Dictionary of Energy System Modelling

ESM Technology & Concept Dictionary

Entries

45Q tax credit (United States)

Definition. A US federal tax credit administered under section 45Q of the Internal Revenue Code that provides a per-tonne payment for CO₂ that is captured and either geologically stored or used. Headline values quoted by the IEA for CCUS deployment include US $85 / t CO₂ for capture-and-storage (sufficient to cover capture, transport and storage in low-cost configurations such as bioethanol CCS) and US $180 / t CO₂ for direct air capture with storage (DACS). (IEA 2026, pp. 26, 41)

Notes. Eligibility for 45Q underpins the project economics of US CCUS deployment, supporting the Trailblazer CO₂ pipeline (bioethanol CCS) and Occidental’s Stratos DAC facility (the latter via a USD 500 million joint venture with BlackRock developing a 500,000 t y⁻¹ DAC facility in Texas). Insurance products tailored to recapture risk for 45Q credits exist; tax-credit transferability has been a key enabler of project finance in North America. (IEA 2026, pp. 41, 46)

Related terms. Carbon contract for difference (CCfD); EU Emissions Trading System; bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS); direct air capture (DAC); non-recourse project finance.

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, headline values, role in US CCUS deployment.

Age of Electricity (IEA)

Definition. A framing introduced by the IEA to describe the current period in which electricity is the fastest-growing fuel in the global energy system, with electricity demand growing at well over twice the rate of total energy demand. The “Age of Electricity” rests on three drivers: rising electrification of end-uses (electric vehicles, heat pumps, electrified industry); the rapid expansion of clean power generation (solar PV, wind, nuclear); and electricity demand growth from data centres and AI workloads. (IEA GER 2026, pp. 5, 10–11, 381; IEA ETP 2026, p. 12)

Attributes — 2025 confirmation (GER-2026).

Indicator Value Year
Global electricity demand growth ~3% (≈800 TWh added) 2025
Energy demand growth 1.3% 2025
Electricity-to-energy demand growth ratio ~2.3× 2025
EV electricity demand growth +38% YoY 2025
Data-centre electricity demand growth +17% YoY 2025
US data-centre share of electricity demand growth ~50% 2025
Solar PV share of all electricity generation growth ~70% 2025
Solar PV absolute generation increase 600 TWh (largest ever for any source) 2025
Solar PV share of global electricity >8% 2025
Solar PV total generation (2025) ~2,700 TWh (>2× 2022) 2025
Combined clean energy technology market value nearly USD 1.2 trillion (2025) → ~USD 2 trillion (CPS 2035) → ~USD 3 trillion (STEPS 2035) 2025–2035

(IEA GER 2026, pp. 5, 10–11, 21; IEA ETP 2026, pp. 12, 15–16)

Notes. The Age of Electricity framing aligns with ETP-2026’s Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS) and underpins the central role assigned to clean energy technologies (solar PV, wind, batteries, electric cars, electrolysers, heat pumps) in IEA’s clean-tech market sizing. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 12, 15–17)

Related terms. Electric cars; clean energy technologies; solar PV; wind power; battery storage (stationary); electricity demand growth; data-centre electricity demand.

Source history. - IEA GER 2026 — added 2026-05-08: framing, 2025 statistics confirming the framing. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: cross-reference to clean-tech market value.

100% renewable energy (RE) system

Definition. An energy framework in which all input energy sources are derived exclusively from renewable resources (solar, wind, hydropower, bioenergy, geothermal, ocean), with fossil fuels and nuclear power not used. In practice, Khalili et al. apply a minimum threshold of at least 95% renewable energy in at least one energy sector within a defined geographic context to qualify a study for inclusion in their systematic review. (Khalili et al. 2026, abstract; pp. 2, 4)

Attributes — review of 1,067 articles 1975-2023.

Dimension Dominant choice Share
Sector covered Power 99.5%
Power-only studies — 47%
Optimisation target function Yes 68%
Time resolution Hourly 73%
Modelling approach Overnight greenfield 77%
Top-2 generation technologies Solar PV; wind power 94% each
Top storage technology Batteries 60%

(Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 2, 9–14)

Notes — historical milestones. First article: Sørensen 1975 (Denmark). First US analysis: Lovins 1976. First global analysis: Sørensen 1996. Most-cited article in the field: Lund 2007. Most-influential modern paper: Jacobson and Delucchi 2011. The Bogdanov & Breyer cost-optimised hourly global-local 145-region model (LUT-ESTM) marks the current state-of-the-art transition-pathway approach. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 2–3)

Related terms. Sector coupling; energy system models (100% RE); power-to-X (PtX); e-fuels; overnight vs transition pathway modelling; temporal resolution (energy modelling).

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, dimensions table, historical milestones.

ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene)

Aliases. ABS resin; acrylonitrile butadiene styrene; ABS plastic.

Definition. A thermoplastic copolymer composed of three monomers — acrylonitrile (giving chemical resistance and rigidity), butadiene (giving toughness and impact resistance), and styrene (giving processability and surface finish) — produced by graft / blend polymerisation. The acrylonitrile-styrene (SAN) phase is the rigid continuous matrix; the polybutadiene rubber phase is dispersed as toughening particles grafted with SAN. ABS is the workhorse engineering thermoplastic for housings, automotive trim, and durable goods. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Attributes — properties and uses.

Property Value
Density 1.04–1.07 g/cm³
Tensile strength 30–50 MPa
Glass transition (matrix Tg) ~105 °C
Notched Izod impact 200–400 J/m (strong)
Production process emulsion / suspension polymerisation with grafting onto polybutadiene rubber
Global ABS production ~10 Mt/yr
Largest end-use automotive interior trim (~30%); appliances (refrigerator liners, vacuum housings, ~25%); electronics housings (~15%); construction pipe & fittings (~10%); LEGO bricks; 3D-printing filament

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11)

Notes — variants. ABS is one of a wider family of styrene-acrylonitrile / styrene-butadiene copolymers including SAN (styrene-acrylonitrile, no rubber phase, transparent rigid), MBS (methacrylate-butadiene-styrene, used as PVC impact modifier), and ASA (acrylate-styrene-acrylonitrile, weather-resistant ABS analogue using acrylate rubber instead of polybutadiene). (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11)

Related terms. Acrylonitrile; butadiene; styrene; SAN; SBR; polystyrene; engineering plastics; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, three-monomer composition, end-uses, ~10 Mt/yr global. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: ABS in chemical-sector mass-balance.

Abandoned mine shaft

Definition. An abandoned mine shaft repurposed for the storage of energy fluids, with engineered barriers (such as cement or resin) installed at the rock boundary to provide containment. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 79)

Notes. Identified as one of two further geological options (alongside engineered rock caverns) for hydrogen storage; both have raised much less interest than salt caverns or saline formations because of technical challenges and host-rock suitability requirements. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 79)

Related terms. Engineered rock cavern; salt cavern; porous rock hydrogen storage.

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition and contextual notes.

Acetic acid

Aliases. Ethanoic acid; CH₃COOH; AcOH; glacial acetic acid.

Definition. A weak organic acid produced industrially by the catalytic carbonylation of methanol with carbon monoxide over an iridium-iodide catalyst (Cativa process, BP) or rhodium-iodide catalyst (Monsanto process, older): CH₃OH + CO → CH₃COOH. Both are C1-chemistry routes that combine methanol (from syngas) with CO (also from syngas) to deliver the second-largest-volume organic acid globally. (Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production ~17 Mt/yr
Cativa (Ir-I, BP) catalyst conditions 150–200 °C, 30–50 bar
Monsanto (Rh-I, older) conditions 150–200 °C, 30–60 bar
Per-pass selectivity >99%
Largest end-use — vinyl acetate (VAM) ~30%
Acetic anhydride ~10%
PTA (terephthalic acid solvent) ~15%
Cellulose acetate ~5%
Other (esters, food/pharma) ~40%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Notes — Cativa vs Monsanto. The Cativa process (BP, commercial 1996) replaced Monsanto’s Rh-based process at most large units because Ir is cheaper, the reaction runs at lower water content (lower energy for distillation), and selectivity is higher. Both are landmarks of homogeneous-catalysis industrial application. (Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5)

Related terms. Methanol (commodity); C1 chemistry; vinyl acetate (VAM); high-value chemicals (HVCs); PET (terephthalic acid solvent); cellulose acetate.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, Cativa vs Monsanto, end-use shares. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 17 Mt/yr global production.

Acrylonitrile

Aliases. AN; vinyl cyanide; CH₂=CH-CN; propenenitrile.

Definition. A colourless, volatile, toxic vinyl-nitrile monomer produced industrially by the catalytic ammoxidation of propylene with ammonia and oxygen over a multicomponent bismuth-molybdate catalyst (SOHIO process, INEOS): C₃H₆ + NH₃ + 1.5 O₂ → CH₂=CH-CN + 3 H₂O. The principal monomer for acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) resin, styrene-acrylonitrile (SAN), nitrile-butadiene rubber (NBR), and acrylic fibre (polyacrylonitrile, PAN). (Speight 2019, Chapters 7.3.9, 11.3.11; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production ~6 Mt/yr
Synthesis route propylene + NH₃ + 1.5 O₂ → AN + 3 H₂O (SOHIO process)
Catalyst Bi-Mo-O multimetal mixed oxide (with V, Co, Ni, K promoters)
Reactor type fluidised bed
Temperature / pressure 400–500 °C / 1.5–3 bar
Per-pass yield 80–82%
End-use ABS / SAN ~30%
Acrylic fibre (PAN) ~30%
Adiponitrile / HMDA / Nylon 6,6 ~15%
NBR rubber ~5%
Other (acrylamide, carbon-fibre precursor, methyl acrylate) ~20%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3.9)

Notes — carbon-fibre precursor. PAN-derived carbon fibre dominates the high-strength-fibre market for aerospace, wind turbine blades, automotive bodies and hydrogen pressure vessels (Type IV). Acrylonitrile is therefore strategic for the wind / hydrogen / electrification supply chain — not just plastics. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11)

Notes — defossilised AN. Bio-acrylonitrile from glycerol or 3-hydroxypropionic acid is at pilot scale (NREL/Cytec, Genomatica). Bio-AN remains a small share but matters for low-carbon carbon-fibre supply chains. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 3 — cross-ref alternative-feedstock pathways)

Related terms. Propylene; ammonia (as hydrogen carrier); ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene); SAN; NBR; polyacrylonitrile (PAN); carbon fibre; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, SOHIO ammoxidation, end-use shares. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 6 Mt/yr global production.

Adipic acid + HMDA + caprolactam (Nylon-feedstock chain)

Aliases. Adipic acid (AA); hexamethylenediamine (HMDA / HMD); ε-caprolactam (CPL); Nylon precursors.

Definition. Three industrial intermediates that anchor the polyamide (Nylon) supply chain: adipic acid (HOOC-(CH₂)₄-COOH) + HMDA (H₂N-(CH₂)₆-NH₂) → Nylon 6,6; ε-caprolactam (cyclic 7-ring amide, ring-opening monomer) → Nylon 6. All three intermediates ultimately derive from benzene (via cyclohexane) or from butadiene (via adiponitrile, ADN). (Speight 2019, Chapters 8 (benzene chain), 11.3.5)

Attributes — production routes and volumes.

Intermediate Route Catalyst / conditions Global production Comments
Cyclohexane benzene + 3 H₂ → cyclohexane Pt/Al₂O₃ or Ni ~6 Mt/yr 70% used for adipic acid
KA-oil (cyclohexanol/cyclohexanone) cyclohexane + O₂ → KA-oil Co or Mn naphthenate intermediate only side-product N₂O significant
Adipic acid KA-oil + HNO₃ → adipic acid + N₂O Cu/V ~3 Mt/yr N₂O abatement standard since 1990s
Adiponitrile (ADN) butadiene + 2 HCN → ADN (Invista) Ni-phosphite ~1.5 Mt/yr replaces some adipic-acid-route HMDA
HMDA ADN + 4 H₂ → HMDA + 2 NH₃ Co or Ni ~1.4 Mt/yr also from adipic acid via ammonolysis
ε-Caprolactam cyclohexanone + NH₂OH → oxime → Beckmann → CPL acid (oleum) ~5 Mt/yr ~5 t (NH₄)₂SO₄ co-product per t CPL

(Speight 2019, Chapter 8 and 11.3.5)

Notes — N₂O emissions. Conventional adipic acid production releases ~300 g N₂O per kg adipic acid (HNO₃ oxidation step). N₂O has a 273× warming potential vs CO₂. Catalytic N₂O abatement (thermal destruction or selective catalysis) deployed since the 1990s reduced emissions >95%; modern adipic-acid plants meet stringent regulatory limits. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.5; cross-ref process emissions)

Notes — Beckmann rearrangement and ammonium sulfate. Caprolactam production from cyclohexanone-oxime via Beckmann rearrangement (oleum-catalysed) generates ~5 t of (NH₄)₂SO₄ per t of CPL. This co-product is sold as fertiliser; the economics of CPL depend on the (NH₄)₂SO₄ market. Modern HPO+ and ammoxidation routes (Sumitomo, EniChem) reduce the (NH₄)₂SO₄ load. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.5)

Related terms. Polyamides (Nylon); benzene; butadiene; ammonia (as hydrogen carrier); process emissions; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: chain definition, production routes, N₂O emissions, Beckmann rearrangement.

Adsorption-induced dislocation emission (AIDE)

Definition. A proposed mechanism of hydrogen embrittlement in which hydrogen-induced surface adsorption assists dislocation emission; predominant in cleavage-like and dimpled intergranular fractures. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 376)

Related terms. Hydrogen embrittlement; hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE); hydrogen-enhanced localised plasticity (HELP).

Source history. - Ghadiani et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definitional sentence and fracture-mode association.

Alcohol-to-jet (ATJ)

Definition. A family of biofuel pathways producing aviation kerosene (ATJ-SPK) from intermediate alcohols (typically ethanol or isobutanol) generated through the fermentation of carbohydrate-rich or lignocellulosic biomass. The ATJ umbrella aggregates the sugar fermentation with alcohol upgrading (SuF) and syngas fermentation (SF) pathways. Both ethanol and isobutanol intermediates are certified by ASTM D7566. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 6)

Notes. ATJ-SPK is produced via four key steps after the fermentation: dehydration of the alcohol, oligomerisation of the resulting alkenes, hydrogenation, and distillation. A variation enriches the heavier olefin fraction with aromatics (~20 vol%) prior to hydrogenation to obtain a synthetic kerosene with aromatics that is potentially blending-limit-free (under ASTM certification process). The maximum ATJ-SPK blending limit with conventional kerosene is up to 50 vol%. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 6–7)

Related terms. Sugar fermentation with alcohol upgrading (SuF); syngas fermentation (SF); synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK); drop-in fuel; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, process steps and ASTM certification status.

Alkylation (refinery)

Aliases. HF alkylation; H₂SO₄ alkylation; ionic-liquid alkylation; alkylate.

Definition. A refinery process that combines isobutane (i-C₄H₁₀) with light olefins (typically butenes, sometimes propylene) over a strong acid catalyst (sulfuric acid H₂SO₄ or hydrofluoric acid HF, or modern ionic liquids / solid acid alternatives) to produce alkylate — a high-octane, low-vapour-pressure, sulfur-free, aromatic-free gasoline blendstock. Alkylate is one of the highest-value gasoline-pool components (RON 92–98, MON 88–94) and is critical for meeting reformulated-gasoline specifications. (Speight 2019, Chapters 4.3, 6.2.3.14, 7.2.2)

Attributes — typical operating envelope.

Indicator H₂SO₄ alkylation HF alkylation
Reactor temperature 5–15 °C 25–40 °C
Reactor pressure 4–6 bar 8–12 bar
Acid concentration 88–95% H₂SO₄ ~90% HF
i-C4 / olefin ratio 6–10:1 10–15:1
Alkylate octane (RON) 92–96 94–98
Acid consumption 70–100 kg / t alkylate 0.5–1 kg / t alkylate (recycled)
Reactor design cascade or contactor with cooling riser with HF settler
Olefin feed predominantly butenes propylene + butenes

(Speight 2019, Chapter 6.2.3.14)

Notes — feedstock origin. Alkylation feedstock comes from the FCC unit (C4 olefin and isobutane streams) and from steam cracker C4 raffinates after butadiene extraction. Butane isomerisation supplements isobutane supply when needed. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2.2)

Notes — safety and replacement. Both H₂SO₄ and HF acid catalysts are hazardous. HF is particularly dangerous (volatile, lung-penetrating); modern alternatives include ionic-liquid alkylation (Honeywell ISOALKY, commercial since 2016) and solid-acid alkylation (AlkyClean, commercial). New refinery alkylation units overwhelmingly use ionic liquid or solid-acid technology. (Speight 2019, Chapter 6.2.3.14)

Related terms. Catalytic cracking (FCC); isomerisation (refinery); petroleum refining (umbrella); naphtha; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, conditions, feedstock origin, safety/replacement options.

Blue ammonia and green ammonia (production routes)

Aliases. Blue NH₃; green NH₃; brown ammonia (legacy fossil-only); turquoise ammonia (from methane pyrolysis); pink ammonia (nuclear-electrolysis); orange / yellow ammonia (other low-emission variants).

Definition. A colour-coded taxonomy of ammonia production routes based on the carbon-emission profile of the input hydrogen and process energy: - Brown ammonia — conventional Haber-Bosch using grey H₂ from natural gas SMR (or coal gasification, “black” sub-variant) + fossil-fired process heat. ~70% of global production. Carbon intensity ~1.6–2.5 kg CO₂eq/kg NH₃ (NG-based) to 4–5 kg CO₂eq/kg (coal-based). - Blue ammonia — Haber-Bosch using blue H₂ from SMR / ATR with CCS (>85% CO₂ capture). Carbon intensity ~0.5–0.8 kg CO₂eq/kg NH₃, conditional on no significant methane leakage (Mayer 2023 critique). - Green ammonia — Haber-Bosch using green H₂ from electrolysis of water powered by renewable electricity (PV, wind) + N₂ from cryogenic air separation. Carbon intensity 0.05–0.6 kg CO₂eq/kg NH₃ depending on electricity-source emission factor. Mingolla 2025 confirms this minimises emissions but at 2–3× the cost of brown ammonia. (Royal Society 2020, pp. 12–20; Mayer et al. 2023; Mingolla & Rosa 2025)

Attributes — comparison of routes (Mayer 2023 + Mingolla 2025).

Route Carbon intensity (kg CO₂eq/kg NH₃) LCOH ammonia (€/t NH₃) Land area (m²/t NH₃) Water (L/t NH₃) TRL
Brown — SMR (natural gas) 1.6–2.5 200–400 minimal 4–10 m³ 9
Brown — coal gasification 4.0–5.0 250–500 minimal higher 9
Blue — SMR + CCS 0.5–0.8 (no CH₄ leak); up to 1.8 (3% leak) 350–600 minimal 4–10 m³ 7–8
Green — PEM + PV (sun-rich) 0.05–0.4 (0% grid) 600–1,200 100–300× brown 100–300× brown 6–8
Green — PEM + wind 0.04–0.2 600–1,000 smaller than PV smaller 7
Turquoise — methane pyrolysis + N₂ ~0.5 (with solid carbon byproduct) n/a n/a minimal 5
Pink — nuclear-electrolysis very low comparable to green small varies 6
Biochemical / electrolytic novel 0.05–0.3 800–1,500 100–300× brown 100–300× brown 4–5

(Mayer et al. 2023, Tables 2–3; Mingolla & Rosa 2025, Fig. 2)

Notes — Mayer 2023 methane-leakage warning. Mayer et al. emphasise that methane upstream leakage dramatically affects blue-ammonia climate performance: at 3% methane leakage, blue ammonia’s GWP100 climbs from 0.5 to 1.8 kg CO₂eq/kg NH₃, narrowing the gap with brown ammonia. Using the Technology Warming Potential (TWP) — a time-dependent metric — methane leakage exacerbates blue ammonia’s climate impact in short time horizons (2030–2040) while improving in long horizons. Reducing upstream methane leakage to <0.5% is essential for blue ammonia to be a credible bridge technology. (Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 6–10)

Notes — Mingolla 2025 land-and-water trade-off. Green ammonia’s principal economic / sustainability hurdle is the land and water requirement. Producing 1 t of green NH₃ via PV-electrolysis requires ~150–300 m² of solar PV land (vs ~minimal for brown) and ~100–300× the water of brown ammonia (~100–300 m³/t vs 4–10 m³/t for SMR-based). In water-stressed regions this is a binding constraint; coastal locations enable seawater electrolysis after desalination. Decentralised production (smaller distributed green-NH₃ plants) reduces transport emissions but loses scale economies. (Mingolla & Rosa 2025, pp. 1–7)

Related terms. Ammonia (as hydrogen carrier); Haber-Bosch process; Methanol-to-Olefins (MTO); steam methane reforming (SMR); Coal gasification (to hydrogen); Carbon capture and storage (CCS); Hydrogen colour taxonomy; near-zero emissions materials; e-fuels (electricity-based fuels); Technology Warming Potential.

Source history. - Royal Society 2020 — added 2026-05-08: blue/green ammonia definitions, decarbonisation framework. - Mayer et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: TEA + LCA comparison, methane-leakage TWP analysis. - Mingolla & Rosa 2025 — added 2026-05-08: land/water trade-off, decentralised-production framing.

Ammonia (as hydrogen carrier)

Definition. Liquid ammonia (NH₃) used as a hydrogen storage and transport medium. With a vapour pressure of 9.2 bar at room temperature, ammonia can be contained in cost-efficient pressure reservoirs; it has a hydrogen content of 17.65 wt% and a volumetric hydrogen density approximately 4.5 times larger than that of liquid hydrogen. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 31, citing Klerke et al. 2008)

Attributes.

Property Value
Hydrogen content 17.8 wt%
Volumetric energy density 107 kg/m³
Advantages cheap energy; direct use possible; existing infrastructure usable
Drawbacks special treatment due to smell and toxicity; ~13% of H₂ needed for dehydrogenation and purification

(AlZohbi et al. 2023, Table 1, pp. 32–33, citing Aziz et al.; Klerke et al. 2008)

Notes. Ammonia is well-developed for amalgamation, distribution and combustion; the combustion of pure ammonia does not emit CO₂. However, ammonia is poisonous and traces may persist in hydrogen produced after decomposition, requiring purification. A high energy expenditure is associated with the liberation of hydrogen from ammonia. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 31)

Related terms. Hydrogen storage; chemisorption; liquid organic hydrogen carriers; chemical hydrides; Haber-Bosch process.

Source history. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, properties and trade-offs as a hydrogen carrier.

Ammonia and methanol propulsion ships

Definition. Ocean-going vessels propelled by combustion of synthetic ammonia (NH₃) or methanol (CH₃OH) — either pure-fuel or dual-fuel with conventional marine diesel/LNG — produced from low-emissions hydrogen and (for methanol) biogenic or atmospheric CO₂. Identified by ETP-2026 as the most cost-competitive long-distance shipping decarbonisation route on a TCO basis, alongside drop-in biofuels. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 129, 6739–6780)

Indicator Value Year
Conventional ships’ share of 2028 planned deliveries (gross tonnage) ~1/3 2028 (orders)
LNG-propulsion ships’ share of 2028 planned deliveries >1/2 2028 (orders)
Methanol-propulsion ships’ share of orders ~10% (levelled off for 2026 / 2028 deliveries) 2026–2028
Ammonia-propulsion vessels expected from 2026 ≥30 medium-to-large vessels 2026+
TCO of methanol/ammonia ships vs oil (today) up to 2× higher 2024
Alternative-propulsion ship share of 2035 sales (gross tonnage, CPS & STEPS) >1/3 2035

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 129, 6739–6780, 7757–7762)

Notes — policy drivers. Demand has been pushed by expanding IMO Emission Control Areas, EU GHG limits and IMO 2025 GHG-pricing decisions. Off-take agreements with fuel suppliers remain a bottleneck — shipowners report difficulty securing long-term firm offtake. Some cargo owners are willing to pay a green premium for low-carbon shipping but not yet at the levels required to bridge the cost gap. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 129, 6745–6770)

Adaptive thermal comfort

Aliases. Adaptive comfort model; de Dear-Brager model; ASHRAE 55 adaptive method; modèle adaptatif (FR); naturally-ventilated comfort model.

Definition. A thermal-comfort framework — alternative to the steady-state Fanger PMV/PPD approach — that explicitly recognises occupants of naturally-ventilated buildings physiologically and behaviourally adapt to outdoor conditions: changing clothing, adjusting metabolic rate, opening windows, drinking cold beverages. The de Dear-Brager (1998) model proposes that the comfort temperature in a naturally-ventilated building is a linear function of the prevailing outdoor temperature (mean outdoor temperature over preceding days), rather than a fixed comfort range. ASHRAE 55 (2020) standardises the model: T_comfort = 0.31 · T_outdoor_running_mean + 17.8 °C (with ± 2.5 to ± 3.5 °C acceptable bands). (Goessel 2025, pp. 27–28, citing ASHRAE 55-2020 and de Dear-Brager 1998)

Attributes — adaptive vs PMV/PPD model.

Aspect PMV/PPD (Fanger) Adaptive (de Dear-Brager)
Building type mechanically-conditioned (steady-state HVAC) naturally-ventilated (free-running)
Comfort temperature fixed (~22 °C) function of outdoor T (T_comf = 0.31·T_out + 17.8)
Acceptable bands PMV ± 0.5 → PPD ≤ 10% ± 2.5 °C (90% acceptability) or ± 3.5 °C (80%)
Required inputs 6 parameters (Ta, Tr, RH, v, clo, met) outdoor temperature only
Application offices, hospitals, hotels with HVAC residential, schools, naturally-cooled offices
Sensitivity to behaviour low high (window-opening, clothing, beverage)
Standards ISO 7730, ASHRAE 55 (Method I) ASHRAE 55 (Method II / V), EN 16798-1

(Goessel 2025, pp. 27–28)

Notes — Goessel choice rationale. Goessel’s residential-renovation methodology applies naturally-ventilated boundary conditions (no active cooling for the baseline scenario), making the adaptive model conceptually more applicable than PMV/PPD. However, Goessel ultimately uses SET-DH (Standard Effective Temperature degree-hours) because it provides a single continuous metric for cumulative discomfort severity (not just count of “uncomfortable” hours) and remains valid into heat-wave conditions where adaptive comfort breaks down. (Goessel 2025, pp. 27–31)

Related terms. Standard Effective Temperature (SET); PMV / PPD (Fanger model); Thermal comfort (umbrella); Heat-wave health risk; building renovation (umbrella); ASHRAE 55; EN 16798-1.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, adaptive-vs-PMV comparison table, ASHRAE 55 method context (translated from French).

Annualised electricity system cost (RTE 2050)

Aliases. Coût complet annualisé du système électrique (FR); full annualised system cost.

Definition. The total annual cost (in € per year) of the French electricity system at a given horizon, integrating (i) the depreciation of capital expenditure (CAPEX) and associated financing cost, (ii) operation and maintenance costs (OPEX), (iii) fuel costs for any combustion-based generation, and (iv) the annualised costs of the transport network, distribution network and flexibility means (storage, demand-side response, decarbonised thermal) — for a given electricity mix and demand trajectory. RTE uses this indicator as the canonical measure for comparing the economic merit of its six 2050 scenarios. (RTE 2022, Sections 11.2.1, 11.5.2.1, translated from French)

Attributes — RTE reference cost trajectory (all six mix scenarios).

Year Annualised system cost (Md€/an, 2020 EUR) Comment
2020/2021 ~45 Reference baseline
2030 mild increase Investment ramp-up phase
2040 continued growth Renewable build-out + early EPR2
2050 50–70 Range across six scenarios
2060 60–80 Range across six scenarios; +20 to +40 Md€/an vs today

(RTE 2022, Figure 11.25, p. 587, translated)

Notes — perimeter and demand sensitivity. The cost perimeter is generation + flexibility + transport network + distribution network. It excludes end-use equipment (e.g. heat pumps, EV chargers) and end-use electricity bills as such. The 60–80 Md€/an 2060 range is broken down by scenario: (i) M0 / M1 (no new nuclear) sit at the high end (~80 Md€/an) due to higher renewable build-out and flexibility needs; (ii) N1 / N2 / N03 (with new EPR2) sit at the low end (~60 Md€/an); (iii) the deep-reindustrialisation variant adds +10 to +15 Md€/an across all six mixes; (iv) sufficiency saves several Md€/an across all six. (RTE 2022, Sections 11.6.5, 11.8.1, 11.8.2)

Notes — driver decomposition. The electricity system’s cost is rising in absolute terms because (a) electricity is replacing fossil fuels in heating, mobility, industry, hydrogen, lifting electricity from ~25% to >50% of final-energy use; (b) renewable build-out, network reinforcement and flexibility investment all involve large up-front CAPEX; (c) the existing nuclear fleet needs partial replacement post-2040 either by EPR2 or renewables. Per-MWh costs in 2060 are bounded between ~70 €/MWh (N03, low) and ~110 €/MWh (M0/M1 stress test, high). (RTE 2022, Section 11.5.2.1, p. 587 chart commentary)

Related terms. RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 scenarios; Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC); Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE); Sufficiency (sobriété); Deep reindustrialisation; EPR2 programme; Power system flexibility.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, perimeter, six-scenario range (60–80 Md€/an in 2060), demand-variant sensitivities (translated from French).

Abatement cost (greenhouse gas)

Aliases. Coût d’abattement (FR); cost of avoided emissions; €/tCO₂eq avoided; marginal abatement cost.

Definition. The unit cost (in € per tonne of CO₂eq avoided) of a decarbonisation action, evaluated as the additional cost (CAPEX + OPEX, life-cycle annualised) of the low-carbon alternative minus the cost of the fossil-fuel counterfactual, divided by the volume of CO₂ emissions avoided by the substitution. The abatement cost is the canonical metric for ranking decarbonisation actions in cost-of-carbon terms and for comparison against the Value of Climate Action (VAC; “valeur de l’action pour le climat”), the shadow price of carbon recommended by the Quinet Commission for evaluating French public investments. (RTE 2022, Sections 11.9.1.1, 11.9.2; Quinet Commission, France)

Attributes — RTE 2022 abatement cost estimates by action.

Decarbonisation action Abatement cost (€/tCO₂) Counterfactual
Heat pumps replacing gas heating (residential) low; well below VAC natural gas boiler
Electric vehicles (BEV) replacing ICE well below VAC by 2030 gasoline ICE
Hydrogen production (electrolysis) replacing SMR ~200 €/tCO₂ achievable grey H₂ from natural gas
Industrial process electrification varies, often below VAC gas / coal process heat
Quinet VAC reference 250 €/tCO₂ in 2030, 500 €/tCO₂ in 2040, 750 €/tCO₂ in 2050 (target value)

(RTE 2022, Sections 11.9.2 sub-sections, p. 633, 639)

Notes — methodology. RTE applies the incremental approach with electricity-mix adaptation: for each electrification action (e.g. switching to a heat pump or to an EV), the additional electricity demand is mapped to incremental generation, with both the cost and CO₂ intensity of that increment computed scenario-by-scenario. This avoids the methodological pitfall of attributing average grid emissions to new electricity demand, which would mask the carbon-displacement value of marginal renewables/nuclear additions. (RTE 2022, Section 11.9.1.1)

Notes — perimeter sensitivity. Abatement cost depends critically on (i) the counterfactual chosen (e.g. gas vs coal vs oil for industrial heat), (ii) the GHG-accounting boundary (territorial vs life-cycle, including imported batteries / steel / hydrogen), and (iii) the time horizon over which the substitution is amortised. RTE adopts a life-cycle perimeter to capture imports such as EV battery manufacturing emissions abroad — without this, electrification can be artificially flattered. (RTE 2022, Sections 11.9.1.1, 12.2.3)

Related terms. Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE); Levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH); Carbon contract for difference (CCfD); EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE); Sufficiency (sobriété); SNBC; carbon dioxide removal (CDR); life-cycle assessment.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, methodology (incremental + life-cycle), 200 €/tCO₂ benchmark for hydrogen production, Quinet VAC reference (translated from French).

Anderson-Schulz-Flory (ASF) distribution

Aliases. ASF distribution; chain-growth product distribution; Flory-Schulz distribution.

Definition. A statistical hydrocarbon-product distribution that arises from a surface-polymerisation mechanism in Fischer-Tropsch (FT) synthesis (and related step-growth chain processes). ASF assumes that, at each step of chain growth, a hydrocarbon chain on the catalyst surface either (i) grows by adding one CH₂ unit with probability α or (ii) terminates with probability (1 − α). The mass fraction of n-carbon products is then Wₙ = n · α^(n−1) · (1 − α)². ASF is the canonical bound on FT product selectivity and explains why traditional FT cannot deliver more than ~58% C₂–C₄ olefins or ~15% aromatics on an industrial scale even with optimised catalysts. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109, citing FT literature)

Attributes — ASF chain-growth probability and product peaks.

α (chain-growth probability) Peak product
0.0–0.3 Methane / light gases dominant
0.3–0.5 LPG / naphtha range (C₃–C₅)
0.5–0.7 Gasoline range (C₅–C₁₂)
0.7–0.85 Diesel + jet fuel range
0.85–0.95 Wax (C₂₀+); cracked subsequently
→ 1 High-MW polymer wax

(Zhang et al. 2024, Section 5.1.2 and Fig. 11; Speight 2019, Chapter 7)

Notes — selectivity ceiling on FT. ASF imposes a hard constraint: no single chain-growth probability α can simultaneously maximise both light olefins (C₂–C₄) and aromatics. Aromatic-only FT selectivity is capped near 15% under standard catalysts; light-olefin selectivity caps near 58% (Zhang). Synergistic catalysts (e.g., OXZEO oxide-zeolite) escape the ASF limit by separating chain growth from selective termination/cracking; this can push light-olefin yield to >80% with full CO conversion. (Zhang et al. 2024, pp. 109–110)

Notes — relevance to defossilising chemicals. Because ASF caps the yield of high-value chemicals from FT, electrofuel and biofuel routes built on FT need either (i) downstream cracking/upgrading, (ii) tail-gas recycling, or (iii) non-ASF synergistic catalysis to be economic at scale. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 110)

Related terms. Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process; Methanol-to-Olefins (MTO); methanol-to-aromatics (MTA); synergistic catalysis (OXZEO); high-value chemicals (HVCs); steam cracking.

Source history. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, formula Wₙ = n·α^(n−1)·(1−α)², selectivity ceilings, link to OXZEO synergistic catalysis.

API gravity (and sweet vs sour crude)

Aliases. API °; °API; American Petroleum Institute gravity; sweet/sour crude classification.

Definition. A standardised measure of the relative density of crude oil and petroleum products vs water, defined by °API = (141.5 / SG) − 131.5, where SG is the specific gravity at 60 °F. Higher °API = lighter (less dense) crude. The two principal crude-oil quality dimensions used in trading and refinery configuration are: (i) gravity (light vs heavy), measured in °API; and (ii) sulfur content (sweet vs sour), with a typical threshold of ~0.5 wt% sulfur separating sweet from sour crudes. (Speight 2019, Chapter 1.4)

Attributes — crude classification.

Crude category °API range Density (g/cm³) Examples
Light >31.1 <0.870 West Texas Intermediate (WTI), Brent, Tapis
Medium 22.3–31.1 0.870–0.920 Mars, Arabian Light
Heavy 10.0–22.3 0.920–1.000 Maya, Arabian Heavy, Bachaquero
Extra-heavy / bitumen <10.0 >1.000 Athabasca bitumen, Orinoco extra-heavy
Sweet (sulfur threshold) <0.5 wt% S — Brent, WTI, Bonny Light
Sour >0.5 wt% S (often >2%) — Arabian Heavy, Maya, Urals

(Speight 2019, Chapter 1.4 and Tables)

Notes — refinery configuration sensitivity. Light-sweet crude is the easiest to refine — high naphtha + middle-distillate yield, low hydrotreating duty, low coke yield; commands the price premium. Heavy-sour crude requires more aggressive conversion (FCC, hydrocracker, coker), more hydrogen, more sulfur recovery — discount in the market. The “Brent–Maya spread” or “WTI–Maya spread” is the key economic signal for complex coker-equipped refineries (US Gulf Coast). (Speight 2019, Chapter 1.4)

Notes — heavy-crude upgrading. Athabasca bitumen and Orinoco extra-heavy crude require upgrading — partial dehydrogenation/cracking via on-site cokers / hydrocrackers / SDA solvent deasphalting — to produce a synthetic crude oil (SCO) light enough to ship by pipeline. Without upgrading, bitumen requires diluent (light condensate at 25–30%) for pipeline transport. (Speight 2019, Chapter 1.4)

Related terms. Petroleum refining (umbrella); atmospheric distillation; hydrotreating; delayed coking; visbreaking; Claus process; sulfur recovery.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: API formula, light/medium/heavy/sweet/sour categories, refinery sensitivity.

Antioxidants (plastic additives)

Definition. A class of plastic additives embedded in polymer resins to delay oxidative degradation when the material is exposed to ultraviolet light, heat, or mechanical shear. Highly reactive free radicals — generated by these stresses and exacerbated by metallic impurities — degrade the polymer chain unless intercepted by an antioxidant. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, p. 186)

Attributes — main classes.

Class Examples Role
Arylamines most common in plastic food packaging primary radical scavenger
Phenolics BHT, BHA, BPA, Irganox 1010, Cyanox 2246/425 hydrogen donors
Organophosphites TNPP, Irgafos 168 reduce hydroperoxides to alcohols

(Hahladakis et al. 2018, p. 186)

Notes. The potential for oxidation increases when food packaging is exposed to high temperatures, hot foods, infrared heating, retort processing or microwave heating. Antioxidant migration into food is widely documented and varies with simulant, time and temperature; Irganox 1010 and 1330 have been detected in oily simulants while many low-molecular-weight antioxidants migrate primarily into aqueous simulants. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, pp. 186, 191, Table 2)

Related terms. Plastic additives; plasticizers (phthalate esters); migration (plastic chemicals); chemicals of concern; PoTSs (potentially toxic substances).

Source history. - Hahladakis et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, classes, food-packaging context.

Atmospheric distillation (refinery)

Aliases. Crude distillation unit (CDU); pipe still; topping unit; primary distillation.

Definition. The first separation step in a petroleum refinery, in which preheated crude oil (340–380 °C, near atmospheric pressure) is fed to a distillation column where it is separated by relative volatility into vapour fractions condensed at progressively lower trays: refinery gas, light naphtha, heavy naphtha, kerosene/jet, light gas oil, heavy gas oil, and an undistilled atmospheric residue. The residue is sent to vacuum distillation. Atmospheric distillation produces no chemical change — it is a purely physical separation. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.2)

Attributes — typical operating envelope.

Indicator Value
Crude inlet temperature 340–380 °C
Column top pressure 1.2–1.5 bar
Column bottom pressure 2–2.5 bar
Number of trays 30–50
Side-stream products 4–6 (naphtha + kerosene + 2–3 gas oil cuts + residue)
Steam stripping in side-strippers yes (improves cut sharpness)
Throughput per CDU train typically 100–300 kbbl/d (≈5–15 Mt/yr)
Atmospheric residue yield 30–60% (depending on crude API)

(Speight 2019, Chapter 4.2)

Notes — desalting upstream. Crude oil first passes through electrostatic desalters (water-wash + electric coalescer) to remove inorganic salts (NaCl, CaCl₂, MgCl₂) that would otherwise cause corrosion (HCl) and fouling in the CDU overhead. Salt content is typically reduced from 50–500 ppm in incoming crude to <5 ppm at desalter outlet. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.2)

Related terms. Vacuum distillation; petroleum refining (umbrella); naphtha; high-value chemicals (HVCs); catalytic cracking (FCC).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, conditions, side-stream products, desalter context.

Air Separation Unit (ASU)

Aliases. ASU; cryogenic air separation; cryogenic distillation of air; Linde process / Claude process.

Definition. An industrial plant that separates atmospheric air into its principal components — nitrogen (N₂, 78%), oxygen (O₂, 21%), and argon (Ar, 0.93%) plus minor noble gases — by cooling air to ~−190 °C (cryogenic conditions) and fractionating it via distillation, exploiting the ~13 °C difference between O₂ (−183 °C boiling point) and N₂ (−196 °C boiling point). ASUs are essential infrastructure for: (i) blue-ammonia / e-ammonia (N₂ feed for Haber-Bosch); (ii) blue-hydrogen via ATR (O₂ feed for partial oxidation); (iii) oxy-combustion CCS (O₂-fired combustion produces concentrated CO₂); (iv) coal/biomass gasification (O₂-blown reactors); (v) industrial gases supply (medical-grade O₂, semiconductor-grade N₂, welding gases). (Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 4–6; Royal Society 2020)

Attributes — typical ASU.

Indicator Value
Operating temperature −180 to −196 °C (cryogenic)
Throughput (typical) 100–10,000 t O₂ + 400–40,000 t N₂ per day
Energy intensity (electricity) 220–250 kWh / t O₂
Major suppliers Linde, Air Liquide, Praxair, Air Products
Output purity 99.5%+ O₂, 99.999%+ N₂ (high-purity grades)
Co-product argon (~1% of air, recovered separately)
Capital cost (typical) $50–500 million per unit (depends on scale)
Lifetime 25–40 years

(Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 4–6)

Notes — significance for low-carbon hydrogen + ammonia. ASU is the principal electricity-consuming component of green-ammonia production beyond electrolysis. For green ammonia, ~10–15% of electricity demand goes to ASU + compression + Haber-Bosch loop; ~85% goes to electrolysis. For blue ammonia, ASU is critical for ATR-based routes. Modern ASUs achieve >99% O₂ recovery efficiency, but the cryogenic operation makes them inherently energy-intensive — researchers explore membrane-based and pressure-swing-adsorption (PSA) alternatives for smaller-scale applications. (Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 4–6)

Related terms. Blue ammonia and green ammonia; Autothermal reforming (ATR); Haber-Bosch process; oxy-combustion (CCS); coal gasification (to hydrogen); pressure swing adsorption (PSA); Air Liquide; Linde.

Source history. - Mayer et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: ASU definition, energy intensity, role in low-carbon ammonia + hydrogen production.

Aqueous phase reforming (APR)

Definition. A biofuel pathway in which a sugar-rich hydrolysate (from carbohydrate or lignocellulosic feedstock) undergoes hydrotreating to convert sugars and organic acids through hydrogenation and hydrogenolysis, followed by deoxygenation in two successive steps: aqueous phase reforming and condensation. The pathway produces hydrodeoxygenation synthetic aromatic kerosene (HDO-SAK) or hydrodeoxygenation synthetic kerosene (HDO-SK; cycloparaffin-rich). (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 4–5)

Attributes — operating conditions.

Parameter Value
APR temperature 175–300 °C (448–573 K)
APR pressure 10–90 bar (1–9 MPa)
Catalysts Cu, Re, Ni, Fe, Co, Ru, Pd, Rh, Pt

(Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 5)

Notes. A gas phase rich in H₂, CO₂, CO and light alkanes is produced alongside the liquid mixture and can be used directly for heat/power; alternatively the H₂ can be separated and recirculated. Both HDO-SK and HDO-SAK are currently under consideration for ASTM certification. The APR pathway is also a route for synthetic aromatic kerosene (SAK), which can be blended with HEFA-SPK to overcome aromatics-content limits. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 5, 30)

Related terms. Synthetic aromatic kerosene (SAK); synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK); HEFA pathway; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); drop-in fuel.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, operating conditions, certification status.

Bankability (CCUS projects)

Definition. The set of conditions under which a CCUS project can secure debt and equity financing, given the predictability of revenues and clarity of risk allocation across the value chain. Because CCUS does not produce a standalone commodity (there is no natural market for stored CO₂), bankability hinges on the underlying business model — whether the project is structured around enhanced oil recovery (EOR/EGR) revenues, low-emissions product sales, carbon-removal credits, or policy-mediated revenue streams (carbon contracts for difference, regulated tariffs, tax credits). (IEA 2026, pp. 7–8, 16–18)

Notes — bankability determinants identified in IEA’s 2026 financier interviews. (i) Revenue uncertainty is the core risk for project finance — without long-term offtake or predictable revenue, projects struggle to attract debt or equity; revenue stacking is a key tool. (ii) Cross-chain interdependence requires clear risk allocation through regulation or contracts. (iii) Sponsor quality (SOEs, industrials, energy majors) directly affects debt pricing. (iv) Insurance is necessary but not sufficient; FOAK technology premiums can be high. (v) FOAK projects typically rely on government backstops for long-term liability and revenue. (IEA 2026, pp. 23–24)

Related terms. Final investment decision (FID); first-of-a-kind (FOAK); cross-chain risk; carbon contract for difference (CCfD); regulated asset base (RAB); long-term storage liability; non-recourse project finance.

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, financier-survey determinants.

Basic oxygen furnace (BOF)

Aliases. Basic oxygen vessel (BOV).

Definition. A primary steel-making vessel that converts pig iron from the blast furnace into crude steel by oxygen blowing; in the integrated steel-mill configuration, it is the second stage after the blast furnace. (Kushnir et al. 2020, p. 4 and Fig. 1A)

Notes. “The well understood technical relationship between the basic oxygen furnace (BOF) and the final steel composition and properties” is identified as a constraint that any transition away from blast-furnace ironmaking must respect. (Kushnir et al. 2020, p. 5)

Related terms. Blast furnace; coke oven; electric arc furnace; primary steel; BF-BOF route.

Source history. - Kushnir et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-07: definition and integration role.

Air-tightness (building / blower-door test)

Aliases. n50 (air-changes per hour at 50 Pa); Q4 (m³/h·m² at 4 Pa); blower-door test; perméabilité à l’air (FR); building air-tightness.

Definition. A measure of unintentional air infiltration / exfiltration through the building envelope at a standardised pressure differential, typically 50 Pa for n50 (Europe) or 4 Pa for Q4 (France). Air leakage occurs through gaps around windows, doors, electrical boxes, plumbing penetrations, junctions, and intermediate floors. Poor air-tightness causes (i) uncontrolled heat losses (typically 20–30% of total heating energy in unrenovated French residential), (ii) cold drafts and reduced thermal comfort, (iii) reduced effectiveness of MVHR ventilation, and (iv) condensation risk in cold climates. Measured by blower-door test (BSI EN ISO 9972). (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35; AFNOR EN ISO 9972)

Attributes — typical air-tightness levels (French residential).

Building category n50 (ach @ 50 Pa) Q4 (m³/h/m² @ 4 Pa)
Pre-1948 traditional construction 7–15 1.7–4.0
1950–1990 standard residential 4–10 1.0–2.5
RT2012 mandate < 3 (target) 0.6 (single-family)
RE2020 mandate < 1.5 (target) 0.3
Passivhaus < 0.6 0.1
Common renovation goal 1.5–3.0 0.3–0.6

(Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35; AFNOR Q4 protocol)

Notes — significance for deep renovation. Achieving good air-tightness during renovation is critical — uninsulated leaky walls dominate winter heat losses, but after insulating, residual air-leakage becomes the new dominant loss path. Good detailing at junctions, vapour-control membranes, and quality-controlled installation are essential. Blower-door testing before and after renovation provides quality-assurance. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35)

Notes — interaction with VMC. Strict air-tightness only delivers comfort and IAQ benefits if combined with mechanical ventilation (VMC). Without controlled ventilation, well-sealed buildings accumulate humidity, CO₂ and indoor pollutants — the “tight house = sick house” problem. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35)

Related terms. Building envelope; Mechanical ventilation (VMC / MVHR); building renovation (umbrella); RE2020 / RT2012; passive house (Passivhaus); thermal bridge.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, n50/Q4 metrics, French stock benchmarks, VMC interaction (translated from French).

Autothermal reforming (ATR)

Aliases. ATR; autothermal reformer; partial-oxidation reforming; combined SMR + POX.

Definition. A hybrid hydrogen-production technology that combines partial oxidation of natural gas with steam methane reforming (SMR) in a single reactor: CH₄ + ½ O₂ → CO + 2 H₂ (POX, exothermic) + CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3 H₂ (SMR, endothermic) — operating at 950–1100 °C and 30–80 bar. The exothermic POX heat balances the endothermic SMR heat, eliminating the need for an external furnace and enabling higher pressure operation (better suited to downstream chemical synthesis). ATR is the preferred route for large-scale blue hydrogen projects because it integrates more cleanly with carbon capture (single concentrated CO₂ stream from the reactor, vs SMR’s mixed flue + process gas). (Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 4–6; Speight 2019)

Attributes — ATR vs SMR comparison.

Indicator SMR ATR
Operating temperature 800–950 °C 950–1100 °C
Operating pressure 15–30 bar 30–80 bar
Heat source external fired furnace internal POX combustion
Oxygen requirement none (steam only) yes — requires ASU
H₂/CO ratio (raw syngas) ~3 (high — good for methanol) ~2 (good for FT synthesis)
CO₂ capture rate (with CCS) 60–70% (split flue + process) 90–95% (concentrated stream)
Best for small-medium scale H₂; methanol large-scale blue H₂ + ammonia
Capital cost (relative) reference similar but ASU adds capex
Typical commercial deployment ubiquitous (~75% of refinery H₂) growing for blue-H₂ + GTL

(Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 4–6)

Notes — blue-ammonia preference. Mayer et al. find that ATR + CCS is the preferred route for blue ammonia because the higher CO₂ capture rate (90–95% vs 60–70% for SMR + CCS) substantially reduces blue-NH₃ embodied carbon. The capital-cost penalty (ASU + larger reformer) is offset by the cleaner CO₂ stream which simplifies and cheapens the CCS step. (Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 4–6)

Related terms. Steam methane reforming (SMR); Air Separation Unit (ASU); Carbon capture and storage (CCS); blue and green ammonia; Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process; methanol synthesis; Power-to-X (PtX).

Source history. - Mayer et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: ATR definition, vs-SMR comparison, blue-ammonia preference rationale.

Aviation gasoline (avgas)

Aliases. Avgas; AVGAS 100LL; aviation petrol.

Definition. A specialised motor-fuel category used in piston-engine aircraft (light aircraft, helicopters, training aircraft), distinguished from automotive gasoline by tighter octane, RVP, and impurity specifications. The dominant grade is AVGAS 100LL (“100 Low-Lead”) — a leaded gasoline with 100 RON minimum (motor octane MON ≥99.5) and ~0.56 g Pb/L (vs 0.6–0.8 g/L in legacy auto gasoline), still containing tetraethyl lead because no fully unleaded replacement has yet met all performance specifications for the global piston-aircraft fleet. AVGAS 100LL remains a controversial residual use of leaded fuel even after the global elimination of leaded auto gasoline (2021). (Addicott 1971, p. 60; cross-ref Tetraethyl lead)

Attributes — typical AVGAS 100LL specification.

Property Value
Octane (RON) ≥100
Octane (MON) ≥99.5
Lead content ~0.56 g Pb/L (TEL)
RVP 38–49 kPa (tighter than auto gasoline)
Distillation final boiling point 170 °C
Sulfur content <0.05 wt%
Density (kg/m³ @ 15 °C) 700–760
Global production ~5–7 Mt/yr (small relative to jet kerosene at 270 Mt/yr)
Replacement candidates UL94 (94-octane unleaded), UL100 (FAA-certified 2022), G100UL (Swift Fuels)

(Addicott 1971, p. 60; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4; FAA certifications)

Notes — vs jet kerosene. Aviation gasoline is for piston-engine aircraft; jet fuel (Jet A / Jet A-1 / JP-8) is a kerosene cut for turbine aircraft and is the much-larger-volume aviation fuel globally. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) targets jet-kerosene replacement, not avgas. Avgas elimination depends on FAA / EASA certification of unleaded high-octane replacement fuels and fleet-wide engine modification — a long-running regulatory process. (Cross-ref Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); Addicott 1971, p. 60)

Related terms. Motor fuels (umbrella); octane number (RON / MON); tetraethyl lead (TEL); sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); HEFA pathway; aviation industry decarbonisation.

Source history. - Addicott 1971 — added 2026-05-08: definition, distinction from automotive gasoline. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): AVGAS 100LL specification, replacement candidates.

Battery electric vehicle (BEV)

Definition. A road, rail or marine vehicle propelled solely by electricity drawn from an onboard rechargeable battery (typically lithium-ion). Batteries can also act as grid-connected storage via vehicle-to-grid (V2G), allowing BEVs to discharge electricity back to the grid during peak demand. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7–8)

Attributes — coverage in 100% RE systems analyses.

Vehicle category Coverage
LDV BEV 92% of LDV studies
LDV FCEV 46% of LDV studies
LDV PHEV 21% of LDV studies
MDV/HDV/BUS BEV balanced across powertrains in most regions

(Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 18)

Notes. BEVs are the most common transport-sector technology in the 100% RE systems database, appearing in 33% of studies. Direct electrification of road and rail transport represents the first phase of transport-sector decarbonisation; indirect electrification via e-fuels handles harder-to-abate segments such as long-distance maritime and aviation. Battery deployment necessitates affordable batteries and widespread charging infrastructure, with rising integration also enabling V2G flexibility. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 1, 3, 7)

Related terms. Lithium-ion battery (aviation); fuel cell electric vehicle (FCEV); vehicle-to-grid (V2G); sodium-ion battery; sector coupling; e-fuels.

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, coverage in 100% RE database.

Bbio / Cep / DH (RE2020 indicators)

Aliases. Bbio (besoins bioclimatiques); Cep (Consommation d’Énergie Primaire); DH (Degrés-Heures, summer indicator); Ic_construction; Ic_énergie; RE2020 indicators.

Definition. A set of complementary technical indicators used in the French RE2020 building regulation to evaluate the energy, environmental, and summer-comfort performance of new buildings: - Bbio (besoins bioclimatiques) — bioclimatic demand index, points-based metric for useful heating + cooling + lighting energy derived purely from envelope and orientation (independent of HVAC system efficiency). Captures envelope quality. - Cep (Consommation d’Énergie Primaire) — primary-energy consumption (kWh/m²/yr), measured in primary-energy units using French conversion factors (×2.3 for electricity). - DH (Degrés-Heures) — degree-hours of overheating above 26 °C operative temperature in summer. Threshold of 350 K·h indicates “passoire de chaleur” warning. - Ic_construction (life-cycle GWP100 of construction materials, kg CO₂eq/m²) — RE2020 carbon-budget for embodied emissions; tightening from <640 (2022) to <415 (post-2031) for residential. - Ic_énergie (operational GWP, kg CO₂eq/m²/yr) — RE2020 carbon-budget for operational emissions. (Goessel 2025, pp. 75–88; Code de la Construction RE2020 specifications)

Attributes — RE2020 indicator hierarchy.

Indicator What it measures Unit Goal
Bbio bioclimatic demand (envelope only) points minimise
Cep primary-energy consumption kWh PE/m²/yr minimise (≤ Cep_max)
Cep_nr non-renewable primary-energy share kWh PE/m²/yr minimise
Cef final-energy consumption kWh FE/m²/yr secondary
DH summer overheating K·h above 26 °C < 1,250 K·h
Ic_construction embodied GWP100 (life-cycle) kg CO₂eq/m² < 640 → < 415 (over time)
Ic_énergie operational GWP100 kg CO₂eq/m²/yr < 4 (life-cycle weighted)

(Goessel 2025, pp. 80–86; CCH RE2020)

Notes — innovations vs RT2012. RE2020 introduces (i) Ic_construction — first national regulation to cap embodied carbon, driving low-carbon-cement and timber construction; (ii) DH summer-comfort metric, reflecting climate-change adaptation; (iii) tighter Cep with bonuses for biomass boilers; (iv) “Bbio − Bbio_max” relative-performance scoring. Older RT2012 only had Bbio + Cep + Tic (interior temperature). (Goessel 2025, pp. 80–86)

Related terms. RE2020 / RT2012; building renovation (umbrella); Embodied carbon (buildings); Operational carbon (buildings); Standard Effective Temperature (SET); building envelope; DPE.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: Bbio/Cep/DH/Ic detailed definitions, RE2020 hierarchy, vs RT2012 innovations (translated from French).

Battery storage (stationary)

Aliases. Stationary battery storage; grid-scale battery storage.

Definition. Electrochemical energy storage systems — predominantly lithium-ion (Li-ion), and increasingly post-Li-ion chemistries including LFP, NMC, NCA, sodium-ion and solid-state — used for grid-scale electricity storage, distinguished from electric-vehicle battery applications. Used to balance variable renewable supply, provide ancillary services (frequency, reserves), defer transmission upgrades, and shift energy across time. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 152, 6340–6645, Glossary p. 373)

Attributes — deployment, costs and outlook (ETP-2026).

Indicator Value Year
Battery cost decline −75% since 2015 (continued through 2025) 2015–2025
2024 battery pack price (utility-scale) falling steeply (USD million / GWh basis, BNEF) 2015–2025
Average battery-storage growth rate (last 5 y) ~70% per year ~2020–2025
Pumped-storage hydropower (PSH) <200 GW global capacity (≈8,500 GWh storage) early 2020s
2025 stationary battery capacity (estimated) ~270 GW / ~625 GWh (battery surpasses PSH in power by end-2025) 2025
Long-duration mechanical storage (CAES, liquid-CO₂, liquid-air) ~1 GW combined 2025
Other long-duration storage in operation ~4 GW total 2025
2035 battery capacity (CPS) 1.4 TW / 4.2 TWh 2035
2035 battery capacity (STEPS) 1.7 TW / 4.9 TWh 2035
2035 battery capacity (NZE) 2.9 TW / 8.5 TWh 2035
Storage share of dispatchable capacity by 2035 (NZE) 30% (≈2× STEPS, >2× CPS) 2035

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 152, 6340–6645)

Notes. The post-2020 surge in stationary battery storage has been driven primarily by EV-driven cost reductions, plus rising solar PV penetration that creates demand for short-duration storage to integrate variable renewables — particularly in regions with weak transmission. China is the dominant manufacturer; Chinese ownership of battery cell capacity outside China is currently ~5%, projected to rise to ~25% by 2030 based on FID/under-construction projects. Long-duration storage (>4 hours) remains a niche but growing market — including CAES, liquid-air, liquid-CO₂ and emerging chemistries — with policy support and falling LCOEs needed to scale. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 152, 6340–6645, 18–19)

Indicator Value
Today’s BESS in France several hundred MW (mostly FCR-providing)
2050 BESS capacity (M0) ~26 GW
2050 BESS capacity (M1) ~21 GW

Average daily injection profile charge mid-day (PV peak), discharge evening / overnight

(RTE 2022, Sections 7.4.1, 7.4.2, 7.10.2, Figures 7.29–7.30, 7.60, pp. 327–331, 378)

Notes — RTE diminishing-returns capacitive contribution. The capacity contribution of 4-hour batteries to security of supply is 30–40% of installed power for the first GW of deployment, but falls progressively as penetration rises. The reason: with more batteries, the residual periods of system tension are longer than the 4-hour discharge window, so additional batteries cannot extend their coverage of those periods. RTE explicitly contrasts this against H₂-CCGT (P2G2P) which covers extreme long-duration events. (RTE 2022, Section 7.4.2, pp. 329–331)

Notes — second-life batteries. RTE evaluates the use of second-life EV batteries for stationary applications: cost is lower than new batteries but residual capacity is lower (~70–80%) and re-assembly costs erode the benefit. RTE concludes second-life batteries are economic in some niche stationary applications but new batteries dominate the bulk of stationary storage build-out by 2050. (RTE 2022, Section 7.4.3, Figure 7.49, pp. 366–367)

Related terms. Biorefinery

Aliases. Integrated biorefinery; multi-product biomass processor.

Definition. A facility that converts biomass feedstock (sugar/starch crops, oils, lignocellulose, algae) into a portfolio of multiple value-added outputs — fuels, chemicals, materials, animal feed, and process heat/power — through a combination of physical, chemical and biochemical conversion steps, analogous to how a petroleum refinery produces multiple products from crude oil. The biorefinery concept is the canonical industrial architecture for valorising biomass at scale, particularly lignocellulose (non-food / 2nd-generation feedstock). (Keim 2010, pp. 301–302; Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Attributes — biorefinery generations.

Generation Feedstock Status
1G — Sugar/starch + oils Corn, sugar cane, soybean Commercial (bioethanol, biodiesel)
2G — Lignocellulose Straw, bagasse, forestry residues, energy crops Pre-commercial (POET-DSM, Iogen, Borregaard)
3G — Algae Microalgae R&D / pilot
4G — Engineered biology + CO₂ Synthetic biology + CCU Concept / early R&D

(Keim 2010, pp. 300–301)

Attributes — typical 2G biorefinery output portfolio.

Output Conversion route
Bioethanol (cellulose → glucose → fermentation) Major; gasoline blending or ethylene feedstock
Lignin-based aromatic chemicals Lignin depolymerisation → BTX, vanillin
Furfural, 5-HMF Hemicellulose → sugar dehydration
Bio-naphtha (HVO route) Hydroprocessing of lipids/oils
Biogas / biomethane Anaerobic digestion of residues
Process heat + power Lignin combustion
Animal feed protein Hydrolysis residues

(Keim 2010, pp. 301–302)

Notes — gasification-as-biorefinery hub. Zhang et al. 2024 propose that universal gasification — biomass + crude + coal + waste plastic, all to syngas — becomes the unifying biorefinery hub of the future, with C1 chemistry providing the molecular reconstruction step. This vision merges petrochemical and biorefinery infrastructure into a single defossilised platform. (Zhang et al. 2024, pp. 105–106 and Fig. 9)

Notes — connection to Fischer-Tropsch. Keim emphasises FT synthesis via biomass gasification as a “promising pathway” for converting non-food biomass into drop-in fuels and chemicals, citing the early Choren Carbo-V process and demonstration plants. Modern syngas-from-biomass + FT routes are studied for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). (Keim 2010, pp. 301–302; cross-ref Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF))

Related terms. Lignocellulose; modern bioenergy; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process; coal gasification (to hydrogen); methanol-to-olefins (MTO); high-value chemicals (HVCs); C1 chemistry; petrochemicals (umbrella); HEFA pathway; bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS).

Source history. - Keim 2010 — added 2026-05-08: definition, generations 1G/2G/3G, 2G output portfolio. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: gasification-as-biorefinery-hub vision.

Building envelope

Aliases. Building skin; thermal envelope; enveloppe (FR); building shell.

Definition. The physical separator between the interior conditioned space and the exterior environment of a building, comprising the opaque elements (walls, roof, floor) and the transparent elements (windows, glazed doors, skylights). The envelope’s thermal performance — characterised by the heat-loss coefficient (U-value, W/m²K), thermal mass (J/K), air-tightness (n50, ach@50Pa), and solar-heat-gain coefficient (g-value, glazing) — determines the building’s heating and cooling demand, summer overheating risk, and operational carbon footprint. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35; AFNOR EN 13790 / ISO 6946)

Attributes — typical U-values for a French residential renovation.

Element Pre-renovation U-value (W/m²K) Post-renovation target
External walls (uninsulated 1960s) 1.5–2.0 0.20–0.30
External walls (modern, RE2020) — <0.18
Roof / attic (uninsulated) 2.5–3.5 0.13–0.20
Floor (over crawl space, uninsulated) 1.0–2.0 0.27
Single glazing 5.6 (replaced)
Double glazing (legacy) 3.0 —
Triple glazing (modern) — 0.6–1.0
Air-tightness (n50, ach @ 50 Pa) 5–15 1.5–3

(Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35; INIES / RE2020)

Notes — building stock heterogeneity. Goessel emphasises that the existing French building stock is highly heterogeneous: the 1969–1974 Chalandon house typology and the pre-1915 stone maison de bourg typology have very different envelope characteristics, requiring different optimal renovation strategies. Pre-1948 buildings often have heritage-protection constraints that exclude exterior-insulation interventions. (Goessel 2025, pp. 75–80)

Notes — “envelope-first” vs “systems-first” debate. Renovation strategies historically emphasised envelope insulation first, with HVAC upgrades second. Goessel’s analysis shows envelope-only strategies fail to capture the full Pareto-optimal set: the optimal renovations combine envelope upgrades with electrification of HVAC (heat-pump replacement) and DHW. Wall insulation + heat pump is the most consistent feature of optimal renovations across French climate zones and existing-system configurations. (Goessel 2025, Sections 3.3–3.4)

Related terms. Building renovation (umbrella); ITI (interior insulation) / ITE (exterior insulation); heat pump (HP); Standard Effective Temperature (SET); RE2020 / RT2012; DPE (Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique); Cooling and Heating degree days (CDD / HDD); building energy simulation (BES / SED).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, U-value table, French stock heterogeneity, envelope-vs-systems debate.

Biomass heating (wood-pellet, log boiler, stove)

Aliases. Chauffage bois (FR); chauffage à granulés (FR — wood pellets); poêle à bois (FR — wood stove); chaudière à granulés (FR — pellet boiler); biomass boiler.

Definition. A residential heating system that burns wood biomass — split logs (bûches), wood pellets (granulés), wood chips (plaquettes), or wood briquettes — as the primary fuel. Three principal categories: (i) wood stove (poêle à bois) — single-room space heater, log or pellet, 3–14 kW; (ii) wood-log boiler (chaudière à bûches) — central boiler with wood-log feed, 15–50 kW; (iii) pellet boiler (chaudière à granulés) — automated central boiler with pellet auger feed and storage silo, 10–30 kW. Biomass heating is widely used in rural France (~7.5 million dwellings) and is a major lever for residential decarbonisation when replacing oil boilers. (Goessel 2025, Annexe A; ADEME 2024)

Attributes — biomass heating system performance.

Indicator Wood stove (log) Wood log boiler Pellet boiler Pellet stove
Efficiency (η) 70–80% 80–90% 88–95% 80–90%
Power (kW) 3–14 15–50 10–30 5–14
Fuel storage local (~100 kg) log basement (~m³) dedicated silo (1–6 t) small bin (~30 kg)
Automation level manual semi-automatic fully automatic semi-automatic
CO₂ emissions (combustion + biogenic credit) near-zero (with sustainable forestry) near-zero near-zero near-zero
Particulate emissions (PM2.5) high (legacy) → low (modern Flamme Verte 7-star) medium very low low
Capital cost (typical, 2024) €2,000–6,000 €10,000–18,000 €15,000–25,000 €5,000–10,000
Annual maintenance low medium medium low

(Goessel 2025, Annexe A; ADEME 2024)

Notes — RE2020 incentive. RE2020 includes a bonus modulation of the Cep_max threshold for buildings using biomass heating, recognising the low-carbon nature of sustainable wood. This effectively favours biomass-renovation in Pareto-optimal strategies under regulatory-compliance criteria. MaPrimeRénov’ provides up to €11,000 grant for replacing oil-boiler with pellet-boiler (low-income households). (Goessel 2025, pp. 80–86; ANAH MaPrimeRénov’)

Notes — air-quality concerns. Older wood-burning stoves emit substantial PM2.5 (fine particulates), undermining outdoor and indoor air quality, particularly in dense settlements. Modern Flamme Verte 7-star (7-étoiles) certification limits stove emissions; outdoor-air-quality regulation increasingly restricts log-burning in pollution-sensitive cities (Île-de-France low-emission zones). (Goessel 2025, Annexe A)

Related terms. Heat pump (HP); Domestic Hot Water (DHW / ECS); building renovation (umbrella); biomass; Modern bioenergy; RE2020 / RT2012; MaPrimeRénov’ / CEE / Eco-PTZ; SO₂ air pollution; secondary organic aerosol (SOA).

Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS)

Definition. A negative-emissions technology in which biomass (typically purpose-grown high-yield crops, grass or wood, or by-products such as pulp-mill bio-CO₂) is combusted or fermented to release energy, and the resulting CO₂ — biogenic in origin — is captured and permanently stored. Because the underlying carbon was atmospheric, BECCS yields verified removal credits eligible for voluntary or compliance carbon markets. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 8, 16; IEA 2026, pp. 17, 41)

Attributes — flagship BECCS project (BECCS Stockholm).

Item Value Source
Project sponsor Stockholm Exergi (50% City of Stockholm) IEA 2026, p. 38
Total estimated investment ~USD 1.3 billion IEA 2026, p. 38
Commercial debt raised >USD 1 billion (2025) IEA 2026, p. 37
Revenue support reverse-auction carbon-removal contracts; long-term forward purchase agreements (Microsoft, Frontier) + low-emission heat sales IEA 2026, pp. 37–38, 41

Notes. Khalili et al. note that integrated assessment models predominantly favour BECCS over DACCS, but the large-scale deployment of BECCS faces extensive land-use, water-stress, EROI and societal constraints. The IEA observes that BECCS together with DACS are the two main technology-based CDR options recognised by financiers; BECCS benefits from being more commercially mature than DACS. (Khalili et al. 2026, p. 16; IEA 2026, p. 17)

Related terms. Carbon dioxide removal (CDR); direct air carbon capture and sequestration (DACCS); 45Q tax credit; pulp and paper industry; carbon capture and storage (CCS); natural climate solutions (NCS).

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, BECCS-vs-DACCS framing, deployment constraints. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: financing-side details for BECCS Stockholm flagship project.

BF-BOF route

Definition. The conventional primary-steel production pathway combining a blast furnace (BF) for iron-ore reduction with a basic oxygen furnace (BOF) for steel-making. In 2019, 93% of primary steel was produced via the BF-BOF route, which consumes large amounts of coal and coke, particularly in the iron-ore reduction step. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Attributes. Energy intensity is around 21 GJ per tonne of steel, depending on operational and technological conditions. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Notes. Modifications to the BF-BOF route can be made to reduce energy consumption (e.g. the HISarna process) or to enable use of biomass or partial hydrogen injection. Carbon capture offers another decarbonisation route, with capture rates between 50% and more than 90%. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Related terms. Blast furnace; basic oxygen furnace; primary steel; secondary steel; DRI-EAF pathway; coke oven.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition, energy intensity, modification options.

Building renovation (umbrella)

Aliases. Rénovation énergétique (FR); building retrofit; renovation strategy; renovation wave (EU framing).

Definition. A set of physical interventions on an existing building — replacing or upgrading the envelope (walls, roof, floor, windows, air-tightness), the heating-ventilation-air-conditioning (HVAC) systems, the domestic-hot-water (DHW) system, lighting and on-site renewables (solar PV, solar thermal) — aimed at improving energy performance, lowering operational and embodied carbon, improving thermal and indoor-air-quality comfort, and extending the useful life of the existing building stock. Building renovation is the principal lever for decarbonising the existing building stock (~40% of EU energy consumption, 36% of EU GHG emissions); the EU “Renovation Wave” strategy (2020) targets doubling the annual renovation rate and 50–60% energy-savings depth by 2030. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7; cross-ref Heat pump (HP), Sufficiency, Deep reindustrialisation)

Attributes — typical renovation-strategy categories.

Category Examples
Envelope insulation — external exterior-insulation-finishing system (ITE); rendered EPS / mineral wool / wood fibre
Envelope insulation — internal interior insulation (ITI); plasterboard + mineral wool
Roof / attic insulation spray foam; mineral wool; cellulose fibre
Floor insulation crawl-space EPS; perimeter insulation
Windows / glazing double / triple glazing; low-E coatings; argon fill
Air-tightness sealing, ventilation membranes, blower-door testing
Heating system heat pump (air-source, ground-source); biomass boiler; condensing gas boiler
HVAC ventilation mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR / CMV double-flux)
Domestic hot water heat-pump water heater; thermodynamic; solar thermal
Solar PV / solar thermal rooftop installations
Cooling / passive shading exterior blinds (volets roulants); brise-soleil; reflective coatings
Active cooling air conditioning (split, multi-split); ceiling fans (brasseur d’air)

(Goessel 2025, Sections 2.3, 3.2.3)

Notes — Goessel 2025 multi-criteria framing. Goessel proposes a prospective multi-criteria optimisation methodology that simultaneously minimises (i) carbon footprint over 50-year life, (ii) Direct Global Cost (CGD), and (iii) summer thermal discomfort (SET-DH) — captured via Pareto dominance and clustered into renovation archetypes. Wall insulation + electrification (heat pump) consistently appears on the Pareto front across French climate zones and existing-system configurations. Renovation strategies focus on the envelope are insufficient alone — HVAC + DHW upgrades are essential for deep decarbonisation. (Goessel 2025, pp. 88–133)

Notes — typical performance reductions. A “deep” residential renovation in temperate climate typically achieves: −60 to −90% heating energy demand; −30 to −70% lifecycle GHG emissions; −20 to −50% summer thermal discomfort (with passive measures); 15–30 year economic payback at ~5% discount rate. Carbon payback time (the time over which embodied carbon of new components is offset by operational savings) is typically 3–15 years for envelope retrofits; can be longer for full equipment replacement. (Goessel 2025, Sections 3, 4)

Related terms. Heat pump (HP); Life Cycle Assessment (LCA); Life Cycle Costing (LCC); Embodied carbon (buildings); Operational carbon (buildings); Standard Effective Temperature (SET); Pareto dominance / Pareto front; Multi-objective optimisation (MOO); RE2020 / RT2012; DPE (Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique); Sufficiency (sobriété énergétique).
