Building energy simulation (BES / SED)

Aliases. SED (FR — Simulation Énergétique Dynamique); dynamic energy simulation; building energy modelling (BEM); whole-building simulation; transient thermal simulation.

Definition. A computational technique for modelling the time-dependent thermal and energy behaviour of a building — typically at hourly or sub-hourly timestep across one or more years — by solving the coupled energy-balance equations for the building envelope, interior zones, HVAC systems, occupant behaviour, and external climate. BES is the standard tool for evaluating renovation strategies, sizing HVAC systems, validating compliance with energy regulations (RT2012, RE2020), and certifying energy-performance ratings. Major commercial / open-source BES software include EnergyPlus, TRNSYS, IDA-ICE, IES VE, COMETh (French RT-Bâtiment standard), DOE-2. (Goessel 2025, pp. 35–41, Fig. 2.7)

Attributes — BES model categories.

Category Description Examples
White-box (physics-based) full first-principles heat-transfer + airflow EnergyPlus, TRNSYS
Grey-box (simplified physics) reduced-order RC-network thermal models COMETh 5RC, ISO 13790 5RC
Black-box (data-driven) regression / machine-learning on measured data building-stock statistics
Quasi-steady (monthly) simplified for regulatory compliance EN 13790 monthly method
Transient (hourly + sub-hourly) hour-by-hour solution dominant in modern BES

(Goessel 2025, pp. 35–37 and Fig. 2.6)

Notes — COMETh 5RC model (French context). The French regulatory tool COMETh, developed by CSTB and used in RE2020 calculations, uses a 5-resistance-capacitance (5RC) simplified thermal model: each thermal zone is represented by 5 thermal resistances and a single thermal capacitance, capturing the dominant heat-transfer paths (envelope conduction, infiltration, solar gains, internal gains, ventilation). The 5RC model is a compromise between the high-fidelity (and expensive) full physics-based approach and the over-simplified monthly steady-state approach. Goessel uses COMETh as the BES engine for renovation simulation. (Goessel 2025, pp. 37–41 and Fig. 2.7)

Notes — input data. BES requires: building geometry, envelope material properties (U-value, thermal mass), window properties (g-value, U-value), HVAC system definitions and efficiencies, occupant schedules + internal-load schedules, climatic file (typical meteorological year — TMY format), control-setpoint schedules. Output includes hourly energy demand by end-use, internal temperatures, comfort indicators (PMV, SET, operative temperature), peak loads. (Goessel 2025, pp. 35–41)

Related terms. Thermal comfort (umbrella); Standard Effective Temperature (SET); PMV / PPD; Typical Meteorological Year (TMY); building renovation (umbrella); RE2020 / RT2012; Cooling and Heating degree days (CDD / HDD); building envelope.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: BES definition, model categories, COMETh 5RC, input data (translated from French).

Bias correction (climate downscaling)

Aliases. Statistical downscaling; bias adjustment; bias removal; correction des biais (FR).

Definition. A family of statistical methods used to correct the systematic bias in climate-model outputs (GCMs / RCMs) when compared with observed local meteorological data over a historical reference period — bringing the model output closer to local reality and making it suitable for impact studies (building energy, hydrology, agriculture). Climate-model biases arise from incomplete physics, sub-grid-scale parameterisation, and topography-resolution mismatch; biases of ±2 °C in temperature and ±20% in precipitation are typical at 12.5 km resolution. (Goessel 2025, pp. 59–61, citing Maraun 2016)

Attributes — major bias-correction methods.

Method Description Strengths Limitations
Delta change (additive / multiplicative) apply model anomaly to observations simple, preserves observation patterns doesn’t capture extreme-event evolution
Quantile Mapping (QM) match model distribution to observed distribution quantile-by-quantile handles bias across the full distribution can alter the climate-change signal in high quantiles
CDF-t (Cumulative Distribution Function transform) combine historical-period calibration with future-period model shift preserves climate-change signal assumes scale-invariant evolution of distributions
LOCI (Local Intensity Scaling) adjust precipitation occurrence frequency + intensity good for precipitation with drizzle days precipitation-specific
Multivariate methods (MBC, R²D²) correct multiple variables jointly preserving inter-variable correlation robust for compound events data-intensive (T, P, RH, wind, radiation)

(Goessel 2025, pp. 59–61, citing Cannon 2015, Michelangeli 2009, Jaiswal 2022)

Notes — Goessel choice (CDF-t). Goessel uses CDF-t for bias correction of EURO-CORDEX 11 outputs against ERA5 reanalysis (1981–2019, 8 km resolution for France). CDF-t is preferred over simpler QM because it preserves the climate-change signal that QM can dampen — particularly important for studying future heat waves under RCP8.5. (Goessel 2025, p. 60)

Related terms. EURO-CORDEX; General Circulation Model (GCM); Regional Climate Model (RCM); Quantile Mapping; CDF-t; Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs); Typical Meteorological Year (TMY); building energy simulation (BES / SED).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: bias-correction methods, CDF-t choice rationale (translated from French).

Bisphenol A (BPA)

Aliases. CAS RN 80-05-7.

Definition. A multi-functional plastic chemical that serves as a co-monomer for polycarbonates and epoxy resins, a crosslinking agent in fluoroelastomers, an intermediate for producing the flame-retardant tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA, CAS RN 79-94-7), an antioxidant, and a light stabiliser. Used as the canonical example illustrating that a single plastic chemical can serve multiple functions across different stages of the plastic life cycle. (Monclús et al. 2025, p. 351)

Notes. Identified as a chemical of concern. The bisphenol family (10 of the 28 grouped chemical groups identified in PlastChem) is a priority group under the structural-similarity grouping framework, with strong evidence of group-level hazard. (Monclús et al. 2025, p. 351, Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 9)

Related terms. Plastic additives; chemicals of concern; plastic chemicals; PlastChem inventory; per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

Source history. - Monclús et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-07: multi-function definition and hazard-group context.

Blast furnace (BF)

Definition. The traditional ironmaking vessel in which iron ore is reduced to pig iron using coke as both fuel and reducing agent. (Kushnir et al. 2020, p. 1, Fig. 1A; Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Notes. In the integrated steel-mill configuration the blast furnace receives iron-ore pellets and coke (from the coke oven), and outputs pig iron to the basic oxygen vessel; off-gases (H₂, CH₄) are also recovered as energy. In Sweden, the coke oven responsible for the bulk of national steel CO₂ emissions has been in continuous operation since the late 1950s. (Kushnir et al. 2020, pp. 1–2 and Fig. 1)

Related terms. Basic oxygen furnace; coke oven; coke; BF-BOF route; direct reduction; hydrogen direct reduction.

Source history. - Kushnir et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-07: definition and integration with coke oven. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: BF-BOF prevalence (93% of primary steel in 2019).

Blended wing body (BWB)

Definition. A novel airframe design in which the fuselage and wings are integrated into a single lifting surface, providing extra internal volume that can accommodate cryogenic hydrogen storage tanks while minimising drag penalty. Identified as the airframe of choice for hydrogen aviation in the Airbus ZEROe project and the Multi-Fuel Blended Wing Body (MFBWB) AHEAD concept aircraft. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 17, 30, 32)

Notes. BWB allows hydrogen tanks to be placed inside the fuselage (integral storage) rather than outside (non-integral), reducing drag penalty at the cost of overhead luggage storage on short-to-medium range airplanes. NASA’s N3-X is another turboelectric BWB concept that demonstrated ~63% energy and 90% NOₓ reductions versus conventional configurations. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 24, 31)

Related terms. Hydrogen aviation; turboelectric propulsion; liquid hydrogen storage; cryo-compressed hydrogen storage.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition and integration role for hydrogen aviation.

Blow moulding (plastic processing)

Aliases. Extrusion blow moulding (EBM); injection blow moulding (IBM); injection-stretch blow moulding (ISBM); blow forming.

Definition. A plastics processing method for producing hollow articles (bottles, containers, drums, fuel tanks) by inflating a softened tubular plastic parison against the inside surface of a closed mould. Three principal variants: EBM — continuous extrusion of a parison, mould-clamping, then air injection (most HDPE bottles, drums); IBM — pre-injected preform, reheated, blown (small-volume containers); ISBM — pre-injection of preform, biaxial stretch + blow (PET water/soft-drink bottles, dominant for PET). (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Attributes — typical blow-mould products.

Variant Typical polymer Wall thickness Example products
EBM HDPE, LDPE, PVC 0.5–5 mm bleach bottles, milk jugs, IBC drums (1,000 L), fuel tanks
IBM HDPE, PP, PET 0.5–3 mm pharma bottles, small consumer packaging
ISBM PET (dominant), PP 0.2–0.6 mm water bottles, soft-drink bottles, oil bottles

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Related terms. Injection moulding; extrusion (plastic processing); thermoforming; rotomoulding; PET; polyethylene (HDPE); polypropylene (PP); plastic processing (umbrella).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, EBM/IBM/ISBM variants, applications.

Boil-off loss

Definition. Hydrogen evaporation losses occurring in liquid-hydrogen storage when heat transferred to the cryogenic liquid causes vaporisation. Boil-off depends on the thermal insulation, design and size of the vessel and can reach up to 0.4% per day. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 29)

Notes. Cryo-compressed hydrogen storage was developed in part to mitigate boil-off; insulated pressure vessels expand the dormancy period and minimise losses by allowing pressure rise inside the tank. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 30)

Related terms. Liquid hydrogen storage; cryo-compressed hydrogen storage; ortho-hydrogen / para-hydrogen.

Source history. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition and mitigation note.

BTX aromatics (benzene, toluene, xylenes)

Aliases. BTX; aromatic hydrocarbons; cracker aromatics.

Definition. A core group of aromatic petrochemicals — benzene (C₆H₆), toluene (C₇H₈), and the three xylene isomers (o-, m-, p-C₈H₁₀) — that forms the building-block stream for the aromatic-chemicals supply chain. BTX is recovered from (i) catalytic-reformer reformate streams in petroleum refineries, (ii) pyrolysis gasoline (pygas) from naphtha steam crackers, and (iii) on-purpose routes such as methanol-to-aromatics (MTA) and toluene disproportionation/hydrodealkylation. BTX feeds polymer (polystyrene, polyester PET, nylon), solvent, and pesticide industries. (Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727; Speight 2019, Chapter 6; Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Attributes — global flows and end-uses (Levi & Cullen 2018, 2013 mass balance).

Aromatic Global production (2013) Principal end-uses
Benzene ~46 Mt/yr Styrene → polystyrene; cumene → phenol; cyclohexane → nylon
Toluene ~21 Mt/yr Solvent; toluene diisocyanate (TDI); disproportionation to benzene + xylenes
Xylenes (mixed + p-xylene) ~50 Mt/yr p-xylene → terephthalic acid → PET (polyester fiber + bottle resin)
Total BTX ~117 Mt/yr ~40% from refinery reformate, ~57% from steam crackers (heavy feed), ~3% on-purpose

(Levi and Cullen 2018, pp. 1727, 1729–1731 and Fig. 1; Speight 2019, Chapter 6)

Notes — recovery and conversion. BTX co-produces with C4 olefins from naphtha steam crackers; lighter ethane-fed crackers produce essentially no aromatics. Toluene is often hydrodealkylated to benzene or disproportionated (TDP) to balance benzene/xylene supply with downstream demand. P-xylene is selectively crystallised or sorbed from the mixed-xylene stream; the m- and o-isomers are isomerised back to feed equilibrium toward p-xylene (UOP Parex / Mobil MX-Sorbex). (Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727)

Notes — methanol-to-aromatics (MTA) route. A non-naphtha route in which methanol (from coal/natural-gas/biomass syngas via methanol synthesis) is dehydrated and aromatised over a zeolite catalyst (typically modified ZSM-5) to deliver up to ~80% aromatics selectivity at moderate conversion (Zhang et al. 2024, Zn-ZrO₂/ZSM-5 catalyst). MTA is one of three on-purpose aromatic routes that diversify away from naphtha. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Related terms. Naphtha; steam cracking (vapocracking); catalytic reforming; methanol-to-olefins (MTO); methanol-to-aromatics (MTA); high-value chemicals (HVCs); pyrolysis gasoline (pygas); benzene; toluene; xylene.

Source history. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: global mass balance, end-use shares, refinery vs steam-cracker split. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: production routes, downstream conversions. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: MTA on-purpose route and 80% selectivity.

Brominated flame retardants (BFRs)

Definition. A family of plastic additives used to delay or suppress combustion of polymer products, in which one or more bromine atoms are incorporated into the molecular structure to interrupt free-radical chain reactions during pyrolysis. Includes hexabromocyclododecane (HBCDD), tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA), polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs), and polybrominated dibenzo-p-dioxins/furans (PBDD/Fs) as combustion by-products. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, pp. 187, 192)

Notes. BFRs are extensively studied for migration and release from plastic products such as electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) casings, textiles and packaging. Several are listed as persistent organic pollutants (POPs) under the Stockholm Convention. The thermal degradation of brominated polymers releases hydrogen bromide and can generate PBDD/Fs as unintended chain-stripping by-products, complicating end-of-life management of WEEE. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, pp. 187, 192)

Related terms. Plastic additives; chemicals of concern; persistent organic pollutants (POPs); migration (plastic chemicals); PoTSs (potentially toxic substances); plastic chemicals.

Source history. - Hahladakis et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, examples, end-of-life concerns.

Capacity factor (by technology)

Aliases. Facteur de charge (FR); CF; load factor (UK); plant utilisation factor.

Definition. The ratio of the average power produced over a period to the rated maximum (nameplate) capacity of the plant, expressed as a percentage. CF = (annual energy output, MWh) / (nameplate capacity, MW × hours/year). Capacity factor reflects (i) the resource availability (sun, wind, fuel), (ii) the planned and unplanned outages, and (iii) the dispatch decisions of the operator (i.e. whether the plant is called to produce). For VRE, capacity factor is largely resource-driven; for dispatchable units, it is largely dispatch-driven. (RTE 2022, Section 4.3.8, pp. 185–187, translated from French)

Attributes — RTE 2050 capacity factors by technology (France).

Technology RTE-2050 mean CF Range / variability Driver
Onshore wind ~23% 21.9–26.6% historical inter-annual Stability hypothesis; site saturation balances technology gain
Offshore wind (fixed-bottom + floating) ~41% 37.3–46.2% inter-annual Technology improvement + site selection
Solar PV (utility + rooftop) ~13–14% 13.1–15.5% historical Mature cell tech; geographic distribution; M1 lower due to non-optimal rooftops
Hydropower (excl. PHES) ~30% effective weather-driven (drought sensitivity) River regime
Nuclear (existing 2nd gen) ~71% declining toward end of life Aging-fleet availability + modulation
Nuclear (EPR Flamanville series) ~73% (incl. FA3) RTE prudent Limited series-effect
Nuclear (EPR2 series) ~84% RTE prudent (vs 91% EDF target, 90.9% Taishan-1) Better-availability assumption
CCGT (gas, today 2019) 47% will collapse Today’s market dispatch
CCGT (decarbonised, 2050) ~10% insurance role Residual-load coverage only
OCGT (peaker, today) tens to hundreds of h/yr (~1–3%) extreme peak only Capacity-adequacy role
OCGT (decarbonised, 2050) <5% insurance only Last-resort capacity

(RTE 2022, Sections 4.3.8, 7.5.3, 7.10.3, pp. 185–187, 336, 380; figures throughout)

Notes — RTE conservatism on RES CF. RTE adopts a prudent stance, projecting onshore-wind CF to remain stable around 23% rather than rising as some studies suggest. Reason: French height-of-mast restrictions (aviation, visual-impact regulations) prevent the larger, taller wind turbines that have driven CF gains in the US, China and Germany. Offshore wind CF can rise toward 41% as technology matures (next-generation turbines from late-2020s). Solar PV CF is essentially flat — cell-technology improvements have plateaued, with future cost gains driven by manufacturing rather than CF. (RTE 2022, Section 4.3.8, pp. 185–187)

Notes — modulation impact on nuclear CF. Today French nuclear runs at ~75% CF in part because of modulation (load-following): demand-side variability + must-run renewables push some nuclear units to reduce output during low-demand periods. By 2050, modulation requirements rise sharply (more VRE), and RTE projects existing-fleet CF to fall toward 71% partly for this reason; new EPR2s achieve 84% partly because they will be designed with modulation flexibility built-in. (RTE 2022, Section 7.10.3, p. 380)

Notes — geographic vs technical CF. RTE distinguishes two effects on CF: (i) site saturation — best wind / sun sites are developed first; later capacity goes to lower-resource sites, lowering average CF; (ii) technology improvement — taller masts, larger blades, better tracking, better cell efficiency raise CF. The two effects largely offset in France, justifying RTE’s stability assumption. (RTE 2022, Section 4.3.8, p. 185)

Related terms. Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); Solar PV; Wind power; Nuclear power; Combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT); Open cycle gas turbine (OCGT); Modulation nucléaire; Curtailment; Residual load.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: French CF values for all major technologies (~23% onshore wind, ~41% offshore, ~13–14% PV, 71% existing nuclear, 84% EPR2, 47%→10% CCGT), prudent stability assumption, modulation impact (translated from French).

C1 chemistry

Aliases. One-carbon chemistry; C1 building blocks; CO/CH₄/CO₂-based chemistry.

Definition. The branch of organic chemistry and process engineering devoted to the synthesis of fuels and chemicals from one-carbon building blocks — methane (CH₄), carbon monoxide (CO), methanol (CH₃OH), formaldehyde (HCHO), and carbon dioxide (CO₂). C1 chemistry is the canonical conversion stage in coal-to-chemicals, gas-to-chemicals, biomass-to-chemicals, and Power-to-X (PtX) value chains. Zhang et al. 2024 propose C1 chemistry combined with universal gasification as the central architecture of a “simplified” net-zero petrochemical industry, replacing the molecule-selective distillation/cracking architecture of today. (Zhang et al. 2024, pp. 104–110; Speight 2019, Chapter 7)

Attributes — main C1 building-block chemistry.

Building block Source Key downstream products
CH₄ Natural gas; biomethane Syngas via SMR; methanol; ethylene via OCM (oxidative coupling)
CO + H₂ (syngas) Coal/biomass gasification; SMR; rWGS Methanol; FT liquids; DME; aldehydes (oxo); acetic acid
Methanol Syngas Olefins (MTO); aromatics (MTA); propylene (MTP); formaldehyde; DME
CO₂ DAC; industrial capture; biogenic Methanol (CRI Iceland); urea; cyclic carbonates; methanation
HCHO Methanol partial oxidation Phenolic resins; formaldehyde-based polymers

(Zhang et al. 2024, Fig. 6 and pp. 105–110; Levi and Cullen 2018, pp. 1726–1727)

Attributes — Zhang’s “future petrochemical” architecture.

Stage Today Zhang 2024 vision
Carbon source Crude oil distillation Universal gasification of crude/coal/biomass/waste plastic to CO + H₂
Reconstruction 50+ refining/cracking units One C1 reconstruction step (CO + green H₂ → target product)
Hydrogen Grey/blue from SMR Green H₂ from electrolysis with renewables/nuclear
Energy Heat from fossil combustion Electrified heat / nuclear high-temp heat
CO₂ Vented or limited CCUS CCUS plus electrocatalytic reduction of CO₂ to CO
Process complexity High (path-dependence) Low (modular, standardised)

(Zhang et al. 2024, Sections 4.3, 5.1, Fig. 9)

Notes — limits today. C1 chemistry already underpins commercial methanol synthesis (~100 Mt/yr global), MTO, MTP, MTA, and FT synthesis; the bottleneck is FT’s ASF distribution ceiling and the high CO₂ footprint of grey-syngas routes. Zhang argues that synergistic catalysts (OXZEO) plus electrocatalytic CO₂-to-CO will turn C1 chemistry into the primary petrochemical platform by mid-century. (Zhang et al. 2024, pp. 109–110)

Notes — connection to electricity refinery. Zhang’s “electricity refinery” concept is the operationalisation of C1 chemistry powered by renewables: electrolysis water → green H₂; electrocatalytic CO₂ reduction → CO; CO + H₂ → target chemicals via FT/MTO/MTA. Estimated cost of CO from electrocatalysis: ~130 USD/t at 300 mA/cm²; cost of ethylene via CO ~40% lower than via direct one-step CO₂ electroreduction. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 111)

Related terms. Methanol synthesis (electrofuels and biofuels); Methanol-to-Olefins (MTO); methanol-to-aromatics (MTA); Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process; Anderson-Schulz-Flory (ASF) distribution; coal gasification (to hydrogen); steam methane reforming (SMR); reverse water gas shift (rWGS); Power-to-X (PtX); synergistic catalysis (OXZEO); high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, building-block table, “simplified petrochemical” architecture, electricity-refinery cost estimates. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): industrial C1 routes (methanol, FT, oxo). - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): mass-balance role in syngas-to-methanol-to-MTO.

Calendering (plastic processing)

Aliases. Calender; calender line; sheeting line.

Definition. A plastics processing method in which molten polymer is forced between a series of heated counter-rotating rolls (typically 4 or 5 rolls in an L, F, Z, or inverted-L configuration) to produce continuous flat sheet or thin film of precise thickness. Calendering is the dominant production method for flexible PVC sheet and film (flooring, wall coverings, roofing membranes), and is also used for thermoplastic elastomer sheets, conveyor belts, and tyre cord coating. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Attributes — typical calendered products.

Polymer Output thickness End-use
Flexible PVC 0.05–1.0 mm flooring, wall coverings, automotive interior, conveyor belts
Rigid PVC 0.2–2.0 mm sheets for thermoforming, signage
HIPS / ABS 0.2–3.0 mm refrigerator liners, packaging
Tyre cord ply various automotive tyres

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Related terms. Polyvinyl chloride (PVC); polystyrene (PS / HIPS / EPS); plasticizers (phthalate esters); plastic processing (umbrella); extrusion (plastic processing).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, roll configurations, products.

Capacity expansion model (CEM / CEP)

Aliases. CEM; CEP; capacity expansion planning; generation-expansion planning; investment-planning model.

Definition. A class of optimisation models that determine the cost-minimising schedule of capacity additions and retirements for a power or energy system over a planning horizon — the “expansion” question — given a forecast of demand growth, technology costs, and constraints. CEMs are a subset of Energy System Optimisation Models (ESOMs); the boundary between the two is fuzzy, with CEMs typically focused on power-sector expansion (often without operational hourly resolution), while ESOMs typically span the full energy system (electricity + heat + transport + industry). (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 1–3; cross-ref Energy System Optimisation Model)

Attributes — CEM vs ESOM.

Aspect CEM (narrow sense) ESOM (broad sense)
Sector scope electricity only full energy system
Operational detail aggregated load duration curves hourly time series typical
Planning horizon 10–30 years 30–80 years
Formulation LP, often with relaxed unit-commitment LP / MILP, often with sector coupling
Typical use utility / regulator IRP national / global decarbonisation pathway
Main constraints reliability, reserve margin, RPS emissions budget, sector coupling, technology learning

(Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 1–3; cross-ref ESOM)

Notes — historical. CEM literature predates ESOM by decades — the WASP (Wien Automatic System Planning) model from IIASA / IAEA in the 1970s–1980s and the EGEAS / GEMINI / PROVIEW utility-industry tools popularised the formulation. Modern CEMs (PLEXOS, ABB GridView, NREL ReEDS) increasingly add operational sub-hourly detail to capture renewable variability. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 1)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); Integrated Assessment Model (IAM); pathways (vs scenarios); investment milestones (modelling); foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); Loss of Load Expectation (LoLE); Capacity adequacy.

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: CEM-vs-ESOM distinction, historical context.

Caprock

Definition. An impermeable layer (typically mudstone or evaporite) overlying a porous reservoir and forming a seal that traps stored gases and the formation brine within the reservoir. Caprock integrity is a primary requirement for secure subsurface gas storage. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 79)

Notes. Caprock integrity may be compromised by pressure-induced geomechanical failure, by hydrogen–rock–brine wettability changes that reduce capillary sealing, and by swelling or drying-out of clays during operation, all of which can create leakage pathways. (Miocic et al. 2023, pp. 80–81, citing Hashemi et al. 2021, 2022; Iglauer et al. 2021; Al-Mukainah et al. 2022; Wentinck and Busch 2017)

Related terms. Porous rock hydrogen storage; saline aquifer; depleted gas field; capillary entry pressure; storage complex.

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition and integrity-related notes.

Capital Recovery Factor (CRF)

Definition. A finance factor that converts a one-time capital expenditure (CAPEX or Total Capital Investment, TCI) into an equivalent annualised payment over the project lifetime, given a discount rate. CRF = i (1+i)^n / [(1+i)^n − 1], where i is the discount rate (commonly the weighted average cost of capital, WACC) and n is the project lifetime (years). (Khan et al. 2021, p. 19; Raillard-Cazanove 2024, abbreviation list)

Attributes — illustrative values used in Khan et al. 2021’s hydrogen-pipeline case study.

Parameter Value
Discount rate (WACC) 8%
Pipe lifetime 50 years
Compressor lifetime 15 years
CRF (compressor, 8%, 15 y) 0.1168

(Khan et al. 2021, p. 20 and Tables 5.2, 6.5)

Notes. The annualised CAPEX is then divided by the annual production to yield the capital component of the levelised cost (e.g. LCOH). CRF is also used in financing CCUS infrastructure, where the regulated asset base (RAB) tariff design depends on similar capital-recovery economics with a regulated rate of return. (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 19–20; IEA 2026, p. 43)

Related terms. Levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH); total capital investment (TCI); discount rate; weighted average cost of capital (WACC); regulated asset base (RAB).

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — listed in Pending 2026-05-07. - Khan et al. 2021 — added 2026-05-08: formula, hydrogen-pipeline application; promoted from Pending.

Clean energy technologies

Definition. An IEA-defined umbrella class for energy technologies that result in minimal or zero CO₂ and pollutant emissions. In ETP-2026 the term refers specifically to six categories: batteries, electric cars, electrolysers, heat pumps, solar PV and wind. The combined global market value of these six technologies grew at ~20% per year over the past decade to reach nearly USD 1.2 trillion in 2025. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary p. 374; Executive Summary p. 15)

Attributes — 2025 market context (ETP-2026).

Item Value
Combined global market value ~USD 1.2 trillion (2025)
Annual market growth (past decade) ~20% per year
Largest sub-segment by value electric cars (≈ ¾ of total in 2035)
Share of generation now below coal/gas LCOE ~80% of solar PV and wind
Battery price decline (last decade) −75%

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 15–16)

Notes. ETP-2026 distinguishes “clean energy technologies” (this list) from “low-emissions fuels” (bioenergy, low-emissions hydrogen, hydrogen-based fuels) and “near-zero emissions materials” (steel, cement, aluminium, ammonia). The six clean energy technologies share characteristics that have driven cost reductions through modularity and mass-manufacturing, contrasting with capital-intensive technologies (nuclear, geothermal, hydrogen) where innovation rather than scale has been the cost-reduction driver. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 15–17, 374)

Related terms. Low-emissions hydrogen; low-emissions hydrogen-based fuels; near-zero emissions materials; modern bioenergy; battery electric vehicle (BEV); heat pump (HP); solar PV; manufacturing capacity (clean energy technologies).

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: umbrella definition, six-technology list, market context.

Carbon payback time (TRC)

Aliases. TRC (FR — Temps de Retour Carbone); carbon payback period; embodied-carbon payback; CO₂ payback time.

Definition. The time over which the operational GHG-emission savings of a low-carbon investment (e.g. building insulation, heat-pump replacement, solar PV) cumulatively offset the embodied GHG emissions of manufacturing, transporting, and installing that investment. After the payback period, every additional year of operation delivers net GHG reduction. Essential for evaluating whether a renovation strategy actually delivers a net climate benefit over its lifetime — short-payback measures are clearly beneficial; long-payback measures (>20 years) may not be net-positive given typical asset lifetimes. (Goessel 2025, pp. 203–204, Annexe D)

Attributes — typical carbon-payback periods (residential renovation).

Renovation measure Carbon payback (typical, French climate)
LED lighting upgrade <1 year
Heat-pump replacing oil boiler 1–3 years
Heat-pump replacing gas boiler 3–6 years
Wall insulation (ITE, mineral wool) 3–8 years
Wall insulation (ITI) 4–10 years
Roof insulation (high R) 2–6 years
Triple glazing replacing double 8–20 years
Solar PV (residential, 5 kWp) 1–4 years (with French electricity mix)
Whole-house deep retrofit 5–15 years
Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) 5–12 years

(Goessel 2025, Annexe D)

Notes — vs investment payback time (TRI). Carbon payback (TRC) is the climate-policy counterpart to investment payback (TRI / REI — Rapport Économies sur Investissement). TRI = years for energy-cost savings to repay capital cost. The two payback times can diverge sharply — a measure with very short carbon-payback (PV) may have long financial-payback if electricity prices are low; a measure with long carbon-payback (triple glazing) may have favourable economics under high gas-price scenarios. (Goessel 2025, pp. 203–204)

Notes — methodological subtlety. TRC depends on (i) the future CO₂-intensity trajectory of the displaced energy carrier (a heat-pump replacing gas saves more CO₂ in 2030 than 2050 because grid decarbonises further); (ii) the embodied carbon of the replacement equipment; (iii) the baseline against which savings are computed (no renovation? business-as-usual replacement?). Goessel emphasises that prospective TRC calculations capture more accurately the long-run benefit by reflecting grid decarbonisation. (Goessel 2025, p. 203)

Related terms. Embodied carbon (buildings); Operational carbon (buildings); Life Cycle Assessment (LCA); building renovation (umbrella); heat pump (HP); investment payback time; abatement cost (greenhouse gas).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: TRC definition, typical periods, vs TRI distinction, methodological-subtlety note.

Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)

Aliases. CBAM; EU CBAM; carbon border tariff; carbon border tax; border carbon adjustment.

Definition. A carbon-pricing trade-policy instrument introduced by the European Union (Regulation EU 2023/956, transitional reporting from October 2023; full financial obligation from 1 January 2026) that imposes a border charge on imports of carbon-intensive goods (initially: cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity, hydrogen) equivalent to the EU ETS price for the embodied emissions, minus any carbon price already paid in the country of origin. The CBAM is designed to (i) prevent carbon leakage — the relocation of EU industrial production to lower-carbon-price jurisdictions — as the EU phases out free-allocation of EU ETS allowances to trade-exposed industries; and (ii) incentivise non-EU exporters to decarbonise to maintain market access. (Johnson et al. 2025, p. 1; cross-ref EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS))

Attributes — CBAM scope and timeline.

Indicator Value
Initial scope (2026) Cement, iron + steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity, H₂
Steel share of CBAM goods (by reported weight) 69%
Free-allocation phase-out gradual 2026 → 2034 (full phase-out by 2034)
CBAM coverage of direct (scope-1) emissions from 2026
CBAM coverage of indirect (scope-2) emissions initially excluded; under review
Default emission factors published by Commission for compliance simplicity
Verification independent verifier required for embedded-emission declarations
Carbon price reduction exporter can deduct any CO₂ price already paid in country of origin

(Johnson et al. 2025, p. 1; EU Reg. 2023/956, cited)

Notes — Johnson 2025 modelling findings. Combined with the 2024 EU ETS revision (which extends free allocation to H₂-DRI / pelletising / hydrogen production benchmarks during 2026–2033), the CBAM creates a market in which: - Hydrogen-DRI-EAF green steel becomes cost-competitive with BF-BOF on the EU market starting 2026 in best-resource locations (Northern Scandinavia, Iberia). - BF-BOF imports become non-competitive from ~2030 (at ETS price ≥ €150/t CO₂) or from ~2033 (at ETS price ≥ €90/t). - Without sufficient EU green-steel capacity, BF-BOF capacity is replaced by imports of low-emission steel — reshaping global value chains. - A “decarbonisation race” dynamic emerges: third countries can collectively decarbonise more steel capacity than they currently export to the EU, gaining market share. - Adding scope-2 (electricity) emissions to CBAM mitigates an additional 12.9 Mt CO₂/yr of imported embedded emissions.

(Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 2–7)

Notes — Hot-Briquetted-Iron (HBI) trade as relocation strategy. Johnson explicitly studies “trading HBI” — relocating the energy-intensive ironmaking step (DRI) to renewable-resource-rich third countries while keeping EAF + downstream processing in the EU. This decouples the EU steel value chain across borders, preserving domestic steel-making while accessing global low-cost green H₂. (Johnson et al. 2025, p. 1; cross-ref Hot briquetted iron entry)

Related terms. EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); H₂-DRI-EAF route; hot briquetted iron (HBI); near-zero emissions materials; non-recourse project finance; carbon contract for difference (CCfD); carbon leakage; deep reindustrialisation; abatement cost.

Source history. - Johnson et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, scope, timeline, dynamic-modelling findings on green-steel cost-competitiveness, HBI trade strategy.

Carbon capture and storage (CCS)

Aliases. Carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS); carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) when storage is omitted.

Definition. - A set of technologies in which CO₂ produced by fossil-fuelled power, gasification or reforming plants is captured and transported to geological storage options such as saline aquifers, depleted oil or gas fields, or other suitable underground cavities (onshore or offshore). (Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8810) - An industrial decarbonisation lever that drives up electricity demand, particularly when oxyfuel combustion is employed; the term is used interchangeably with CCUS in the recent industry-decarbonisation literature, with CCUS additionally encompassing utilisation of captured CO₂. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, pp. 8, 10–11, 14)

Attributes — capture pathways (Baufumé et al. 2011, pp. 8810, 8812).

Capture pathway Description
Pre-combustion CO₂ absorbed after the shift reaction in IGCC by a commercial physical solvent (Rectisol, Selexol).
Post-combustion (NGCC) CO₂ chemically absorbed from NGCC flue gas by a monoethanolamine solution.
Post-combustion (SMR) CO₂ chemically absorbed after the shift reaction by a methyl diethanolamine solution.
Oxyfuel Combustion in pure oxygen (e.g. oxyfuel NGCC).

Attributes — costs (where reported by source).

Item Value Source
ULCOS test-furnace modifications with CCS at LKAB 50% reduction of CO₂ emissions; full system costs from €56/t and up Kushnir et al. 2020, p. 1, citing Quader et al. 2015; Leeson et al. 2017
Onshore CO₂ storage in saline aquifers €4 / t CO₂ Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8816, footnote 15 (citing IEA-GHG)
Offshore CO₂ storage €8 / t CO₂ Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8816, footnote 15
CO₂ emission allowance price (assumed 2030) €31 / t CO₂ Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8812
Industrial capture rates 50–95% (cement); 60–90% (varied processes) Raillard-Cazanove 2024, pp. 8, 10

Notes — divergence in cost estimates. Reported costs reflect different scopes: Kushnir 2020 gives a sectoral steelmaking estimate (system cost from €56/t up) for the ULCOS + LKAB programme; Baufumé 2011 reports geological-storage tariffs (€4–8/t CO₂) plus an emission-allowance price (€31/t CO₂); Raillard 2024 reports capture-rate ranges across multiple industries (50–95%) without per-tonne cost figures. The terminology drift between CCS and CCUS reflects extension of scope from storage-only to also include utilisation of captured CO₂.

Related terms. Pre-combustion capture; post-combustion capture; oxyfuel; Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle; Natural Gas Combined Cycle; steam methane reforming; coal gasification; depleted gas field; saline aquifer; storage complex.

Cross-source comparison — CCS / CCUS costs and deployment metrics.

Source Metric Value Year
Baufumé et al. 2011 Onshore CO₂ storage in saline aquifers €4 / t CO₂ 2011 (IEA-GHG)
Baufumé et al. 2011 Offshore CO₂ storage €8 / t CO₂ 2011
Baufumé et al. 2011 CO₂ allowance assumed for 2030 €31 / t CO₂ 2011 assumption
Kushnir et al. 2020 ULCOS test-furnace + CCS at LKAB from €56 / t CO₂ system cost 2020 ref
Raillard-Cazanove 2024 Industrial capture rates (cement) 50–95% 2024
Raillard-Cazanove 2024 Industrial capture rates (varied) 60–90% 2024

IEA Financing CCUS 2026 Annual CCUS investment >USD 5 billion (2025) 2025 (15-fold growth since 2020)

IEA Financing CCUS 2026 Operational track record 70+ large-scale capture facilities; 9,000+ km CO₂ pipelines 2026
