(Compiled from Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8816; Kushnir et al. 2020, p. 1; Raillard-Cazanove 2024, pp. 8, 10; Grimaud and Girard 2024, p. 28; IEA Financing CCUS 2026, pp. 7–8, 26–28, 52–53; IEA ETP 2026, p. 16.)

Notes — convergence on cost and progress. The five sources span the 2011–2026 evolution from pioneer cost-curve estimation (Baufumé 2011 — €4–8/t storage; €31/t allowance) through industry-decarbonisation cost ranges (Raillard 2024; Grimaud 2024) to financing-side metrics (IEA Financing CCUS 2026 and ETP 2026 — multi-billion debt deals). Cost dispersion mirrors scope: €4–8/t for pure storage, €56–170/t for industrial-process CCS systems, and US $94–232/t for DAC-with-storage (the latter reported in the Direct air capture entry). Industrial capture rates cluster at 60–95% across sectors (cement, steel, chemicals).

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — listed in Pending 2026-05-07 (mentioned but not defined). - Kushnir et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-07: ULCOS+CCS reference and cost estimate from steelmaking context. - Baufumé et al. 2011 — added 2026-05-07: functional definition, capture-pathway breakdown, geological-storage cost data. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: CCUS terminology drift, industrial capture-rate ranges. - Grimaud and Girard 2024 — added 2026-05-08 (round 4 cross-ref): cracker-CCS CAPEX and cost. - IEA Financing CCUS 2026 — added 2026-05-08 (round 4 cross-ref): financing metrics and pipeline operating record. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08 (round 4 cross-ref): UK landmark deals and RAB support.

Carbon leakage

Aliases. Leakage; emissions leakage; competitiveness leakage; pollution-haven effect.

Definition. The phenomenon in which carbon-pricing or other emissions-regulation in one jurisdiction causes industrial production (and its associated emissions) to relocate to less-regulated jurisdictions, partially or fully offsetting the domestic emissions reductions. Carbon leakage thus undermines the climate effectiveness of unilateral carbon pricing while damaging the competitiveness of the regulating jurisdiction’s trade-exposed industries. Two principal channels: (i) operational leakage — production shifts to existing facilities abroad; (ii) investment leakage — new capacity is built abroad rather than in the regulated jurisdiction. (Johnson et al. 2025, p. 1; cross-ref EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), CBAM)

Attributes — leakage rate quantification.

Sector Estimated leakage rate (literature)
Cement 30–70% (very high — bulky, low value-add)
Steel 20–50%
Aluminium 50–70%
Chemicals (basic) 20–40%
Refining 20–30%
Paper / pulp 10–25%
Glass 20–40%
EU sectors not on ETS typically <5%

(Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 1, 2; literature meta-analyses)

Notes — policy responses. The EU has historically addressed leakage via free allocation of EU ETS allowances to trade-exposed industries (since 2005), giving them effectively zero net carbon cost on existing production. The 2024 EU ETS revision phases out free allocation gradually 2026–2034 in concert with the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) phase-in. Together, free-allocation phase-out + CBAM are designed to maintain leakage protection while eliminating the cost-effectiveness penalty of free allocation. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 1–2)

Notes — Johnson 2025 modelling finding. Johnson finds that the CBAM is fully effective at protecting EU industry against operational and investment leakage in steelmaking through 2035, if the CBAM scope is extended to include scope-2 (electricity) emissions. With scope-1-only CBAM, EU green-steel investment is at competitive disadvantage with low-grid-emission third-country imports because EU electricity is partially fossil-derived even after climate policy. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 5–7)

Related terms. Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM); EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); EU ETS 2024 revisions; H2-DRI-EAF route; deep reindustrialisation; abatement cost; marginal abatement cost (MAC).

Source history. - Johnson et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, leakage-rate empirical estimates, policy responses, scope-1-vs-2 CBAM finding.

Carbon lock-in

Aliases. Lock-in; technological lock-in; institutional lock-in; carbon lock-in (Unruh); fossil-fuel lock-in.

Definition. A concept from sociology of technology and political economy (Unruh 2000), describing how fossil-fuel-based technological systems become entrenched through self-reinforcing positive feedbacks between technologies, institutions, organisations, knowledge, finance, and consumer behaviour — creating a path-dependent system that resists transformative low-carbon alternatives even when those alternatives are technically and economically competitive. Carbon lock-in operates at multiple scales: device-level (sunk-cost ICE vehicles), infrastructure-level (gas-distribution networks, oil pipelines), industry-level (petrochemical clusters), institutional-level (subsidies, regulations, education systems), and cultural-level (consumer expectations, employment dependencies). (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 607–610, citing Unruh 2000)

Attributes — five classic carbon-lock-in dimensions.

Dimension Description Examples
Technological sunk-cost in fossil-tech infrastructure + supply chains gas grid, ICE engines, refineries
Institutional / regulatory rules, taxes, building codes designed for fossil systems gasoline taxes, fossil-fuel subsidies
Organisational firms organised around fossil-fuel value chains oil majors, utility monopolies
Knowledge / education curricula + R&D pipelines aligned to fossil paradigms petroleum-engineering departments
Financial banks, insurers, pension funds invested in fossil assets pension-fund energy holdings

(Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 608; Unruh 2000)

Notes — escape mechanisms. Lock-in literature identifies several unlocking mechanisms: (i) disruptive technologies (solar PV cost decline disrupted incumbent power-plant economics); (ii) crisis events (Fukushima → German nuclear phase-out); (iii) policy windows (Paris Agreement creating CBAM legitimacy); (iv) generational change in incumbent firms (Ørsted’s transformation from coal/gas to wind); (v) institutional creative destruction (1973 oil crisis → French nuclear program). Successful unlocking is rare and depends on aligning multiple conditions. (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 611–612)

Notes — petrochemical-specific intensity. Petrochemical lock-in (Tilsted) is especially deep because the same fossil molecules are used as both fuel and feedstock — making the alternative-feedstock transition harder than the energy-system transition (which only needs to substitute energy carriers). (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 608–610; cross-ref Petrochemical lock-ins entry)

Related terms. Petrochemical lock-ins / political economy; Just transition; deep reindustrialisation; stranded assets; planetary boundaries; political economy.

Source history. - Tilsted et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: definition, five-dimension framework, unlocking mechanisms, petrochemical-specific intensity.

Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) — as hydrogen storage medium

Definition. Graphite sheets rolled up into a cylindrical shape, used as a physisorption hydrogen-storage material. Adsorption capacity depends on pore size and curvature of the tubes; the rolling direction influences mechanical, electrical and thermal properties. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 30, citing Mohan et al. 2019)

Attributes.

Configuration Capacity / conditions
Multi-walled CNTs gravimetric storage 7.75 wt%; volumetric 0.209 kg H₂/L at room temperature, 650 atm
Single-walled CNT (1300 m²/g) 3.0 mass% adsorbed at 77 K
Multi-walled BN nano-tubes 1.8–2.6 mass% at ~10 MPa, room temperature

(AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 30, citing Lyu/Kudiarov; Utsumi/Kaneko 2011; Ma et al. 2004)

Notes. CNTs are dominated by van der Waals forces with binding strength below 10 kJ/mol; valued for high mass density, high surface area and chemical stability. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 30)

Related terms. Physisorption; hydrogen storage; metal-organic frameworks.

Source history. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, capacities, structural notes.

Carbon contract for difference (CCfD)

Aliases. CCfD; CO₂ contract for difference.

Definition. A government-backed risk-sharing instrument in which a counterparty (typically a state-owned vehicle or grid manager) pays the project developer the difference between a fixed strike price (set per tonne of CO₂ abated or per MWh of low-emissions output) and the prevailing market reference price (e.g. the EU ETS allowance price). CCfDs reduce revenue uncertainty by making project cash flows largely independent of carbon-price volatility, and have been instrumental in reaching FIDs for major European CCUS projects. (IEA 2026, pp. 18, 26, 43)

Attributes — adoption by jurisdiction.

Jurisdiction Status / vehicle
United Kingdom Track-1 CCUS programme; 15-year Dispatchable Power Agreement
Netherlands SDE++ scheme covers gap between capture cost and EU ETS price
Sweden Reverse-auction carbon-removal contracts (BECCS Stockholm)
Canada Canada Growth Fund — 15-year carbon-credit offtake (Glacier project)
Germany CCfD-type Klimaschutzverträge auctions for industry
Japan Long-Term Decarbonized Power Source Auction (CCfD for power CCUS)

(IEA 2026, pp. 26, 38, 43, 48)

Notes. CCfDs are now being adapted for CCUS in several jurisdictions, with reverse-auction variants being especially important for BECCS and DAC where reference prices for carbon removals are nascent. The IEA distinguishes “two-sided” CCfDs (where the developer pays back when the carbon price exceeds the strike) from “one-sided” CfDs that resemble subsidies. (IEA 2026, pp. 26, 43)

Related terms. EU Emissions Trading System; bankability; regulated asset base (RAB); reverse auction; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF).

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, jurisdictional table, role in European FIDs.

Carbon dioxide removal (CDR)

Aliases. Negative emissions technologies; greenhouse gas removal.

Definition. A portfolio of technologies and natural-system practices that remove CO₂ from the atmosphere and store it durably, distinguished from emissions abatement by their net-negative carbon flux. Khalili et al. divide CDR into natural climate solutions (NCS — afforestation/reforestation, soil carbon sequestration, etc.) and technical solutions (BECCS, DACCS, biochar, enhanced weathering, desalination-based afforestation). (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 8–9; IEA 2026, p. 17)

Attributes — coverage in the 100% RE systems database.

CDR option Studies (n=1067) Share
BECCS 11 1.0%
DACCS 7 0.7%
NCS / agriculture, forestry 1 0.1%
Other (enhanced weathering, biochar, soil C, CCUS materials) 0 not yet covered

(Khalili et al. 2026, p. 16, citing the database review)

Notes — financing context. From the IEA (2026) financier perspective, CDR projects can earn voluntary-market removal credits at premium prices (DAC ~US $500/t CO₂ on voluntary markets historically) which combined with policy supports such as the 45Q tax credit (US $180/t for DACS, US $85/t for BECCS) materially improve project economics; however, mid-sized projects (USD 10–100 m) face a “missing middle” financing gap between venture-capital-funded pilots and bankable large-scale facilities. (IEA 2026, pp. 40–41)

Notes — stabilisation requirement. Studies on rebalancing within planetary climate boundaries imply massive net-negative CO₂ emissions on the order of 40 Gt CO₂/y by end-of-century to return atmospheric CO₂ to ~350 ppm. (Khalili et al. 2026, p. 16)

Related terms. Direct air capture (DAC); direct air carbon capture and sequestration (DACCS); bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS); natural climate solutions (NCS); 45Q tax credit; carbon contract for difference (CCfD).

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, taxonomy, coverage in database, climate-stabilisation context. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: financing dynamics and missing-middle gap.

Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA)

Definition. An ICAO market-based mechanism launched in 2016, requiring aircraft operators with annual emissions greater than 10,000 t CO₂ (and aircraft above 5,700 kg maximum certified take-off mass) to monitor, report and offset CO₂ emissions exceeding a defined baseline through the purchase of certified carbon offsets via the Aviation Carbon Exchange (ACE). The scheme is the first economic-sector-wide global, universal and binding system to control GHG emissions from international flights and aims to achieve carbon-neutral growth (CNG2020 target) for international aviation. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 1, 26–27)

Attributes — implementation phases.

Phase Years Status
Pilot phase 2021–2023 81 states volunteered (≈76% of international RTK)
First phase 2024–2026 Voluntary participation
Second phase 2027–2035 Legally binding for ICAO members (with exceptions for least-developed and small states)

(Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 27)

Notes. Year 2019 is the baseline for the pilot phase (originally proposed as an average of 2019–2020, revised due to the COVID-19 impact). CORSIA Eligible Fuels are biofuels meeting CORSIA sustainability criteria; default life-cycle GHG values are published for five biomass-based pathways (LCA-based, with 87.5 g CO₂e MJ⁻¹ as the fossil-kerosene baseline). Default values for “lower carbon aviation fuels” (electrofuels) and the CHJ pathway had not been announced at the time of writing. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 27, 18)

Related terms. EU Emissions Trading System; ReFuelEU Aviation; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, phasing, baseline and CORSIA Eligible Fuels framework.

Catalytic hydrothermolysis jet (CHJ)

Definition. A biofuel pathway based on high-temperature water chemistry (hydrothermal processes), converting oil-based feedstock (vegetable oils, oleochemical wastes, brown grease) into a mixture of straight, branched and cyclic hydrocarbons. The four steps are: hydrothermal pre-conditioning, catalytic hydrothermolysis (CH), hydrotreatment and product fractionation. The kerosene product is denoted CHJ-SK and was certified by ASTM in 2020. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 10–11)

Attributes — operating conditions.

Stage Temperature Pressure
Pre-conditioning 150–300 °C (423–573 K) 5–50 bar (0.5–5 MPa)
Catalytic hydrothermolysis (CH) unit 240–450 °C (513–723 K) 15–250 bar (1.5–25 MPa)

(Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 11)

Notes. The CH unit’s organic phase (“CHJ bio-crude”) is decarboxylated, hydrogenated and distilled into naphtha, kerosene (CHJ-SK) and diesel; aviation biofuels obtained by this process contain high-density aromatics, iso-paraffins and cyclo-paraffins. CHJ-SK is one of the synthetic kerosene types (SK) close in composition to fossil kerosene, supporting use without blending. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 11, 30)

Related terms. Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL); HEFA pathway; synthetic kerosene (SK); sustainable aviation fuels (SAF).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, operating conditions, ASTM certification status.

Catalytic cracking (FCC)

Aliases. Fluid catalytic cracking; FCC; cat cracking.

Definition. A petroleum-refining process in which heavy hydrocarbon feedstocks (vacuum gas oil, residue) are converted at 480–540 °C and near-atmospheric pressure over a fluidised bed of acidic zeolite catalyst into lighter, higher-value products: gasoline-range naphtha, light olefins (propylene), C4 olefins, and refinery LPG. Unlike steam cracking (which targets ethylene/propylene from naphtha + steam), FCC operates on heavier feedstocks and primarily targets transport fuels with olefins as a high-value co-product. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3; Zhang et al. 2024, Fig. 2)

Attributes — typical product yields and conditions.

Indicator Value
Reactor temperature 480–540 °C
Reactor pressure ~1.5–3 bar
Catalyst Y-zeolite + matrix; rare-earth modified
Riser residence time 2–4 s
Catalyst-to-oil ratio 4–10
Typical yield (gasoline) 40–55 wt%
Typical yield (LPG, incl. propylene) 15–25 wt%
Typical yield (light olefins) 5–10 wt% (depending on operation)
Typical yield (LCO + slurry) 15–25 wt%
FCC propylene global share ~30% of global propylene supply
Coke yield (combusted in regenerator) 4–6 wt%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3, Tables; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727)

Notes — FCC as olefin source. Levi & Cullen find that ~40% of global olefins (propylene + butadiene) are sourced from refinery FCC and catalytic-reformer streams rather than from steam crackers. FCC is the largest single refinery contributor to the petrochemical olefin pool. High-severity FCC variants (e.g., DCC, PetroFCC) push propylene yield from ~5% to ~20% by raising temperature and modifying catalyst. (Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Notes — coke balance and energy. Coke deposited on the catalyst is burned in the regenerator at ~700 °C, providing the heat for the endothermic cracking reactions. The energy balance is essentially closed (auto-thermal). FCC units are operated continuously for 3–5 years between turnarounds. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Related terms. Steam cracking (vapocracking); catalytic reforming; hydrocracking; naphtha; pyrolysis gasoline (pygas); propylene; high-value chemicals (HVCs); BTX aromatics.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, conditions, yields, energy balance. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 40% global olefin share from refinery streams. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: FCC’s role in current vs future petrochemical architecture.

Catalytic reforming

Aliases. Cat reforming; platinum reforming; reformer.

Definition. A petroleum-refining process in which low-octane straight-run naphtha is converted at 480–525 °C and 5–25 bar over a bifunctional Pt/Re or Pt/Sn catalyst on chlorinated alumina into a high-octane reformate stream rich in aromatic hydrocarbons (BTX) plus hydrogen as a co-product. The principal reactions are dehydrogenation of cyclohexanes to aromatics, dehydrocyclisation of paraffins, and isomerisation of n-paraffins to iso-paraffins. Catalytic reforming is the dominant non-cracker source of BTX aromatics globally and a major refinery hydrogen source. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3 and Chapter 6.5; Zhang et al. 2024, Fig. 2)

Attributes — typical operating envelope.

Indicator Value
Reactor temperature 480–525 °C
Reactor pressure 5–25 bar (semi-regen → continuous regen lower-end)
Catalyst Pt-Re or Pt-Sn on Cl-Al₂O₃
H₂/HC molar ratio 3–8
Typical reformate yield 80–85 wt%
Typical reformate aromatic content 60–70%
H₂ co-production 2–3 wt% of feed; ~1,500–2,000 Nm³/t feed
Octane improvement RON +20–40
Global BTX share from reforming ~40% (vs ~57% from steam crackers)

(Speight 2019, Chapters 4.3, 6.5; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Notes — refinery hydrogen role. Catalytic reformers are the largest refinery hydrogen producers, supplying H₂ that is consumed downstream in hydrotreating (sulphur removal) and hydrocracking. As refineries adopt heavier and sourer feeds, hydrogen demand rises, and reformer hydrogen is increasingly supplemented by SMR units. In a defossilised future, green H₂ from electrolysis can replace this supplementary SMR. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Notes — continuous catalyst regeneration (CCR). Modern reformers use continuous catalyst regeneration (CCR), which moves catalyst between reactor stages and a regenerator continuously, allowing operation at lower pressure and higher selectivity to aromatics. Older “semi-regenerative” units regenerate catalyst on a 6–24 month cycle. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Related terms. Catalytic cracking (FCC); steam cracking (vapocracking); BTX aromatics; naphtha; pyrolysis gasoline (pygas); steam methane reforming (SMR); hydrocracking; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, conditions, catalyst, yields, hydrogen co-production. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: ~40% BTX share from reforming. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: role in 1950s–1960s petrochemical industry development.

Cathodic protection (CP)

Definition. A pipeline corrosion-control system, in use on steel pipelines since the 1930s, in which sacrificial metal anodes are connected near the pipeline to counteract the natural electrical current that flows from a steel pipe to the surrounding soil. Applicable to steel pipelines irrespective of whether the pipe transports natural gas or hydrogen. (Khan et al. 2021, p. 5)

Notes. Cathodic protection is one of three common corrosion-control methods for pipelines (alongside pipeline coatings and corrosion inhibitors). For US natural-gas transmission pipelines, ~96% are wrapped/coated and cathodically protected. For hydrogen service, additional R&D is underway to develop specialty internal coatings minimising hydrogen embrittlement; common external coatings remain fusion-bonded epoxy (FBE) and polyethylene heat-shrink sleeves, with older pipelines using coal-tar enamel wrap. (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 5–6)

Related terms. Hydrogen pipeline; hydrogen embrittlement; hydrogen-natural gas blending; pipeline coatings.

Source history. - Khan et al. 2021 — added 2026-05-08: definition, integration with coatings/inhibitors, prevalence on US gas pipelines.

Cetane number

Aliases. CN; cetane index; CCI (calculated cetane index); diesel ignition quality.

Definition. A standardised measure of a diesel fuel’s ignition quality under compression-ignition conditions — i.e. how readily the fuel auto-ignites once injected into the hot compressed air in a diesel engine cylinder. Higher cetane = shorter ignition delay = smoother combustion = lower NOₓ emissions and reduced engine knock. The cetane scale uses cetane (n-hexadecane, CN = 100, ignites readily) and 1-methylnaphthalene (CN = 0, ignites poorly) as reference compounds. The Calculated Cetane Index (CCI) is a refinery-blend-property estimate from API gravity and mid-boiling temperature, used when actual cetane testing is not feasible. (Addicott 1971; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Attributes — typical cetane values.

Fuel Cetane number
n-hexadecane (cetane reference) 100
1-methylnaphthalene (reference) 0
Premium ULSD (EU EN 590) 51 minimum
Standard US diesel (ASTM D975) 40 minimum
Hydrocracker diesel 50–60
FCC light cycle oil (raw) 18–25 (poor diesel blendstock)
GTL / biodiesel (FAME) 55–75
HVO (renewable diesel) 70–90
Gasoline ~−20 (deliberately low)

(Addicott 1971, p. 67; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Notes — vs octane (opposite scales). Cetane and octane measure opposite combustion behaviours: high octane = resistance to autoignition (good for spark-ignition engines); high cetane = readiness for autoignition (good for compression-ignition diesel engines). A high-cetane fuel is a low-octane fuel and vice versa. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Related terms. Octane number (RON / MON); knock; motor fuels (umbrella); diesel fuel; ULSD (ultra-low-sulfur-diesel); HVO (renewable diesel); HEFA pathway.

Source history. - Addicott 1971 — added 2026-05-08: definition, scale, vs octane. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): typical CN values across fuel grades.

Chemical hydrides

Definition. Hydrogen-storage materials in which the hydrogen absorption process occurs in a host material (water-based or solid). Chemical hydrides can be solid or liquid with storage capacities of 6–8 wt% and higher energy densities than metal hydrides at mild operating temperatures. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 31, citing Staubitz et al. 2010)

Attributes (AlZohbi et al. 2023, Table 1, pp. 32–33).

Property Value
Hydrogen content 6–8 wt%
Volumetric energy density up to 150 kg/m³ (e.g. Mg₂FeH₆)
Advantages good volumetric density
Drawbacks thermal management needed; off-board regeneration required

Notes. Common chemical hydrides include borohydrides and ammonia borane. The drawback is that activation energies for absorption exceed the energy provided by hydrogen pressure, so hydrogenation is performed independently and the dehydrogenation reaction is irreversible on-board, making chemical hydrides more convenient for one-time use than reversible metal-hydride absorption/desorption. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 31)

Related terms. Metal hydrides; chemisorption; liquid organic hydrogen carriers; ammonia.

Source history. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, capacity, on-board reversibility constraint.

Chemical looping (umbrella)

Aliases. Chemical looping technologies; CLC / CLR / CL-ODH / ROC umbrella; oxygen-carrier-mediated processes.

Definition. A family of process-intensification technologies in which a circulating oxygen carrier (typically a metal-oxide particle: Fe₂O₃, NiO, CuO, Mn₃O₄, perovskites) shuttles oxygen between two physically-separated reactors — a fuel reactor (where the metal oxide is reduced by reaction with fuel/feedstock, releasing the desired product) and an air reactor (where the reduced metal is re-oxidised by air, releasing heat). Chemical looping eliminates direct gas-phase contact between fuel and air, with the consequences: (i) intrinsic CO₂ separation in the fuel-reactor outlet (no N₂ dilution); (ii) no NOₓ formation; (iii) no air-separation unit needed; (iv) tighter temperature control via solids circulation. Originally developed for combustion (CLC) but now extended to reforming (CLR), oxidative dehydrogenation (CL-ODH), oxy-cracking (ROC), gasification, and steam-reforming. (Haribal et al. 2018, pp. 714–715; cross-ref Redox oxy-cracking (ROC) entry)

Attributes — major chemical-looping process variants.

Variant Application Status (TRL)
Chemical-Looping Combustion (CLC) power generation with intrinsic CO₂ capture 6–7 (1 MW pilot demonstrated)
Chemical-Looping Reforming (CLR) H₂ production from natural gas with capture 5–6
Chemical-Looping Oxidative Dehydrogenation (CL-ODH) ethylene from ethane 4–5 (lab-to-pilot)
Redox Oxy-Cracking (ROC) ethylene from naphtha (Haribal 2018) 4 (lab + simulation)
Chemical-Looping Air Separation (CLAS) O₂ production from air 4
Chemical-Looping Steam Methane Reforming SMR with intrinsic capture 5

(Haribal et al. 2018, pp. 714–715; literature)

Notes — significance for industrial decarbonisation. Chemical looping is identified by IEA, IPCC and major corporates (Sasol, ExxonMobil, ARC) as a candidate technology for deep decarbonisation of high-temperature industrial heat and feedstock conversion, with intrinsic CO₂ capture as the strategic advantage over conventional combustion + post-combustion capture. The principal challenge is oxygen-carrier durability over 1,000s of redox cycles and oxygen-carrier mechanical attrition in fluidised-bed circulation. (Haribal et al. 2018, p. 715)

Related terms. Redox oxy-cracking (ROC); oxidative dehydrogenation (ODH); steam methane reforming (SMR); carbon capture and storage (CCS); near-zero emissions materials; oxygen carrier; high-value chemicals (HVCs); ethylene; methanol synthesis.

Source history. - Haribal et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: chemical-looping family taxonomy, ROC as one variant, decarbonisation significance.

Oxygen carrier (chemical looping)

Aliases. Oxygen-storage material; redox-active material; metal-oxide carrier; OC particle.

Definition. A solid metal-oxide material that can repeatedly cycle between a fully oxidised state (donating lattice oxygen to a reaction) and a reduced state (accepting oxygen back from air) without irreversible degradation. Oxygen carriers are the central enabling material of chemical-looping processes — fluidised between fuel-reactor and air-reactor, they shuttle oxygen between the two zones at controllable temperature and rate. Performance metrics are: (i) oxygen-carrying capacity (g O₂ / kg carrier), (ii) reduction-rate kinetics, (iii) re-oxidation kinetics, (iv) attrition resistance (mechanical durability over 1,000s of cycles), (v) sintering resistance at high T, (vi) cost. (Haribal et al. 2018, pp. 715–717)

Attributes — common oxygen carriers.

Material Redox couple O-carrying capacity Comment
Mn₃O₄ / MnO Mn(III/II) ~7 wt% Haribal 2018 ROC reference (alkali-doped Ca-Mn-O)
Fe₂O₃ / Fe₃O₄ / FeO / Fe Fe(III/II/0) up to ~30 wt% high capacity but low T-stability
NiO / Ni Ni(II/0) ~22 wt% high reactivity but Ni cost + toxicity
CuO / Cu₂O / Cu Cu(II/I/0) ~20 wt% exothermic reduction (advantage in CLOU)
CaSO₄ / CaS sulfate / sulfide ~47 wt% very high capacity but kinetically slow
Perovskites (LaMnO₃, LaFeO₃) flexible non-stoichiometry ~4 wt% tunable redox properties
Ilmenite (FeTiO₃) Fe(III/II) ~4 wt% low cost, naturally occurring

(Haribal et al. 2018, pp. 715–716; CLC literature)

Notes — Haribal Ca-Mn-K oxide. The ROC oxygen carrier reported by Haribal et al. 2018 (alkali-doped Ca-Mn-K mixed oxide) achieves 79% n-hexane conversion with 61% light-olefin selectivity in lab tests, with >100 redox cycles demonstrated. The alkali doping enhances the selectivity for hydrogen combustion (preferred) over hydrocarbon over-oxidation (undesired), making the carrier suitable for selective oxy-cracking. (Haribal et al. 2018, p. 717)

Related terms. Chemical looping (umbrella); redox oxy-cracking (ROC); oxidative dehydrogenation (ODH); carbon capture and storage (CCS); high-value chemicals (HVCs); ethylene.

Source history. - Haribal et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, performance metrics, common-carrier table, Ca-Mn-K specifics.

Chemical recycling

Definition. An umbrella term for plastic recycling processes that decompose long polymer chains back to monomers or to a hydrocarbon mixture (which can be re-polymerised), as opposed to mechanical recycling which preserves the polymer chain. Two main mechanisms: (i) depolymerisation (chemolysis) by reaction with a chemical agent (methanolysis, glycolysis, hydrolysis, aminolysis); (ii) thermochemical recycling by heating with or without oxygen (pyrolysis, gasification, hydrocracking, plasma routes). (Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 23–25)

Attributes — comparative table of routes.

Route Typical T TRL Strength Limitation
Chemolysis (glycolysis, methanolysis, hydrolysis) 180–280 °C 9 Already integrated; low energy input Only for homogeneous PET, PU, PC; high cost
Pyrolysis 300–700 °C 9 Flexible; suits hard-to-depolymerise plastics High energy; low PVC tolerance
Gasification 700–1200 °C 9 Suits mixed plastic waste Char/tar by-products; energy-intensive
Hydrocracking 375–500 °C 7 High product quality High H₂ cost; PVC poisoning
Plasma gasification 1200–1500 °C 8 Tolerant to feedstock variability Very high electricity demand
Microwave-assisted pyrolysis up to 1000 °C 4 Uniform heating; rapid Diverse waste dielectric properties
Catalytic cracking 400–450 °C 8 Lower T, fast reaction Catalyst sensitivity, deactivation

(Grimaud and Girard 2024, p. 25, Fig. 23)

Notes — European projects (early 2022). ~1.5 Mt/y announced chemical-recycling capacity for non-sorted plastic waste, dominated by pyrolysis. Country distribution: France 720 kt/y (13 projects); Spain 503 kt/y (5); Finland 440 kt/y (2); Germany 382 kt/y (7); Netherlands 252 kt/y (8); Austria 200 kt/y (1). Plastic chemical recycling produces virgin-quality monomer feedstock but typically incurs material losses of >50% and significant energy penalties, alongside technical difficulties. (Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 19, 25, Fig. 22)

Related terms. Mechanical recycling; solvolysis; pyrolysis (PL); gasification; methanol-to-olefins (MTO); steam cracking; plastic chemicals.

Source history. - Grimaud and Girard 2024 — added 2026-05-08: umbrella definition, comparative routes, European deployment status (translated from French).

Chemicals of concern (plastic chemicals)

Definition. Plastic chemicals classified as hazardous on the basis of one or more of four broad criteria — persistence (P), bioaccumulation (B), mobility (M) and toxicity (T) — using a hazard-based approach drawing on 15 regulatory sources aligned with the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling and the EU Classification, Labelling and Packaging (CLP) regulation. Of 16,325 known plastic chemicals in the PlastChem inventory, 4,219 (≈26%) are identified as chemicals of concern. (Monclús et al. 2025, pp. 350–351)

Attributes — combined hazard categories among chemicals of concern.

Category Number Description
PBT (persistent, bioaccumulative, toxic) 56 Three criteria fulfilled
PMT (persistent, mobile, toxic) 98 Three criteria fulfilled
vPvB (very persistent, very bioaccumulative) 47 Stockholm Convention category
vPvM (very persistent, very mobile) 97 EU CLP category
POP (persistent organic pollutant) 179 Stockholm Convention listed
EDC (endocrine-disrupting chemical) 47 Toxicity criterion
CMR (carcinogenic, mutagenic, reprotoxic) 1,489 Toxicity criterion
STOT (specific target organ toxicity) 1,774 Toxicity criterion
Aquatic toxicity 2,760 Toxicity criterion

(Monclús et al. 2025, Fig. 2, p. 351)

Notes. Only 6% of plastic chemicals (980) are globally regulated under the Basel, Stockholm and Minamata Conventions, and the Montreal Protocol; 568 of the 4,219 chemicals of concern are covered by these multilateral agreements, leaving 3,651 (≈87%) unregulated globally. National regulations cover an additional 1,021 chemicals. 1,322 known chemicals of concern are marketed for use in plastics manufacturing; 850 have empirical evidence of presence in plastics and 508 of release. The hazard-based approach is described as conservative; 10,726 plastic chemicals (66%) lack official hazard classifications by regulatory agencies or industry. (Monclús et al. 2025, pp. 351–353)

Related terms. Plastic chemicals; PlastChem inventory; per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS); bisphenol A (BPA); UVCB substances; non-intentionally added substances (NIAS); essential use concept.

Source history. - Monclús et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-07: definition, hazard categories, regulatory coverage.

Chemisorption (hydrogen storage)

Definition. A material-based hydrogen-storage method in which hydrogen is robustly attached within molecular structures by chemical bonding (as distinct from physisorption, which uses adsorption forces). Chemisorption materials include metallic and chemical hydrides, ammonia and liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHCs). (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 31, citing Makowski et al. 2009)

Notes. Chemisorption offers the highest volumetric energy density among hydrogen-storage technologies but is costly and requires high operating temperatures. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 31)

Related terms. Physisorption; metal hydrides; chemical hydrides; ammonia; liquid organic hydrogen carriers; hydrogen storage.

Source history. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition and trade-off note.

Climate risk in power-system planning

Aliases. Risque climatique systémique; weather-year stress test; canicule / sécheresse / grand froid sensitivity.

Definition. The exposure of a power system to weather-driven shocks affecting (i) demand (heating peaks during cold spells; cooling peaks during heat waves), (ii) generation availability (river-cooled thermal plants in droughts; PV in heat waves; wind in stagnation events; hydropower in droughts), and (iii) network operations. Climate risk is increasingly integrated into long-term planning via stress tests — projecting the system response under specific anomalous-weather scenarios derived from historical events and climate-change projections. (RTE 2022, Sections 8.2–8.4, translated from French)

Attributes — RTE 2022 stress tests.

Stress test Scenario Magnitude Implication
#1 — Anticyclone winter “vague de froid” Cold spell + low wind for 5–10 days +20 GW peak demand vs typical winter; residual load near total load Capacity adequacy hit
#2 — Heat wave “canicule” Extreme heatwave (Aug 2003 / July 2019 type) Up to 6 GW (~10% of fleet) of nuclear unavailable due to river-cooling limits Production capacity hit
#3 — Drought “sécheresse” Severe multi-year drought Hydropower CF drops 20–30%; thermal cooling restricted Annual energy reduction
#4 — Combined “grand froid + low wind/PV” Compound event Several GW deficit possible if no adequate flexibility Highest-stress event
#5 — Compound canicule + drought (Aug 2003 type) Nuclear unavailability + low hydro + high cooling demand Highest summer-stress event

(RTE 2022, Sections 8.4.1–8.4.4, pp. 410–414, translated)

Notes — quantified historical reference. During the July 2019 heatwave, simultaneous unavailability of French nuclear units due to river-cooling restrictions reached ~6 GW (~10% of installed nuclear capacity), concentrated on 4 of the 18 fleet sites with river-cooled tranches. RTE projects this risk to increase under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 climate trajectories; the share of fleet affected can rise to a higher percentage by 2050. New EPR2 reactors will be specified for higher-temperature cooling tolerance. (RTE 2022, Sections 8.3.3.2–8.3.3.3, pp. 411–413)

Notes — interaction with renewable generation. RTE finds that wind and solar PV output are largely insensitive to mean climate change to 2050 (no consensus in IPCC scenarios; magnitudes within natural inter-annual variability). The principal climate risk is therefore on the thermal-fleet availability side, not on the RES-supply side. This makes the risk worse in N-scenarios (which keep more thermal capacity) than in pure-RES scenarios. (RTE 2022, Sections 8.3.4.1–8.3.4.2, pp. 416, 418)

Notes — heating demand. Climate change reduces winter peak demand (CDD/HDD shift) by ~10–15 TWh/yr by 2050 (vs +5–10 TWh/yr extra summer cooling). Net demand impact is slightly negative but small. (RTE 2022, Section 8.3.1, p. 408 area)

Related terms. Capacity adequacy; Loss of Load Expectation (LoLE); Cooling and Heating degree days (CDD / HDD); Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); Hydropower; Nuclear power; Power system flexibility; Stress test (RTE).

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, five stress tests (cold spell / canicule / drought / compound), 6 GW July-2019 historical loss, RCP4.5/8.5 implications, asymmetric risk on thermal vs RES (translated from French).

Chlor-alkali process

Aliases. Chlor-alkali; sodium chloride electrolysis; mercury / diaphragm / membrane cell.

Definition. The electrolysis of brine (saturated aqueous NaCl) in an electrolyser cell to co-produce chlorine gas (Cl₂) at the anode, hydrogen gas (H₂) at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide (NaOH, “caustic soda”) in solution: 2 NaCl + 2 H₂O → Cl₂ + H₂ + 2 NaOH. The process operates at ~3–5 V cell voltage and ~3,000 A/m² typical current density. Three historical cell technologies: mercury cell (legacy, banned in EU since 2017 due to mercury emissions), diaphragm cell (asbestos-free since the 1990s), and ion-exchange membrane cell (modern, dominant since the 1990s — most efficient and cleanest). (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Attributes — production and product split.

Indicator Value
Global Cl₂ production ~85 Mt/yr
Global NaOH production ~95 Mt/yr (co-product, slightly higher Mt as more NaOH made per Cl)
Global H₂ co-production ~3 Mt/yr (often used as fuel; sometimes upgraded to industrial H₂)
Largest Cl₂ end-use — VCM/PVC ~30%
Other Cl₂ end-uses water treatment, isocyanates (TDI/MDI), epichlorohydrin, solvents, bleach
Largest NaOH end-use pulp & paper, alumina (Bayer process), soaps, detergents, chemical synthesis
Membrane-cell electricity demand ~2,200 kWh / t Cl₂
Mercury / diaphragm-cell demand ~3,000–3,500 kWh / t Cl₂

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2)

Notes — by-product hydrogen. Chlor-alkali generates ~28 kg H₂ per t Cl₂, totalling ~3 Mt H₂/yr globally — a significant industrial-H₂ source often vented or burned for process heat. Capturing and upgrading this H₂ to fuel-cell grade is a low-cost industrial-H₂ supply lever. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2)

Notes — Cl₂ / NaOH co-product economics. The Cl₂ and NaOH markets are coupled by the chlor-alkali process — when one demand grows faster, the other floods the market. The “ECU” (electrochemical unit) is the standard tradable bundle of 1 t Cl₂ + 1.13 t NaOH + ~28 kg H₂. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2)

Related terms. Vinyl chloride monomer (VCM); polyvinyl chloride (PVC); ammonia (as hydrogen carrier); hydrogen; petrochemicals (umbrella); high-value chemicals (HVCs); near-zero emissions materials.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, three cell technologies, product split, ECU. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: ~85 Mt/yr Cl₂ production.

Claus process (sulfur recovery)

Aliases. Sulfur Recovery Unit (SRU); Claus plant; modified Claus; SuperClaus.

Definition. A two-stage industrial process for converting hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) — recovered from refinery sour gas, natural gas sweetening, and amine-treating-unit acid gas — into elemental sulfur. Stage 1: thermal combustion of one-third of the H₂S with air to SO₂, then thermal reaction H₂S + ½ O₂ → ½ S₂ + H₂O at 1,000–1,400 °C. Stage 2: catalytic Claus reaction 2 H₂S + SO₂ → 3/8 S₈ + 2 H₂O over alumina or titania catalysts at 200–340 °C across 2–4 catalytic stages. Modern SRUs achieve >99.5% sulfur recovery with tail-gas treatment (SCOT, Beavon, Stretford). (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Attributes — typical operating envelope.

Indicator Value
Inlet H₂S concentration 5–95% (variable by source)
Stage-1 thermal temperature 1,000–1,400 °C
Catalytic stages (typical) 2–3
Catalyst activated Al₂O₃ or TiO₂
Sulfur recovery (basic Claus) 95–98%
Sulfur recovery (with tail-gas treatment) >99.5%
Global Claus sulfur production ~70 Mt S/yr (most of global elemental-sulfur supply)

(Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Notes — sulfur as fertiliser feedstock. ~95% of recovered Claus sulfur goes to sulfuric acid manufacture (~70% of which goes to phosphate fertiliser). Sulfur recovery is therefore a bottleneck on global fertiliser supply; without it, oil-and-gas-derived sulfur could not meet demand. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Related terms. Petroleum refining (umbrella); hydrotreating (HDS); sweet vs sour crude; phosphate fertiliser; sulfuric acid.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, two-stage chemistry, recovery efficiency, sulfur-fertiliser link.

Class VI well permit (United States)

Definition. The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Underground Injection Control (UIC) authorisation specifically for wells used to inject CO₂ into deep rock formations for long-term geological storage. Permitting authority can be retained by the EPA or, where states have applied for and been granted “Class VI primacy”, administered by the state. (IEA 2026, pp. 36, 47)

Notes. Slow federal Class VI permitting is identified as a major bottleneck for US dedicated-storage projects; states with Class VI primacy (e.g. North Dakota, Wyoming, Louisiana) move significantly faster. Initiatives such as the US Department of Energy’s CarbonSAFE programme reduce subsurface and regulatory uncertainty by funding feasibility studies, site characterisation and permit preparation for large-scale storage resources. (IEA 2026, pp. 36, 47)

Related terms. Carbon capture and storage (CCS); long-term storage liability; saline aquifer; Class VI primacy.

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition and permitting-bottleneck note.

Clinker

Definition. The intermediate product of cement manufacture, formed by the high-temperature decomposition of limestone (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂) in a rotary kiln. Process CO₂ emissions from this decomposition represent about two-thirds of cement’s direct emissions. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 9)

Attributes.

Stage Temperature
Preheating 200–750 °C
Pre-calcination 750–1000 °C
Rotary kiln 1200–1450 °C

Specific thermal energy demand for one tonne of clinker varies between 3.5 and 5.5 GJ depending on kiln size, presence of pre-calcination, and feedstock moisture content. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 9)

Notes. The European cement industry aims to move from an average 77% clinker rate in cement (2020) to 74% in 2030 and 65% in 2050 by adopting less clinker-intensive cements. Alternative cement chemistries can reduce associated emissions and energy consumption by up to 60% and 51% respectively. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 10)

Related terms. Pre-calcination; rotary kiln; cullet; process emissions.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition, kiln stages and clinker-rate trajectory.

Co-electrolysis

Definition. A high-temperature electrolysis process in which water (steam) and CO₂ are jointly converted into syngas (H₂ + CO) by combining water thermal splitting and the reverse water-gas-shift reaction in a single solid-oxide electrolyser cell, typically operated at 600–1000 °C (873–1273 K). The syngas is then converted to liquid electrofuels via Fischer–Tropsch or methanol synthesis. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 11–12)

Notes. Co-electrolysis benefits from high conversion and energy efficiencies when industrial waste heat (e.g. from FT synthesis) is utilised. The technology is part of the SOE family alongside straight high-temperature steam electrolysis. The reverse water-gas-shift step requires 300–800 °C and a catalyst (typically copper-based). (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 12)

Related terms. Solid oxide electrolysis (SOE); reverse water gas shift; electrofuels; methanol synthesis; Fischer–Tropsch (FT) process.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, operating temperature, integration with electrofuel pathways.

Cumene process (Hock process — phenol + acetone)

Aliases. Hock process; cumene-phenol process; cumene oxidation.

Definition. A two-step industrial route to phenol (C₆H₅OH) and acetone (CH₃COCH₃) as co-products. Step 1: alkylation of benzene with propylene over a zeolite catalyst at 200–250 °C and 25–35 bar to produce cumene (isopropylbenzene). Step 2: liquid-phase aerobic oxidation of cumene to cumene hydroperoxide (CHP) at ~100 °C, then cleavage of CHP with sulfuric acid catalyst at ~50 °C to give phenol + acetone in a stoichiometric 1:0.6 mass ratio. The Hock process supplies >95% of global phenol and ~50% of global acetone. (Speight 2019, Chapter 8 benzene chemistry)

Attributes — production and end-uses.

Indicator Value
Global phenol production ~12 Mt/yr
Global acetone production ~7 Mt/yr
Phenol:acetone mass ratio (Hock) 1.000 : 0.620 (stoichiometric)
Cumene catalyst (alkylation) zeolite (ZSM-5 / β / Y) — replaced AlCl₃ in 1990s
Phenol largest end-use — bisphenol A (BPA) → polycarbonate + epoxy ~45%
Phenol — phenolic resins (phenol-formaldehyde) ~25%
Phenol — caprolactam (Nylon 6) ~10%
Acetone — methyl methacrylate (MMA / PMMA) ~30%
Acetone — bisphenol A ~25%
Acetone — solvent / general chemistry ~45%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 8)

Notes — bisphenol A coupling. Phenol + acetone → bisphenol A is one of the largest downstream uses of both phenol and acetone, creating an internally-coupled supply chain. The phenol/acetone byproduct ratio (1:0.6) drives a chronic over-supply of acetone vs phenol, which is partially absorbed by the BPA market. (Speight 2019, Chapter 8)

Notes — alternative phenol routes. Direct benzene-to-phenol (e.g., Solutia AlphOx N₂O oxidation, Chinese benzene-to-phenol via toluene) routes exist but are pre-commercial. Hock dominates because of the integrated phenol+acetone economics. (Speight 2019, Chapter 8)

Related terms. Benzene; propylene; cumene; phenol; acetone; bisphenol A (BPA); polycarbonate (PC); methyl methacrylate (MMA / PMMA); polyamides (Nylon); high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: two-step Hock chemistry, end-use shares, BPA-coupling.

Cyclohexane

Aliases. Hexamethylene; C₆H₁₂.

Definition. A saturated cyclic hydrocarbon (C₆H₁₂) produced predominantly by catalytic hydrogenation of benzene with hydrogen over Pt/Al₂O₃ or Ni catalyst at 200–225 °C and 20–35 bar (essentially complete conversion). Cyclohexane is the principal feedstock for adipic acid (via KA-oil oxidation, Nylon 6,6 chain) and ε-caprolactam (via cyclohexanone oxime + Beckmann, Nylon 6 chain) — making it the gateway chemical of the polyamide (Nylon) industry. (Speight 2019, Chapter 8 benzene chemistry, Chapter 11.3.5)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production ~6 Mt/yr
Boiling point 80.7 °C
Synthesis route benzene + 3 H₂ → cyclohexane
Catalyst Pt/Al₂O₃ (or Raney Ni)
Conversion (per pass) >99%
H₂ consumption 3 mol H₂ / mol cyclohexane (~70 kg H₂/t)
End-use — adipic acid (Nylon 6,6) ~70%
End-use — caprolactam (Nylon 6) ~25%
Other uses (solvent, general chemistry) ~5%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 8 and 11.3.5)

Related terms. Benzene; adipic acid + HMDA + caprolactam (Nylon-feedstock chain); polyamides (Nylon); high-value chemicals (HVCs); BTX aromatics; hydrogen.

Curtailment (variable renewable energy)

Definition. A power-system operation in which available wind, solar PV or other variable renewable generation is intentionally not used — i.e. the operator dispatches less of it than is technically available — typically because of transmission constraints, system-balancing needs, frequency-stability constraints (e.g. minimum-inertia requirements), or oversupply at low marginal cost. Curtailment is one of the principal flexibility mechanisms enabling high VRE shares. (Guerra et al. 2022, p. 1 and Sections 3.3, 3.4)

Attributes — Guerra Spanish-system curtailment levels for future scenarios.

Level Hydro Solar thermal Wind (ST) Wind (DG/GCA) Solar PV (ST) Solar PV (DG/GCA)
Level 1 (technical inflexibility) n1h n1t 60% 60% 60% 70%
Level 2 (technical inflexibility) 20% 20% 60% 60% 60% 70%
Level 3 (inertia stability) — — 90% 60% 90% 90%

(Levels 1–2 cover surplus from inflexible thermal/dispatch constraints; Level 3 covers the additional curtailment forced by minimum-inertia requirements when synchronous generation is displaced.) (Guerra et al. 2022, Table 1)

Notes — recent context. ETP-2026 reports VRE curtailment reaching 16% in some regions; China demonstrated that grid upgrades, market reforms and demand-side flexibility can drive average wind curtailment from a >15% peak (2016) to <5% (2024) and bring solar PV curtailment to similarly low levels. (IEA ETP 2026, p. 145)

Attributes — RTE 2050 curtailment volumes by scenario (TWh / year, France).

Scenario 2050 curtailment 2060 curtailment Share of variable RES output
M0 (no nuclear, max RES) ~20 TWh/an rises to ~25 TWh/an ~3% (rising to ~4% in 2060)
M1 (diffuse RES) ~15 TWh/an ~18 TWh/an ~2.5%
M23 (concentrated RES) ~5 TWh/an ~7 TWh/an ~1%
N1 (8 EPR2 + RES) ~3 TWh/an ~5 TWh/an <1%
N2 (14 EPR2 + RES) ~2 TWh/an ~3 TWh/an <1%
N03 (max nuclear) <2 TWh/an <3 TWh/an <1%

(RTE 2022, Figure 7.60, Section 7.10.2, p. 378)

Notes — RTE distinction: economic vs grid-constraint curtailment. RTE distinguishes (i) economic curtailment that arises when total VRE output exceeds residual demand plus export capacity plus storage uptake (the values in the table above), from (ii) local-grid-constraint curtailment driven by transmission/distribution bottlenecks. The two do not add directly because their occurrence partially overlaps in time. The “optimum economic curtailment” is the lowest-cost balance between (a) extra grid investment to absorb peak surplus, and (b) accepting some lost RES output. RTE designs the transport-network long-term plan around a target ~1% optimal curtailment for grid-design purposes. (RTE 2022, Sections 7.10.2, 10.2.7, p. 378, p. 522 area; cited 1% target, Section on transport-network sizing)

Notes — non-failure framing. RTE explicitly notes that curtailment volumes of 1–4% of variable RES output are not a failure: they reflect an economic trade-off with the cost of additional storage or grid expansion. Pushing curtailment to zero would require disproportionate over-build of flexibility means. (RTE 2022, Section 7.10.2, p. 378)

Related terms. Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); inertia (power system); Rate of Change of Frequency (ROCOF); flexibility (power system); pumped hydro energy storage (PHES); battery storage (stationary); residual load; Power-to-gas-to-power loop.

Source history. - Guerra et al. 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, curtailment-level table for inflexibility vs inertia. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: China’s curtailment-reduction trajectory. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: France 2050 curtailment volumes by scenario (1–4% of variable RES output), distinction between economic and grid-constraint curtailment, ~1% optimum-grid-design target (translated from French).

Combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT)

Aliases. CCG (FR — Cycle Combiné Gaz); combined cycle gas plant; CCGT.

Definition. A thermal-power plant configuration in which a gas turbine (Brayton cycle) generates electricity, with its hot exhaust gases routed through a heat-recovery steam generator (HRSG) to produce steam that drives a steam turbine (Rankine cycle) for additional electricity output. The double cycle delivers significantly higher net thermal efficiency (~55–60% at full load on natural gas) than a simple-cycle gas turbine or a conventional steam plant, and a CO₂ emission factor approximately half that of coal per kWh. (RTE 2022, Section 4.4, p. 195, translated from French)

Attributes — France-2021 fleet and 2050 projections.

Indicator Value
France CCGT fleet (Sept 2021) 14 units, >6 GW total
Last CCGT under construction Landivisiau (commissioned 2022) — last fossil thermal plant in mainland France per Loi Énergie-Climat
CCGT thermal efficiency (NG) ~55–60% (RTE)
CCGT efficiency on H₂ (assumed) ~55–60% (similar to NG)
H₂ CCGT efficiency in P2G2P loop ~60%
2019 CCGT capacity factor (France) 47%
2050 CCGT capacity factor (RTE scenarios) ~10% (assurantial role)
New decarbonised thermal CCGT (M0) ~29 GW
New decarbonised thermal CCGT (N03) 0 GW (replaced by EPR2)
Cost ratio CCGT vs OCGT (CAPEX) CCGT ~3× OCGT

(RTE 2022, Sections 4.4, 7.5.3, Figures 4.26 and 7.32–7.36, pp. 195–196, 333–336)

Notes — role transition under RTE 2050 scenarios. Existing fossil-fuel CCGTs progressively phase out by 2030–2040 as European RES build-out reduces their capacity factor. Under the SNBC, only decarbonised CCGTs remain by 2050: hydrogen-CCGT or biomethane-CCGT, operating at ~10% capacity factor in an “insurance” role to cover residual-load peaks during low-RES periods (anticyclone winter weeks, dunkelflaute analogues). Their role is no longer baseload but long-term flexibility / capacity adequacy. (RTE 2022, Sections 4.4.2, 7.5.3, p. 195)

Notes — Power-to-gas-to-power loop. A H₂-CCGT operating on hydrogen produced by electrolysis from VRE forms the power-to-H₂-to-power loop, with cycle round-trip efficiency ~40% (~70% electrolyser × ~60% CCGT). The CH₄ variant adds a methanation step (~80% efficiency), giving cycle round-trip efficiency ~30%. RTE uses both as candidate long-duration storage solutions to address inter-seasonal mismatch in 100%-RE scenarios. (RTE 2022, Section 7.5.2.3, Figures 7.32–7.33, pp. 333–334)

Related terms. Open cycle gas turbine (OCGT); Power-to-gas-to-power loop; Hydrogen Combined Cycle (H₂ CC); Natural Gas Combined Cycle (NGCC); Capacity adequacy; Residual load; Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); SNBC; RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 scenarios; Hydrogen pipeline.

Compounding (plastics)

Aliases. Polymer compounding; resin compounding; master-batch production.

Definition. The industrial step that combines virgin polymer resin (the “binder”) with additives, fillers, reinforcements, and pigments to deliver a finished plastic compound with the target properties for downstream processing (injection moulding, extrusion, blow moulding, etc.). Compounding is performed in twin-screw extruders, Banbury mixers, or kneaders that melt the polymer and disperse the additives uniformly. The output — pellets — is the actual feedstock that plastics-product factories purchase. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic compounding section)

Attributes — additive categories.

Additive Function Typical loading Examples
Plasticisers flexibilise, lower Tg 10–80% (PVC-P) DEHP, DINP, DOTP
Antioxidants retard oxidative degradation 0.05–1% Irganox 1010, BHT
UV stabilisers block UV-induced degradation 0.1–1% HALS, benzophenones
Flame retardants suppress combustion 1–20% BFRs, ATH, MgOH₂, phosphate esters
Heat stabilisers (PVC-specific) prevent HCl release on heating 1–4% Ca-Zn, organotins, Pb (legacy)
Lubricants improve flow / mould release 0.1–2% wax, stearates
Colourants / pigments aesthetics 0.1–5% TiO₂ (white), carbon black
Fillers reduce cost, modify properties 5–60% CaCO₃, talc, glass beads
Reinforcements increase strength 10–60% glass fibre, carbon fibre, mineral fibre
Impact modifiers toughness 5–25% EPDM, MBS, ABS modifier
Compatibilisers blend miscibility 1–10% maleated PP, EPDM-g-MA

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic compounding section)

Notes — master-batch. Concentrated additive packages (“master-batches”) at 20–50% loading on a polymer carrier are pre-blended at compounding lines and added at low ratios (1–5%) to the main polymer feed at the moulder/extruder. Master-batches simplify additive handling and improve dispersion uniformity. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic compounding section)

Related terms. Plastic additives; plasticizers (phthalate esters); antioxidants (plastic additives); brominated flame retardants (BFRs); compatibilisers (polymer blends); plastic processing (umbrella); injection moulding; extrusion (plastic processing).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, additive categories with typical loadings, master-batch concept.

Compatibilisers (polymer blends)

Definition. Plastic additives used to enable miscibility and adhesion between two otherwise incompatible polymer phases when blending different resins. They improve interfacial adhesion and blend morphology, allowing co-polymers and recycled-feedstock blends to retain mechanical performance. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, pp. 184, 186)

Notes. Compatibilisation is widely used to create new polymer blends with combined attributes; it is also exploited in plastic recycling where contamination of one polymer (e.g. PLA) by another (e.g. LDPE) can be turned into an advantage if the two are properly compatibilised, potentially commanding a price premium for recycled materials. Ethylene-propylene diene rubber (EPDM) is a common compatibiliser for PP/PE blends in bottles. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, p. 186)

Related terms. Plastic additives; mechanical recycling; plastic chemicals.

Source history. - Hahladakis et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, recycling-relevance note.

Compressed air energy storage (CAES)

Definition. A bulk electricity-storage technology that uses electrically powered compressors to convert excess renewable electricity into compressed air (potential exergy) stored in pressurised vessels, salt caverns or other underground formations. The compressed air is later expanded through an air turbine to generate electricity on demand. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 16)

Attributes — coverage in the 100% RE systems database.

Storage technology Share of 1,067 articles
Batteries 60.2%
e-hydrogen 45.5%
Pumped hydro energy storage (PHES) 29.8%
Thermal energy storage (TES) 19.4%
e-methane 12.8%
Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) 11.6%
Compressed air energy storage (CAES) 9.7%

(Khalili et al. 2026, p. 16)

Notes. Underground storage potential of CAES exceeds the global storage demand by orders of magnitude. CAES remains a niche option in 100% RE systems analyses despite its theoretically large potential, with much higher representation given to batteries and e-hydrogen. The first study to numerically analyse all seven major storage options (batteries, e-hydrogen, PHES, e-methane, TES, V2G, CAES) within a single article appeared in 2023. (Khalili et al. 2026, p. 16)

Related terms. Pumped hydro energy storage (PHES); thermal energy storage (TES); battery electric vehicle (BEV); vehicle-to-grid (V2G); hydrogen storage.

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — listed in Pending 2026-05-07. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, share in 100% RE systems analyses; promoted from Pending.

Coefficient of Performance (COP / SCOP)

Aliases. COP (Coefficient of Performance); SCOP (Seasonal COP); EER (Energy Efficiency Ratio, cooling); SEER (Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio); η_thermal.

Definition. A dimensionless efficiency metric for heat-pump and refrigeration systems, defined as the ratio of useful thermal energy delivered to the electrical energy consumed. For heating: COP = Q_heating / E_electrical (typical 3.0–5.0 for modern air-source heat pumps; >5 for ground-source). For cooling: EER = Q_cooling / E_electrical. The seasonal variants (SCOP / SEER) integrate performance over a full heating or cooling season, capturing varying outdoor conditions and part-load behaviour — usually 0.5–1.0 lower than the rated COP at standard test points (B-7/W35 for ASHP). (Goessel 2025, Sections 2.4, 3.3; AFNOR EN 14511, EN 14825)

Attributes — typical COP / SCOP values.

Heat pump type Test condition COP rated SCOP (heating season, France)
Air-source HP (ASHP, air-water) A2/W35 4.0–4.5 3.0–3.7
Air-source HP (ASHP, air-air, split) A7/A20 3.5–4.5 3.5–4.5
Ground-source HP (GSHP, brine-water) B0/W35 4.5–5.5 4.0–5.0
Water-source HP (WSHP) W10/W35 5.0–6.0 4.5–5.5
Hot-water HP / CET A20/W55 3.0–3.5 2.5–3.0
Window AC (cooling) A35/A27 EER 2.5–3.5 SEER 3.0–4.5
Reversible split AC (heating) A7/A20 3.5–4.5 3.5–4.5

(Goessel 2025, Annexe A; AFNOR EN 14511 test points)

Notes — significance. The COP/SCOP gap (typically 0.5–1.0) reflects the cycling, defrost-cycle, low-temperature degradation, and part-load operation of heat pumps in real climate. Goessel’s economic optimisation uses SCOP values (not COP) because they better represent actual operational performance. A heat pump with SCOP 3.5 replacing a gas boiler delivers a real-world primary-energy reduction of ~50% (with French 2.3 PE conversion factor for electricity) and operational-CO₂ reduction of ~70%. (Goessel 2025, p. 92)

Notes — temperature sensitivity. ASHP performance drops sharply at low outdoor temperature: COP 4.0 at 7 °C falls to ~2.5 at −7 °C. Hybrid heat-pump + gas-boiler systems use the heat pump above ~5 °C and switch to gas below. Modern inverter-driven ASHPs maintain higher SCOP at low temperature than fixed-speed predecessors. (Goessel 2025, p. 92)

Related terms. Heat pump (HP); Building renovation (umbrella); Industrial heat pumps; refrigerant; air-source heat pump; ground-source heat pump; CET (chauffe-eau thermodynamique); operational carbon (buildings); RE2020 / RT2012.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: COP/SCOP definitions, typical values by HP type, gap rationale, temperature sensitivity (translated from French).

Condensing gas boiler

Aliases. Chaudière à condensation gaz (FR); high-efficiency gas boiler; HE gas boiler; modulating gas boiler.

Definition. A natural-gas-fired residential or commercial boiler that recovers the latent heat of water-vapour combustion product by condensing the flue gases — increasing thermal efficiency from ~80% (legacy non-condensing) to 95–110% (relative to lower heating value, LHV). Condensing requires the return-water temperature to be below the dew point of flue gas (~58 °C), achieved with low-temperature heating distribution (radiators sized for 50/40 °C, or underfloor heating at 35 °C). Mandatory for all new gas-boiler installations in France since RT2012. Will be progressively phased out in EU member states from 2025–2040 under EPBD 2024 fossil-boiler ban. (Goessel 2025, Annexe A; AFNOR EN 297)

Attributes — typical condensing-boiler performance.

Indicator Value
Efficiency η (LHV basis) 95–110%
Efficiency η (HHV basis) 88–98%
Modulation range 20–100% (modern modulating boilers)
Power output 5–35 kW (residential), up to 1 MW (commercial)
Capital cost (residential, 2024) €3,500–7,000 (replacing legacy boiler)
Lifetime 15–20 years
CO₂ emissions (combustion + upstream) ~0.24 kg CO₂eq / kWh delivered (~half of oil)
Replacing oil boiler — CO₂ savings ~25% (gas vs oil)
Replacing legacy gas boiler — energy savings ~15–25% (efficiency uplift)

(Goessel 2025, Annexe A; ADEME 2024)

Notes — declining role. Although technically efficient, condensing gas boilers remain fossil-fuel heating with non-zero CO₂ emissions. France’s new-build sales of gas boilers fell from ~50% (2018) to ~25% (2024) as heat-pump market share grows. The MaPrimeRénov’ subsidy schedule excludes gas-boiler replacements (only allowing decarbonised replacements: heat pump, biomass, district heating). (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7)

Related terms. Heat pump (HP); Coefficient of Performance (COP / SCOP); Domestic Hot Water (DHW / ECS); building renovation (umbrella); EPBD; RE2020 / RT2012; MaPrimeRénov’ / CEE / Eco-PTZ.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: condensing-boiler definition, performance, declining-role context (translated from French).

Combined Heat and Power (CHP)

Aliases. CHP; cogeneration; heat-and-power; combined cycle (in some contexts); cogénération (FR).

Definition. A power-plant or industrial-facility configuration in which a single fuel-combustion or process-heat source generates both electricity and useful thermal energy (process steam, district heat, hot water) — capturing waste heat that would otherwise be rejected to the environment in a single-output power plant. Total efficiency 70–90% (vs ~35–55% for power-only generation). CHP is widely deployed in petrochemical plants, refineries, paper mills, district-heating systems, and large industrial facilities where steady steam demand is co-located with power demand. The petrochemical industry is one of the largest CHP users globally (~25% of European industrial CHP capacity). (Bennett 2012, pp. 344–346; Speight 2019)

Attributes — typical CHP configurations.

Configuration Description Total efficiency
Steam-extraction CHP extract steam from condensing-steam-turbine cycle 70–80%
Backpressure steam turbine exhaust steam directly to process 75–85%
Gas-turbine + heat-recovery steam generator (HRSG) gas turbine + steam from exhaust 80–90%
Combined-cycle CHP gas + steam turbines + steam extraction 80–90%
Reciprocating engine CHP engine + jacket-water + exhaust heat 70–85%
Fuel-cell CHP fuel cell + waste heat 70–85%
Industrial-park CHP shared facility serving multiple users 75–90%

(Bennett 2012, pp. 344–346)

Notes — petrochemical relevance. Bennett 2012 highlights that CHP retrofits in petrochemical facilities deliver 15–25% energy-efficiency improvements at moderate capital cost — a major short-term decarbonisation lever. The integration is site-specific: a petrochemical complex’s steam balance, electrical demand, and existing infrastructure determine optimal CHP configuration. EU ETS + national CHP-bonus schemes incentivise deployment. (Bennett 2012, p. 345)

Notes — climate trade-off. CHP improves fuel efficiency but, when burning fossil fuel, still emits CO₂. Decarbonised CHP requires either (i) biomass-CHP, (ii) biogas / hydrogen-fired gas turbines, (iii) electric boilers + heat pumps replacing fossil-CHP. Electrification often eliminates the CHP-paradigm entirely as separate sourcing (grid electricity + heat pumps) becomes more efficient end-to-end. (Bennett 2012, p. 346)

Related terms. Petrochemicals (umbrella); refinery-petrochemical integration; district heating (DH); combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT); steam cracking; hydrogen aviation; energy efficiency; cogénération.

Source history. - Bennett 2012 — added 2026-05-08: CHP definition, configuration table, petrochemical-deployment context, climate-trade-off discussion. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): refinery CHP integration.

Concentrated solar power (CSP)

Aliases. Concentrated solar thermal power.

Definition. A power-generation technology that uses mirrors or lenses to concentrate solar irradiation on a fluid, creating superheated steam that drives a turbine. Four main configurations exist: parabolic trough (the most mature and widely used), solar tower, dish Stirling, and Fresnel CSP. (Khalili et al. 2026, p. 6)

Attributes — share of 100% RE systems studies.

Wind power 1,002 94%
Bioenergy 660 62%
Hydropower 620 58%

(Khalili et al. 2026, p. 12)

Notes. Solar tower may gain market share over parabolic trough due to lower cost potential. CSP first appeared in 100% RE systems analyses in 1978; despite its pre-commercial origins dating to the 1970s, lower priority is currently given to it relative to solar PV and wind. Key barriers include heat-transfer-fluid choices, energy-storage system integration, cooling methods, water management, and electricity costs. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 6, 13)

Cotton (textile fibre)

Aliases. Coton (FR); cotton fibre; cotton lint; conventional / organic / Better Cotton Initiative cotton.

Definition. A natural cellulosic fibre obtained from the seed bolls of Gossypium cotton plants — the largest natural-fibre source globally and the second-largest textile fibre after polyester. Cotton fibre is ~95% cellulose with traces of pectins, waxes and minerals; staple-length classified as short (<25 mm), medium (25–35 mm) or long (>35 mm), with longer staples commanding higher prices for fine textiles. Cotton growing is agriculture (annual or perennial crop), making the fibre fundamentally different from synthetic / petrochemical fibres in its supply chain, water requirements, pesticide use, and climate footprint. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 191–193)

Attributes — global cotton statistics.

Indicator Value
Global cotton production (lint, 2018) ~26 Mt/yr (~25% of total textile fibres)
Top producers (2024) India, China, US, Brazil, Pakistan, Australia
Cotton share of global pesticide use ~6% (despite occupying only ~2.5% of arable land)
Water footprint per kg cotton fibre 5,000–10,000 L (rainfed varies)
Water footprint per cotton T-shirt ~2,700–3,800 L
Water footprint per pair of cotton jeans ~7,500–10,000 L
Cotton consumption — fashion industry water share ~70% of fashion-industry water use traceable to cotton
Organic cotton CO₂ vs conventional ~60% lower (per Niinimäki 2020)
Better Cotton Initiative (BCI) certified ~25% of global cotton (2024)
GMO cotton (Bt cotton) ~80% of global cotton (US, India, China, Brazil)

(Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 191–193, Fig. 4 and citations)

Notes — water-stress impact. Cotton cultivation is concentrated in arid / semi-arid regions where it is the dominant agricultural water user — the Aral Sea catastrophe (Uzbekistan, Soviet-era cotton irrigation) is the canonical case. Niinimäki cites that cotton production from outside the EU drives the EU’s “virtual water” footprint sharply upward — 7% of global groundwater + drinking-water losses are attributable to textiles + fashion via the cotton supply chain. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, p. 192)

Notes — pesticide-and-fertiliser intensity. Conventional cotton uses 16% of global insecticides and 7% of global pesticides while occupying 2.5% of arable land — making it one of the most chemical-intensive crops. Bt-cotton (genetically-modified to express Bacillus thuringiensis insecticidal protein) reduces some insecticide use but doesn’t eliminate it. Organic cotton (no synthetic fertiliser, no synthetic pesticide) has lower per-kg footprint but lower yield, requiring more land for equivalent output. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, p. 193)

Related terms. Textile fibres (synthetic and natural); fast fashion (and slow fashion); microfibre pollution; circular economy; nitrogen fertilisers (umbrella); pesticides; agricultural water use.

Cooling and Heating degree days (CDD / HDD)

Definition. Standardised metrics quantifying how far ambient temperature deviates from a comfort baseline, used to estimate weather-driven heating and cooling demand. Cooling degree days (CDD) sum the temperature excess above the baseline (typically 18 °C); heating degree days (HDD) sum the deficit below the baseline. The two measures together provide the principal weather-correction tool in energy demand statistics. (IEA GER 2026, pp. 12, 571–572)

Notes — 2025 weather context.

Indicator Value Year
2025 vs 2024 global cooling degree days −6% 2025
2025 vs 2000–2019 average cooling degree days still well above 2025
Advanced-economies winter HDD increase (2025) up vs 2024 2025
Estimated weather contribution to 2025 NG demand growth >16 bcm of ~40 bcm total 2025
Estimated weather contribution to 2025 fossil-fuel CO₂ emissions +90 Mt CO₂ 2025
Counterfactual coal-demand growth without cooler weather 0.5% (vs observed 0.4%) 2025

(IEA GER 2026, pp. 12, 715–720, 1001, 1332)

Notes — application. GER-2026 uses HDD/CDD changes year-over-year to disaggregate weather-driven from structural drivers in energy demand, and to support its scenario projections under the IEA Global Energy and Climate model. ETP-2026 uses the same baseline framework for projecting heat-pump and air-conditioning demand by region. (IEA GER 2026, p. 717; IEA ETP 2026, pp. 131, 133)

Related terms. Energy intensity; primary energy demand; Power system flexibility; heat pump (HP); air-conditioning systems.

Critical materials (clean energy technologies)

Aliases. Critical minerals.

Definition. A wide range of minerals and metals that are essential to clean energy technologies and other modern technologies and have supply chains that are vulnerable to disruption. Critical-minerals lists differ between jurisdictions; the IEA’s working list for clean energy includes chromium, cobalt, copper, graphite, lithium, manganese, molybdenum, nickel, platinum-group metals, zinc and rare earth elements (REEs). (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 374, citing IEA 2021 Role of Critical Minerals in Clean Energy Transitions)

Notes — supply-chain concentration in 2025–2030. Each of the major clean energy supply chains contains at least one step where less than one-quarter of demand outside China can be met from non-Chinese supply. Magnet rare earth elements (MREEs) used in wind turbines, electric cars, drones and data centres are particularly affected: refining is dominated by China and an export-restriction announcement in 2025 highlighted the dependence. Battery supply-chain disruption from China would cost an estimated USD 17 billion per month in lost output at electric-car factories elsewhere; solar-PV component disruption would cost ~USD 1 billion/month outside China. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 18–19, 269 ff.)

Related terms. Manufacturing capacity (clean energy technologies); clean energy technologies; rare earth elements; battery electric vehicle (BEV).

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, mineral list, concentration metrics.

Cross-chain risk (CCUS)

Definition. A category of CCUS project risk arising from the interdependency of capture, transport and storage along a single value chain: the failure or delay of any one segment (e.g. capture facility, pipeline, storage well) can strand the others. Capture facilities depend on transport and storage being operational; infrastructure providers depend on sustained CO₂ volumes from emitters; and shared infrastructure faces project-on-project risks. (IEA 2026, pp. 19, 22)

Notes — examples and mitigants. - Denmark 2025 auction: 80% of industrial bidders pulled their proposals after cross-chain risks could not be managed. - UK Track-1: government provides a backstop covering project delays, unavailable storage capacity, and infrastructure-failure cost recovery. - Netherlands (Porthos, Aramis): integrated commercial contracts allocate transport and storage costs and risks among value-chain entities. - Common contractual mitigants include take-or-pay/store-or-pay contracts, back-to-back capacity bookings, minimum volume commitments (MVCs) and termination/delay compensation clauses.

(IEA 2026, pp. 8, 22, 42, 44)

Related terms. Bankability; long-term storage liability; hub and cluster model; take-or-pay/store-or-pay contract; regulated asset base (RAB); minimum volume commitment.

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, examples, contractual mitigants.

Current Policies Scenario (CPS)

Definition. An IEA exploratory scenario that sets out a pathway for the energy system in which no change in energy-related policies is assumed beyond what is already in place. The CPS builds on a narrow reading of today’s policy settings, considering only policies that are adopted in legislation and regulation; where existing policies target a range of outcomes, the CPS assumes the lower end of the range and treats time-bound policies as not strengthened beyond expiry. The CPS also offers a generally cautious view of new-technology adoption, projecting slower growth than seen in recent years or in the STEPS. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 374)

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 15–16, Executive Summary)
