Ethylbenzene / styrene share ~6%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 6.2.3; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1; Zhang et al. 2024, pp. 100–101)

Notes — production routes. Steam cracking dominates (>95%); the feed determines the co-product slate (ethane → ethylene-pure; naphtha → ethylene + propylene + C4 + BTX). Defossilised routes include bioethanol-dehydration to ethylene (commercial in Brazil, India), biomethanol-to-olefins (MTO), bionaphtha cracking, and electrocatalytic CO₂ reduction directly to ethylene (~60% Faradaic efficiency at lab scale). (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 110; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 3)

Notes — geographic concentration. Ethylene production is heavily geographically concentrated: ~90% of US ethylene from ethane-rich NGLs (Gulf Coast); Middle East from ethane (cheap feedstock); China from coal-to-MTO and naphtha; Europe from naphtha. This concentration makes the global ethylene market sensitive to shale-gas economics, NGL prices, and Middle East gas pricing. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastics intro)

Related terms. Olefins; high-value chemicals (HVCs); steam cracking (vapocracking); naphtha; polyethylene; ethylene oxide / ethylene glycol (EO / MEG); vinyl chloride monomer (VCM); styrene; methanol-to-olefins (MTO).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, properties, end-use shares. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 150 Mt/yr global, polymer end-use breakdown. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: 26.8 GJ/t energy intensity, electrocatalytic route.

Propylene (C₃H₆)

Aliases. Propene; propilen; propylene monomer.

Definition. A colourless, flammable gas (CH₃-CH=CH₂), the second-largest-volume light olefin globally and the principal feedstock for polypropylene (PP) — the second-largest commodity thermoplastic after polyethylene. Globally, ~65% of propylene goes to PP; the remainder is split between propylene oxide / polyols / polyurethanes (~7%), acrylonitrile / ABS / acrylic fibres (~7%), cumene / phenol / acetone (~6%), and oxo-alcohols (~5%) and others. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production (recent) ~110 Mt/yr
Bond C=C double, 632 kJ/mol
Boiling point −47.6 °C
LHV 45.8 MJ/kg
Steam-cracker yield (naphtha feed) ~15 wt%
Steam-cracker yield (ethane feed) ~3 wt%
FCC propylene yield (high-severity) 5–20 wt%
Refinery share of global propylene ~30%
Steam-cracker share ~50%
On-purpose (PDH, MTO, MTP, metathesis) ~15–20%
Polypropylene share of end-use ~65%
Propylene oxide / polyols share ~7%
Acrylonitrile share ~7%
Cumene share ~6%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Notes — supply tightness. Propylene supply has been chronically tight relative to PP demand because most propylene is a co-product of ethylene-targeted steam cracking (yields fixed by feed) or of FCC gasoline production (yields fixed by FCC operation). On-purpose propylene technologies — propane dehydrogenation (PDH), methanol-to-propylene (MTP, Lurgi process), olefin metathesis (ABB/Lummus OCT) — fill the gap and have grown rapidly since 2010, especially in China. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 3)

Notes — defossilisation routes. Bionaphtha cracking, biomethanol-to-propylene (MTP), bio-PDH (from bio-propane), and electrocatalytic CO₂-to-propylene (still pre-commercial) are the principal alternative-feedstock options. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 3 and Fig. 3)

Related terms. Olefins; high-value chemicals (HVCs); steam cracking (vapocracking); catalytic cracking (FCC); polypropylene (PP); propylene oxide; acrylonitrile; methanol-to-olefins (MTO); methanol-to-propylene (MTP); propane dehydrogenation (PDH); ethylene.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, end-use shares, supply-tightness dynamics. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 110 Mt/yr global, refinery share 30%, on-purpose share growth.

Butadiene (1,3-butadiene)

Aliases. 1,3-BD; BD; butadiene monomer.

Definition. A colourless, flammable C₄ diolefin (CH₂=CH-CH=CH₂) and the principal monomer for synthetic rubber production — particularly styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), polybutadiene (BR), nitrile rubber (NBR) and ABS resin. Butadiene is recovered primarily as a co-product of naphtha steam cracking (where it appears in the C4 stream alongside butenes and butane), with smaller volumes from on-purpose dehydrogenation of n-butane (Catadiene / Houdry process) and on-purpose dehydration of bioethanol (Ostromislensky process). (Speight 2019, Chapters 7.5, 11.3.11)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production (recent) ~12–13 Mt/yr
Bond conjugated C=C-C=C
Boiling point −4.4 °C
LHV 44.9 MJ/kg
Steam-cracker C4 yield (naphtha feed) ~10 wt% (50% of which is butadiene)
On-purpose (Catadiene, ethanol-to-BD) ~5–10% of global supply
SBR share of butadiene end-use ~30% (tires)
Polybutadiene (BR) share ~25% (tires)
ABS / SAN share ~15%
Nitrile rubber (NBR) share ~5%
Adiponitrile / hexamethylenediamine (HMDA) share ~10% (Nylon 66)
Other (chloroprene, latex, plastics) ~15%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.5; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Notes — extraction from C4 stream. The cracker C4 stream (butadiene + butenes + butane) is separated by extractive distillation with a polar solvent (NMP, DMF, or sulfolane) to recover purified butadiene (>99.5%). Butenes are then sent downstream to alkylation, MTBE production, isomerisation, or recycled to crackers; butane is used as fuel. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.5)

Notes — alternative routes. Houdry Catadiene (n-butane → butadiene over alumina-chromia) operated commercially during WWII (US synthetic rubber program); displaced by cracker C4 economics post-war but remerged in some Middle East / China plants. Ethanol-to-butadiene (Ostromislensky / Lebedev) operates over various metal-oxide catalysts at 350–450 °C and is being revisited as a route to bio-butadiene (Synthos, IFP Axens, Versalis-Genomatica). (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11)

Related terms. Olefins; high-value chemicals (HVCs); steam cracking (vapocracking); styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR); polybutadiene; ABS; ethylene; propylene; pyrolysis gasoline (pygas).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, end-use shares, Catadiene + ethanol-to-BD routes. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 12–13 Mt/yr global, end-use breakdown.

Engineering plastics (umbrella)

Aliases. Performance plastics; high-performance polymers; technical plastics.

Definition. A category of thermoplastic polymers that exhibit higher mechanical strength, thermal stability, and chemical resistance than commodity thermoplastics (PE, PP, PVC, PET, PS), and which are used in technically demanding applications — automotive engine compartments, electrical/electronics housings, gear and bearing components, medical devices, aerospace structures. Engineering plastics typically command 2–10× the price of commodity plastics and are produced in much smaller volumes. (Speight 2019, Chapters 11.3.7–11.3.10, 11.6)

Attributes — major engineering plastics.

Polymer Tg / Tm Tensile strength Global production Key applications
Polycarbonate (PC) Tg 145 °C 60–70 MPa ~5 Mt/yr optical media, glazing, automotive headlamps
Polyamides (PA66, PA6) Tm 220–265 °C 70–85 MPa ~9 Mt/yr tyre cord, automotive intake manifolds
Polyacetal (POM) Tm 175 °C 65 MPa ~1 Mt/yr gears, bearings, fasteners, plumbing
Poly(phenylene oxide) (PPO) blends Tg 205 °C 55 MPa ~0.5 Mt/yr electrical housings, medical instruments
Polysulfone (PSU) / PES Tg 190–225 °C 70 MPa ~0.1 Mt/yr medical sterilisable devices, membranes
PMMA (acrylic) Tg 105 °C 70 MPa ~3 Mt/yr optical sheet (Plexiglas), automotive lighting
PEEK (polyetheretherketone) Tg 143 °C, Tm 343 °C 100 MPa ~10 kt/yr aerospace structural, oil & gas, medical implants
PTFE (Teflon) crystalline (no Tg) Tm 327 °C 25 MPa (low!), self-lubricating ~0.2 Mt/yr non-stick, chemical-resistant linings, gaskets
LCP (liquid crystal polymer) Tg ~120 °C 100–200 MPa ~50 kt/yr electronic connectors, medical devices

(Speight 2019, Chapters 11.3.7–11.3.10)

Notes — vs commodity polymers. Engineering plastics are characterised by glass-transition or melting temperatures above ~100 °C, low creep under load, and chemical resistance suited for repeated thermal-mechanical cycling. They overlap somewhat with commodity-polymer “engineered grades” (engineering-grade PP with talc reinforcement, for instance) but the canonical engineering-plastics taxonomy excludes commodity polymers regardless of how reinforced they are. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.7)

Related terms. Polycarbonate (PC); polyamides (Nylon); high-value chemicals (HVCs); plastic additives; plastic processing (umbrella); injection moulding.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: umbrella definition, taxonomy of major engineering plastics, vs commodity polymers.

EURO-CORDEX (regional climate-projection ensemble)

Aliases. EURO-CORDEX 11; EURO-CORDEX 0.11°; CORDEX-Europe; coordinated regional downscaling experiment (Europe domain).

Definition. A coordinated set of high-resolution (typically 0.11° ≈ 12.5 km, hence “EURO-CORDEX 11”) regional climate projections covering the European domain, produced by dynamically downscaling Global Climate Model (GCM) outputs through Regional Climate Models (RCMs) under standardised RCP forcing scenarios. The EURO-CORDEX ensemble combines ~13 RCMs × ~9 GCMs × 3 RCP scenarios (RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP8.5), producing >100 climate-projection time series at 12.5 km resolution across Europe through 2100. EURO-CORDEX is the standard data source for European-scale climate-impact studies on buildings, hydrology, agriculture and energy. (Goessel 2025, pp. 56–62, citing Gobiet 2012, Evin 2021)

Attributes — EURO-CORDEX ensemble structure.

Element Value
Spatial resolution 0.11° (~12.5 km, “EURO-CORDEX 11”) and 0.44° (~50 km, “EURO-CORDEX 44”)
Temporal resolution 3-hourly (raw); requires interpolation to hourly for BES
Time range 1981–2100 (historical + projection)
RCP scenarios RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP8.5 (CMIP5) — being extended to SSP scenarios (CMIP6)
GCMs (driving) ~9 (CNRM-CM5, EC-EARTH, HadGEM2-ES, IPSL-CM5A-MR, MPI-ESM-LR, etc.)
RCMs (downscaling) ~13 (CCLM, RACMO22E, REMO, ALADIN, RegCM4, etc.)
Output variables temperature, precipitation, humidity, radiation, wind speed, pressure
Public access CORDEX ESGF data portals (free)

(Goessel 2025, Annexe B; Gobiet 2012; Evin 2021)

Notes — uncertainty decomposition (Evin 2021). EURO-CORDEX projections decompose total uncertainty into three sources: (i) RCP scenario uncertainty (politics + emissions trajectory); (ii) GCM-RCM model uncertainty (different climate models predict differently); (iii) internal variability of the climate system (multi-decadal natural variability). Evin et al. 2021 quantify that for 2021–2050 mean summer temperature in central Europe, GCM-RCM choice contributes 78% of total variance — model uncertainty dominates over scenario choice for the next 30 years. By 2071–2099, scenario choice (RCP) becomes dominant (53% of variance). (Goessel 2025, pp. 56–60 and Fig. 2.13)

Notes — bias correction required. EURO-CORDEX outputs at 12.5 km resolution still contain systematic biases vs local meteorological-station observations (typically ±2 °C systematic temperature error, ±20% precipitation). Bias-correction methods (Quantile Mapping, CDF-t, LOCI) are routinely applied before the data is used in building-impact studies. (Goessel 2025, p. 60)

Related terms. Bias correction (climate); General Circulation Model (GCM); Regional Climate Model (RCM); Quantile Mapping; CDF-t; Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs); Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs); Typical Meteorological Year (TMY); building energy simulation (BES / SED); building renovation (umbrella).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: EURO-CORDEX 11 definition, ensemble structure, uncertainty decomposition (Evin 2021), bias-correction need.

Energy intensity (primary)

Definition. The amount of primary energy required to generate a unit of economic output, typically expressed as MJ per USD or toe per USD of GDP. Lower energy intensity means a given amount of GDP requires less energy. Improvements in energy intensity (“intensity gains”) arise from energy-efficiency upgrades, structural shifts towards less energy-intensive industries, and substitution of low-conversion-loss technologies (e.g. renewables-to-electricity vs fossil-fuel-to-electricity). (IEA GER 2026, pp. 11, 514–520, 555)

Attributes — 2025 trends (GER-2026).

Region / period Energy intensity improvement
World — 2010–2019 average ~2% per year
World — 2019–2024 average ~1.3% per year
World — 2025 ~2% (notable acceleration)
China — 2010–2019 average ~4% per year
China — 2019–2024 average ~0.6% per year
China — 2025 >3%
2024 → 2025 GDP growth 3.3% → 3.1%

(IEA GER 2026, pp. 11, 514–520)

Notes. GER-2026 attributes the 2019–2024 slowdown in global energy intensity improvements largely to China’s slowdown — itself reflecting adverse weather and structural shifts in China’s economy after Covid-19 toward a more export- and industry-intensive model. The 2025 reacceleration brings global intensity improvement back in line with the 2010–2019 long-run trend. Outside China, intensity improvements have been more stable. (IEA GER 2026, pp. 11, 520)

Related terms. Cooling and Heating degree days (CDD / HDD); primary energy demand; Age of Electricity; total system inertia (TSI).

Source history. - IEA GER 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, 2025 reacceleration context, China’s role.

Erosional velocity

Definition. The upper-bound gas velocity in a transport pipeline, beyond which prolonged operation causes erosion of the pipe wall. It can be approximated as V_max = 100·√(0.05131 · Z·R·T / (G·P)), where Z is the compressibility factor, R the ideal-gas constant (8.314 kPa·m³/kg·mol·K), T the gas temperature (K), G the specific gravity, and P the pressure (kPa). (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 13, 22)

Attributes — illustrative values at 70 bar inlet pressure, 15 °C.

Gas Erosional velocity (m/s)
Methane 17.1
Hydrogen 49.9

(Khan et al. 2021, p. 15, Table 4.1)

Notes. Hydrogen’s erosional velocity is ~2.91× higher than methane at 70 bar transmission-pipeline conditions. Combined with the 3.29× higher volumetric flow rate required to deliver the same energy via H₂ as via methane, the maximum energy density a hydrogen pipeline can carry is limited to ~88.4% of the equivalent methane pipeline. The higher H₂ flow rates also imply ~3× the compression energy per MJ of fuel delivered. (Khan et al. 2021, p. 15)

Related terms. Hydrogen pipeline; general flow equation; compressibility factor (Z); Reynolds number; hydrogen-natural gas blending.

Source history. - Khan et al. 2021 — added 2026-05-08: definition, formula, hydrogen/methane comparison.

Extrusion (plastic processing)

Aliases. Profile extrusion; pipe extrusion; sheet/film extrusion; blown-film extrusion; cast-film extrusion.

Definition. A continuous plastics processing method in which thermoplastic resin pellets are gravity-fed into a heated barrel containing one or two screws that compress, melt, and homogenise the polymer, then push the melt through a shaped die at a controlled rate to produce a continuous profile of constant cross-section: pipe, tube, sheet, film, fibres, monofilaments, or coated cable. The output is cooled (in air, water bath, or by chilled rollers) and cut/wound. Extrusion is the dominant production method for plastic pipes, films, and sheets — by tonnage the largest plastic-processing method globally. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Attributes — variants and outputs.

Variant Output Polymer Throughput
Pipe / profile extrusion constant-section pipe (10–800 mm) HDPE, PVC-U, PP up to 5 t/h
Sheet extrusion flat sheet (0.5–20 mm) PP, HIPS, PVC, PET 0.5–3 t/h
Blown-film extrusion tubular film (LDPE, LLDPE, HDPE) LDPE/LLDPE/HDPE for shopping bags, food film
Cast-film extrusion flat clear film LLDPE, PP, PET for packaging
Wire & cable insulated cable jacket XLPE, PVC, PP continuous
Fibre / monofilament continuous filament PP, polyester, nylon for textile, ropes

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Notes — twin-screw vs single-screw. Single-screw extruders dominate basic shaping; twin-screw extruders (co-rotating intermeshing) dominate compounding and reactive extrusion (incorporating additives or running chemical reactions in-line). Co-extrusion combines multiple polymer streams through a single die to create multilayer structures (e.g., barrier films with EVOH or PA layers between PE layers). (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Related terms. Injection moulding; blow moulding; thermoforming; compounding (plastics); polyethylene (HDPE / LDPE / LLDPE); polypropylene (PP); polyvinyl chloride (PVC); plastic processing (umbrella).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, variants, twin-screw vs single-screw, co-extrusion.

Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)

Definition. A regulatory and economic instrument that makes producers (manufacturers, importers, brand owners) financially and/or operationally responsible for the end-of-life management of their products and packaging — typically through a fee paid into a producer responsibility organisation (PRO) that funds collection, sorting and recycling. EPR creates an incentive for producers to design for recyclability, reduce material use and switch to less hazardous substances (“eco-design”). (OECD 2022, pp. 25–27, 626; Goel and Tripathi 2024, p. xi)

Notes — implementation lessons. Among 50 countries surveyed by the OECD’s plastics policy inventory, only 13 (covering 4% of the surveyed population) had national instruments providing direct financial incentives to sort plastic waste at source. EPR can be paired with “fee modulation” — varying the producer fee by the recyclability of the product — to strengthen design incentives. EPR for tyres, batteries, packaging and electronics is the most common application; full coverage of plastic packaging EPR remains the EU baseline benchmark. (OECD 2022, pp. 25–27, 121–122; Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 6–7)

Related terms. Deposit-refund scheme; pay-as-you-throw (PAYT); plastic leakage; secondary plastics market; mismanaged plastic waste.

Source history. - OECD 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, deployment status, fee-modulation note. - Goel and Tripathi 2024 — added 2026-05-08: India implementation context. - Grimaud and Girard 2024 — added 2026-05-08: regulatory framework note (translated from French).

EU ETS 2024 revisions (Fit-for-55 reform)

Aliases. EU ETS Phase IV revisions; 2023 / 2024 reform; CBAM-aligned ETS reform; free-allocation phase-out.

Definition. A package of legislative revisions to the EU Emissions Trading System adopted in 2023–2024 as part of the EU’s Fit-for-55 climate package, designed to (i) deepen the emissions cap to align with the EU 2030 −55% target and 2050 climate neutrality, (ii) phase out free allocation of EU allowances (EUAs) to trade-exposed industrial sectors gradually 2026 → 2034, and (iii) reform the benchmark definitions used to allocate free EUAs so that low-emission technologies (H₂-DRI for steel, electrolytic hydrogen, pelletising) can also qualify for free allocation rather than only incumbent emission-intensive technologies. The revisions are timed to coincide with the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) phase-in to maintain leakage protection. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 1–4 and Fig. 2)

Attributes — Johnson 2025 detailed benchmark changes.

Benchmark Pre-2024 scope Post-2024 scope Effect
Sintered ore sintering only sintering + pelletising pellet producers receive free EUAs from 2026
Hot metal blast-furnace only BF + DRI reactors + sponge iron DRI producers receive free EUAs from 2026
Hydrogen grey-H₂ from SMR SMR + electrolysis electrolytic green H₂ receives free EUAs from 2026
Result only incumbent emission-intensive routes get free EUAs low-emission routes also receive subsidy in transition levels playing field for green steel

(Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 2–4 and Fig. 2)

Notes — net negative EU ETS cost. Because benchmarks are based on incumbent emission intensity and updated only gradually toward lower-emitting technologies (Supplementary Methods 1: Free allocation), producers operating below benchmark receive more free EUAs than they need to cover their emissions — a “net negative EU ETS cost”, effectively a subsidy. Johnson finds that during 2026–2033, H₂-DRI-EAF steel producers receive net negative EU ETS costs (effectively €−10 to €−118 per tonne steel), giving them a transitional cost advantage. (Johnson et al. 2025, p. 2 and Fig. 2)

Notes — phase-out trajectory. Free-allocation phase-out follows a non-linear schedule: 2.5% phase-out 2026, rising to 50% by 2030, 100% by 2034. CBAM ramps up symmetrically. The non-linearity creates a sharp “post-2029 stress” on EU BF-BOF producers (Johnson Fig. 6), driving major investment-decision pressure for 2026–2029. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 5–7)

Related terms. EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM); H2-DRI-EAF route; carbon leakage; near-zero emissions materials; decarbonisation race; abatement cost; marginal abatement cost (MAC).

Source history. - Johnson et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, benchmark changes, net-negative-cost subsidy mechanism, phase-out trajectory.

EPBD (Energy Performance of Buildings Directive)

Aliases. EPBD; Directive 2010/31/EU (recast); Directive (EU) 2024/1275 (latest revision); European Union building-energy regulation.

Definition. The principal EU directive regulating building energy performance, originally adopted in 2002, revised in 2010 (Directive 2010/31/EU), 2018 (Directive 2018/844/EU), and most recently in 2024 (Directive (EU) 2024/1275 — the “EPBD recast”). The directive sets minimum energy-performance requirements for new and existing buildings, establishes the Energy Performance Certificate system (EPC — known as DPE in France), and from 2024 mandates Zero-Emission Buildings (ZEB) for all new buildings from 2030 (2028 for public-authority buildings) plus mandatory deep renovation of the worst-performing buildings. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7; Directive (EU) 2024/1275)

Attributes — EPBD 2024 recast key provisions.

Provision Description
Zero-Emission Buildings (ZEB) for new construction mandatory from 2030 (2028 for public)
Minimum Energy Performance Standards (MEPS) residential: 16% reduction by 2030, 20–22% by 2035
Worst-performing buildings target 16% lowest must be renovated by 2030
Building Renovation Passport (BRP) mandatory tool for staged-renovation planning, 2030
Mortgage Portfolio Standards banks must improve average energy class of mortgaged buildings
Solar mandate new public + commercial buildings must integrate solar by 2027–2030
Phase-out of fossil-fuel boilers new fossil boilers banned 2040; subsidy ban 2025
Fossil-fuel-only heating phase-out 2040
EU Renovation Wave target 35 million renovated buildings by 2030

(Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7; Directive (EU) 2024/1275 final text)

Notes — relationship to national laws. EPBD sets EU-wide minimums; national-implementation laws (RE2020 in France, GEG in Germany, Building Regulations in UK, etc.) typically exceed the EU minimum. The 2024 recast was strengthened during EU Parliament + Council negotiations to align with the European Green Deal 2050 climate-neutrality target. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7)

Notes — EU Renovation Wave. The EU Renovation Wave (October 2020) targets doubling the EU annual renovation rate from ~1% to ~2% by 2030 — translating to 35 million renovated dwellings cumulatively. Goessel’s methodology is designed to support the renovation-strategy decisions implied by this scale of activity. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7)

Related terms. RE2020 / RT2012; DPE (Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique); Building renovation (umbrella); passoire thermique; Net Zero Energy Building (NZEB); Energy poverty; EU climate policy (Fit-for-55).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: EPBD definition, 2024 recast provisions, EU Renovation Wave target, national-laws relationship (translated from French).

EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS)

Definition. The EU’s principal mandatory cap-and-trade policy instrument for climate-change mitigation, covering approximately 40% of total EU GHG emissions from industrial activities including the aviation and maritime sectors. Tradable allowances (EUAs) put a price on carbon and are used to drive economy-wide emission-reduction targets. Currently for aviation the EU ETS covers only CO₂ tail-pipe emissions on intra-EEA flights. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 25–26)

Attributes — aviation allowance distribution and prices.

Item Value Year
Free allowances 82% (allocated by airline efficiency) 2013–2020
Auctioned 15% 2013–2020
Reserved (new entrants, fast-growing airlines) 3% 2013–2020
EUA price ~€25/t CO₂ end-2019
EUA price ~€85/t CO₂ May 2021
Free-allowance cap 95% of avg. 2004–2006 emissions (~210–220 Mt CO₂) 2013–2020
Linear Reduction Factor (LRF) 2.2% per year (proposed 4.2% from 2025 under Fit for 55) 2021–

(Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 26)

Notes. The Fit for 55 package proposes phasing out free allowances over 2024–2026 (full phase-out from 2027), capping at current level, and including flights to outermost regions, Switzerland and the UK; international (extra-EEA) flights involving CORSIA participating states will also be integrated. The EU ETS counts SAF as zero-emission fuels (no allowances surrendered), but the high SAF price relative to the EUA price (>€160/t CO₂ break-even required) limits the incentive. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 26)

Related terms. CORSIA; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); ReFuelEU Aviation; Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).

Source history. - Kushnir et al. 2020 — listed in Pending 2026-05-07. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, allowance distribution, Fit for 55 revision; promoted from Pending.

Fatigue crack growth rate (FCGR) test

Definition. A test that measures the rate at which existing cracks propagate under cyclic loading, used to assess the effect of hydrogen on fatigue resistance of pipeline steels. Typically performed on compact tension (CT) specimens with dimensions specified in the ASTM E647 standard. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 377)

Notes. Hydrogen significantly accelerates crack growth rates in many high-strength steels, but a threshold hydrogen concentration may exist below which FCGR decreases with increasing hydrogen and above which it increases. Tests can be conducted in-situ (specimens charged during testing) or ex-situ. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 377, citing Dmytrakh et al.; Yamabe et al.; An et al.)

Related terms. Hydrogen embrittlement; fatigue life test; hydrogen charging; slow strain rate test.

Source history. - Ghadiani et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition, specimen and standard, hydrogen-effect notes.

Fatigue life test

Definition. A test that assesses the overall lifespan of a material until failure under cyclic loading. The hydrogen-embrittlement literature emphasises FCGR tests with relatively few studies addressing fatigue life directly. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 377)

Notes. Faucon et al. (cited) reported a 37% reduction in fatigue life for API X60 pipeline steel charged at 70 and 150 barg; Meng et al. demonstrated a fall from 24 431 cycles in nitrogen to 2130 cycles in a 5 vol% H₂ blend at 12 MPa for X80 pipeline steel. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 377)

Related terms. Hydrogen embrittlement; fatigue crack growth rate test; hydrogen-natural gas blending.

Source history. - Ghadiani et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition and example fatigue-life findings.

Fast fashion (and slow fashion)

Aliases. Fast fashion; ultra-fast fashion; Shein-style fashion; Zara/H&M model; slow fashion (the antithesis).

Definition. A textile-and-apparel business model that relies on high-frequency, low-cost, trend-led clothing production and short garment-use periods. Fast-fashion retailers (Zara, H&M, Forever 21) compress design-to-shelf cycles to ~2–6 weeks (vs traditional 6–12 months) and offer ~52 collections per year (vs 2–4 traditional). Ultra-fast-fashion players (Shein, Temu) push this further to weekly micro-collections, AI-driven trend prediction, and prices below €5–10 per garment. The model has driven a doubling of global clothing production since 2000 — ~62 Mt/yr → ~102 Mt/yr projected by 2030 — alongside a 36% reduction in average garment-use time since 2005. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 189–190; Tilsted et al. 2023)

Attributes — quantified impacts (Niinimäki 2020).

Indicator Value
Global apparel production (2018) ~62 Mt/yr
Projected 2030 production ~102 Mt/yr
Annual growth ~2%/yr
Per-capita textile production 5.9 kg (1975) → 13 kg (2018)
Industry share of global CO₂ 8–10% (4–5 GtCO₂/yr)
Industry share of industrial water pollution ~20%
Annual textile waste >92 Mt
Annual water consumption 79 trillion litres
Marine primary microplastic pollution from textiles ~35% (190 kt/yr)
Average US consumer purchases 1 garment every 5.5 days
EU clothing-purchase increase 1996–2012 +40%
Average expenditure share on clothing (EU/UK) 30% (1950s) → 12% (2009) → 5% (2020)

(Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 189–192)

Notes — slow-fashion antithesis. Slow fashion is a counter-movement emphasising garment durability, quality manufacturing, fewer purchases per year, repair / mend / second-hand circular practice, transparent supply chains, and local production. It aligns with the EU Sustainable & Circular Textiles Strategy (March 2022) and EPR (Extended Producer Responsibility) for textiles (effective 2025 in many EU member states). (Niinimäki et al. 2020, p. 192; EU Strategy)

Notes — five environmental impact categories. Fast fashion concentrates impact on (i) water use — cotton cultivation 3,800 L/T-shirt; (ii) chemical pollution — 8,000+ chemicals in textile manufacturing, 35% of microplastic ocean pollution; (iii) CO₂ emissions — synthetic fibres (polyester) from petrochemical naphtha; (iv) textile waste — 92 Mt/yr; (v) labour rights — Bangladesh, Cambodia, India production geography concentrated where wages are lowest. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 189–195)

Related terms. Textile fibres (synthetic / natural); microplastics; mechanical recycling; chemical recycling; plastic chemicals; circular economy; petrochemicals (umbrella); polyester (PET); cotton; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR).

Source history. - Niinimäki et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-08: definition, quantified impacts, slow-fashion counter-movement, five environmental-impact categories. - Clark 2022 (ref.pdf, Current Opinion in Green & Sustainable Chemistry) — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): green-chemistry circular-fashion framing.

FEPPS (Future Renewable Energy Performance into the Power System)

Definition. A linear, rule-based power-system simulation model developed by Guerra et al. (2022) to represent the operation of a real power grid with high VRE penetration on an hourly resolution. Distinguished from optimisation-based models (which compute investment decisions endogenously) by its rule-based dispatch following a fixed merit order, with curtailment levels triggered by inflexibility and inertia constraints. (Guerra et al. 2022, Sections 1, 3)

Attributes — model scope.

Element Choice
Country case Spain (limited international interconnections)
Time resolution Hourly
Generation technologies All Spanish technologies: nuclear, coal, CC, CR, TR, hydro (impoundment + diversion), PHS, solar PV, wind, solar thermal, biomass, biogas, marine, geothermal, cogeneration
Approach Rule-based; linear dispatch by merit order
Modelled scenarios Sustainable Transition (ST), Distributed Generation (DG), Global Climate Action (GCA)
Curtailment levels 3 (Levels 1–2 for inflexibility; Level 3 for inertia stability)
Stability constraint Total System Inertia (TSI) ≥ Critical Inertia Level (CIL); ROCOF ≤ ENTSO-E threshold

(Guerra et al. 2022, Sections 3.2–3.4 and Tables 1–2)

Notes — key results. FEPPS finds that the Spanish 2030 ST scenario (33% VRE) produces 157 kg CO₂/MWh and the 2040 ST scenario (35% VRE) produces 159 kg CO₂/MWh — well above the Paris-aligned target of ~75–80 kg CO₂/MWh in 2030 / near zero in 2040. Beyond ~39% VRE, new low-emissions firm technologies are required with emissions ≤113 kg CO₂/MWh, max LCOE €134/MWh, and inertia constant ≥5 s. (Guerra et al. 2022, abstract; Section 4)

Related terms. Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); Inertia (power system); Rate of Change of Frequency (ROCOF); curtailment (VRE); Power system flexibility; energy system models (100% RE analyses).

Source history. - Guerra et al. 2022 — added 2026-05-08: model definition, scope, key 2030/2040 ST findings.

Final investment decision (FID)

Definition. The formal decision by a project’s sponsors and financiers to commit funds to construction and proceed to delivery, marking the transition from project development (feasibility studies, FEED, permitting) into execution. FID is the central inflection point at which financing structures must be in place, contracts executed, and risks allocated. (IEA 2026, pp. 7–8, 15, 23)

Notes — recent CCUS FID activity.

Indicator Value Period
FIDs reached worldwide >30 last 2 years
Total commercial debt raised >USD 15 billion last 2 years
Annual CCUS investment >USD 5 billion 2025
Projects announced for 2035 still pre-FID ~90% as of 2026

(IEA 2026, pp. 7–8)

Notes. A number of projects have been cancelled or withdrawn from government tenders in the face of uncertain financing conditions. Hydrogen and CDR projects in particular have struggled to secure offtake agreements, leading to project cancellations in many regions; in Denmark, 80% of industrial bidders pulled their proposals from a recent auction after cross-chain risks could not be managed. (IEA 2026, p. 8)

Related terms. Bankability; first-of-a-kind (FOAK); cross-chain risk; non-recourse project finance; carbon contract for difference (CCfD).

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, recent FID activity statistics.

First-of-a-kind (FOAK)

Definition. A project, technology configuration or industrial application deployed at commercial scale for the first time, characterised by greater performance and integration uncertainty than subsequent installations of the same technology. FOAK projects typically face higher financing costs, more demanding insurance and contingency requirements, and greater dependence on government-backed risk-sharing mechanisms. (IEA 2026, pp. 8, 21, 23–24)

Notes — FOAK considerations highlighted in the IEA’s 2026 financier survey. (i) Technology risk remains modest if the technology is proven at smaller scales or in other sectors. (ii) Lender scrutiny of performance guarantees, insurance coverage and contingency provisions intensifies during FOAK deployment. (iii) Specialised insurance products are emerging for FOAK operational risks. (iv) Several CCUS projects seeking financing today represent either new applications of existing capture technologies (e.g. capture on more dilute streams) or significant scale-ups, retaining FOAK elements even where underlying technology is well understood. (v) Many of the most valuable lessons (e.g. from Boundary Dam) emerged from unforeseen FOAK operational challenges resolved through experience over time. (IEA 2026, pp. 23–24, 51)

Related terms. Bankability; final investment decision (FID); cross-chain risk; technology readiness level (TRL).

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, FOAK financing considerations.

Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process

Definition. A series of catalytic processes that convert purified syngas (mostly H₂ and CO) into liquid hydrocarbons ranging from gases to waxes via three main reactions: 2H₂ + CO → (CH₂) + H₂O; (2n+1)H₂ + nCO → CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + nH₂O; (2n)H₂ + nCO → CₙH₂ₙ + nH₂O. The product distribution is strongly influenced by operating temperature, pressure, syngas composition and catalyst. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 8)

Attributes — operating regimes.

Variant Temperature Typical product slate
High-temperature FT (HTFT) 310–340 °C (583–613 K) Gasoline, solvent oil, olefins
Low-temperature FT (LTFT) 210–260 °C (483–533 K) ~50% solid wax (C20–C23⁺); aromatics + cyclo-paraffins in liquid

Common catalysts: Fe (HTFT), Co (LTFT). Wax can be hydrocracked to naphtha, kerosene and diesel. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 8)

Notes. FT-SPK (FT-derived synthetic paraffinic kerosene) consists of a high proportion of n- and iso-paraffins with up to 15 wt% cyclo-paraffins, providing high cetane number, high specific energy, and high thermal stability without sulfur or nitrogen impurities. FT-SPK with added aromatics (SPK/A) was certified in 2015. In aviation electrofuels, the FT route is the only currently-certified gas-to-liquid pathway. FT-LB (Biomass gasification + Fischer–Tropsch from lignocellulosic biomass) is identified by Su-ungkavatin et al. as the highest-scoring biofuel pathway for both 2030 and 2050 in their semi-quantitative ranking, owing to a 91% well-to-wake GHG reduction and decoupling from arable land. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 8, 18–19)

Related terms. Synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK); coal gasification; co-electrolysis; methanol synthesis; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); electrofuels.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, HTFT/LTFT regimes, FT-SPK characteristics, FT-LB ranking.

Formaldehyde (HCHO)

Aliases. Methanal; formalin (37–55% aqueous solution); HCHO; oxomethane.

Definition. The simplest aldehyde (HCHO), produced industrially by partial oxidation of methanol over either silver-metal catalyst (~650 °C, 1 bar — BASF / methanol-rich variant) or iron-molybdate catalyst (250–400 °C — Formox process, methanol-lean variant): 2 CH₃OH + O₂ → 2 HCHO + 2 H₂O (and CH₃OH → HCHO + H₂ on Ag). Formaldehyde is sold and shipped as 37–55% aqueous solution (“formalin”, containing methanol stabiliser) or as paraformaldehyde (solid oligomer). It is the principal monomer for amino and phenolic resins (urea-formaldehyde, melamine-formaldehyde, phenol-formaldehyde) and the precursor to polyacetal (polyoxymethylene, POM). (Speight 2019, Chapters 6.5, 11.3.10)

Attributes — production and end-uses.

Indicator Value
Global production ~30 Mt/yr (HCHO basis; ~50 Mt/yr formalin solution)
Synthesis routes silver process (~30%) + Formox iron-molybdate process (~70%)
End-use — urea-formaldehyde (UF) resins ~30% (wood adhesives, particleboard)
End-use — phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins ~12% (plywood, insulation, abrasives)
End-use — melamine-formaldehyde (MF) resins ~8% (laminate decorative surfaces, cooking utensils)
End-use — methylenedianiline (MDA → MDI for PU) ~10%
End-use — polyacetal (POM) ~5%
Other (1,4-butanediol, pentaerythritol, hexamine, etc.) ~35%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5)

Notes — health concerns. Formaldehyde is classified as a Group 1 IARC human carcinogen (nasopharyngeal cancer). Indoor-air emissions from UF / MF resins in particleboard and laminates are regulated (EU E1, US CARB Phase 2), driving low-emission “E0” formulations and isocyanate-based wood adhesives. (Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5)

Related terms. Methanol (commodity); urea-formaldehyde resin; phenol-formaldehyde resin; polyoxymethylene (POM / polyacetal); polyurethane (PU); plastic chemicals; chemicals of concern.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, silver vs Formox routes, end-use shares, health concerns.

Foresight (perfect / limited / myopic) — energy-system modelling

Aliases. Model foresight; planning horizon; decision horizon; perfect foresight; myopic; limited / rolling-horizon foresight.

Definition. The degree of visibility that a multi-period optimisation model has into future system conditions when making investment and operational decisions. Three principal regimes: - Perfect foresight — the model has full visibility of the entire investment horizon (price trajectories, future policies, decommissioning requirements) and optimises over all milestone years jointly. Provides global cost-optimum but assumes unrealistic anticipation. - Limited / rolling-horizon foresight — the investment horizon is divided into overlapping windows; the model solves each window with full visibility within the window, then “rolls” forward, possibly reconsidering some decisions in the next window. Approximates real-world adaptive planning with periodic policy reviews. - Myopic foresight (no foresight) — the model solves only one investment milestone at a time without anticipating future developments; agents face price/policy changes as they occur. Most realistic for short-sighted decision-making but risks lock-in to suboptimal pathways. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 2–3 and Fig. 2)

Attributes — Manuel 2025 systematic-review distribution.

Foresight type Share of ESOM studies (n=308)
Perfect foresight 71%
Myopic (rolling horizon, single-period) 11%
Limited foresight (rolling horizon, multi-period) 2%
Indeterminate / unspecified 16%
Myopic studies in last half-decade (2020–2025) 69% of all myopic studies

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8)

Notes — implications. Choice of foresight regime materially affects results: - Perfect foresight tends toward overly-optimistic decarbonisation pathways with disruptive jumps from one technology to another, “unicorn” assumptions about future cost reductions and infrastructure availability. - Myopic foresight risks lock-in (e.g., natural-gas turbine investment that becomes stranded as carbon prices rise) but reflects how policymakers actually behave under uncertainty. - Limited foresight is a compromise — recent studies show it captures more realistic delayed-investment dynamics while preserving some long-term planning.

The pre-2010 ESOM literature predominantly used perfect foresight; the post-2020 literature is shifting toward myopic and limited variants. Pathway studies should explicitly justify their foresight choice. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 3, 8–9)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); end effects (modelling); pathways (vs scenarios); Integrated Assessment Model (IAM); investment milestones; myopic vs anticipatory planning.

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, three regimes, systematic-review distribution, implications.

End effects and decision horizon (modelling)

Aliases. End-effect distortion; horizon truncation; finite-horizon distortion; decision horizon; planning horizon.

Definition. Distortions in the optimal solution of a finite-horizon optimisation model caused by the model’s terminal date — investments made near the end of the horizon are charged the full installation cost but credited only the operational savings within the horizon, biasing the model toward technologies with low CAPEX / high OPEX (gas turbines) and against high-CAPEX / low-OPEX renewables. The decision horizon is the minimum length of the foresight horizon required so that the first investment year is unaffected by end effects — i.e., extending the model beyond the decision-horizon date does not change the first-year decision. ESOMs are particularly susceptible because their assets often have 30–80 year lifetimes and target dates 20–30 years out. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 3–5; Grinold 1980, 1983 cited)

Attributes — typical end-effect mitigation methods.

Method Description Frameworks using
Discounting apply discount factor DFₘ = 1/(1+d)^(m−m₀) to compress future costs universal; d ~ 1–10%
Salvage value subtract residual undepreciated value of investments still operating at horizon end TIMES, OSeMOSYS
Annuity factor (AFᵢ) spread CAPEX over annuitised payments; technologies compared by within-horizon payments only TEMOA, PyPSA
Truncation (no correction) charge full CAPEX, credit only within-horizon OPEX crude — still common in literature
Horizon extension run model beyond target year, report only pre-target results conservative; high computational cost

(Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 4–5 and eqs. 4–9)

Notes — Manuel 2025 critique. Even with discounting, salvage values and annuity factors, end effects remain present in ESOMs (Grinold 1980, 1983); the methods reduce but do not eliminate distortions. Models with complex long-term formulations (decreasing efficiencies, long-term storage, endogenous cost evolution, carbon-budget constraints) need extended horizons to avoid distorted pathways. The decision horizon is rarely reported, and modellers often choose horizons too short to be safe. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 4–5)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); pathways (vs scenarios); discount rate; salvage value (modelling); annuity factor (modelling); investment milestones.

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, mitigation methods, decision horizon concept, modelling-framework comparison.

Frequency control (power system)

Aliases. Frequency response; primary/secondary frequency control; FFR (fast frequency response).

Definition. A hierarchy of control mechanisms that hold AC grid frequency near its nominal value (50 Hz in Europe, 60 Hz in North America) following a load–generation imbalance. Inertial response (provided automatically by rotating masses or synthetic inertia from converters) acts on sub-second timescales. Primary frequency control (governor response of synchronous generators) corrects deviations within seconds. Secondary frequency control (automatic generation control) restores frequency to nominal within minutes. Tertiary control re-optimises dispatch over longer horizons. (Guerra et al. 2022, pp. 2, 4, 949)

Notes — emerging contributions from non-synchronous sources. Modern Voltage Source Converter (VSC) HVDC interconnections and grid-forming wind/PV converters can provide synthetic inertia plus primary and secondary frequency response, partially compensating for the loss of rotating-mass inertia as conventional thermal plants retire. Fast Frequency Response (FFR) products from battery storage are becoming important ancillary services in high-VRE systems. (Guerra et al. 2022, p. 2 references [19,20])

Related terms. Inertia (power system); Rate of Change of Frequency (ROCOF); Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); battery storage (stationary); Power system flexibility; Critical Inertia Level (CIL).

Source history. - Guerra et al. 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, hierarchy, synthetic-inertia/grid-forming-converter note.

Functional Unit (LCA)

Aliases. FU; UF (FR — Unité Fonctionnelle); reference flow; service unit.

Definition. A quantified description of the function delivered by the system being studied in a Life Cycle Assessment, used as the reference unit against which all environmental impacts are normalised. The functional unit specifies what the system does (function), how much (magnitude), for how long (time / lifetime), to what level (quality / performance threshold). All LCA results — kg CO₂eq, ozone-depletion potential, eutrophication, etc. — are reported per functional unit, allowing direct comparison between alternative systems delivering the same function. (Goessel 2025, pp. 22, 47–48; ISO 14040)

Attributes — typical functional-unit examples.

Sector Typical functional unit
Building (renovation) “1 m² of building over a 50-year reference period” (Goessel)
Transport vehicle “1 vehicle-km” or “1 passenger-km”
Power generation “1 kWh delivered to the grid”
Cement “1 t cement at 32.5 N strength class”
Packaging “1,000 L of beverage packaged + delivered + disposed”
Plastic “1 kg PET resin delivered”
Lighting “1 Mlm·hr of light delivered”
Heat pump “1 kWh of useful heat delivered to building”

(Goessel 2025, p. 22; ISO 14040 examples)

Notes — significance for like-for-like comparison. The choice of functional unit is the most sensitive methodological decision in LCA — comparing two alternatives must be done on the same FU. For example, comparing two renovation strategies must use the same building, same climate, same occupant load. Goessel uses “1 m² of existing building over 50 years” as the FU for all renovation strategies, allowing direct comparison across many strategies on a single Pareto plot. (Goessel 2025, p. 47)

Related terms. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA); Life Cycle Costing (LCC); Embodied carbon (buildings); building renovation (umbrella); ISO 14040.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: FU definition, examples, role in like-for-like LCA comparison.

Fuel cell (aviation)

Definition. An electrochemical device converting hydrogen-based or hydrocarbon-based fuels into electricity (continuously, while fuel is supplied) without combustion, with water vapour and a small amount of heat as the only by-products. Two main variants are considered for aviation: proton/polymer exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFC) and solid oxide fuel cells (SOFC), distinguished by their electrolytes, operating conditions and fuel compatibility. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 23)

Attributes.

Parameter Value
Current power density ~0.75 kW/kg
Required for commercial aircraft ≥2 kW/kg
Energy converter (not storage) continuous output while fuel supplied
First commercial H₂ fuel-cell aircraft (announced) ZeroAvia, 10–20 passengers, ≤555 km
Airbus ZEROe entry-into-service target 2035 (100–200 passengers)

(Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 23, 31)

Notes. Excess electricity from a fuel cell can be stored in batteries as backup. Fuel-cell propulsion is unlikely to be competitive for heavy payloads and long distances — current designs would require ~4× the mass of conventional aircraft engines for the same power output. Hybridisation of fuel cells with hydrogen combustion engines (takeoff/climb on H₂ turbines, cruise on fuel cells) is investigated to reduce fuel consumption and NOₓ emissions. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 23, 31)

Related terms. Hydrogen aviation; PEM electrolyser; solid oxide electrolysis (SOE); turboelectric propulsion; hybrid electric propulsion.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, PEMFC/SOFC distinction, performance constraints.

Fuel cell electric vehicle (FCEV)

Definition. A vehicle propelled by an electric motor whose electricity is generated onboard by a hydrogen fuel cell (rather than drawn from a battery as in a BEV). In practice FCEVs run on two propulsion systems — electricity (powering the motor) and hydrogen (feeding the fuel cell) — sometimes combined with a small battery for transient response. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7–8)

Notes — coverage in the 100% RE systems database. FCEVs are considered the most often next to BEVs within road transport, with 46% of LDV studies covering them. For aviation and marine modes, hydrogen-based propulsion (combustion or fuel-cell) sees relatively higher representation given the limits of battery electrification for long-distance travel. In Europe, road categories (LDV, MDV, HDV, BUS) predominantly rely on BEV with FCEVs less prevalent, reflecting the further move towards electrification, regulatory support and charging infrastructure development. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 18)

Related terms. Battery electric vehicle (BEV); plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV); fuel cell (aviation); hydrogen aviation.

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, coverage, regional patterns.

Grand carénage (French nuclear life-extension programme)

Aliases. Grand carénage (FR); GC; nuclear long-term operation programme.

Definition. A large-scale industrial maintenance and refurbishment programme run by EDF on the existing French nuclear fleet (56 second-generation PWRs of the 900 MW, 1300 MW and N4-1450 MW palliers), aimed at extending operating life from the original 40-year design horizon to 50 or 60 years and beyond. The programme replaces several major components (steam generators, turbines), retrofits post-Fukushima safety upgrades, and brings sûreté requirements towards those of third-generation reactors (EPR-class). It is the principal vehicle for prolongation (life extension) under the periodic ten-yearly safety reviews supervised by the Autorité de sûreté nucléaire (ASN). (RTE 2022, Sections 4.2.3, 4.2.3.2, translated from French)

Attributes — programme parameters.

Indicator Value
Reactor count 56 second-generation PWRs
Original design life 40 years
Target extended life 50 → 60 years (and beyond for some)
ASN generic ruling, palier 900 MW February 2021 (Décision n° 2021-DC-0706) — validated 40 → 50-year extension subject to GC works
Cost provisioning per reactor accounted for in CAPEX amortisation under RTE economic analysis
Assumed in RTE reference trajectory success of GC for all reactors up to 5th periodic review
Closure rhythm post-2045 (if N-scenarios) ~3 reactors / year on average, 2045–2055

(RTE 2022, Sections 4.2.3.1–4.2.3.2, p. 154)

Notes — economic analysis. RTE concludes that GC-based life extension is by far the cheapest source of low-carbon electricity available — production cost (full-cycle including GC) of the existing fleet stays in the 30–40 €/MWh range. This is the primary reason scenarios with maximised existing-fleet life extension (N03) deliver the lowest annualised system cost. The trade-off is that GC commits the system to a finite extension window — by 2060, the entire current fleet will close on age criteria absent a programme of new EPR2 build. (RTE 2022, Sections 11.4, 11.6.5, p. 591)

Notes — ASN safety review process. France has no statutory limit on nuclear plant operating life; authorisations are granted without time limit, with a periodic safety review every 10 years assessing fitness for the next decade. The ASN’s February 2021 avis générique on the 900 MW palier is structuring because it confirmed the 40 → 50-year extension principle subject to extensive Fukushima-era safety improvements being completed under GC. ASN has not yet ruled on similar extensions for the 1300 MW or N4 paliers. (RTE 2022, Section 4.2.3.2, p. 154)

Notes — RTE caution. RTE flags GC as a non-trivial prerequisite, not a given: the programme’s success requires industrial mobilisation, supply-chain capacity, ASN approval at each individual reactor, and political commitment over 20+ years. Scenarios are run also with GC partial failure to test robustness. (RTE 2022, Section 4.2.3.2)

Related terms. Nuclear power (incl. small modular reactors); EPR2 programme; RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 scenarios; Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE); Annualised electricity system cost (RTE 2050); SNBC (Stratégie nationale bas-carbone).

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, ASN 2021 ruling on palier 900 MW, 30–40 €/MWh production cost, role in N-scenarios, programme prerequisites (translated from French).

General Circulation Model (GCM) and Regional Climate Model (RCM)

Aliases. GCM (Global Climate Model); MCG (FR — Modèle de Circulation Générale); RCM (Regional Climate Model); MCR (FR — Modèle de Circulation Régionale).

Definition. Two complementary classes of physics-based numerical climate models: - GCM (Global Climate Model) — solves the coupled ocean-atmosphere-land-cryosphere system at typical resolution 100–300 km horizontal grid, simulating climate evolution over centuries-to-millennia at the global scale. ~35 GCMs are currently maintained worldwide (CMIP5, CMIP6 ensembles). GCMs provide the boundary conditions under various GHG-concentration trajectories (RCPs / SSPs). - RCM (Regional Climate Model) — dynamically downscales the GCM output to higher resolution (typically 10–50 km) over a limited regional domain by solving the same physics equations on a finer grid, with GCM outputs imposed at the regional-domain boundaries. RCMs capture orographic effects, coastal circulation, and small-scale weather systems that GCMs cannot resolve.

The IPCC AR6 (2021–2023) integrates results from 35 GCMs (run by 20 laboratories worldwide) under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6). (Goessel 2025, pp. 56–58)

Attributes — typical resolution.

Model class Horizontal grid Time-step Domain
GCM (CMIP5/CMIP6) 100–300 km hours global
RCM (EURO-CORDEX 44) 50 km hours regional
RCM (EURO-CORDEX 11) 12.5 km hours regional
Convection-permitting (CP-RCM) 1–3 km sub-hourly small region

(Goessel 2025, pp. 56–60)

Notes — uncertainty decomposition. Combined GCM-RCM choice contributes a major share of total uncertainty in regional climate projections — 78% of variance in 2021–2050 mean summer temperature in central Europe (Evin et al. 2021). For longer-horizon projections (2071–2099), RCP-scenario choice becomes the dominant uncertainty (53% of variance). For building-design analysis spanning 30+ years, both GCM-RCM ensemble breadth and RCP scenario choice must be considered. (Goessel 2025, pp. 56–60)

Related terms. EURO-CORDEX; Bias correction (climate); Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs); Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs); CMIP (Coupled Model Intercomparison Project); Integrated Assessment Model (IAM); Climate risk in power-system planning.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: GCM/RCM definition, resolution table, uncertainty decomposition (translated from French).

Glazing technology (windows)

Aliases. Vitrage (FR); double glazing (DG); triple glazing (TG); low-emissivity (low-E) glass; argon-fill; gas-filled glazing.

Definition. A multi-component window-glass assembly designed to balance four conflicting performance objectives: (i) low thermal-loss U-value (insulation), (ii) controlled solar-heat-gain coefficient g (solar gain regulation), (iii) high visible-light transmittance Tv (daylight admission), (iv) protection from UV / break-resistance / acoustic. Modern double / triple glazing combines 2–3 panes of glass separated by warm-edge spacers, filled with argon or krypton gas, and one or two panes coated with thin transparent metal-oxide layers (low-E coatings) that reflect long-wave thermal radiation while transmitting visible light. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35; AFNOR EN 12898)

Attributes — typical glazing performance.

Variant U-value (W/m²K, glass-only) g-value (solar) Tv (visible)
Single glazing 5.6 0.85 0.90
Double glazing (4-12-4 air) 2.8 0.76 0.81
Double glazing low-E + argon (4-16-4) 1.1 0.62 0.78
Triple glazing (4-12-4-12-4 air) 1.5 0.65 0.72
Triple glazing low-E + argon (4-16-4-16-4) 0.5–0.7 0.55 0.69
Triple glazing low-E + krypton (slim-profile) 0.4–0.6 0.50 0.67
Vacuum-insulated glazing (VIG) 0.4–1.0 0.50 0.78
Solar-control glazing (warm climates) 1.6 0.30–0.50 0.50–0.70

(Goessel 2025, Annexe A; manufacturer data)

Notes — frame-conduction effect. The whole-window U-value (Uw) is typically 30–50% higher than the glass-only U-value (Ug) due to frame conduction. Modern Passivhaus-grade triple-glazed wood-aluminium windows achieve Uw ~0.7–0.9 W/m²K. PVC-frame triple glazing achieves Uw ~1.0–1.2; aluminium-frame (without thermal break) can be Uw 2.0+. Frame choice is therefore as important as glass choice for thermal performance. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35)

Notes — Goessel optimisation finding. Window replacement (legacy single → modern triple) typically has long carbon-payback time (8–20 years) due to high embodied carbon of float glass and aluminium frames. Pareto-optimal renovations more often retain existing windows + add adjustable solar protection, especially in moderate climates. Triple glazing dominates only in cold-climate renovations (H1a — Strasbourg, Paris). (Goessel 2025, Sections 3.3–3.4)

Related terms. Building envelope; Building renovation (umbrella); Solar protection (umbrella); Embodied carbon (buildings); Carbon payback time (TRC); RE2020 / RT2012.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: glazing variants table, frame-conduction effect, optimisation finding (translated from French).

Glass

Definition. A class of industrial materials produced by melting raw materials (predominantly sand) at temperatures up to ~1500 °C in a furnace, then forming and finishing. Four main types account for global production: flat glass (30%), container glass (37%), fibre glass (10%) and speciality glass (10%). (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 10)

Attributes. Specific energy consumption for conventional furnaces typically ranges from 4 to 7 GJ per tonne of glass; melting accounts for most of energy demand and emissions. Process emissions account for 13–43% of total emissions depending on recycling rate and glass type. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, pp. 10–11)

Notes. Decarbonisation options include cullet (recycled glass) increases, fuel switching to biogas or hydrogen, oxyfuel combustion (recommended for hydrogen), CCUS, and electrification of heating. Soda ash, limestone and dolomite emit CO₂ when heated, contributing to process emissions. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, pp. 10–11)

Related terms. Cullet; process emissions; carbon capture and storage.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: production process, energy intensity, glass-type breakdown.

Nitrogen fertilisers (umbrella)

Aliases. N-fertilisers; synthetic nitrogen fertilisers; engrais azotés (FR); fertiliser N.

Definition. A category of synthetic fertilisers providing the macronutrient nitrogen essential for plant protein and nucleic-acid synthesis. Globally, ~107 Mt N/yr are applied as ammonia-based synthetic fertilisers (~67% of total N applied to crops; the remainder comes from animal manure and biological nitrogen fixation). The principal nitrogen fertilisers are derived from anhydrous ammonia via further chemical processing into solid / granular / liquid forms easier to transport and field-apply: urea (CO(NH₂)₂), ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃), ammonium sulfate ((NH₄)₂SO₄), calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN), and compound NPK / NP / NK blends. Nitrogen fertilisers feed approximately half the world’s population (Erisman 2008 estimate) and underpin modern food security. (Mingolla & Rosa 2025, pp. 1–3 and Fig. 1; Royal Society 2020, pp. 6–10)

Attributes — global N-fertiliser flows (Mingolla 2025).

Fertiliser product N share (Mt N/yr 2020) Properties
Urea (CO(NH₂)₂) 53.8 (~50% of total N) 46% N by weight, easy transport, slow-release
NPK compound (NP / NK / NPK) 21.3 combined macronutrients
Ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃) 6.1 high N (33%), explosive risk
Urea-ammonium nitrate (UAN) 6.1 liquid, easy fertigation
Ammonium sulfate ((NH₄)₂SO₄) 4.2 high S co-nutrient
Calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN) 3.7 safer than AN
Ammonium phosphate (DAP/MAP) 7.5 combined P + N
Direct ammonia application 3.5 injection into soil
Potassium nitrate (KNO₃) 0.6 combined K + N
Total ammonia for fertiliser 107 Mt N/yr ~70% of global ammonia

(Mingolla & Rosa 2025, p. 3 and Fig. 1)

Notes — emissions across the supply chain. Mingolla 2025 quantifies the cradle-to-grave nitrogen-fertiliser GHG footprint: - Production — ~450–500 Mt CO₂eq/yr (1.3% of global emissions) from ammonia synthesis (mainly NG-SMR + Haber-Bosch). - Transportation — ~30 Mt CO₂eq/yr. - Use phase (field application) — ~660 Mt CO₂eq/yr from N₂O emissions (nitrification / denitrification of applied N) — the dominant share! - Total cradle-to-grave — 1,100–1,300 Mt CO₂eq/yr.

This means field-application N₂O dominates total fertiliser-N emissions (50%+); even with full decarbonisation of production (green ammonia), the application-phase N₂O remains. Precision application (4R nutrient stewardship) and circular nitrogen (anaerobic-digestion recovery from manure) are essential complements. (Mingolla & Rosa 2025, pp. 1–3)

Notes — global supply-chain vulnerability. Mingolla 2025 documents that ~1.8 billion people depend on imported fertilisers or imported natural gas for fertiliser production. Concentrated production geography (~50% of N capacity in 4 countries) creates supply-chain fragility — the 2022 Russia-Ukraine war drove EU N-fertiliser prices up 4× in months and triggered yield losses in import-dependent African countries. Decentralised green-ammonia production at smaller scales (1–10 t/d vs centralised 1,000+ t/d) is a possible resilience strategy. (Mingolla & Rosa 2025, pp. 1–7)

Related terms. Ammonia (as hydrogen carrier); Haber-Bosch process; Blue ammonia and green ammonia; urea; nitrous oxide (N₂O); food security; decentralised production; sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄); phosphate fertiliser.

Source history. - Mingolla & Rosa 2025 — added 2026-05-08: N-fertiliser flow taxonomy, emissions across supply chain, supply-chain-vulnerability framing. - Royal Society 2020 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): fertiliser-supply role of ammonia.

Haber-Bosch process

Definition. The industrial process for ammonia (NH₃) synthesis from hydrogen and nitrogen. Hydrogen is typically produced from natural gas in most regions and from coal in 66% of Asian production. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 12)

Notes. Decarbonising ammonia production requires low-carbon hydrogen production (water electrolysis or fossil-route + CCS), electrified heating, and/or substitution of fossil fuels with bioenergy. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 12)

Related terms. Ammonia (as hydrogen carrier); hydrogen colour taxonomy; carbon capture and storage; steam methane reforming.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition and decarbonisation levers.

Hall-Héroult electrolysis process

Definition. The dominant industrial process for primary aluminium production: electrolysis of aluminium oxide (alumina, refined from bauxite) between a carbon anode and a molten aluminium cathode, governed by 2 Al₂O₃(non-aq) + 3 C(s) → 4 Al(l) + 3 CO₂(g). (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 6)

Attributes. Current processes consume 12.8–16 MWh per tonne of aluminium and emit roughly 1.5 tCO₂/t Al. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 6)

Notes. Newer technologies use inert (carbon-free) anodes that avoid the chemical CO₂ emission, generating pure oxygen instead, though inert anodes increase total energy consumption by ~20%. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Related terms. Inert anode; process emissions.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: chemistry, intensity, inert-anode alternative.

Geothermal energy (next-generation)

Definition. A power and heat generation technology that exploits heat stored in the Earth’s subsurface. Conventional geothermal relies on naturally formed hydrothermal reservoirs (location-constrained); next-generation geothermal — using directional drilling and hydraulic fracturing techniques imported from oil and gas — accesses heat at much greater depth and is not location-dependent. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 149, 7390–7410)

Attributes — capacity, costs and outlook.

Next-gen geothermal LCOE ~USD 230 / MWh (today) 2024
Projected next-gen LCOE reduction by 2035 up to −80% (with innovation, scale, oil-and-gas learnings) 2024–2035
Net 2025 additions (mostly conventional) ~0.5 GW 2025
