2035 capacity (STEPS) 32 GW 2035
2035 capacity (NZE) >55 GW 2035
Technical potential <8 km depth (next-gen) 600 TW (~2,000× current conventional) —
Technical potential <5 km depth 42 TW —

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 149, 7390–7410)

Notes. ~30 countries already have supportive geothermal policies. In Costa Rica, El Salvador, Iceland, Kenya, New Zealand and Nicaragua, geothermal contributes >10% of annual electricity supply. Multiple large-scale enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) projects are scheduled to begin operations in 2026–2027. (IEA ETP 2026, p. 149)

Related terms. Solar PV; wind power; clean energy technologies; pumped hydro energy storage (PHES); levelised cost of energy (LCOE); concentrated solar power (CSP).

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, conventional vs next-gen, cost trajectory, capacity outlook.

General Flow Equation (gas pipeline hydraulics)

Aliases. Fundamental Flow Equation.

Definition. The principal steady-state equation in gas pipeline hydraulics, derived from Bernoulli’s equation, relating volumetric flow rate Q to inlet/outlet pressures, pipe geometry, gas properties and friction. It is used for sizing, capacity calculation, and pressure-drop estimation:

Q = 1.1494 × 10⁻³ · (T_b/P_b) · [(P₁² − e^s · P₂²) / (G · T_f · L_e · Z · f)]^0.5 · D^2.5

where Q is gas flow rate in Sm³/day, T_b/P_b are base temperature and pressure (288.706 K, 101.352 kPa), P₁/P₂ are inlet/outlet absolute pressures, G is specific gravity (0.0696 for H₂), T_f the average flowing temperature, L_e the equivalent pipe length adjusted for elevation, Z the compressibility factor, f the Darcy friction factor, and D the inside diameter. (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 10–11, citing Menon 2005)

Notes — implications for hydrogen pipelines. - Q ∝ √(P₁² − P₂²): the pressure gradient is curved, not linear. - Q ∝ D^2.5: pipe diameter has a strong effect on capacity. - Q ∝ 1/√(G·Z·L·T): higher gravity, compressibility, length or temperature reduce capacity. - For turbulent flow (Re > 4000) the Darcy friction factor is computed iteratively using the Colebrook-White equation. - Friction factor f at typical H₂ transmission conditions (36-inch pipe, 70 bar, 35 m/s outlet velocity) is ~0.0094, with Re ~ 1.65 × 10⁷.

(Khan et al. 2021, pp. 12–13, 22–23)

Related terms. Compressibility factor (Z); Darcy-Weisbach friction factor; Reynolds number; erosional velocity; hydrogen pipeline; pipeline efficiency.

Source history. - Khan et al. 2021 — added 2026-05-08: equation, illustrative numerical values.

HDCJ pathway (hydrotreated depolymerized cellulosic jet)

Definition. A biofuel pathway in which residual biomass is converted to liquid fuels via either pyrolysis (denoted HDCJ-PL) or hydrothermal liquefaction (HDCJ-HTL) for wet substrates. The bio-oil is fractionated by distillation, centrifugation and extraction; the bio-crude oil phase is hydrotreated (deoxygenation, decarboxylation, decarbonylation, hydrogenation) and distilled into liquid fuels including naphtha, kerosene and diesel. Currently under development; not yet ASTM-certified. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 9)

Notes. Pyrolysis bio-oil has higher acidity and weaker thermal stability than HTL bio-oil and so requires more extensive upgrading. Wet biomass (5–35% dry-matter content) is suitable for the HTL route without prior drying. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 8–9)

Related terms. Pyrolysis (PL); hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL); HEFA pathway; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, PL vs HTL variants, certification status.

HEFA pathway (hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids)

Aliases. Hydroprocessed renewable jet (HRJ) — equivalent terminology in aviation literature.

Definition. A biofuel pathway converting triglycerides containing saturated/unsaturated fatty acids (from non-edible oil crops, oleochemical wastes such as waste cooking oil, animal fats, palm fatty acid distillate, tall oil pitch, etc.) into liquid hydrocarbons (naphtha, kerosene, diesel) by hydroprocessing. The pathway sequences hydrogenation (saturating double bonds, releasing propane and free fatty acids), hydrotreating (deoxygenation, decarboxylation, decarbonylation), isomerisation, and hydrocracking, followed by distillation. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 9–10)

Attributes.

Parameter Value
Overall energy efficiency ~75% (vs ~40% for FT-SPK)
Current production capacity ~100,000 t SPK y⁻¹ (2019, Neste) ≈ 0.1 Mt y⁻¹
Maximum blend with conventional kerosene 50 vol%
Variant: HEFA+ (HFP HEFA-SK) high freeze-point HEFA-SK; near final ASTM approval
Variant: HH HEFA-SPK (incl. Bb oil from microalgae Botryococcus braunii) 10 vol% blend, ASTM-approved 2020

(Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 10, 29)

Notes. HEFA is the most mature aviation biofuel pathway at commercial scale; in 2019 it was the dominant route, with current aviation biofuel production essentially deriving from HEFA. The availability and cost of sustainable oleochemical feedstock (waste-based or marginal-land crops) is identified as a limiting factor for scale-up. Supplying the 2045 aviation demand of 16.73 EJ y⁻¹ entirely with HEFA would require ~77 EJ of waste oils and fats, whereas the global potential of waste fats, oils and greases is only ~1 EJ y⁻¹. HEFA from oleochemical wastes is identified as one of the two most promising near-term (2030) biofuel pathways in the semi-quantitative ranking. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 18, 29)

Related terms. Drop-in fuel; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK); CHJ; Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, energy efficiency, capacity, feedstock constraint, near-term ranking.

Heat-wave health risk

Aliases. Vague de chaleur (FR); heat wave; canicule; extreme heat event; heat-related mortality.

Definition. A meteorological phenomenon defined by sustained extreme high temperatures (usually 3+ consecutive days above a regional threshold), with elevated daytime maxima and elevated nocturnal minima preventing physiological recovery. Heat waves cause excess mortality (especially among elderly, infants, chronically-ill), exacerbate respiratory and cardiovascular conditions, and create acute thermal-discomfort and productivity-loss risks for the general population. Climate change is making heat waves more frequent, longer, and more intense — a major adaptation driver for the building sector. (Goessel 2025, pp. 4–7, 202; Vellei 2017 cited; CSTB 2025b)

Attributes — heat-wave reference points.

Indicator Value
French definition (Météo-France) T > 30 °C daytime + T > 18 °C night-time, 3+ consecutive days
2003 European heat wave deaths ~70,000 (peer-reviewed)
France 2003 deaths ~15,000
2022 European heat wave deaths ~62,000
France 2022 deaths ~10,000
SET threshold for serious health risk (Goessel) 30 °C
Population exposure (France) ~70% live in regions with rising heat-wave risk by 2050
Heat-wave projection (RCP8.5, France 2050) 5–10 events/yr (vs 1–2 in 1990)

(Goessel 2025, pp. 4–7, 202; Vellei 2017; INSEE Cassini)

Notes — building-sector implications. Goessel highlights that the thermal comfort (PMV/PPD) models are inadequate for heat-wave conditions because they assume moderate thermal environments; SET-DH above health-risk threshold (30 °C) is the better metric for heat-wave-risk evaluation. Renovation strategies that reduce winter heating demand (heavy insulation) can increase summer overheating risk if not coupled with passive-cooling measures (exterior shading, ventilation, ceiling fans, reflective coatings). Active air-conditioning is a fall-back but adds operational carbon. (Goessel 2025, pp. 11–12, 202; Koelblen 2018)

Notes — adaptation policy. France’s PNACC (Plan National d’Adaptation au Changement Climatique, 2018, revised 2024) identifies building-stock adaptation as a key lever. The French Ministry of Health issues a daily heat-wave-risk alert during summer; designated “rooms cool” (“îlots de fraîcheur” — cooling islands) in cities provide air-conditioned public refuge during canicules. (Goessel 2025, pp. 4–7)

Related terms. Standard Effective Temperature (SET); PMV / PPD (Fanger model); Thermal comfort (umbrella); building renovation (umbrella); Cooling and Heating degree days (CDD / HDD); Climate risk in power-system planning; PNACC (Plan National d’Adaptation au Changement Climatique).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: heat-wave definition, mortality reference points, building-sector implications, French adaptation policy (translated from French).

Heat pump (HP)

Definition. A device that transfers thermal energy from a lower-temperature source (ambient air, ground, wastewater) to a higher-temperature sink, using a small electricity input. Three main types are distinguished: air-source, wastewater-source, and ground-source heat pumps. (Khalili et al. 2026, p. 7)

Attributes.

Parameter Value
Coefficient of performance (COP) ratio of heat output to electricity input
COP sensitivity air-source HP COP drops at low ambient T
Coverage in 100% RE systems database 32% of 1,067 articles
Most used in regions Europe, Northeast Asia (except Middle East where DH dominates)

(Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 12, 18)

Notes. Heat pumps are the leading heating technology in the 100% RE systems database, ahead of electric heating (25%) and combustion boilers (21%). Research confirms that the combination of individual heat pumps and district heating provides the best heating-strategy solution for current and future energy systems. The combination is more efficient than direct electric heating in terms of fuel use. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 12)

Notes — buildings sector deployment (IEA ETP 2026). Global heat-pump sales for heating slowed in 2023 and 2024 after a record 2022 surge, against a backdrop of high interest rates, inflation, energy-price spikes and a weaker construction sector; sales have nevertheless more than doubled over the past decade. China is the world’s largest market (1 in 3 installations in 2024), followed by the United States and the European Union. Upfront costs are typically 2–3× higher than fossil-fuel boilers, while electricity-to-gas price ratios remain unfavourable in many regions (UK ~4×, Germany ~3×). In the STEPS, annual sales double by 2035; in the CPS sales rise 85%; in the NZE Scenario sales nearly double STEPS levels. The performance metric COP (or seasonal COP, SCOP) usually delivers heat that is several multiples of the electric input. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 131, 374–375)

Related terms. District heating (DH); thermal energy storage (TES); sector coupling; load shifting and load shedding; Industrial heat pumps; clean energy technologies.

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, COP framework, leadership in 100% RE database. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: 2024 sales dynamics, electricity-vs-gas price ratios, CPS/STEPS/NZE outlook.

High-value chemicals (HVCs)

Aliases. HVCs; primary chemicals; basic chemicals; cracker olefins and aromatics.

Definition. A standard category in petrochemical industry analysis comprising the largest-volume, lowest-degree-of-derivatisation chemicals that anchor the petrochemical product chain: light olefins (ethylene, propylene), C₄ olefins (butadiene, butenes) and BTX aromatics (benzene, toluene, xylenes). HVCs are co-produced primarily from naphtha and ethane steam cracking, supplemented by refinery FCC, catalytic reforming, on-purpose technologies (PDH, MTO, MTA, metathesis), and emerging bio/CCU pathways. Together, the HVCs are the gateway from fossil-fuel feedstocks to the >800 Mt/yr global chemical-product portfolio. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 1; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727; Speight 2019, Chapter 6)

Attributes — global HVC production (2013 / recent baselines).

HVC Global production Principal source
Ethylene ~150 Mt/yr Steam cracking (naphtha 50%, ethane 30%, others 20%)
Propylene ~110 Mt/yr Steam cracking ~50%, FCC ~30%, PDH 15%, MTO/MTP small
C4 olefins (butadiene + butenes) ~50 Mt/yr Steam-cracker C4 stream; FCC C4 stream
BTX aromatics ~117 Mt/yr Catalytic reforming ~40%, steam-cracker pygas ~57%, MTA ~3%
Total HVCs ~430 Mt/yr
Steam-cracker share of HVCs ~62% Naphtha + ethane crackers
Refinery share of HVCs ~35% FCC + catalytic reformer
On-purpose share of HVCs ~3% PDH + MTS + MTO + MTA

(Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 2)

Notes — defossilisation challenge. Zanon-Zotin et al. find that under stringent climate scenarios, alternative carbon feedstocks (biomass, CO₂ via CCU, recycled plastics) could supply up to 62% of total chemical-sector feedstock by 2050. Achieving this requires major scale-up of biomass mobilisation, electrolytic hydrogen, CCS, and on-purpose biomass-to-HVC routes (bionaphtha steam cracking, bioethanol-dehydration to ethylene, biomethanol-to-olefins/aromatics, ethanol-to-butadiene). Even so, oil-derived naphtha cracking persists in their models throughout the 21st century via “gasoline-naphtha substitution flexibility” — refinery streams that would have made gasoline are diverted to HVC production as transport-fuel demand falls. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, pp. 2–3 and Fig. 2)

Notes — ETP-2026 alignment. IEA ETP-2026 names “near-zero ammonia and methanol” production as the principal chemical-sector decarbonisation lever; HVCs are the next layer down. Bionaphtha + biomethanol + electrolytic hydrogen are the three input vectors that anchor near-zero HVCs in the ETP architecture. (IEA ETP 2026, p. 16; cross-ref to Near-zero emissions materials)

Related terms. Steam cracking (vapocracking); catalytic cracking (FCC); catalytic reforming; naphtha; BTX aromatics; methanol-to-olefins (MTO); methanol-to-aromatics (MTA); propane dehydrogenation (PDH); olefins; near-zero emissions materials; non-energy use of fossil fuels; petrochemicals (umbrella).

Source history. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: global production volumes, refinery vs cracker vs on-purpose split. - Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: defossilisation pathways, 62% alternative-feedstock share by 2050, gasoline-naphtha substitution dynamic. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): industrial HVC routes and conversions. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): near-zero chemicals architecture.

HBI trade strategy (relocation of ironmaking)

Aliases. Green-iron trade; HBI export; ironmaking relocation; cross-border DRI value chain.

Definition. A green-steel decarbonisation strategy in which the energy-intensive ironmaking step (DRI production from iron ore using green hydrogen) is relocated to countries with abundant low-cost renewable energy and competitive green-H₂ production (Australia, Brazil, Chile, Morocco, Saudi Arabia, Namibia), while the steelmaking step (DRI → liquid steel in EAF) and downstream rolling / processing remain in the importing country (typically the EU). The HBI form (Hot Briquetted Iron — DRI compacted into briquettes) is preferred for sea transport because it has higher density and is less prone to re-oxidation than direct DRI. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 1, 7; cross-ref Hot briquetted iron)

Attributes — strategic logic.

Aspect Description
Geographic split ironmaking → low-cost renewable countries; steelmaking → demand centres
Driver renewable-electricity-cost differential (Spain ~€40/MWh vs Germany €100+/MWh)
H₂ cost differential competitive locations: ~€2/kg; high-cost: ~€5/kg
Cost saving on iron up to 30–40% lower per tonne DRI
Trade product HBI (briquetted DRI), shippable like coal
EU market access via CBAM-aligned border adjustment for embedded emissions
Domestic value retained EAF + steelmaking + rolling + downstream processing
Lost value ironmaking labour, capex, taxes

(Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 1, 7)

Notes — Johnson 2025 modelling output. Under the EU ETS + CBAM framework, Johnson finds the HBI-trade strategy is cost-optimal for European steel-makers from ~2030 onwards: domestic green-H₂ would be too expensive vs imported HBI from Australia / Morocco / Chile. The result is a partial reconfiguration of the global steel value chain — energy-intensive ironmaking relocates internationally; downstream processing remains co-located with end-use demand. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 1, 7)

Notes — political tension. The HBI-trade strategy is contentious in EU policy circles because it implies loss of integrated steel manufacturing in Europe (loss of high-paid industrial jobs in ironmaking communities), even as climate-emissions are reduced. Trade unions and industrial-policy advocates push for domestic green-H₂ deployment instead. The tension between climate cost-optimisation and industrial-base preservation is one of the principal political debates around the EU ETS / CBAM / green-steel transition. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 7–8)

Related terms. Hot briquetted iron (HBI); H2-DRI-EAF route; Direct reduced iron (DRI); Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM); EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); decarbonisation race; deep reindustrialisation; carbon leakage; near-zero emissions materials.

Source history. - Johnson et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, strategic logic, modelling output, political tension.

Hot briquetted iron (HBI)

Definition. A transportable, briquetted form of direct reduced iron (DRI) used when iron-ore reduction and steelmaking facilities are not co-located. HBI carries the “emission-free” iron content from a reduction site to remote steel operations, e.g. for export of low-emission iron pellets from Europe. (Kushnir et al. 2020, pp. 5, 10)

Related terms. Direct reduced iron; direct reduction; electric arc furnace.

Source history. - Kushnir et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-07: definition and transport role.

Hybrid electric propulsion

Definition. A family of aviation propulsion configurations that combine an electric motor (powered by batteries and/or a fuel cell) with a (hydrogen) gas turbine to deliver mechanical power to the aircraft propulsor (propeller, fan, or shaft). Two parameters quantify the relative contributions: the degree of energy hybridisation (HE), the share of stored battery energy in total energy supplied (HE = 0 if no battery, HE = 1 if fully battery-powered); and the degree of power hybridisation (HP), the share of mechanical power supplied by electric motors (HP = 1 if only electric motors propel the aircraft). (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 22)

Attributes — main configurations.

Configuration HE HP Notes
All-electric (full electric) 1 1 Battery only; no hydrocarbon fuel or H₂
Parallel hybrid electric 0–1 0–1 Mechanical power from both gas turbine and electric motor; gearbox required
Series hybrid electric 0–1 1 Generator (driven by gas turbine) charges battery and powers electric motor
Fuel-cell electric 0–1 1 Fuel cell powers electric motor; batteries optional backup
Full turboelectric 0 1 Gas-turbine-driven generator powers electric motor; no battery
Partial turboelectric 0 0–1 Mechanical power partially diverted to generator + electric motor

(Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 22–24, Fig. 17)

Notes. The integration of electrical components introduces mass penalties; benefits are achieved by optimising aircraft design (boundary-layer ingestion, wingtip propulsors, blended wing body). NASA’s STARC-ABL demonstrated 12% fuel-burn reduction; Wright ECO-150R demonstrated 44% reduction. NASA’s N3-X turboelectric BWB demonstrated ~63% energy and 90% NOₓ reductions versus conventional configurations. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 24)

Related terms. Turboelectric propulsion; fuel cell (aviation); hydrogen aviation; lithium-ion battery (aviation); blended wing body (BWB).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, HE/HP framework, configuration table.

HYBRIT

Definition. A Swedish hydrogen-direct-reduction (H-DR) initiative — formally HYdrogen BReakthrough Ironmaking Technology — comprising a research project and a company (HYBRIT AB), set up as a joint venture of the steel producer SSAB, the iron-ore producer LKAB, and the utility Vattenfall. (Kushnir et al. 2020, p. 1 and Abbreviations p. 12)

Attributes — milestones (Kushnir et al. 2020, Fig. 2, p. 4).

Phase Period Capacity
Prestudy 2016–2017 —
Pilot design and construction 2017–2020 —
Pilot 2020–2024 1 t/h
Demonstration 2025–2035 1/8 to 1/4 of full scale
Full operation (assumed) 2040 —

Notes. HYBRIT is identified as the centrepiece of the Swedish steel TIS, intended to develop the inter-actor cooperations needed to overcome systemic transition barriers. Initial funding (pilot and research programme) came in part from the Swedish Energy Agency. The HYBRIT consortium is also developing a 100 m³ hard-rock cavern for hydrogen storage in Sweden as part of the steelmaking-decarbonisation programme. (Kushnir et al. 2020, pp. 7, 10; cf. Miocic et al. 2023, Table 3, p. 78)

Related terms. Hydrogen direct reduction; technological innovation system; engineered rock cavern.

Source history. - Kushnir et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-07: definition, consortium, milestones, role within Swedish steel TIS. - Miocic et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: cross-reference to engineered-rock-cavern hydrogen-storage component.

Hydrogen

Definition. The lightest chemical substance and a low-carbon energy carrier of central interest for the decarbonisation of transportation, power, heating and fuel-intensive industries. Hydrogen has the highest gravimetric energy density of all known substances (120 kJ g⁻¹) but the lowest atomic mass of any substance (1.00784 u), and as such has a relatively low volumetric energy density. (Miocic et al. 2023, abstract and p. 73, citing NIST 2022; Hanley et al. 2018; McPherson et al. 2018)

Extended definition. Because of its small size, low molecular weight, low viscosity, low density and positive buoyancy over c. −251 °C, hydrogen gas is highly diffusive. It has low solubility in water, although solubility rises with increasing pressure. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 73, citing Chabab et al. 2020)

Attributes. Physical properties at NTP (293 K, 101 325 Pa).

Parameter Value
Molecular weight 1.09784 u
Molar mass 2.01594 g mol⁻¹
Triple-point temperature 13.8 K
Triple-point pressure 7.041 kPa
Critical-point temperature 32.938 K
Critical-point pressure 1.2858 MPa
Density at NTP 0.08990 kg m⁻³
Viscosity at NTP 89.48 µPoise
Solubility in water at NTP 0.0016 g gas per kg water
Diffusion coefficient at NTP 0.000061 m² s⁻¹
Diffusion velocity at NTP <0.02 m s⁻¹
Buoyant velocity 1.2–9 m s⁻¹
Specific heat at NTP 14.85 kJ (kg K)⁻¹
Thermal conductivity at NTP 0.187 W (m K)⁻¹
Flammability limits in air 4–75 vol%
Explosion limits in air 15–59 vol%
Auto-ignition temperature in air 793–1023 K (mean 858 K)

(Miocic et al. 2023, Table 1, p. 74, citing NIST 2022)

Notes. Hydrogen density, viscosity and solubility in pure water all vary with reservoir depth; for a hypothetical reservoir under a geothermal gradient of 33 °C km⁻¹ and a hydrostatic gradient of 10 kPa m⁻¹, density and energy density rise sharply over the first ~1500 m and then plateau, while viscosity and solubility rise more linearly with depth. Salinity of the reservoir brine influences solubility. (Miocic et al. 2023, Fig. 1, p. 74)

Notes — energy-system role. Hydrogen has the highest energy per mass compared to other chemical fuels and is described as an ideal candidate for handling the intermittency of renewable generation. It can be stored in gas, liquid or solid state and does not change over time if unused, making it suitable for generating units and other mission-critical energy uses. It is viewed as a core element in the development and growth of hydrogen and fuel technologies in portable, stationary and transportation applications. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 28)

Notes — aviation applications. All sustainable aviation pathways examined by Su-ungkavatin et al. require hydrogen (with the exception of pure battery-electric SA), whether for hydrogenation of biofuels (3–75-fold more H₂ per MJ than fossil kerosene), production of electrofuels (~169 Mt H₂ to satisfy 16.73 EJ of FT electrofuels in 2045), or for direct combustion / fuel-cell use as cryogenic LH2. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 11, 28–29)

Related terms. Underground hydrogen storage; hydrogen storage; hydrogen colour taxonomy; town gas; hydrogen aviation.

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: physical properties, behavioural traits, and depth-dependence note. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: energy-system role and storage-state characterisation. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: aviation-pathway demands.

Hydrocracking (HCK)

Aliases. Hydrocracker; HCK; hydrocracking unit (HCU).

Definition. A petroleum-refining process in which heavy petroleum fractions (vacuum gas oil, hydrowax, residue) are converted at 300–450 °C and 70–200 bar over a bifunctional Ni-Mo or Ni-W sulfide catalyst on an acidic support (zeolite or amorphous silica-alumina) in the presence of hydrogen. The combination of cracking (acid sites) and hydrogenation (metal sites) produces high-quality middle distillates (jet, diesel) and light naphtha with low sulfur, low aromatic and high cetane content. Hydrocracking is the second-largest hydrogen consumer in a refinery (after hydrotreating). (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 2)

Attributes — typical operating envelope.

Indicator Value
Reactor temperature 300–450 °C
Reactor pressure 70–200 bar
Catalyst Ni-Mo (or Ni-W) sulfide on zeolite or amorphous SiO₂-Al₂O₃
Conversion 60–100% (single- vs two-stage)
H₂ consumption 200–400 Nm³/m³ feed (1.5–3 wt%)
Jet+diesel yield 50–80% (depending on severity)
Naphtha yield 10–25%
LPG yield 3–8%
Octane of HCK naphtha low (~50–55 RON) — sent to reformer
Cetane of HCK diesel high (~50–60)

(Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Notes — role in defossilising chemicals. Zanon-Zotin emphasise hydrocracking as a key flexibility lever in fuel-oriented refineries: as gasoline demand falls (transport electrification), refiners can re-route hydrocracker output toward jet and chemical naphtha, prolonging the role of fossil oil throughout the 21st century. Hydrocrackers also process bionaphtha and waste-plastic-derived oils when these feedstocks scale up. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, pp. 2–3)

Related terms. Catalytic cracking (FCC); catalytic reforming; naphtha; high-value chemicals (HVCs); steam methane reforming (SMR); refinery-petrochemical integration.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, conditions, yields, hydrogen consumption. - Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: flexibility role in 21st-century refinery transformations.

Hydrotreating (HDS / HDN / HDM)

Aliases. Hydrodesulphurisation (HDS); hydrodenitrogenation (HDN); hydrodemetalisation (HDM); hydrofining; hydroprocessing.

Definition. A family of catalytic refinery treating processes in which hydrocarbon fractions are reacted with hydrogen at 280–400 °C and 30–130 bar over a sulfided Co-Mo or Ni-Mo (or Ni-W for higher severity) on alumina catalyst to remove heteroatom contaminants — sulphur (HDS, → H₂S), nitrogen (HDN, → NH₃), oxygen (HDO, → H₂O) and metals (HDM, capture on catalyst). Hydrotreating also saturates olefins and aromatics. Every refinery stream that goes to a fuel pool or to a downstream catalyst-sensitive unit (FCC, reformer) is hydrotreated; HDS is by far the highest-volume hydrotreating duty. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3 hydrotreating section)

Attributes — typical operating envelopes by feed.

Feed Temperature Pressure Catalyst H₂ consumption Sulfur removal target
Naphtha (reformer feed) 280–340 °C 30–60 bar Co-Mo / Al₂O₃ 0.05–0.2 wt% <0.5 ppm
Kerosene / jet 320–360 °C 40–80 bar Co-Mo / Al₂O₃ 0.1–0.4 wt% <10 ppm (jet)
Diesel ULSD 340–380 °C 60–100 bar Ni-Mo / Al₂O₃ 0.4–0.8 wt% <10 ppm
FCC feed VGO 360–400 °C 80–130 bar Ni-Mo / Al₂O₃ 0.7–1.2 wt% varies
Atmospheric residue 370–400 °C 130–200 bar guard + Ni-Mo 1.2–2.0 wt% varies

(Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Notes — global hydrogen demand. Hydrotreating is the largest refinery hydrogen consumer (along with hydrocracking). Global refinery H₂ demand ~50 Mt/yr, of which ~80% comes from steam methane reforming (SMR) and the rest from catalytic-reformer co-product H₂. Tightening fuel-sulphur specifications (ULSD 10 ppm, IMO 2020 marine 0.5%, jet 10–15 ppm) have driven sustained growth in hydrotreating capacity since the 2000s. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Notes — defossilisation linkage. Hydrotreating is the gateway for feeding bionaphtha, HVO/HEFA renewable diesel, and chemically-recycled-plastic oils into petrochemical and fuel pools — these alternative feedstocks contain heteroatoms (oxygen, nitrogen, chlorine, metals) that must be removed before downstream catalyst-sensitive units. Replacing SMR-grey H₂ with electrolytic green H₂ in hydrotreating is one of the largest H₂-substitution levers in refinery decarbonisation roadmaps. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 3; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Related terms. Petroleum refining (umbrella); catalytic reforming; catalytic cracking (FCC); hydrocracking; steam methane reforming (SMR); steam cracking (vapocracking); naphtha; refinery-petrochemical integration; bionaphtha.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, operating envelopes by feed, global demand. - Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: defossilisation linkage.

Hydroformylation (oxo synthesis)

Aliases. Oxo synthesis; OXO process; Roelen reaction; carbonylation of olefins.

Definition. A homogeneous-catalysis industrial reaction in which an olefin (R-CH=CH₂) reacts with carbon monoxide and hydrogen (syngas) to form an aldehyde with one additional carbon atom: R-CH=CH₂ + CO + H₂ → R-CH₂-CH₂-CHO. The process operates at 70–200 °C and 10–300 bar over a homogeneous Co or (modern, dominant) Rh complex catalyst with phosphine or phosphite ligands. The aldehydes are generally hydrogenated downstream to “oxo-alcohols” — n-butanol, 2-ethylhexanol (2-EH), iso-nonanol — used as solvents and as plasticiser-alcohol precursors. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7 olefin chemistry)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global oxo-aldehyde + alcohol production ~12 Mt/yr
Largest output — 2-ethylhexanol (2-EH) ~3.5 Mt/yr (DEHP plasticiser precursor)
n-butanol ~3 Mt/yr (solvent, butyl acrylate)
iso-nonanol (INA) ~1 Mt/yr (DINP plasticiser precursor)
Catalyst (modern) Rh-bisphosphite (LP Oxo / Ruhrchemie / Mitsubishi / UCC)
n/iso ratio (Rh-modified) 20:1 → 100:1 (favours linear)
End-use — phthalate plasticisers ~50% (via 2-EH and INA → DEHP/DINP)
End-use — solvents (butyl acetate, etc.) ~25%
End-use — acrylates (butyl acrylate) ~15%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7)

Notes — significance. Oxo synthesis is one of the largest-scale industrial applications of homogeneous catalysis (alongside Cativa acetic-acid). Modern Rh-bisphosphite catalysts deliver near-quantitative yields and tunable n/iso selectivity. The reaction is a major demand sink for syngas (CO + H₂) — coupling refining, gasification, and downstream petrochemicals. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7)

Related terms. Olefins; propylene; ethylene; syngas; methanol synthesis (electrofuels and biofuels); plasticizers (phthalate esters); high-value chemicals (HVCs); C1 chemistry.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, Roelen reaction, oxo-alcohol product taxonomy, plasticiser linkage.

HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning) — buildings

Aliases. HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning); CVC (FR — Chauffage, Ventilation, Climatisation); building services; mechanical / electrical (M&E).

Definition. The umbrella term for the systems that provide thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and humidity control in buildings — typically about 50–70% of total building operational energy in temperate climates. HVAC systems comprise (i) heating production (boilers, heat pumps, district heat); (ii) cooling production (chillers, AC units, reversible heat pumps); (iii) heat distribution (radiators, underfloor heating, fan-coils, ducted air); (iv) ventilation (mechanical ventilation, air-handling units, MVHR); (v) controls (thermostats, BMS — Building Management Systems). HVAC system selection is one of the principal renovation-strategy categories in Goessel’s optimisation methodology. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–41)

Attributes — HVAC sub-system taxonomy.

Sub-system Sub-categories Examples
Heating production combustion boiler, heat pump, district heating, electric resistance gas/oil/biomass boiler; ASHP/GSHP; CET
Cooling production reversible HP, chiller, evaporative, passive split AC; reversible ASHP; chilled water
Heat distribution radiators (low-/high-T), underfloor, fan-coil, ducted air wall radiators (60/45 °C); plancher chauffant (35 °C)
Ventilation natural, single-flux, double-flux MVHR VMC simple flux hygro; VMC double flux
Domestic hot water combined-boiler, dedicated tank, heat-pump water heater CET; CESI
Controls thermostatic, programmable, BMS, smart TRV (thermostatic radiator valve); BMS
Auxiliary pumps, fans, control systems ECM circulator pumps; demand-controlled fans

(Goessel 2025, Annexe A)

Notes — Goessel optimisation finding. HVAC-system replacement is consistently part of Pareto-optimal renovation strategies — pure envelope upgrades are not sufficient alone. Heat-pump replacement of legacy boilers (especially oil) is the highest single-measure CO₂-saving lever; combined with envelope insulation, deep-renovation strategies typically reduce HVAC energy demand by 60–85%. (Goessel 2025, Sections 3.3–3.4)

Notes — IAQ vs energy trade-off. Indoor Air Quality (IAQ) and energy efficiency are inherently in tension — fresh-air ventilation removes pollutants but loses heat. MVHR resolves this by recovering ~80% of ventilation heat. Modern French RE2020 mandates minimum CO₂ ventilation rates (~30 m³/h per occupant) regardless of energy implications. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35)

Related terms. Heat pump (HP); Mechanical ventilation (VMC / MVHR); Domestic Hot Water (DHW / ECS); Coefficient of Performance (COP / SCOP); building renovation (umbrella); RE2020 / RT2012; air conditioning; condensing gas boiler.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: HVAC umbrella definition, sub-system taxonomy, Goessel optimisation finding, IAQ-vs-energy trade-off.

Hydrogen aviation

Definition. A family of sustainable-aviation systems in which hydrogen is used as the primary energy carrier — either burned directly in modified gas turbines or piston engines, or converted to electricity in fuel cells that drive electric propulsion. Onboard hydrogen storage is in cryogenic liquid form (LH₂) at below −253 °C (20 K) in double-walled vacuum-insulated tanks. Identified by Su-ungkavatin et al. as the only available option for long-range aviation completely decoupled from fossil-based hydrocarbon fuels. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, abstract; pp. 17, 30–31)

Notes — challenges. Mass penalty of the storage system is currently ~2× the conventional kerosene-based APU. Cryogenic LH₂ has a high boil-off rate and small molecule size, raising leak-related safety concerns. Conversely H₂ has lower flammability than kerosene, a higher auto-ignition temperature (550 °C vs 300 °C) and rapid dispersion in air. Newly developed materials for hydrogen tanks are expected to reach 10–21 kWh/kg gravimetric storage-system energy density, competitive with conventional storage (~8.9 kWh/kg). (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 17, 31)

Notes — example projects. Airbus ZEROe targets 100–200-passenger entry into service by 2035 (with hydrogen combustion-mode and fuel-cell variants). The A380 MSN1 demonstrator powered by H₂ combustion is expected to fly by 2026. Boeing Phantom Eye, ZeroAvia and the AHEAD MFBWB project illustrate further variants. Ammonia-based aviation (e.g. ZAPturbo) is a related but separate avenue for the same underlying decarbonisation aim. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 17, 20–21, 23, 32)

Related terms. Liquid hydrogen storage; fuel cell (aviation); turboelectric propulsion; hybrid electric propulsion; ammonia (as hydrogen carrier); blended wing body (BWB).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, challenges, example projects.

Hub and cluster model (CCUS)

Definition. A CCUS deployment configuration in which multiple emitters share a common CO₂ transport and storage infrastructure (typically operated as a regulated or jointly-owned vehicle), allowing aggregation of supply and distribution of construction, volume and revenue risk among multiple participants. Hubs are typically organised as joint ventures or special-purpose vehicles spanning capture, transport and storage segments, with capacity bookings allocated by contract. (IEA 2026, pp. 7, 22, 26, 47)

Attributes — examples.

Project Country Configuration
Northern Lights Norway Offshore storage hub serving multi-emitter and cross-border CO₂ from Norwegian and European sources
Porthos / Aramis Netherlands Open-access transport-and-storage operated by SOEs (EBN, Gasunie, Port of Rotterdam)
Net Zero Teesside / NEP United Kingdom Cluster combining gas-fired CCUS power and offshore Endurance storage
Kalundborg Hub Denmark Industrial cluster integrating SLB Capturi capture with shared transport infrastructure
Jubail CCS hub Saudi Arabia Industrial cluster led by national oil company

(IEA 2026, pp. 26, 38, 39, 44)

Notes. Hub and cluster models effectively distribute risk among participants, but they may also introduce greater complexity in contracts and interfaces. Cross-chain risk amplifies in hub structures: 80% of industrial bidders pulled their proposals from a recent Danish auction after these risks could not be managed. The IEA observes that hubs are well-suited to regions with regulated infrastructure frameworks (UK regulated asset base; Dutch SOE-led deployment), while in North America private partnerships have advanced lower-cost projects without formal hub structures. (IEA 2026, pp. 8, 22, 24, 47)

Related terms. Cross-chain risk; regulated asset base (RAB); take-or-pay/store-or-pay contract; final investment decision (FID); non-recourse project finance; bankability.

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, project examples, risk-distribution role.

Hydrogen charging (H-charging)

Definition. A laboratory technique for inducing hydrogen absorption into metal specimens, accomplished through electrochemical, chemical or gaseous methods. Gaseous H-charging using high-pressure gas best simulates pipeline transport conditions but requires specialised equipment and poses safety risks. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 376)

Notes. In electrochemical H-charging, a specimen is held as the cathode in an electrolyte (e.g. 0.1 M NaOH with 3.3 g/L NH₄SCN as a recombination poison), with a potentiostat applying a constant current to promote the hydrogen evolution reaction at the steel surface; charging current density and time are derived from prior permeation tests via the Devanathan-Stachursky method (per ISO 17081). Hydrogen concentration correlates with the square root of charging current density per the relation C_H = K · √i. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, pp. 379–380)

Related terms. Hydrogen embrittlement; hydrogen permeation test; slow strain rate test; fatigue crack growth rate test.

Source history. - Ghadiani et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition, electrochemical method, current-concentration relation.

Hydrogen colour taxonomy

Definition. A naming convention that assigns colour labels to hydrogen production processes based on feedstock, energy source, and production method. The “primary colour” refers to the most commonly used label for a process; “alternative colours” refer to less common labels. The taxonomy is not standardised and the literature differs over which colour applies to a given process. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 75 and Table 2, p. 76, citing Newborough and Cooley 2020)

Extended definition. A preferable differentiation for hydrogen production processes is to consider the life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions related to both the production process itself and other related processes (e.g. mining of fuel). (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 76, citing Parkinson et al. 2019)

Hydrogen Combined Cycle (H₂ CC)

Definition. A combined-cycle power plant fuelled by hydrogen and used for central, decoupled electricity generation; envisaged in CCS-bridge scenarios in which hydrogen is centrally produced (e.g. via gasification or reforming with carbon capture) and delivered by pipeline to the consumption centre. (Baufumé et al. 2011, pp. 8810–8811)

H2-DRI-EAF route (hydrogen-based green steel)

Aliases. H₂-DRI-EAF; green steel; hydrogen direct-reduced iron + electric arc furnace.

Definition. A two-step low-emission primary-steelmaking route in which iron ore (typically as pelletised hematite) is reduced to direct-reduced iron (DRI / sponge iron) using green hydrogen as the reducing agent in a shaft furnace at 800–1100 °C, then melted and refined into liquid steel in an electric arc furnace (EAF). The reduction reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3 H₂ → 2 Fe + 3 H₂O replaces the carbon-based reduction of the conventional blast-furnace–basic-oxygen-furnace (BF-BOF) route, eliminating direct CO₂ emissions from ironmaking. The H₂-DRI-EAF chain is identified by IEA, IPCC, and Johnson et al. 2025 as the leading low-emission primary-steel option for the 2026–2050 deployment window. (Johnson et al. 2025, p. 1; cross-ref Hydrogen direct reduction (H-DR), Direct reduced iron (DRI), Electric arc furnace (EAF), HYBRIT)

Attributes — Johnson 2025 cost-competitiveness benchmarks (EU market, 2026 onwards).

Indicator Value
H₂ consumption ~55 kg H₂ / t steel (low-emission case); ~70 kg / t (with NG-DRI partial replacement)
Electricity consumption (EAF + auxiliaries) ~600–800 kWh / t steel
CO₂ intensity (low-emission H₂-DRI-EAF) 64 kg CO₂ / t steel (Johnson “low-emission” reference)
CO₂ intensity (high-emission H₂-DRI-EAF, with grid emissions) 437 kg CO₂ / t steel
BF-BOF reference CO₂ intensity ~1.9 t CO₂ / t steel
H₂ price for cost-competitiveness 2025 €1.91 / kg H₂
H₂ price for cost-competitiveness 2026 (post-ETS revision) €4.12 / kg H₂ (low-emission case)
First-mover competitive locations (EU market) Northern Scandinavia, Iberian peninsula, Portugal — €4.1–5.5 / kg H₂
Free-allocation period (EU ETS) 2026–2033 for H₂ benchmark
Existing pilot / first-of-a-kind plants HYBRIT (Sweden, 2026), H2 Green Steel / Stegra (Sweden, 2026), thyssenkrupp Tk (Germany, 2027–2030), Salzgitter, ArcelorMittal Sestao

(Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 2–4; cross-ref HYBRIT entry)

Notes — comparison with NG-DRI-EAF. Natural-gas-based DRI (Midrex, Energiron) is the established commercial DRI technology — used for ~115 Mt/yr of DRI production globally (chiefly in the Middle East, India, Russia). Switching from NG to H₂ as the reducing agent retains the DRI–EAF process flow while eliminating most direct CO₂ emissions. Johnson 2025 finds NG-DRI-EAF is not competitive with BF-BOF under realistic NG prices (€30–60/MWh), even with the EU ETS, except under extreme assumptions of extended free-allocation. H₂-DRI-EAF therefore is the only low-emission route that is structurally competitive on the EU market under the new ETS + CBAM framework. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 3–5)

Notes — global market dynamics. Johnson’s modelling identifies a global decarbonisation race in which countries with low-cost renewable hydrogen (Australia, Brazil, Chile, Morocco, Saudi Arabia) become competitive green-iron exporters; the EU shifts toward importing low-emission DRI (HBI form) for processing in domestic EAFs. The result is a partial reconfiguration of the global steel value chain — energy-intensive ironmaking relocates; downstream steel processing remains co-located with end-use demand. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 2–7)

Related terms. Hydrogen direct reduction (H-DR); Direct reduced iron (DRI); Electric arc furnace (EAF); HYBRIT; BF-BOF route; Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM); EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); near-zero emissions materials; hot briquetted iron (HBI); low-emissions hydrogen.

Source history. - Johnson et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, cost-competitiveness benchmarks (€4.12/kg H₂ threshold), EU market dynamics, NG-DRI-EAF comparison, global decarbonisation race.

Hydrogen direct reduction (H-DR)

Definition. A primary-steel iron-reduction process in which hydrogen replaces coke (in the BF-BOF route) or natural gas (in NG-DR) as the iron-ore reductant, producing direct reduced iron (DRI) for downstream steelmaking in an electric arc furnace. (Kushnir et al. 2020, p. 1; Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 9)

Notes. H-DR is identified by Kushnir as the only option at sufficient technology readiness level (TRL) for Sweden to retain primary-steel capability while meeting its 2045 climate targets. The Swedish HYBRIT consortium (SSAB, LKAB, Vattenfall) targets full-scale H-DR operation by 2040, preceded by pilot (2018–2024, 1 t/h) and demonstration (2025–2035, 1/8–1/4 of full scale) phases. Estimated electricity demand: full conversion of the Swedish steel industry would require ~17 TWh/y of new generation capacity, of which 10.5 TWh/y for the reduction step alone. (Kushnir et al. 2020, pp. 2–3, Fig. 2 p. 4, p. 10)

Notes — costs. Estimated production-cost increase relative to conventional BF-BOF is 20–30% with a wide margin of error; cost increase is roughly split between capital and energy costs. Achieving competitive electricity prices around €30/MWh (or lower) would significantly improve the economics; the HYBRIT project’s internal estimate of WACC is 9%. (Kushnir et al. 2020, p. 11, citing SSAB et al. 2018; Vogl et al. 2018; IRENA 2018)

Related terms. Direct reduction; direct reduced iron; electric arc furnace; HYBRIT; BF-BOF route; DRI-EAF pathway.

Source history. - Kushnir et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-07: definition, system implications, cost notes. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: pathway naming alignment.

Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) — standalone

Aliases. HDS; sulfur removal; deep-HDS; hydrotreating-for-sulfur.

Definition. A specialised refinery process — the dominant subset of hydrotreating — in which sulfur compounds (mercaptans, sulfides, disulfides, thiophenes) in petroleum products are reacted with hydrogen over a sulfided Co-Mo or Ni-Mo catalyst at 280–400 °C and 30–130 bar to remove sulfur as hydrogen sulfide (H₂S): R-S-R’ + 2 H₂ → R-H + R’-H + H₂S. The H₂S is then sent to a Claus sulfur-recovery unit. HDS is required to meet modern fuel-sulfur specifications (≤10 ppm under Tier 3 / Euro 6 / ULSD rules), to protect downstream catalysts (FCC, reformer, hydrocracker), and to enable on-board emission-control systems in modern vehicles. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 3–4; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Attributes — Praxair/Linde 2017 quantitative reference.

Indicator Value
H₂ consumption per S removed ~1.85 mol H₂ per mol S (varies by sulfur-compound class)
H₂ consumption (engineering-rule-of-thumb) 70 scf H₂ per barrel feed per % S removed
US refinery H₂ for HDS (2016) 1.33 billion scf/day
Total US refinery H₂ supply ~5.0 billion scf/day (captive 3.0 + merchant 1.95)
HDS share of total refinery H₂ ~20%
US sulfur removed by HDS (2016) ~30,000 short tons/day
Equivalent SO₂ avoided (US) ~21.9 Mt SO₂/yr
Recovery efficiency (HDS + Claus combined) ~90% of crude-feed sulfur recovered as elemental S
US elemental sulfur production ~12 Mt/yr (essentially all by-product)

(H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 3–6)

Notes — sulfur-compound difficulty hierarchy. Different sulfur-containing compounds in crude have very different removal difficulty: mercaptans and aliphatic sulfides react readily under mild HDS conditions; thiophenes and especially dibenzothiophenes require harsher conditions (higher T, P, more H₂). Deep-HDS to 10 ppm requires removing the sterically-hindered 4,6-dimethyl-dibenzothiophenes, which is what drives the large hydrogen consumption per percentage point of sulfur reduction at the deep end of the curve. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 3–4; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Related terms. Hydrotreating (HDS / HDN / HDM); Claus process (sulfur recovery); ULSD (ultra-low-sulfur diesel); sulfur compounds in crude; sulfur dioxide (SO₂); sweet vs sour crude; Tier 3 fuel standards; steam methane reforming (SMR); refinery green-H₂; petroleum refining (umbrella).

Source history. - H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017 — added 2026-05-08: definition, quantitative reference (1.85 mol H₂/mol S, 70 scf H₂/bbl/%S, 1.33 bn scf/d), sulfur-compound difficulty hierarchy. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): catalyst types and operating-envelope detail.

Hydrogen embrittlement (HE)

Definition. A phenomenon in which the mechanical properties of pipe steels degrade due to the infiltration of hydrogen atoms into the metal lattice structure, potentially resulting in sudden and severe failures when the steel is subjected to mechanical stress. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, abstract and p. 376)

Extended definition. Under pressure and flow, molecular hydrogen dissociates into H atoms which penetrate steel through adsorption, react with the metal’s atomic structure and cause microcrack propagation. The interaction between hydrogen and metal microstructure is multi-mechanism and no single theory fully explains it. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 376)

Notes — proposed mechanisms. Identified mechanisms include hydrogen pressure theory (HPT); hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE) — predominant in brittle intergranular fractures; hydrogen-enhanced localised plasticity (HELP) — predominant in slip-band fractures; adsorption-induced dislocation emission (AIDE) — in cleavage-like and dimpled intergranular fractures; hydrogen-enhanced strain-induced vacancy formation (HESIVM); hydrogen-enhanced macroscopic plasticity (HEMP); hydride formation; hydrogen-induced reduction in surface energy; and hydrogen-assisted micro-void coalescence. Multiple mechanisms may operate simultaneously. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 376)

Notes — observed effects. Hydrogen charging increases yield strength (interstitial-hydrogen solid-solution strengthening) but reduces total elongation, toughness and fatigue life; reductions in area at fracture for smooth specimens range from 20% to 50% relative to in-air tests, and fatigue life can fall by 70% at 1 wppm hydrogen content for in-service pipe steels. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, pp. 376, 388–389)

Related terms. Hydrogen-natural gas blending; hydrogen permeation test; hydrogen charging; slow strain rate test; fatigue crack growth rate test; HEDE; HELP; AIDE.

Source history. - Ghadiani et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition, mechanisms, effects on mechanical properties.

Hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE)

Definition. A proposed mechanism of hydrogen embrittlement in which hydrogen weakens interatomic bonds; predominant in brittle intergranular fractures. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 376)

Related terms. Hydrogen embrittlement; HELP; AIDE.

Source history. - Ghadiani et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definitional sentence and fracture-mode association.

Hydrogen-enhanced localised plasticity (HELP)

Definition. A proposed mechanism of hydrogen embrittlement in which the presence of hydrogen around dislocations induces a local decrease in yield stress, facilitating local dislocation movement; predominant in slip-band fractures. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, pp. 376, 388)

Related terms. Hydrogen embrittlement; HEDE; AIDE.

Source history. - Ghadiani et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definitional content from mechanism listing and fatigue analysis.

Hydrogen-natural gas blending

Definition. The injection and transport of hydrogen blended with natural gas in existing natural-gas pipelines, presented as a strategy to reduce carbon emissions in residential and commercial heating. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, abstract and p. 375)

Notes. A critical implementation challenge is hydrogen embrittlement of pipeline steels under varying H₂ concentrations. Numerous field trials have been conducted in Europe, with fewer in the US, Australia, Canada and Germany. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 376)

Notes — Haeseldonckx & D’haeseleer thresholds. Haeseldonckx & D’haeseleer (2007) identify a 17 vol% H₂ blend as the upper safe threshold below which the existing NG infrastructure (pipelines, end-use applications) needs no replacement. Above 17 vol%, end-use applications and some pipelines must be replaced. For 100% H₂, an unmodified pipeline can carry 98% of the energy (vs. lean NG / L-gas) or 80% (vs. rich NG / H-gas), assuming an unchanged pressure drop and centrifugal-compressor adaptation; pipeline linepack drops to 65–71% of NG values. (Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007, abstract and Sections 2–4)

Notes — physical comparisons. Hydrogen has HHV 13 MJ/Nm³ vs ~40 MJ/Nm³ for NG, so to deliver the same energy 3× the volumetric flow is required; H₂ density is 9× lower than NG, so 3× the volumetric flow can be achieved for the same pressure drop. Joule-Thomson cooling on pressure reduction is ≈ −0.5 °C/bar for NG but ≈ +0.035 °C/bar (heating) for H₂ — throttling H₂ from 80 to 15 bar yields only ~+2 °C, posing no operational concern. Centrifugal compressor design is the principal challenge: H₂ requires ~3× the impeller tip speeds of NG, near the material-strength limit. (Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007, Section 2; Khan et al. 2021, p. 4)

Related terms. Hydrogen embrittlement; hydrogen charging; fatigue crack growth rate test; hydrogen pipeline; hydrogen pipeline reassignment (NG → H₂); linepack.

Source history. - Ghadiani et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition and deployment status. - Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007 — added 2026-05-08: 17 vol% blend threshold, energy-flow ratios, Joule-Thomson and compressor specifics.

Hydrogen permeation test

Definition. A test that determines hydrogen content and its influence on mechanical properties of metals, conducted in either aqueous or gaseous environment. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 376)

Notes. Used in this study (per the Devanathan-Stachursky method, ISO 17081) to obtain effective diffusivity (D_eff), hydrogen concentration in interstitial lattice and reversible trap sites (C_0R), and time to steady state (t_ss) for the steels under test. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 380, Table 2)

Related terms. Hydrogen embrittlement; hydrogen charging; slow strain rate test.

Source history. - Ghadiani et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition and parameter outputs.

Hydrogen pipeline

Definition. A pipeline transporting hydrogen gas, classified — like the natural-gas analogue — into transmission (6–48 inch diameter, 10–120 bar), distribution (2–10 inch, 2–10 bar), service lines (0.5–2 inch, ~1 bar), and gathering (4–12 inch). Pure-hydrogen pipelines are identified as the most cost-effective method for transporting gaseous H₂ over distances greater than 200 km up to a few hundred km; for very long distances (>2,000 km) shipping liquid H₂ may become cheaper than pipelines. (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 1–2; Khalili et al. 2026, p. 9)

Attributes — illustrative LCOH for a 1,500 km, 36-inch H₂ transmission pipeline (Khan case study).

Cost component | Value (2019 C$) |

|—|—| | Pipeline TIC | 837,789 / km | | Pipeline TCI | 192 M C$ for inlet compressor + system | | Annualized CAPEX (inlet compressor) | 22.5 M C\(/y (CRF = 0.1168) | | LCOH (inlet compressor) | ~0.10 C\)/kg H₂ | | Capacity (36-inch, 70 bar inlet, 35 m/s outlet) | 51.25 MMSCMD ≈ 4,279 t H₂/day |

(Khan et al. 2021, pp. 22–28)

Notes — global existing infrastructure. ~2,500 km of active H₂ pipelines in the United States (90% along the Gulf Coast); 1,100–1,770 km in Europe (Germany has operated a 210 km pipeline carrying ~9,000 kg H₂/h since 1939). The European Hydrogen Backbone (2020) estimates that a 48-inch H₂ pipeline can transport ~1.9 Mt H₂/y (≈13 GW LHV) at 0.07–0.23 €/kg per 1,000 km. A recent Cerniauskas et al. (2020) study suggests repurposing natural-gas pipelines could cut H₂ transport cost by 20–60% versus new construction. (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 1, 37)

Notes — rules of thumb. “A demand of ~1–1.2 t H₂/day per km of pipeline is needed to drive economic viability” for short-distance pipelines without intermediate compressor stations. Pipeline H₂ transport is low-cost (<1 C$/kg H₂; <7 $/GJ) at scales of 100s–1,000s t H₂/day depending on distance. (Khan et al. 2021, pp. xi, 36)

Related terms. Hydrogen embrittlement; hydrogen-natural gas blending; cathodic protection; general flow equation; erosional velocity; levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH); hydrogen colour taxonomy.

Hydrogen pipeline network design

Definition. The combined topology-and-dimensioning optimisation problem for a multi-source, multi-sink hydrogen transmission/distribution network. Inputs include source and sink locations, demand and supply profiles, pipe-cost functions, design-pressure and erosional-velocity constraints. Outputs include arc selection (which links to build), pipeline diameters per arc, and an estimated levelised cost of hydrogen transportation (LCOH-T). (André et al. 2013, abstract; Hammond et al. 2025, abstract and Section 1)

Approaches — André (2013) vs Hammond (2025).

Aspect André et al. 2013 Hammond et al. 2025
Method Local search + Tabu search heuristic Steiner tree with Obstacles Genetic Algorithm (StObGA)
Innovation Joint topology + diameter sizing in a single model Spatially-aware routing on variable-cost surface incl. obstacles
Cost surface Uniform (length × diameter cost) Variable (slopes, transport crossings, water bodies, forests, populated areas)
Topology theorem Arborescence is optimal for distribution Steiner-tree generalisation with non-uniform weights
Cost saving vs uniform-surface graph methods (vs MST) 20–40%
Application case France (local, regional, national) UK industrial clusters

(André et al. 2013, abstract and Sections 3–6; Hammond et al. 2025, abstract and Section 1)

Notes. Both papers treat pipeline routing as fundamentally distinct from telecom-network design because pipeline diameter is a discrete decision variable that must be solved jointly with topology. André et al. demonstrate an arborescence topology is optimal for distribution networks (i.e. trees rooted at a single source). Hammond et al. extend the literature by lifting the uniform-cost-surface assumption that dominates earlier studies (Heijnen et al., Baufumé et al., Johnson and Ogden), producing 20–40% cheaper bespoke routes for given infrastructures. (André et al. 2013, Section 3; Hammond et al. 2025, Section 1)

Related terms. Hydrogen pipeline; hydrogen pipeline reassignment (NG → H₂); levelised cost of hydrogen (LCOH); Erosional velocity; General Flow Equation; Mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP).

Source history. - André et al. 2013 — added 2026-05-08: joint topology-sizing model, French case studies. - Hammond et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: StObGA spatially-aware routing, UK clusters, 20–40% cost saving.

Hydrogen pipeline reassignment (NG → H₂)

Aliases. Pipeline repurposing; pipeline retrofit for H₂.

Definition. Conversion of an existing natural-gas (NG) pipeline so that it carries pure hydrogen rather than NG, achieved through one or a combination of: (i) pipeline-without-modification operation under controlled stress and additional inspection/maintenance; (ii) internal coatings to limit hydrogen adsorption into the steel; (iii) gaseous inhibitor addition to the H₂ stream; (iv) pipe-in-pipe insertion of a dedicated inner H₂ line. Reassignment is one of two main routes for using existing NG infrastructure for hydrogen (the other being H₂-into-NG blending). (Cerniauskas et al. 2019, abstract and Sections 1–2)

Attributes — Cerniauskas et al. Germany case study.

Indicator Value
Technically viable share of analysed German pipeline network >80%
Cost reduction vs newly built H₂ pipeline (transmission cost) >60%
Country-wide cost reduction in 2030 (vs new H₂ pipeline system) ~30%
Suitable steel X70 (yield strength 483 MPa, within Raymond et al. safe range 200–580 MPa for static H₂ load)
Key degradation mechanisms addressed heat-affected-zone (HAZ) cracking; fatigue crack propagation (FCP)

(Cerniauskas et al. 2019, abstract; Sections “Pipeline reassignment options”)

Notes — Khan 2021 cost view. The Khan techno-economic analysis cites a German-network study (Cerniauskas et al. 2020) suggesting H₂ transport cost can be cut 20–60% by repurposing NG pipelines vs new construction. Repurposing has been demonstrated in the United States, where Air Liquide successfully converted two crude-oil pipelines in Texas for H₂ transport. (Khan et al. 2021, p. 37, citing Cerniauskas 2020)

Related terms. Hydrogen pipeline; hydrogen embrittlement; hydrogen-natural gas blending; cathodic protection; fatigue crack growth rate (FCGR) test; Steam cracking (vapocracking).

Hydrogen pressure vessel types

Definition. A four-class classification of pressure vessels for compressed-gas hydrogen storage, distinguished by construction material and lining. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 28, citing Bathélémy 2012)

Type Construction Pressure Application

II Metal-liner hoop-wrapped composite cylinder 26.3–30 MPa Industrial
III Fully wrapped composite with metal (typically aluminium) liner up to 450 bar Vehicle; 25–75% lighter than I/II; expensive; pressure-cycling concerns
IV Fully wrapped composite with plastic liner up to 1000 bar Vehicle; light, durable, simple to manufacture; long lifetime

Hydrogen storage

Definition. The storage of hydrogen in any of three states — gas, liquid, or solid — for later use; viewed as a core element in the development and growth of hydrogen and fuel technologies in portable, stationary and transportation applications. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 28, citing Wolf 2015)

Extended definition. Storage technologies are classified as physical-based (compressed gas, liquid hydrogen, cryo-compressed) or material-based (physisorption and chemisorption, the latter including metallic and chemical hydrides, ammonia and LOHCs). (AlZohbi et al. 2023, pp. 28–31)

Notes — scope distinction. This umbrella entry covers above-ground / vessel-based / material-based hydrogen storage at portable to medium scales. For subsurface, GW–TWh, weeks-to-seasons-scale hydrogen storage, see Underground hydrogen storage (UHS).

Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL)

Definition. A thermochemical process in which residual biomass reacts with water at 200–450 °C (473–723 K) and 50–280 bar (5–28 MPa), with or without a catalyst, to produce bio-crude oil. Suitable for relatively wet biomasses (5–35% dry-matter content), so drying pretreatment is not required. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 9, citing Tian et al.; Castello et al.)

Notes. During HTL, bio-oil is produced through hydrolysis, dehydration, decarboxylation, condensation, cyclisation and polymerisation reactions. HTL bio-oil contains lower oxygen content and moisture, with higher heating value than pyrolysis bio-oil; it also has weaker acidity and stronger thermal stability. HTL is the upstream step of the HDCJ-HTL biofuel pathway and shares high-temperature water-chemistry principles with the catalytic-hydrothermolysis-jet (CHJ) pathway for oil-based feedstock. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 9, 11)

Related terms. HDCJ pathway; pyrolysis (PL); CHJ; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, operating window, comparison with PL bio-oil.

Indirect land use change (ILUC)

Definition. A regulatory and accounting concept used in the EU Renewable Energy Directive II (RED II) to limit the use of high-ILUC-risk biofuel feedstock from land with high carbon stocks. Recognises that diverting agricultural land to fuel-crop production indirectly displaces food/feed production to other (potentially carbon-rich) land, generating additional GHG emissions outside the immediate biofuel production system. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 25, citing EU RED II)

Notes. RED II introduces a multiplication factor of 1.2 (in the energy-content calculation of renewable energy) to incentivise non-food biomass for aviation and maritime fuel production. Sustainable feedstock not inducing additional arable-land demand (residual biomass, oleochemical wastes) is identified as a key concern for aviation biofuels. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 25, 27)

Related terms. Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); ReFuelEU Aviation; HEFA pathway.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition and RED II framing.

Inertia (power system)

Aliases. Total system inertia (TSI); rotational inertia.

Definition. The kinetic energy stored in rotating masses of synchronous generators directly connected to a power grid, which contributes to the system’s resistance to frequency deviations. When system frequency deviates from nominal (e.g. 50 Hz in Europe), synchronous generators inject or absorb kinetic energy automatically, slowing the rate of change of frequency (ROCOF) and giving frequency-control mechanisms time to act. Non-synchronous generators (wind, solar PV) connected via electronic power converters are decoupled from the grid and do not inherently contribute inertia, raising stability challenges as variable renewable energy (VRE) penetration rises. (Guerra et al. 2022, p. 2 and Section 3.4)

Attributes — illustrative inertia constants (Guerra et al. 2022, Table 2).

Source Rotational inertia constant H (s)
Nuclear ~6
Coal-fired thermal ~4
Combined cycle (gas) ~5–6
Reservoir hydro ~3
Pumped hydro storage (PHS) ~3
Biomass / cogeneration ~3–4
Solar PV (no synthetic inertia) 0
Wind (without grid-forming converter) 0
HVDC interconnection 0 (asynchronous; AC interconnections do contribute)

(Guerra et al. 2022, Section 3.4 and Table 2)

Notes — critical inertia level (CIL) and ROCOF. The Total System Inertia (TSI) has a Critical Inertia Level (CIL) below which a contingency event drives ROCOF beyond protection thresholds, triggering frequency relays and generation/load shedding. ROCOF protection relays in 50 Hz systems are typically set between 0.1 and 1.0 Hz/s; ENTSO-E uses 2 Hz/s for future-system simulations. Guerra et al. find that for the Spanish 2030/2040 scenarios, an inertia constant ≥ 5 s is required alongside emissions ≤ ~113 kg CO₂/MWh and a maximum LCOE of ~€134/MWh to meet Paris-aligned decarbonisation. (Guerra et al. 2022, abstract; Section 3.4.3)

Notes — synthetic inertia. Modern Voltage Source Converter (VSC) HVDC technology and advanced wind/PV power-converter controls (grid-forming converters) can provide synthetic inertia and primary/secondary frequency control, partially replacing physical rotating-mass inertia. (Guerra et al. 2022, p. 2)

Related terms. Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); Rate of Change of Frequency (ROCOF); curtailment (VRE); flexibility (power system); critical inertia level (CIL); frequency response.

Source history. - Guerra et al. 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, inertia constants by technology, CIL/ROCOF context, synthetic-inertia note.

Interconnection (cross-border, security-of-supply contribution)

Aliases. Interconnexion (FR); cross-border transmission; international tie-line; HVDC interconnector.

Definition. Cross-border transmission infrastructure (HVAC or HVDC) connecting national power systems, allowing electricity exchanges to optimise operating costs (merit-order dispatch across borders), to balance variable renewable output via geographic smoothing, and to contribute to the security of supply of each connected country via probabilistic import availability. Interconnections are a primary flexibility lever and a structuring component of the European synchronous area. (RTE 2022, Sections 7.2, 14.4.1.3, pp. 309–315, 865 area, translated from French)

Attributes — RTE 2050 French interconnection envelope.

Indicator Today (2020) RTE 2050
Total import capacity ~10 GW 20–25 GW (median config); 39 GW (high config)
Number of interconnected neighbours 6 (Germany, Belgium, UK, Spain, Switzerland, Italy, Ireland via UK) up to 8 (incl. additional sea cables)
HVDC share of new build minor major (>50% of new builds)
Capacity-adequacy contribution ~80% of physical capacity (~8 GW) ~60% of physical capacity (12–15 GW)
Average contribution at top-4 residual-demand hours high (Italy, Switzerland, etc. exporting to France) high but declining
Cost (HVDC subsea, indicative) ~1.5–3 M€/km similar

(RTE 2022, Sections 7.2.4–7.2.5, Figures 7.16–7.18, pp. 313–315)

Notes — declining capacity-contribution coefficient. RTE quantifies that interconnection capacity-adequacy contribution falls from ~80% of physical capacity (today) to ~60% by 2050 — even though physical import capacity rises from 10 GW to 20–25 GW. Reason: neighbouring countries also rely on RES and have less surplus dispatchable capacity to export to France during simultaneous European cold spells or low-wind periods. The structural decline is symmetric across all major European systems. (RTE 2022, Section 7.2.4, pp. 313–314)

Notes — sensitivity to European LoLE. A degraded European-level reliability standard (LoLE rising from 1.4 h/yr in the reference configuration to 3.9 h/yr in major neighbouring countries) could reduce the French capacity-adequacy contribution of interconnections by ~5 GW. RTE thus argues for harmonised European reliability standards as a precondition for relying on interconnections in national capacity-adequacy assessments. (RTE 2022, Section 7.2.4, p. 314)

Notes — exporter/importer dynamics. RTE projects France remains a net exporter in 2050 across all six scenarios — typically 30–80 TWh/yr exports. Net export volume is highest in N03 (~80 TWh/yr) and lowest in M0 (~30 TWh/yr) due to RES variability. Interconnections nonetheless contribute to security of supply via imports during the few hundred hours of French residual-load peak. (RTE 2022, Section 7.10.1, p. 374 area)

Notes — HVDC and grid-forming inverters. Most new interconnections are HVDC (line-commutated converters LCC, or voltage-source converters VSC). VSC HVDC links can provide “synthetic inertia” and reactive-power support, partially offsetting the inertia loss from declining synchronous-generation share. Grid-forming inverter capability is identified by RTE as an essential 2030+ requirement. (RTE 2022, Section 14.4.1.3, p. 865 area)

Related terms. Power system flexibility; Capacity adequacy; Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); Inertia (power system); Loss of Load Expectation (LoLE); ENTSO-E TYNDP; HVDC; Voltage-source converter (VSC); Mismatch energy.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: French envelope (10 GW today → 20–25 GW 2050), declining capacity-adequacy contribution (80% → 60%), European LoLE sensitivity, net-export dynamics, HVDC/grid-forming role (translated from French).

INIES / FDES / PEP (French environmental databases)

Aliases. INIES (INformations sur les Impacts Environnementaux et Sanitaires); FDES (Fiches de Déclaration Environnementale et Sanitaire); PEP (Profils Environnementaux Produits); base INIES.

Definition. The French national environmental database for construction products, equipment, and building services, established under the Ministry of Ecological Transition and used as the standard data source for building Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) and the regulatory RE2020 carbon-balance compliance check. Two principal data formats: - FDES (Environmental & Health Declaration Forms) — standardised LCA data sheets for construction products (insulation, glass, concrete, steel, paint, etc.) following NF EN 15804. - PEP (Environmental Product Profiles) — analogous LCA data sheets for building equipment (heat pumps, boilers, ventilation, lighting, etc.). (Goessel 2025, pp. 47–48; AFNOR EN 15804)

Attributes — INIES base statistics (end 2024).

Indicator Value
Total entries (FDES + PEP) >6,000
FDES (products) majority
PEP (equipment) smaller share
Coverage French market construction products + EU equivalents
Data quality tiers individual (manufacturer-specific), collective (industry consortium), default (DED — Donnée Environnementale par Défaut)
Time horizon 50-year reference (matches building LCA)
Indicators GWP100 (kg CO₂eq), eutrophication, acidification, ODP, abiotic resource depletion, etc.
Free public access yes (since ~2021)

(Goessel 2025, pp. 47–48; INIES website)

Notes — quality hierarchy. Goessel’s methodology (and the RE2020 protocol) ranks INIES data by quality: - Individual data — manufacturer-specific, most accurate, preferred when available. - Collective data — industry-association average for a product category, used when individual data is missing. - Default Environmental Data (DED) — generic worst-case data for products without manufacturer-specific FDES, used as a last-resort regulatory default.

The DED bias toward worst-case incentivises manufacturers to publish individual FDES for their products to escape the default penalty. (Goessel 2025, pp. 47–48)

Notes — international counterparts. Other countries have analogous databases: KBOB (Switzerland), ÖKOBAUDAT (Germany), ICE (UK Bath inventory), NIST BEES (US). The European INIES-comparable PEF (Product Environmental Footprint) initiative aims to harmonise across member states. Ecoinvent is the most-cited international LCA database covering all sectors but with less building-specific resolution than INIES. (Goessel 2025, p. 47)

Related terms. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA); Embodied carbon (buildings); RE2020 / RT2012; building renovation (umbrella); EN 15978; Material Flow Analysis (MFA / Sankey); BBCA (Bâtiment Bas Carbone).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: INIES / FDES / PEP definitions, quality hierarchy, international counterparts (translated from French).

Industrial heat pumps

Definition. High-temperature heat pumps deployed in industrial settings to electrify low-to-medium-temperature process heat. Distinguished from buildings heat pumps by their higher delivered temperatures (up to ~200 °C with waste-heat integration) and larger unit size. Identified by ETP-2026 as a key lever for industrial-sector electrification. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 137, 6995–7010)

Attributes — capacity, costs and outlook.

Indicator Value Year
Share of global industrial heat met by electricity (2024) <5% 2024
Industrial heat-pump CAPEX vs coal boilers ~3× higher indicative
Industrial heat-pump CAPEX vs gas boilers up to 10× higher indicative
Best efficiency window <100 °C (waste-heat integration extends to >200 °C) —
Cost-effective heat-pump share of light industry needs up to 45% —
Cost-effective share of all industrial heating needs ~20% (depending on waste-heat availability) —
2035 installed capacity (STEPS) 80 GWth (~8% of light-industry thermal needs) 2035
2035 capacity (CPS) more muted than STEPS 2035
2035 capacity (NZE) ~3× STEPS level 2035
Industrial-heat electricity consumption growth +2% / y (2010–2020) → +4% / y (since 2020) trend

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 137, 6995–7010, citing HPT TCP 2023)

Notes — barriers. Industrial heat-pump CAPEX (equipment + installation, excluding grid connection) remains a major hurdle, particularly for smaller firms and EMDEs. Hybrid configurations (heat pump + gas backup, or heat pump + thermal energy storage) can narrow the cost gap and improve grid-stress flexibility. Time-of-use electricity tariffs and grid-connection prioritisation are identified as key policy levers. (IEA ETP 2026, p. 137)

Related terms. Heat pump (HP); thermal energy storage (TES); load shifting and load shedding; district heating (DH); coefficient of performance (COP).

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, cost ratios, CPS/STEPS/NZE outlook.

Injection moulding (plastic processing)

Aliases. IM; injection-moulded plastics; reciprocating-screw injection moulder; moulding machine.

Definition. A discrete-batch plastics processing method in which thermoplastic resin pellets are melted in a reciprocating-screw barrel, then injected at high pressure (500–2,000 bar) into a closed steel mould cavity where the polymer cools and solidifies into the final product shape. The mould opens, the part is ejected, the cycle repeats every 10–60 seconds. Injection moulding is the dominant production method for discrete plastic articles (vs continuous extrusion for profiles): caps, cutlery, container closures, automotive bumpers, electronic housings, medical devices, LEGO bricks. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Attributes — process envelope.

Indicator Value
Cycle time 10–60 s (typical small parts); minutes (large parts)
Injection pressure 500–2,000 bar
Mould clamping force 50–10,000 t
Mould temperature 20–120 °C (depending on polymer)
Polymer melt temperature 180–320 °C (depending on polymer)
Typical polymers PP (~30%), PE (~20%), ABS (~10%), PS (~10%), PA (~5%), PC (~5%), PVC, PET
Typical part mass 0.1 g (microparts) to 50 kg (industrial pallets)
Tooling cost high (€10k–€1M+ per mould — economic only for high volumes)

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Notes — variants. Multi-cavity moulds produce multiple identical parts per cycle. Multi-component / overmoulding combines two or more polymers (rigid + soft for grips). Insert moulding overmoulds onto inserted metal or electronic parts. Gas-assisted injection moulding hollows out thick sections, reducing material use and cycle time. Microcellular foam moulding (MuCell) injects supercritical N₂/CO₂ to reduce density and weight. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Related terms. Extrusion (plastic processing); blow moulding; thermoforming; rotomoulding; compounding (plastics); polypropylene (PP); polyethylene (HDPE / LDPE / LLDPE); ABS; polycarbonate (PC); polyamides (Nylon); plastic processing (umbrella).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, process envelope, variants (overmoulding, MuCell, gas-assisted).

Integrated Assessment Model (IAM)

Aliases. IAM; integrated-assessment modelling; climate-economy model; multi-sector long-term model.

Definition. A class of multi-sector models that integrate representations of the energy system, the rest of the economy, and the climate system to evaluate the long-term costs, risks, and pathways of climate-mitigation strategies under different policy and socio-economic scenarios. IAMs typically combine an Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM, often MESSAGE / TIMES / OSeMOSYS at their core) with a macroeconomic / general-equilibrium representation, a land-use / agriculture model, and a simplified climate-emissions-temperature module. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6, 2022–2023) integrated >1,000 IAM-derived scenarios; the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) are the standard IAM scenario taxonomies. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 1–2; cross-ref Pathways entry)

Attributes — major IAM frameworks.

Framework Energy-system core Origin Use
MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM MESSAGE ESOM IIASA IPCC SSPs, IEA collaboration
REMIND-MAgPIE REMIND macro + MAgPIE land PIK (Germany) IPCC SSPs, EU policy
GCAM hybrid optimisation + simulation PNNL (US) US DOE, climate-policy
WITCH Ramsey-style growth model RFF-CMCC climate-economics research
AIM/CGE general equilibrium NIES (Japan) Asian climate policy
IMAGE integrated assessment hub PBL Netherlands IPCC, EU policy
TIAM-ECN TIMES global TNO / ECN / Joint Institute technology-pathway studies
COFFEE MESSAGE-derived global IAM COPPE Brazil Latin-American + global pathways (Zanon-Zotin)

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 1; cross-ref Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024 COFFEE model)
