Notes — IPCC AR6 dependence on IAMs. The 1.5 °C and 2 °C mitigation pathways underpinning the IPCC 6th Assessment Report were generated almost entirely by IAMs. Critiques of these pathways (heavy reliance on negative emissions, optimistic technology cost assumptions, perfect foresight) trace back to underlying ESOM / IAM design choices — the same modelling-methodology issues Manuel et al. 2025 surface. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 1–2)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); pathways (vs scenarios); foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); end effects (modelling); MESSAGE; TIMES; OSeMOSYS; Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE); Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS); Current Policies Scenario (CPS).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, major IAM frameworks, IPCC AR6 dependence, methodology-critique link.

Internal Rate of Return (IRR)

Aliases. Tasa Interna de Retorno (TIR); discounted-cash-flow yield.

Definition. The discount rate at which the net present value (NPV) of a project’s expected cash flows equals zero. Computed by solving NPV(r) = Σₜ (CFₜ / (1 + r)ᵗ) = 0 across the project’s full cash-flow profile (including the initial investment), where CFₜ is the net cash flow in period t. A project is financially viable when IRR exceeds the investor’s hurdle rate (typically the WACC). (Ramírez Del Río 2022, pp. 23–24)

Notes. IRR is the principal metric used in the Ramírez Del Río 2022 PV-vs-hydroelectric Colombia case study, with sensitivity analysis on CAPEX, energy contract price, the Tasa Representativa del Mercado (TRM, exchange rate) and WACC. IRR is preferred where investors compare projects across different scales and currencies; NPV (VPN) is the complementary criterion that maximises absolute project value. (Ramírez Del Río 2022, pp. 23–24, 62–69)

Related terms. Net Present Value (NPV); Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC); Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE); Capital Recovery Factor (CRF).

Source history. - Ramírez Del Río 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, formula, role in PV-vs-hydro financial comparison (translated from Spanish).

Inert anode (aluminium production)

Definition. A carbon-free anode used in primary aluminium electrolysis, enabling the alumina-reduction reaction to generate pure oxygen instead of CO₂, thereby avoiding the chemical-process emissions of conventional Hall-Héroult cells. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Notes. Inert anodes appear to increase total energy consumption by approximately 20%. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Related terms. Hall-Héroult electrolysis process; process emissions.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition, energy-penalty note.

Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle (IGCC)

Definition. A coal-based power-generation technology in which coal is converted to syngas in a commercial gasifier (E-gas, Prenflo, Shell, Texaco), with CO₂ separable after the shift reaction by a physical solvent (Rectisol, Selexol) — a configuration termed pre-combustion capture. (Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8810)

Attributes — Hard Coal IGCC plant assumptions, Baufumé 2011, Table 3, p. 8813.

Parameter Value
Power 670–760 MW(e) Net
Efficiency 45.0 % Net
Capital cost 1550 € (2000) / kW(e) Net
Fixed O&M 64 € (2000) / kW(e) Net / year
Variable O&M 5.0 € (2000) / MWh(e) / year
CO₂ capture rate (assumed) 90 %
Capacity factor 75 %

Notes. IGCC plant capital costs (1550 €/kW(e) Net) are smaller than the equivalent two-step (gasification + combined cycle) configuration (1852 €/kW(e) Net), reflecting the loss of thermal-integration efficiency when these processes are spatially decoupled. (Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8812)

Related terms. Carbon capture and storage; pre-combustion capture; Natural Gas Combined Cycle; Hydrogen Combined Cycle; coal gasification.

Source history. - Baufumé et al. 2011 — added 2026-05-07: definition, plant assumptions, integration vs decoupled cost note.

Integrated hydropyrolysis and hydroconversion (IH2)

Definition. A biofuel pathway in which lignocellulosic biomass is converted to gasoline-, kerosene- and diesel-range hydrocarbons through four key processes: pretreatment, catalytic hydropyrolysis (350–450 °C, 20–35 bar in the presence of hydrogen), hydroconversion (340–400 °C, hydrodeoxygenation and hydrogenation), and steam reforming for in-process hydrogen recovery. Under ASTM certification process; high aromatic content (up to 92 vol% from woody biomass) makes IH2 product suitable as a blending component for low-aromatic SPK. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 9)

Notes. The presence of hydrogen during pyrolysis improves on standard pyrolysis bio-oil quality by reducing acidity and oxygen content and increasing liquid-fuels yield. IH2 is currently used essentially for gasoline production at demonstration scale. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 9, 14)

Related terms. Pyrolysis (PL); HDCJ pathway; synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK); sustainable aviation fuels (SAF).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, operating conditions, certification status.

Life Cycle Assessment (LCA)

Aliases. ACV (FR — Analyse du Cycle de Vie); LCA; eco-balance; cradle-to-grave / cradle-to-cradle assessment; environmental product declaration (EPD).

Definition. A standardised methodology (ISO 14040 / 14044 framework) for quantifying the environmental impacts of a product or service across its full life cycle — from raw-material extraction through manufacturing, distribution, use, and end-of-life disposal/recycling. The LCA process consists of four phases: (i) goal and scope definition, (ii) inventory analysis (LCI — quantifying all input/output flows), (iii) impact assessment (LCIA — translating inventory into impact categories), (iv) interpretation. LCA is the canonical tool for comparing the environmental performance of products, technologies, or services on a like-for-like basis. (Goessel 2025, pp. 22–48; ISO 14040/14044 framework)

Attributes — LCA framework structure.

Element Description
Functional Unit (FU) reference unit (e.g. “1 m² of building over 50 years”; “1 kWh delivered to grid”; “1 t cement”)
System boundary which life-cycle stages and processes are included
Allocation method how to attribute impacts of multi-product processes
Inventory phase (LCI) quantitative input/output flow data for each unit process
Impact assessment (LCIA) midpoint indicators (acidification, eutrophication, GWP100…) and endpoint (DALY, species·yr)
Cradle-to-grave from raw material → end-of-life
Cradle-to-cradle includes recycling / reuse closing the loop
Cradle-to-gate only up to the factory gate (excludes use + end-of-life)
Attributional LCA (ALCA) snapshot of average impacts
Consequential LCA (CLCA) impacts of changes / market dynamics

(Goessel 2025, pp. 22–25 and Fig. 2.2; ISO 14040)

Notes — building-LCA specificities. EN 15804 and EN 15978 are the standardised LCA frameworks for construction products and buildings, with life-cycle phases labelled A1–A5 (raw material → construction), B1–B7 (use phase including B6 operational energy and B7 operational water), C1–C4 (deconstruction → end-of-life), D (benefits beyond system boundaries — recycling). Goessel’s renovation methodology uses the QEC (Quartier Énergie Carbone) variant from ADEME 2022 with “residual-charge” treatment of preserved components. (Goessel 2025, pp. 41–48 and Tables 2.1; AFNOR EN 15978)

Notes — prospective LCA. Standard LCA uses static present-day environmental data; prospective LCA (or forward-looking LCA) updates the data to reflect future scenarios — decarbonising electricity grids, evolving recycling rates, technological learning. Particularly important for long-lived assets (buildings, infrastructure, vehicles); Goessel implements this with energy-mix decarbonisation scenarios (RTE / SNBC) and prospective climate (EURO-CORDEX RCP8.5). (Goessel 2025, pp. 13, 47, 62–65)

Related terms. Life Cycle Costing (LCC); Embodied carbon (buildings); Operational carbon (buildings); Functional Unit (FU); Material Flow Analysis (MFA / Sankey); INIES / FDES (French environmental databases); EN 15978; building renovation (umbrella); midpoint vs endpoint LCA; ISO 14040/14044.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: ISO 14040/14044 framework, four-phase structure, cradle-to-grave/gate variants, prospective LCA, building-LCA specificities (translated from French).

Lignocellulose (non-food / 2nd-generation biomass)

Aliases. Lignocellulosic biomass; non-food biomass; 2G feedstock; second-generation biorefinery feedstock.

Definition. Plant-derived biomass composed of three biopolymers — cellulose (35–50%), hemicellulose (20–35%) and lignin (15–30%) — together forming the structural cell walls of grasses, trees, agricultural residues (straw, bagasse, corn stover) and forestry residues. Lignocellulose is distinct from “first-generation” food-crop biomass (sugar, starch, vegetable oils) and offers far greater theoretical scale (~2 × 10¹¹ t/yr globally available) without competing with human or animal nutrition. Conversion of lignocellulose to chemicals or fuels requires either (i) thermochemical routes (gasification, pyrolysis, hydrothermal liquefaction) or (ii) biochemical routes (enzymatic hydrolysis + fermentation), which are technologically more demanding than first-generation biomass routes. (Keim 2010, pp. 300–301; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 4; Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Attributes — composition and conversion options.

Component Share Principal conversion target
Cellulose (β-D-glucose polymer) 35–50% Glucose → bioethanol → ethylene; glucose → 5-HMF → furanics
Hemicellulose (mixed pentose/hexose polymer) 20–35% Xylose → furfural → polymer building blocks
Lignin (polyphenolic polymer) 15–30% Combustion for process heat; aromatic monomers via depolymerisation
Total renewable scale ~2 × 10¹¹ t/yr Theoretical
Practical sustainable harvest ~10–20 EJ/yr Without competing with food/biodiversity

(Keim 2010, p. 301; Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Notes — chemical vs energy use. Keim 2010 emphasises that lignocellulose is the “2nd generation” feedstock for the chemical industry. Routes to bulk chemicals from lignocellulose are still pre-commercial; bioethanol from cellulosic sources is the most commercially advanced (see Sucden, Borregaard, Iogen, POET-DSM). The biorefinery concept (multi-product output: fuels + chemicals + materials + power) is the canonical industrial architecture for lignocellulose valorisation. (Keim 2010, pp. 301–302)

Notes — competing demand. Zanon-Zotin’s 1.5 °C scenarios with constraints on global biomass availability (PBIO sensitivity) show that competition between energy/transport biofuels, BECCS-for-removal, and chemical-feedstock substitution becomes a binding limit; up to 6 GtCO₂/yr of additional mitigation effort is required if biomass availability is constrained. The chemical sector’s per-tonne carbon-storage value of biogenic carbon in unrecycled biomaterials makes feedstock use of biomass particularly attractive vs combustion. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 2 and Fig. 1)

Related terms. Modern bioenergy; biorefinery; bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS); pyrolysis (PL); hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL); coal gasification (to hydrogen); high-value chemicals (HVCs); near-zero emissions materials; bioethanol; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF).

Source history. - Keim 2010 — added 2026-05-08: definition, composition, “2nd generation” framing. - Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: PBIO-sensitivity competition, chemical-feedstock substitution role. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: scale (~2 × 10¹¹ t/yr global availability).

Lube basestocks (Group I–V)

Aliases. Base oils; lube base oils; API base-oil categories; PAO; Group I/II/III/IV/V.

Definition. Petroleum-derived (or synthetic) hydrocarbon fluids used as the base for blended lubricants (engine oil, gear oil, transmission fluid, hydraulic oil), categorised by the API into five groups based on saturate content, sulfur content, and viscosity index (VI). Higher group numbers correspond to higher purity and performance. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4 lube manufacturing section)

Attributes — API base-oil group classification.

Group Process Saturates Sulfur VI Use
I solvent extraction (legacy) <90% >0.03% 80–120 industrial lubes, less-demanding automotive
II hydrocracking + hydrofinishing >90% <0.03% 80–120 mainstream engine oil, gear oil
III hydrocracking + dewaxing + hydroisomerisation >90% <0.03% >120 (high VI) synthetic-like, modern engine oil (“synthetic blend”)
IV poly-alpha-olefin (PAO, synthetic) >99% 0 130–150 full synthetic engine oil, aviation, military
V esters, polyalkylene glycols, alkylated naphthalenes (other synthetic) varies varies 120–200+ high-performance specialty lubes, refrigeration

(Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Notes — production routes. Group I (~10% of global supply, declining) comes from solvent-extraction-based lube refining (Brightstock, lube SDA, dewaxing). Group II/III (~70% of supply, growing) comes from modern hydrocracking + catalytic dewaxing of vacuum gas oil. Group IV (PAO, ~10%) is synthetic — produced by oligomerisation of decene-1 or other linear α-olefins over a homogeneous catalyst (BF₃, AlCl₃), then hydrogenation. Group V (~10%) is a heterogeneous category used as additive/blend component. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Notes — defossilisation. Group IV PAO and Group V esters can be produced from bio-derived α-olefins or fatty acids, opening a partial bio-route. Group I/II/III remain crude-oil-derived. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Related terms. Petroleum refining (umbrella); vacuum distillation; hydrocracking; non-energy use of fossil fuels; lubricants.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: API five-group classification, production routes, defossilisation options.

Liquefied natural gas (LNG)

Definition. Methane (or biomethane) liquefied at −162 °C (111 K) at atmospheric pressure, primarily considered a fuel for shipping and to some extent aviation. LNG has a slightly higher gravimetric energy density (48–54 MJ kg⁻¹) than conventional kerosene (~43 MJ kg⁻¹) and is reported to reduce CO₂ tail-pipe emissions by ~20–25% relative to fossil kerosene for the same energy content. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 20)

Notes — sustainability pathways. Although LNG is currently derived primarily from fossil natural gas, it can stem from biomethane via anaerobic digestion, biomass gasification, or power-to-methane routes decoupled from biomass. LNG is compatible with both combustion-mode (showcased in the TU-155 aircraft and AHEAD project) and fuel-cell mode (SOFC in the Subsonic Ultra Green Aircraft Research / SUGAR project). Methane has a global warming potential (GWP100) ~28 times that of CO₂, so LNG leakages are a significant climate concern; cryogenic infrastructure (refuelling, storage tanks, liquefaction) is also not yet in place at airports. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 20)

Related terms. Hydrogen aviation; ammonia (as hydrogen carrier); biomethane; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); blended wing body (BWB).

Source history. - Kushnir et al. 2020 — listed in Pending 2026-05-07. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, sustainability pathways, aviation use; promoted from Pending.

Levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH)

Definition. The constant per-unit (typically per kg or per MJ) revenue requirement that, over the project lifetime, equates the present value of all costs (CAPEX, O&M, fuel/energy) to the present value of cumulative hydrogen production. For a hydrogen pipeline system, Khan et al. decompose LCOH into the pipeline’s contribution and the compressor stations’ contribution. (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 16, 19–20)

Attributes — formula structure.

LCOH_pipe-system = LCOH_pipe + LCOH_comp; each component = (annualised CAPEX [TCI × CRF] + non-energy OPEX + energy OPEX) / (availability × design capacity × 365). For Khan et al.’s 1,500 km, 36-inch H₂ pipeline case study: annualized CAPEX 22.5 M C\(/y, electricity OPEX 107.6 M C\)/y, total LCOH ≈ 0.10 C$/kg H₂ for the inlet compressor alone. (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 19–20, 26–27)

Notes. Pipeline LCOH is highly sensitive to scale: a NPS-10 pipe over 1,500 km yields LCOH_pipe of 4.25 C\(/kg H₂ (compressors every 500 km) but only 2.05 C\)/kg H₂ if compressors are placed every 100 km. Larger pipes (>NPS-24) achieve <1 C\(/kg H₂ even with sparse compression. A "low-cost" threshold (~0.5–0.6 C\)/kg H₂) is reached at minimum demands of ~10.5 t H₂/day for 10 km up to ~370 t H₂/day for 300 km — supporting the rule of thumb of ~1–1.2 t H₂/day per km. (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 33–36)

Related terms. Hydrogen pipeline; capital recovery factor (CRF); total capital investment (TCI); discount rate; hydrogen colour taxonomy.

Source history. - Khan et al. 2021 — added 2026-05-08: definition, formula, case-study LCOH values.

Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE)

Aliases. Levelised Cost of Electricity; Costo Nivelado de la Energía.

Definition. The constant per-MWh (or per-kWh) revenue requirement that, over the project lifetime, equates the present value of all life-cycle costs (CAPEX plus OPEX) to the present value of cumulative electricity generation, given a chosen discount rate. Expressed as: LCOE = Σₜ (Cₜ + Oₜ)/(1 + r)ᵗ ÷ Σₜ E₀/(1 + r)ᵗ, where Cₜ is CAPEX, Oₜ is OPEX, E₀ is energy generated, r is the nominal discount rate and T is the project lifetime. (Ramírez Del Río 2022, pp. 25–26, citing Shea and Ramgolam 2019; Shen et al. 2020)

Notes. LCOE is the most widely accepted metric for comparing the cost-competitiveness of generation technologies because it integrates installation cost, financing structure, operating costs and lifetime energy yield into a single number that can be benchmarked against electricity tariffs. LCOE is widely used in 100% RE systems analyses (alongside IRR/NPV) and in the IEA/IRENA technology-cost reports. The hydrogen analogue is the Levelized Cost of Hydrogen (LCOH); the heat analogue is Levelized Cost of Heat (LCOH-thermal). (Ramírez Del Río 2022, pp. 25–26)

Related terms. Levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH); Net Present Value (NPV); Internal Rate of Return (IRR); Capital Recovery Factor (CRF); Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC).

Source history. - Ramírez Del Río 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, formula, methodological context (translated from Spanish).

Levelised cost of hydrogen transportation (LCOH-T)

Aliases. Levelised cost of H₂ transport; LCOH-Transport.

Definition. A unit-cost metric for the transport segment of the hydrogen value chain, computing the per-kg-H₂ revenue requirement that, over the pipeline’s lifetime, equates the present value of all transport-segment costs (pipeline CAPEX, compressor CAPEX, energy OPEX for compression, fixed O&M) to the present value of cumulative H₂ throughput. Conceptually parallel to LCOH (which spans production-plus-transport-plus-distribution) but isolates the transport contribution. (Hammond et al. 2025, Section 1)

Notes — drivers. Hammond et al. 2025 use LCOH-T as the headline metric for spatially-aware pipeline-routing optimisation, achieving 20–40% cost savings vs uniform-surface graph methods. Khan et al. 2021 break the same metric into LCOH_pipe + LCOH_comp components, with the rule of thumb that ~1–1.2 t H₂/day per km of pipeline is needed to drive economic viability for short-distance pipelines. (Hammond et al. 2025, abstract; Khan et al. 2021, p. 36)

Related terms. Levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH); hydrogen pipeline; hydrogen pipeline network design; capital recovery factor (CRF); levelized cost of energy (LCOE).

Source history. - Hammond et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, role in spatially-aware routing. - Khan et al. 2021 — added 2026-05-08: pipe / compressor decomposition note.

Just transition (climate policy)

Aliases. Just energy transition; transition juste (FR); justice climatique (FR); Paris Agreement just-transition principle.

Definition. A climate-policy framework, formalised in the preamble of the 2015 Paris Agreement, recognising that the transition to a low-carbon economy must protect workers and communities who depend on fossil-fuel and high-emissions industries (coal mining, oil refining, petrochemicals, steel, automotive ICE manufacturing) — through retraining, redeployment, social safety nets, and economic-development support for affected regions. The just-transition principle is now central to EU Just Transition Fund (€19.2 billion 2021–2027), German Strukturwandel (coal-region restructuring), and the US Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) job-creation provisions. (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 612–613; ILO Just Transition Guidelines 2015)

Attributes — just-transition policy elements.

Element Description
Worker retraining dedicated programs to redeploy ICE-engine assemblers, oil-refinery operators into clean-tech jobs
Social safety nets unemployment benefits, early-retirement options for transition-affected workers
Regional economic development infrastructure + business-support for transition regions
Climate-investment local sharing local communities receive share of clean-tech project revenues
Indigenous / vulnerable-community protection ensuring climate transition doesn’t exacerbate existing social inequities
Energy-poverty mitigation ensuring decarbonisation doesn’t push poor households into precarité énergétique

(Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 612–613)

Notes — Tilsted 2023 critique. Tilsted argues that just transition must extend to the petrochemical industry — currently underrepresented because petrochemical jobs (~2 million globally) are considered safe in the short term. As global plastic production must peak and decline, petrochemical-cluster regions (Antwerp, Houston, Rotterdam, Singapore, Jubail) face stranded-asset and worker-displacement risk; just-transition principles should apply proactively rather than reactively after closures occur. (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 612–613)

Notes — French context. France’s Loi AGEC + Loi Climat & Résilience integrate just-transition principles: protected jobs for fossil-fuel-sector workers; CEE energy-poverty assistance; Comité d’Adaptation aux Conséquences Économiques de la Transition Énergétique (CACET). (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 612–613)

Related terms. Petrochemical lock-ins / political economy; deep reindustrialisation; SNBC (Stratégie nationale bas-carbone); EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); Energy poverty (précarité énergétique); building renovation (umbrella); EPBD; Paris Agreement.

Source history. - Tilsted et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: just-transition definition, policy elements, petrochemical-sector extension argument.

K-Means clustering

Aliases. K-means; Lloyd’s algorithm; centroidal clustering; partitional clustering.

Definition. An unsupervised machine-learning algorithm that partitions a dataset of n observations into K clusters by iteratively (i) assigning each observation to its nearest cluster centroid, (ii) recomputing centroids as the mean of assigned observations, until convergence. K-Means minimises the within-cluster sum of squared distances and produces K hard-assigned (non-overlapping) clusters with cluster-mean centroids as representatives. Choice of K is a hyperparameter — typically selected via the elbow method (plot of within-cluster variance vs K) or silhouette score (cohesion vs separation). (Goessel 2025, pp. 72–73 and Fig. 3.11)

Attributes — algorithm steps.

Step Description
1. Initialisation randomly select K initial centroids (or use K-Means++ for better starting points)
2. Assignment each observation assigned to nearest centroid (Euclidean distance default)
3. Update recompute each centroid as mean of its cluster members
4. Convergence stop when centroids no longer move (or below tolerance)
5. Validation use silhouette score, ARI / AMI on labels, or domain knowledge

(Goessel 2025, p. 72)

Notes — Goessel renovation-archetype clustering. Goessel applies K-Means with K = 5 to the Pareto-optimal renovation strategies (typically ~50–200 strategies on the front), with each strategy described by a vector of 30+ binary / categorical / continuous renovation features (envelope, HVAC, DHW, etc.). The 5-cluster output identifies renovation archetypes — characteristic strategies on the Pareto front that share common renovation features (e.g. “wall ITE + heat pump”, “deep envelope + biomass boiler”, “PV + active cooling”). Cluster validation uses Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) and Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI). (Goessel 2025, pp. 72–73, 95–96)

Notes — limitations. K-Means assumes (i) clusters are roughly spherical and similar in size; (ii) numerical / distance-based features are well-defined; (iii) K is known a priori. For mixed numerical-categorical features (Goessel’s renovation strategies have both), pre-processing via Factor Analysis of Mixed Data (AFDM / FAMD) is required to project to a continuous space before K-Means application. (Goessel 2025, pp. 72–73)

Related terms. Multi-objective optimisation (MOO / OMO); Pareto dominance / Pareto front; Adjusted Rand Index (ARI); building renovation (umbrella); Factor Analysis of Mixed Data (AFDM / FAMD); machine learning.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: K-Means definition, algorithm steps, Goessel renovation-archetype application, validation methodology.

Knock (engine knock)

Aliases. Engine knock; pinging; detonation; autoignition; abnormal combustion.

Definition. Premature autoignition of unburned end-gas in a spark-ignition engine cylinder, occurring before the spark-initiated flame front reaches it, causing a sharp pressure spike and characteristic metallic “pinging” sound. Knock damages pistons, rings and bearings, reduces engine efficiency (the operator must retard ignition timing to compensate), and limits the maximum compression ratio achievable. Higher-octane fuels are more knock-resistant; engine compression ratio is the principal design parameter that determines minimum required octane. (Addicott 1971, pp. 64–66; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Attributes — knock-resistance hierarchy by hydrocarbon type.

Hydrocarbon class Knock resistance
n-paraffins low (low octane); especially heptane RON 0
iso-paraffins high (high octane); especially highly-branched, e.g. isooctane RON 100
Olefins medium-to-high
Aromatics very high (RON 100–120+)
Cycloparaffins (naphthenes) medium

(Addicott 1971, p. 64; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Notes — anti-knock additives and oxygenates. Tetraethyl lead (TEL) — added at 0.6–0.8 g/L since the 1920s — was the dominant anti-knock additive until phased out (US 1995, EU 2000) for health and environmental reasons. Replacement strategies: higher-octane refinery blendstocks (alkylate, reformate); oxygenates (MTBE — banned in many US states post-2000 due to groundwater contamination; ethanol — now the dominant oxygenate; ETBE; isobutanol). Direct-injection turbocharged engines are increasingly common as a way to extract higher efficiency without raising octane requirements. (Addicott 1971, p. 65; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Related terms. Octane number (RON / MON); motor fuels (umbrella); ethanol; MTBE; aromatic hydrocarbons; alkylation (refinery); isomerisation (refinery); knock-limited compression ratio.

Source history. - Addicott 1971 — added 2026-05-08: definition, hydrocarbon-type knock hierarchy. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): TEL phase-out and modern anti-knock strategies.

Life Cycle Costing (LCC)

Aliases. ACCV (FR — Analyse du Coût du Cycle de Vie); whole-life cost; LCC; total cost of ownership (related but broader); Direct Global Cost (CGD).

Definition. A standardised methodology (ISO 15686-5) for quantifying the total monetary cost of a product, service or building over its full life cycle, including capital expenditure (CAPEX, A1–A5 modules), operational expenditure (OPEX — energy, water, maintenance B1–B7), and end-of-life cost (C1–C4). Unlike Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), LCC strictly follows the same life-cycle module structure as LCA (allowing direct LCA-LCC comparisons of decarbonisation pathways). LCC is the economic-pillar counterpart to LCA in life-cycle sustainability assessment (LCSA). (Goessel 2025, pp. 49–53; ISO 15686-5 standard)

Attributes — LCC components.

Module Description Example for a building renovation
A1–A3 raw materials + manufacture insulation panel manufacturing cost
A4–A5 transport + on-site construction delivery + installation labour
B1–B5 use phase (excluding energy & water) maintenance, repair, replacement
B6 operational energy electricity / gas bill
B7 operational water water bill
C1–C4 end-of-life (deconstruction, transport, processing, disposal) demolition cost
D benefits beyond system boundary resale of recycled materials

(Goessel 2025, pp. 49–50; ISO 15686-5)

Notes — discount rate sensitivity. LCC results are highly sensitive to the discount rate (typically 0–15% in the building-renovation literature) and to the energy-price escalation rate (typically 0–5% per annum). Goessel notes these two parameters together can swing LCC results by ±50%. The choice of discount rate is value-laden: high discount rates favour low-CAPEX / high-OPEX solutions (gas boilers, no-insulation); low discount rates favour high-CAPEX / low-OPEX (heat pumps, deep insulation, solar PV). (Goessel 2025, p. 50)

Notes — Direct Global Cost (CGD) variant. Goessel uses a French Coût Global Direct (CGD) — Direct Global Cost — which is LCC normalised by floor area and study period (€/m²/yr) and excludes externalities. The “indirect” variant (CGE — Coût Global Élargi) adds externalities like health damage from air pollution, social cost of carbon, and biodiversity loss. CGD is the standard French metric for residential renovation economics. (Goessel 2025, pp. 21–22)

Related terms. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA); Total Capital Investment (TCI); Total Cost of Ownership (TCO); Capital Recovery Factor (CRF); Net Present Value (NPV); Internal Rate of Return (IRR); discount rate; building renovation (umbrella); LCSA (Life Cycle Sustainability Assessment).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: ISO 15686-5 framework, LCC module structure, discount-rate sensitivity, CGD variant (translated from French).

Linepack (gas pipeline storage)

Definition. Short-term storage of compressed gas (natural gas or hydrogen) within the pipeline volume itself, achieved by raising operating pressure during periods of supply-greater-than-demand and drawing it down when demand exceeds supply. Allows nearly continuous gas supply despite fluctuating demand without separate storage facilities. (Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007, Section 2)

Attributes — H₂ vs NG linepack.

Indicator Value
H₂ linepack as % of NG linepack 65–71% (depending on operating-pressure assumptions)
Storage volume formula V_storage = V_geom · (p_m / K_m − p_m’ / K_m’) · (1/p_n) · (T_n/T)
Mean pipeline pressure (3-pressure formula) p_m = (2/3)(p₁³ − p₂³)/(p₁² − p₂²)
Lower flow-rate impact More linepack possible at lower flow rates

(Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007, Section 2 and equations)

Notes. Linepack-style operation gives demand-side off-takers the freedom to adjust their off-take independently of injection into the pipeline. For a planned transition from NG to H₂ in the same pipeline, the loss of two-thirds of linepack is one of the principal short-term security-of-supply concerns, alongside centrifugal-compressor limits. (Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007, abstract)

Related terms. Hydrogen pipeline; hydrogen-natural gas blending; hydrogen pipeline reassignment (NG → H₂); compressibility factor (Z); pipeline efficiency.

Source history. - Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007 — added 2026-05-08: definition, H₂-vs-NG ratios, storage formulae.

Levelised Cost of Production (LCOP)

Definition. A measure of the average cost of producing a unit of output from a manufacturing facility over its lifetime. Used in ETP-2026 to compare the cost-competitiveness of clean-energy-technology and material manufacturing across regions, by integrating capital expenditure, operating expenditure (energy, labour, materials), maintenance and end-of-life costs, all discounted to present value and divided by lifetime production. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 377)

Notes — manufacturing-cost gap analyses. - Solar PV: one-third of the gap in cell and module manufacturing costs between China and other regions stems from labour and components. - Heat pumps: the gap relates primarily to cheaper labour, components and integration in China. - LCOP is conceptually parallel to LCOE/LCOH but applies to manufactured-product cost rather than fuel/electricity cost.

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 1740, 1764, 1784 ff.)

Related terms. Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE); Levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH); Total Cost of Ownership (TCO); Manufacturing capacity (clean energy technologies); ad valorem tariff.

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, manufacturing-cost-gap context.

Liquid hydrogen storage

Definition. Storage of hydrogen as a cryogenic liquid (boiling point −253 °C) in super-insulated cryogenic pressure tanks, offering a more compact alternative to compressed-gas storage. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, pp. 28–29)

Attributes.

Property Value
Volumetric density 70 g/L at boiling point and atmospheric pressure
Hydrogen content 16 wt%
Volumetric energy density 50 kg/m³
Liquefaction energy penalty 25–40% of the energy content of hydrogen
Boil-off loss up to 0.4 %/day
Advantages higher gravimetric and volumetric density than gaseous storage; high purity
Drawbacks energy- and time-intensive; costly; existing hydrogen dissipation; safety issues

(AlZohbi et al. 2023, pp. 28–29 and Table 1, p. 32)

Notes. Tanks are spherical or cylindrical; large tanks are usually spherical to minimise surface area for heat-transfer reasons. The liquefaction process and thermal insulation are the two principal cost and energy-loss drivers. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 28)

Related terms. Compressed gas hydrogen storage; cryo-compressed hydrogen storage; boil-off loss; ortho-hydrogen / para-hydrogen; hydrogen storage.

Source history. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, properties, energy-penalty notes.

Liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHC)

Definition. Organic compounds that reversibly absorb hydrogen via a catalytic hydrogenation reaction (charging) and release it via a catalytic dehydrogenation reaction (discharging), remaining in the liquid state throughout the cycle. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 31, citing Preuster et al. 2017; He et al. 2015)

Attributes (AlZohbi et al. 2023, Table 1, pp. 32–33).

Property Value
Hydrogen content 5.5 wt%
Volumetric energy density 60 kg/m³
Storage viability > 1 year
Advantages use of existing infrastructure for storage and transport in liquid form
Drawbacks large amount of generated hydrogen needed for dehydrogenation

Notes. Hydrogenation occurs under high hydrogen pressure; dehydrogenation occurs under low pressure (under 5 bar). Explosion risk is reduced by the low free-hydrogen content in a LOHC system; existing fuel infrastructure is suitable for storage and transport, lowering investment risk. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 31)

Related terms. Chemisorption; chemical hydrides; ammonia; hydrogen storage.

Source history. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, capacity, infrastructure benefits.

Local content requirements (LCRs)

Definition. Industrial and trade-policy provisions that specify a minimum share of domestically manufactured goods, domestically supplied services, or domestic labour that must contribute to a product or service, often expressed as a percentage of the final value. Certain incentives — for example tax credits, subsidies, or eligibility for public-procurement contracts — may be available only for products meeting these local-content thresholds. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 377)

Notes — examples in clean energy. LCRs are a central feature of the US Inflation Reduction Act’s “domestic-content adders” for solar, wind and storage, India’s solar-PV manufacturing-incentive schemes, and the EU’s Net-Zero Industry Act. The IEA notes that LCRs can support domestic manufacturing build-out but tend to raise consumer costs and slow deployment if they constrain supply faster than domestic capacity scales up. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 17, 297 ff.)

Related terms. Ad valorem tariff; Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA); manufacturing capacity; Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, deployment context.

Low-emissions hydrogen

Definition. Hydrogen produced through low-emissions pathways: water electrolysis using renewable or nuclear electricity; biomass-based gasification; or fossil fuels with CCUS, provided that upstream emissions are sufficiently low, capture is applied at high rates to all CO₂ streams, and all CO₂ is permanently stored. Encompasses what is variously labelled “green”, “blue”, “pink”, “yellow” or “white” hydrogen depending on the production route and electricity source. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 377)

Attributes — 2024–2025 deployment (ETP-2026 / Global Hydrogen Review 2025).

Indicator Value Year
Annual investment nearly USD 8 billion 2025 (year-on-year +80%)
Production output ~1 Mt H₂ 2025 (≈1% of total H₂)
2030 production from committed projects >4 Mt H₂ projected
Share from gas + CCUS in 2024 >80% 2024
Share from electrolysis in 2024 ~15% 2024
Largest electrolyser plants 500 MW commissioned, 1 GW under construction 2025
Cumulative installed electrolyser capacity (start–2025) ~5 GW 2025
Capacity at FID for 2030 26 GW committed
Potential 2030 capacity (incl. high-likelihood projects) 65 GW strong-potential

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 52–54)

Notes — boom-and-bust dynamics. Between 2019 and 2021, listed low-emissions-hydrogen company market capitalisation rose by USD 70 billion; since then it has collapsed by >80%, with HydrogenOne Capital Growth winding down in early 2025. ETP-2026 frames this as a typical post-exuberance consolidation rather than a “burst bubble”, noting that electrolyser deployment is tracking the early adoption curve of solar PV and offshore wind. The bulk of investment goes to industrial uses (refining, ammonia, methanol, steel, aviation, shipping) where firm offtake agreements have concentrated. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 52–54)

Related terms. Hydrogen colour taxonomy; hydrogen; low-emissions hydrogen-based fuels; carbon capture and storage (CCS); electrolysers; PEM electrolyser.

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: formal definition, 2025 deployment data, “is the bubble bursting” analysis.

Low-emissions hydrogen-based fuels

Definition. Synthetic fuels produced from low-emissions hydrogen, including ammonia, methanol and other synthetic hydrocarbons (gases and liquids), provided that any carbon inputs are not from fossil fuels or fossil-derived process emissions (i.e. carbon must be biogenic or atmospheric, captured via DAC). (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 377)

Notes. Low-emissions hydrogen-based fuels are a sub-set of “low-emissions fuels” (which also includes bioenergy and hydrogen itself). They are particularly important for hard-to-electrify sectors — aviation, shipping, long-haul road freight, and chemicals — where alternatives to liquid hydrocarbon fuels are constrained. Ammonia is a particularly active near-term market, both as a hydrogen carrier and as a maritime fuel; ETP-2026 aligns this category with Su-ungkavatin’s electrofuels and Khalili’s e-fuels (e-ammonia, e-methanol, e-FTL). (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 15–16, 377)

Related terms. Low-emissions hydrogen; e-fuels; electrofuels; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); ammonia (as hydrogen carrier); methanol synthesis (electrofuels and biofuels); near-zero emissions materials.

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: formal definition, sectoral context.

Isomerisation (refinery)

Aliases. Light naphtha isomerisation; C5/C6 isomerisation; pentane-hexane isom.

Definition. A refinery process in which low-octane straight-chain (n-) pentane and hexane in light naphtha are converted to higher-octane branched (iso-) isomers — iso-pentane (RON 92), 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane (RON 92–105) — over a chlorinated-alumina-supported Pt catalyst (Pt/Cl-Al₂O₃) at 120–180 °C and 20–40 bar in a hydrogen atmosphere. Isomerisation is the standard upgrade for the C5–C6 light-naphtha cut, complementing catalytic reforming (which targets the heavy C7–C10 cut). (Speight 2019, Chapters 6.5.3.3, 7.4.1.3)

Attributes — typical operating envelope.

Indicator Value
Reactor temperature 120–180 °C (Pt/chlorinated alumina; UOP Penex)
Reactor pressure 20–40 bar
Catalyst Pt/Cl-Al₂O₃ (chloriding feed required) or Pt/zeolite (higher T)
H₂/HC molar ratio 1–4
C5+ liquid product RON ~85 (single-pass) → ~89 (with deisopentaniser recycle) → ~92 (with full DIH recycle)
Yield 95–98 wt% C5+

(Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5.3.3)

Notes — alternative catalyst. Zeolite-based isomerisation (Pt/HZSM-5 or Pt/mordenite) operates at higher temperature (~250 °C) without chloriding, gives slightly lower RON but is more robust to sulfur and water contamination. Refiners choose between chlorinated-alumina (high RON, sensitive) and zeolite (lower RON, robust) based on feed quality. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.4.1.3)

Related terms. Catalytic reforming; alkylation (refinery); naphtha; petroleum refining (umbrella); high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, conditions, catalyst variants, role vs catalytic reforming.

Lithium-ion battery (aviation)

Definition. A rechargeable battery technology used for sustainable aviation, in which lithium ions move between the cathode and anode through an electrolyte during charge/discharge. Five Li-based chemistries are reviewed by Su-ungkavatin et al. as candidates for aviation propulsion or onboard (“more electric”) power: lithium-ion (Li-ion), advanced lithium-ion, solid-state battery (Li-SSB), lithium-sulfur (Li-S) and lithium-air (Li-air). (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 14)

Attributes — specific energy and aviation context.

Battery type Specific energy (Wh kg⁻¹) Notes
Li-ion (current) up to 400 (1.44 MJ kg⁻¹) Mature; basis of “all electric” demonstrators
Advanced Li-ion higher than current Li-ion Improved cathodes/anodes
Solid-state battery (Li-SSB) improved safety, energy density Pre-commercial
Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) high theoretical energy density Cycle-life challenges
Lithium-air (Li-air) highest theoretical energy density Identified as best long-term (2050) battery option
Conventional Jet A-1 (reference) ~12,000 Wh kg⁻¹ ~30× current Li-ion

(Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 13–14, 19)

Notes. Battery-electric aviation is essentially a short-haul option due to low energy density. Demonstrator projects include Eviation Alice (9-passenger, 1,046 km range, FAA certification target 2024), magniX e-Caravan (9-passenger, ~160 km), and the EasyJet/Wright Electric 186-seat all-electric aircraft (target 2030). The Lithium-air battery is highlighted as the most interesting battery option in the long-term (2050) ranking, owing to its anticipated high energy density. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 22, 19)

Related terms. Hybrid electric propulsion; turboelectric propulsion; fuel cell (aviation); hydrogen aviation.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, five chemistries, demonstrator projects.

Long-term storage liability (CCUS)

Definition. The post-closure obligation for monitoring, remediation and any compensation associated with stored CO₂ — including risks of leakage, environmental damage, and surrender of carbon credits previously received. Considered the most distinctive CCUS risk, extending decades beyond the operational phase, and a key reason for elevated cost of capital where it is not clearly allocated. (IEA 2026, pp. 21–22, 43)

Attributes — liability-transfer regimes.

Jurisdiction Liability transfer Mechanism
EU (most member states) After 15–20 years Transferred to state once operator demonstrates no significant leakage risk
United Kingdom (NZT/NEP) After 15 years Plus leakage cap mechanism
Norway (Longship, Northern Lights) After 15 years State-owned-enterprise sponsorship
Canada (Glacier, Alberta) Stewardship fund Post-closure pooled fund
United States (High Plains, Wyoming) Stewardship fund Post-closure pooled fund

(IEA 2026, pp. 43, 47)

Notes. Stewardship funds and financial security requirements (insurance, credit lines, surety bonds) help ensure that monitoring and remediation obligations can be met over time. For banks and long-term investors, uncertainty around long-term liability creates risks that cannot be easily priced or insured on private balance sheets, leading to higher cost of capital. Insurance markets are evolving (environmental liability insurance, FOAK technology coverage) but post-closure cover remains limited, expensive or subject to exclusions. (IEA 2026, pp. 21–22, 45–46)

Related terms. Bankability; stewardship fund (post-closure CO₂); cross-chain risk; Class VI well permit; carbon dioxide removal (CDR); regulated asset base (RAB).

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, jurisdictional regimes, financing implications.

Loss of Load Expectation (LoLE) — French 3-hour criterion

Aliases. Critère des trois heures (FR); espérance de défaillance; LoLE; loss-of-load probability adjacent.

Definition. A reliability metric for power-system capacity adequacy, defined as the expected number of hours per year during which generation cannot meet demand without resorting to emergency interruption (load shedding, voltage reduction, post-market actions). The French Code de l’énergie sets the LoLE target at less than 3 hours/year of expected supply-demand imbalance and less than 2 hours/year of expected involuntary load shedding. The target is met today and is the primary quantitative criterion against which the French electricity-mix planning is evaluated. (RTE 2022, Sections 7.1.2.1–7.1.2.2, pp. 290–291, translated from French)

Attributes — RTE 2050 reliability metrics.

Indicator Today RTE 2050 (under reference scenarios)
LoLE target (Code de l’énergie) <3 h/yr <3 h/yr (unchanged)
LoLE for load shedding <2 h/yr <2 h/yr (unchanged)
Expected non-distributed energy ~10 GWh/yr similar order of magnitude
Share of non-distributed energy ~0.002% of total demand ~0.002% of total demand
Expected deficit during failure events ~4 GW today ~10 GW (and more in M-scenarios)
Sizing risk events cold spell + nuclear unavailability cold spell + low wind/solar weeks

(RTE 2022, Sections 7.1.2.1–7.1.2.2, pp. 290–291)

Notes — RTE methodology evolution. RTE flags that the current “3-hour LoLE” criterion is blunt: it captures the probability of supply shortfall but not the depth of the shortfall. As VRE penetration rises, individual failure events become less frequent but deeper (10 GW deficit per event vs 4 GW today). RTE therefore proposes complementing LoLE with an Expected Energy Not Served (EENS, in MWh/yr) indicator and a peak deficit indicator to better characterise tail risk in 100% RE-friendly scenarios. (RTE 2022, Section 7.1.2.2, pp. 290–291)

Notes — vs ENTSO-E / GB practice. The French 3-hour criterion is broadly consistent with ENTSO-E target-LoLE values used elsewhere in continental Europe; Great Britain uses a slightly different reliability standard (~3 h/yr LoLE plus operational margins). Most of these criteria are derived from the cost of expected unserved energy (VOLL × EENS) balanced against the cost of incremental capacity. (RTE 2022, Section 7.1, pp. 287–290)

Related terms. Capacity adequacy; Power system flexibility; Residual load; Combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT); Open cycle gas turbine (OCGT); Operating reserves; Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); Frequency control.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, 3-hour criterion, French Code de l’énergie reference, RTE methodology critique (LoLE blunt vs EENS), 2050 sizing implications (translated from French).

Macroplastics

Definition. Plastic items larger than 5 mm in diameter, distinguished from microplastics (<5 mm) for monitoring and policy purposes. Macroplastics are dominated by mismanaged single-use packaging and account for the majority of plastic mass leaked into the environment. (OECD 2022, pp. 21–22)

Attributes — share of global plastic leakage in 2019.

Class Mass leaked Share
Macroplastics ~19 Mt 88%
Microplastics ~3 Mt 12%
Total plastic leakage 22 Mt 100%

(OECD 2022, p. 21)

Notes. OECD countries account for 14% of global macroplastic leakage but 36% of microplastic leakage. Non-OECD countries account for 86% of total leakage, driven mainly by mismanaged waste reaching the environment. Cleanup of macroplastics becomes more difficult and costly as items fragment into microplastics — strong upstream policy is therefore identified as more cost-effective than downstream cleanup. (OECD 2022, pp. 21–22)

Related terms. Microplastics; mismanaged plastic waste; plastic leakage; single-use plastics; plastic chemicals.

Source history. - OECD 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, leakage statistics, regional breakdown.

Mechanical recycling

Definition. The dominant plastic recycling pathway, in which plastic waste is washed, ground, extruded and pelletised back into a secondary feedstock that retains the polymer chain (no chemical decomposition). Currently accounts for ~99.9% of plastic recycling in Europe, with 5.5 Mt of recycled material used in production in 2021. (Grimaud and Girard 2024, p. 22)

Attributes.

Property Value
TRL 9 (commercially mature)
Energy intensity low
Output secondary granules
Limiting factor upstream sorting (must be mono-material, low contamination)
Geyer 2017 global recycling rate (2014) ~18% of nonfiber plastic waste; only 9% of all plastic ever made has been recycled

(Grimaud and Girard 2024, p. 22; Geyer et al. 2017, pp. 2–3)

Notes. Mechanical recycling is highly efficient and energy-cheap but inherently quality-limited and volume-limited: each cycle entails some loss of mechanical properties due to polymer-chain shortening and additive accumulation. Sensitivity to additives and the need for a clean, mono-material input stream are the main barriers to scale-up. Geyer et al. (2017) note that recycling delays — rather than avoids — final disposal, and only reduces primary plastic production where displacement is robustly demonstrated (counterfactual problem). (Grimaud and Girard 2024, p. 22; Geyer et al. 2017, pp. 2–3)

Related terms. Chemical recycling; secondary plastics market; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR); plastic chemicals.

Source history. - Grimaud and Girard 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, performance characteristics, limits (translated from French). - Geyer et al. 2017 — added 2026-05-08: global recycling-rate context.

Load shifting and load shedding (industrial flexibility)

Definition. Two regimes of industrial demand-side flexibility for electricity. Load shifting refers to temporarily shifting electricity consumption in time without reducing it; load shedding refers to a temporary reduction of consumption. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Attributes — aluminium example. Aluminium consumption can use 1.5–3% of flexibility for load shifting for durations under 12 hours; aluminium is more suitable for load shedding with a maximum of 25% consumption reduction for less than 4 hours. Longer durations would destabilise the electrolytic process. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Related terms. Hall-Héroult electrolysis process.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definitional contrast and aluminium attribute example.

Mechanical pulping vs chemical pulping

Definition. Two primary processes for producing pulp from wood fibres in paper manufacturing, differing in mechanism and energy/emissions profile. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 13)

Attributes (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 13).

Process Energy consumption Direct emissions Output share
Mechanical pulping 6.1–7.5 GJ/t pulp (electricity) — <20% of global primary pulp production
Chemical pulping 15.9 GJ heat + 3 GJ electricity per t pulp 0.5 tCO₂/t pulp majority of global primary pulp
Recycled paper (context) 1.7 GJ/t pulp electricity + 0.2 GJ/t pulp heat — 57% of pulp globally (2014); 71% in Europe

Notes. Mechanical pulping yields shorter fibres and lower-strength paper. Decarbonisation of paper production focuses on heat and chemical-pulping decarbonisation; transitioning CHP systems to bioenergy or hydrogen could reduce emissions by up to 100%. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 13)

Related terms. Process emissions.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition, energy/emissions profile, decarbonisation note.

Metal hydrides

Definition. Hydrogen-storage materials that combine hydrogen with metals (e.g. Fe, Cr, Mn, V, Cu, Co, Ni, Au, Pt) at elevated temperatures, storing hydrogen in solid state via reversible chemical bonding. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 31)

Attributes (AlZohbi et al. 2023, Table 1, pp. 32–33).

Property Value
Hydrogen content 1–2 wt%
Volumetric energy density 50–175 kg/m³
Highest known volumetric H₂ density 150 kg/m³ (Mg₂FeH₆); also Al(BH₄)₃
Reach of metallic-hydride volumetric density 115 kg/m³
Advantages high volumetric density; no high pressure required; lower upfront cost; safe; usable thermal effect
Drawbacks depends on metal properties; low gravimetric capacity; expensive high-temperature operation for release; activation energy higher than supplied by H₂ pressure

Notes. The need for higher activation energy than hydrogen pressure can supply means hydrogenation must be performed separately, making metal hydrides best suited to one-time applications rather than automotive use. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 31)

Related terms. Chemisorption; chemical hydrides; ammonia; hydrogen storage.

Source history. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, capacity, operational constraints.

Manufacturing capacity (clean energy technologies)

Definition. The maximum amount of a material, component or technology that a manufacturing facility is nominally able to produce. ETP-2026 distinguishes between “operational” capacity (currently producing), “committed” capacity (FID reached or under construction) and “preliminary” capacity (announced but pre-FID; feasibility studies underway). (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, pp. 373, 378)

Attributes — 2024 manufacturing investment, key clean technologies.

Item Value Year
Global manufacturing investment ~USD 200 billion 2024
Peak (recent) USD 220 billion 2023
Expected 2025 trend continued gentle decline 2025
China’s share of key supply-chain steps 60–85% (>95% for some) 2024
Chinese ownership of battery capacity outside China 5% (rising to ~25% by 2030 based on under-construction/FID projects) 2024–2030
Chinese-firm share of solar-PV capacity outside China large 2025

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 18–19, 217 ff.)

Notes — investment-spend timing. ETP-2026 models manufacturing investment using “investment overnight” (capital costs assumed to occur at install time, ignoring discount rates) and “investment spending” (overnight investment distributed evenly between FID and start of operations — typically 2 years for materials/most technologies, 1 year for solar-PV cells/modules). Greenfield additions only are counted (upgrades excluded for clean technologies; conversion-to-near-zero allowed for materials). (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, pp. 376–377)

Related terms. Clean energy technologies; critical materials; final investment decision (FID); ad valorem tariff; local content requirements (LCRs); levelised cost of production (LCOP).

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, classification (operational/committed/preliminary), 2024 investment metrics, accounting conventions.

Marginal abatement cost (MAC)

Aliases. MAC; marginal abatement cost curve (MACC); McKinsey curve; cost-of-emissions-reduction curve.

Definition. The cost (in € or US$ per tonne CO₂eq avoided) of the next available emissions-reduction action, evaluated against a defined counterfactual (typically the dominant incumbent technology). The full set of MACs across all available decarbonisation actions, ranked by MAC and plotted as cumulative emissions abated, gives the Marginal Abatement Cost Curve (MACC) — a foundational diagnostic tool in climate-policy economics. The MAC differs from the abatement cost in being marginal (next-action) rather than average (all-actions), and is the canonical metric for ranking decarbonisation options under a least-cost-mitigation criterion. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 3–4; cross-ref Abatement cost entry)

Attributes — MAC vs abatement cost (terminology).

Aspect MAC (marginal) Abatement cost (average)
What is computed next unit of CO₂ avoided total cost / total CO₂ avoided
Used for least-cost ranking; carbon price overall mitigation-strategy economics
Curve construction sort actions by MAC, cumulate abatement not curve-based
Sign of MAC can be negative (no-regret action) usually positive (net cost)

(Johnson et al. 2025, p. 3; cross-ref Abatement cost)

Notes — Johnson 2025 H₂-DRI-EAF MAC. Johnson computes the MAC of switching from BF-BOF (1.9 t CO₂/t steel, reference) to H₂-DRI-EAF in the EU. At an EU ETS price of €100/t CO₂, the LCOH₂ required for marginal-abatement competitiveness with BF-BOF rises by €2.12–3.95/kg H₂ from 2025 to 2026 (post-ETS-revision), reflecting the impact of free-allocation transitioning from H₂ to BF-BOF. By 2030 (high ETS price + free-allocation phase-out), H₂-DRI-EAF achieves MAC competitiveness in best-renewable-resource locations (Northern Scandinavia, Iberia) at €4.12/kg H₂. (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 3–4 and Fig. 4)

Notes — historical use. The McKinsey global GHG MACC (2007–2010) was the iconic application — it showed that cumulative emissions reductions of ~38 GtCO₂eq/yr below business-as-usual were achievable at MAC <€60/t (with ~30% of these at negative MAC, “no-regret” actions). Subsequent MACCs by IEA, IPCC and the World Bank refined the methodology and exposed limitations (static analysis, no learning, uncertain counterfactuals). (Johnson et al. 2025, pp. 3–4; McKinsey 2010 cited in literature)

Related terms. Abatement cost (greenhouse gas); Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM); EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); H2-DRI-EAF route; carbon contract for difference (CCfD); near-zero emissions materials; LCOH (levelised cost of hydrogen).

Source history. - Johnson et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: MAC definition, vs abatement cost, H₂-DRI-EAF MAC quantification, McKinsey-curve historical context.

Mechanical ventilation (VMC / MVHR)

Aliases. VMC (FR — Ventilation Mécanique Contrôlée); MVHR (Mechanical Ventilation with Heat Recovery); double flux; simple flux; HRV (Heat Recovery Ventilation); ERV (Energy Recovery Ventilation).

Definition. A controlled-airflow ventilation system that mechanically extracts stale indoor air and supplies fresh outdoor air through ducts, fans, and (in MVHR variants) a heat-exchanger that recovers heat from outgoing exhaust air to preheat incoming fresh air — recovering up to 90% of ventilation heat losses. VMC is the standard ventilation system in modern French residential and tertiary buildings; replacing legacy natural / passive ventilation (gaps, vents) reduces uncontrolled air infiltration and the associated heat losses while ensuring indoor air quality (humidity, CO₂, VOCs). (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35; AFNOR DTU 68.3)

Attributes — VMC variants.

Variant Description Heat recovery Energy savings
VMC simple flux (single-flux) extract only; supply via passive air vents none reduces uncontrolled infiltration
VMC simple flux hygro-régulé extract rate modulated by humidity none mild
VMC double flux (double-flux MVHR) extract + supply ducted; cross-flow heat exchanger 70–90% major (saves 50–80% ventilation losses)
VMC double flux + earth-pipe (puits canadien) preheat/precool fresh air via ground exchanger yes additional +10–20%
VMC double flux + heat pump dedicated air-air HP on supply duct very high high

(Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35)

Notes — significance. VMC double flux is a near-universal feature of Passivhaus-grade and high-performance residential renovation. It is essential when air-tightness is improved (n50 < 1.5 ach@50Pa) — without controlled ventilation, condensation and indoor-air-quality problems arise. In France, MaPrimeRénov’ subsidies cover VMC double flux installation as part of “BAR-EN-103” renovation packages. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35)

Notes — auxiliary energy and embodied cost. VMC double flux requires continuous fan electricity (~50–150 W per system, 24/7) — auxiliary energy ~400–1,300 kWh/yr. Embodied carbon is ~50–150 kg CO₂eq for the unit + ductwork. The auxiliary-energy and embodied costs must be netted against the heat-recovery benefit; in well-insulated French buildings the heat recovery saves more than the auxiliary cost. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35)

Related terms. Building envelope; air-tightness (blower door); building renovation (umbrella); heat pump (HP); RE2020 / RT2012; passive house (Passivhaus); embodied carbon (buildings); operational carbon (buildings).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: VMC variants table, MVHR significance, auxiliary-energy and embodied-cost trade-off (translated from French).

Maritime chokepoint

Definition. A strategic, narrow passage connecting two larger ocean or sea areas — often a strait or canal — through which a significant share of global shipping must transit. Maritime chokepoints are key vulnerability nodes in clean-energy-technology and critical-mineral supply chains, since most clean-energy components, batteries and refined minerals are moved by container, dry-bulk or wet-bulk shipping. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 378)

Notes. ETP-2026’s supply-chain analysis identifies Strait of Hormuz, Strait of Malacca, Bab el-Mandeb, Suez Canal and Panama Canal as the principal chokepoints for clean energy and fossil-fuel supply chains; cybersecurity, conflict and infrastructure-failure risks at these chokepoints are increasingly material to clean-energy supply security. Distinct shipping classes — container, breakbulk, Ro-Ro, dry bulk, wet bulk, bunkering — face different chokepoint risks. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 269–296, Glossary p. 378)

Related terms. Critical materials; manufacturing capacity; clean energy technologies; international marine bunkers.

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, chokepoint role in clean-energy supply chains.

MaPrimeRénov’ / CEE / Eco-PTZ (French renovation subsidies)

Aliases. MaPrimeRénov’ (MPR); CEE (Certificat d’Économie d’Énergie); Eco-PTZ (éco-prêt à taux zéro); aides à la rénovation (FR); French renovation subsidies.

Definition. A bundle of three principal financial instruments that French households use to finance residential renovation: - MaPrimeRénov’ — direct grant from the state (Anah — Agence Nationale de l’Habitat) to households, sized by household income and renovation depth. Up to €70,000 for “rénovation d’ampleur” (deep renovation) for low-income households. Replaced the older Crédit d’Impôt Transition Énergétique (CITE) in 2020. - CEE (Certificat d’Économie d’Énergie) — energy-savings certificates that energy suppliers (Total, EDF, Engie) must purchase to meet legal obligations; suppliers fund renovation works in exchange for the certificates, partially or fully covering the cost for households. Funding ~€5 billion/yr French total. - Eco-PTZ — interest-free loan up to €50,000 for renovation works (administered through banks); designed to bridge the gap between subsidies and total project cost. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7; ANAH 2024 statistics)

Attributes — French residential renovation funding mix (~2024).

Subsidy Annual budget Average per project Beneficiaries
MaPrimeRénov’ €4–5 billion €5,000–€70,000 ~700,000 households/yr
CEE €5 billion €1,000–€10,000 varies
Eco-PTZ €1 billion (loan volume) €15,000–€50,000 ~50,000 loans/yr
TVA réduite (5.5%) indirect varies universal
Local subsidies (regions, départements) varies varies regional
Crédit d’impôt rénovation various small declining

(Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7; ANAH; Ministère de la Transition Écologique 2024)

Notes — accumulation rules. Multiple subsidies can be combined (cumulé) up to a cap, typically 90–100% of project cost for low-income (très-modeste) households. The “Reste à charge” (remaining out-of-pocket cost) is the principal household-decision-driver — even with subsidies, deep-renovation works typically still require €10,000–€40,000 from the household. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7)

Notes — significance for renovation pace. The financial-instrument bundle is the principal policy lever for the French government’s target of 700,000 deep renovations per year by 2030 (vs ~80,000 in 2022). Goessel’s optimisation methodology is one input to the policy-design question: which combinations of measures should be prioritised by the subsidy schemes for cost-effective decarbonisation. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7)

Related terms. Building renovation (umbrella); DPE (Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique); passoire thermique; CEE (Certificat d’Économie d’Énergie); Energy poverty (précarité énergétique); RE2020 / RT2012.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: subsidy taxonomy, budget statistics, accumulation rules, policy-pace context (translated from French).

Material Flow Analysis (MFA / Sankey diagram)

Aliases. MFA; substance flow analysis (SFA); industrial metabolism; Sankey diagram methodology.

Definition. A systematic accounting of the physical mass flows of a substance, group of substances, or material through a defined system over a defined time period — typically visualised as a Sankey diagram in which the width of each arrow is proportional to the mass flow it represents. The data set must close at every node (mass balance) by accounting for primary inputs, secondary reactants, primary products, secondary products, losses, and stocks. Levi & Cullen 2018 use MFA + Sankey to map global chemical-sector mass flows from fossil-fuel feedstocks through to chemical products. (Levi and Cullen 2018, pp. 1726, 1729; Allwood and Cullen 2012, cited)

Attributes — MFA workflow.

Step Description
1. Define system boundary spatial (global, country) + temporal (year) + scope (process / sector / substance)
2. Identify nodes unit operations, processes, end-uses
3. Identify flows material streams between nodes
4. Compile data top-down (energy balance) + bottom-up (process yields × production volumes)
5. Check mass balance every node closes (Σ inputs = Σ outputs)
6. Visualise Sankey diagram (arrow width ∝ flow magnitude)
7. Sensitivity analysis one-at-a-time variation to identify dominant flows

(Levi and Cullen 2018, Section 2 methodology)

Notes — significance. MFA is the standard tool for industrial-ecology and material-efficiency studies. By making mass flows visible and traceable, MFA exposes downstream demand drivers (fertilisers, plastics, fibres) and enables prioritisation of mitigation levers (lightweighting, yield improvement, recycling). Without an MFA, decarbonisation scenarios for chemicals/plastics tend to focus narrowly on supply-side technology (e.g., carbon capture, hydrogen, biomass) and miss demand-side levers. (Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1726)

Notes — Top-18 chemicals framing. Levi & Cullen apply MFA at the global chemical sector and find that just 18 chemicals account for 63% of process energy and 75% of GHG emissions; ~10 first-tier intermediate transformations dominate upstream chemical consumption; and N-fertilisers + thermoplastics together account for >60% of total chemical-sector output. This concentrated demand structure makes downstream-mitigation-prioritisation feasible despite the chemical sector’s apparent complexity. (Levi and Cullen 2018, pp. 1729–1731)

Related terms. Top-18 chemicals (Levi & Cullen framing); petrochemicals (umbrella); high-value chemicals (HVCs); non-energy use of fossil fuels; near-zero emissions materials; refinery-petrochemical integration.

Source history. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, MFA workflow, Sankey visualisation, Top-18 chemicals framing.

MESSAGE (modelling framework)

Aliases. MESSAGE; MESSAGEix; MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM; Model for Energy Supply Strategy Alternatives and their General Environmental Impact.

Definition. A bottom-up Energy System Optimisation Model framework developed by the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA, Austria), first released in the 1980s and now maintained as the open-source MESSAGEix platform. MESSAGE is the energy-system core of the MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM Integrated Assessment Model used in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report scenarios. Manuel et al. 2025 found MESSAGE in 5% of single-model pathway studies. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8; Huppmann et al. 2019 cited)

Attributes — MESSAGE design features.

Indicator Value
Solver paradigm LP / MILP (GAMS or pyomo)
Foresight perfect or myopic
Milestone interpolation scaling-based with remaining-lifetime correction
End-effect mitigation salvage values + discounting
Endogenous learning yes (optional, used in IIASA SSP scenarios)
Endogenous early retirement optional
Spatial resolution typically 11-region global aggregation
Open-source status yes (MESSAGEix is open)
Use cases global IAM scenarios (IPCC AR6), Asian energy policy, IIASA research
Notable applications SSP scenarios, IIASA energy-transition studies

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8; Huppmann et al. 2019)

Notes — IPCC AR6 dependence. MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM is one of the principal IAM frameworks contributing scenarios to the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report. The combination of MESSAGE (energy + macro) with GLOBIOM (land-use + agriculture) gives a full-system-coverage IAM widely used in 1.5 °C / 2 °C mitigation studies. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 1)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); Integrated Assessment Model (IAM); TIMES; OSeMOSYS; PyPSA; TEMOA; foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); endogenous learning; Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, design features, IPCC AR6 dependence.

Methanation (Sabatier reaction)

Aliases. Methanation; Sabatier process; Sabatier reaction; CO₂-methanation; e-methane synthesis; CCU-methanation; biological methanation.

Definition. A catalytic chemical reaction that combines hydrogen with carbon dioxide (or carbon monoxide) to produce methane (CH₄) and water: CO₂ + 4 H₂ → CH₄ + 2 H₂O (ΔH ≈ −165 kJ/mol, exothermic). Discovered by Paul Sabatier (1902 Nobel Prize 1912), the reaction is the central step of the Power-to-Methane (P2M / PtCH₄) value chain — converting green hydrogen plus captured CO₂ into a drop-in synthetic natural gas that can use existing gas-grid infrastructure. Two principal variants: catalytic methanation (Ni-based catalyst, 250–400 °C, 1–80 bar; commercial scale demonstrated by Audi e-gas, Hitachi-Zosen Inova, Etogas) and biological methanation (anaerobic Methanobacterium archaea, 60–70 °C, near-atmospheric pressure; Electrochaea / Hydrogenics). (EVOLEN 2023, pp. 17–21)

Attributes — methanation routes.

Route Catalyst Temperature Pressure Per-pass conversion
Catalytic (Ni-based) Ni / Al₂O₃ 250–400 °C 1–80 bar >99% with recycle
Catalytic (Ru-based) Ru / Al₂O₃ 200–300 °C 1–10 bar >95%
Biological Methanobacterium archaea 60–70 °C ~1 bar >95%
Plasma-assisted non-thermal plasma + Ni 100–200 °C atmospheric emerging
Direct dual-function (DFM) Ni + sorbent 250–500 °C 1–10 bar emerging

(EVOLEN 2023, pp. 17–18)

Notes — significance for hydrogen storage and gas grid. Methanation enables seasonal-storage of green H₂ as CH₄ in the existing gas-grid infrastructure (much higher capacity than dedicated H₂ storage). The downside is the thermodynamic penalty — converting H₂ to CH₄ and back loses ~30% of the original energy (round-trip H₂→CH₄→H₂ via SMR efficiency 70%). This is why direct H₂ use is preferred where possible; methanation is the fallback when H₂ infrastructure is unavailable. (EVOLEN 2023, p. 21)

Notes — biological vs catalytic. Catalytic methanation has higher throughput and lower CAPEX but requires high-purity CO₂ feed and significant heat-integration. Biological methanation is more tolerant of impurities (including some CO₂ + H₂S mixtures, e.g. raw biogas), operates at lower temperature (no high-T process heat), but throughput is lower and bioreactors are larger. Both routes are commercial — Audi’s Werlte plant (catalytic, 6.3 MW) and Avedøre BioCat (biological, 1 MW Denmark) are reference installations. (EVOLEN 2023, p. 18)

Related terms. E-fuels — molecule-by-molecule (e-methane); Methanol synthesis (electrofuels and biofuels); Power-to-X (PtX); reverse water gas shift (rWGS); Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process; e-methane; CCU (carbon capture and utilisation); biogas; biomethane.

Source history. - EVOLEN 2023 — added 2026-05-08: definition, routes, hydrogen-storage role, biological vs catalytic comparison (translated from French).

Methanol synthesis (electrofuels and biofuels)

Definition. A catalytic process in which syngas (H₂ + CO + CO₂) is converted to methanol (CH₃OH) at 150–300 °C (423–573 K) and 10–100 bar (1–10 MPa) over copper-based catalysts (e.g. Cu/ZnO). Reactions: CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH (ΔH = −91 kJ mol⁻¹); CO₂ + 3H₂ → CH₃OH + H₂O (ΔH = −50 kJ mol⁻¹); the water gas shift CO + H₂O ↔︎ CO₂ + H₂ (ΔH = −41 kJ mol⁻¹) occurs simultaneously. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 12–13)

Notes. Methanol can be processed to gasoline (ExxonMobil’s Methanol-to-Gasoline) or to olefins via dimethyl ether (Methanol-to-Olefins, MTO), but no aviation electrofuels have yet been produced via the methanol pathway; the Fischer–Tropsch route is currently the only ASTM D7566–certified gas-to-liquid pathway for aviation electrofuels. Direct use of methanol as aviation fuel has been initially explored but is scarcely documented. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 12–13, 21)

Related terms. Fischer–Tropsch (FT) process; co-electrolysis; reverse water gas shift; electrofuels; olefins.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, reactions, FT vs methanol-route comparison.

Methanol (CH₃OH, commodity chemical)

Aliases. Methyl alcohol; wood alcohol; MeOH.

Definition. A colourless, volatile liquid alcohol (CH₃OH), the simplest C1-aliphatic alcohol and one of the largest-volume base chemicals globally. Industrial methanol is produced almost exclusively by catalytic synthesis from synthesis gas (CO + 2 H₂ → CH₃OH) over a Cu-Zn-Al₂O₃ catalyst at 200–300 °C and 50–100 bar. The synthesis gas comes from steam methane reforming (in natural-gas-rich regions) or from coal gasification (China). Methanol is the gateway molecule to MTO, MTP, MTA, formaldehyde, acetic acid, MTBE, biodiesel transesterification, and increasingly to renewable maritime fuel. (Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production (recent) ~110 Mt/yr
Boiling point 64.7 °C
LHV 19.9 MJ/kg
Synthesis catalyst Cu/ZnO/Al₂O₃
Synthesis temperature 200–300 °C
Synthesis pressure 50–100 bar
Per-pass conversion 5–10% (with recycle to total ~99%)
Feedstock split (global) NG/SMR ~75%; coal ~20%; oil ~3%; biomass ~2%
Methanol-to-olefins (MTO) share of end-use ~25–30% (mostly China)
Formaldehyde share of end-use ~25%
MTBE / DME / fuel share ~15%
Acetic acid (Cativa / Monsanto) share ~10%
Other (solvents, biodiesel, methacrylate) ~20%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727)

Notes — colour-coded methanol. Conventional fossil methanol is “grey”; with CCS on the SMR or coal-gasification step it becomes “blue”; from green H₂ + captured CO₂ it is “e-methanol” or “renewable methanol” (CRI Iceland: ~5 ML/y from geothermal CO₂); from biomass gasification it is “bio-methanol”. Renewable methanol total capacity is small but growing (<2 Mt/yr 2024) — the largest defossilisation route via methanol is to scale e-methanol with renewable electricity. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 110; cross-ref Methanol synthesis entry)

Notes — maritime fuel role. Methanol is one of the leading IMO-approved low-carbon marine fuels alongside ammonia. Maersk has ordered ~25 methanol-dual-fuel container ships (first delivered 2023); shipyards report ~10% of 2026–2028 ship orders are methanol-fuelled. This emerging end-use could grow methanol demand by 15–30 Mt/yr by 2035 if shipping decarbonisation accelerates. (IEA ETP 2026 — cross-ref Ammonia and methanol propulsion ships entry)

Related terms. Methanol synthesis (electrofuels and biofuels); Methanol-to-Olefins (MTO); methanol-to-aromatics (MTA); methanol-to-propylene (MTP); ammonia and methanol propulsion ships; e-fuels (electricity-based fuels); coal gasification (to hydrogen); steam methane reforming (SMR); high-value chemicals (HVCs); near-zero emissions materials.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, synthesis chemistry, end-use shares. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 110 Mt/yr global, feedstock split. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: colour-coded methanol, defossilisation route.

Multi-objective optimisation (MOO / OMO)

Aliases. MOO; OMO (FR — Optimisation Multi-Objectifs); MOOP (multi-objective optimisation problem); multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM); vector optimisation.

Definition. A class of optimisation problems with two or more conflicting objective functions to be simultaneously optimised — typically minimisation of cost + carbon + discomfort, or maximisation of profit + sustainability. Unlike single-objective optimisation (which has one optimal solution), multi-objective optimisation produces a set of optimal solutions: the Pareto front — solutions where no objective can be improved without worsening at least one other objective (Pareto dominance criterion). MOO is the standard analytical framework for sustainability-design decisions where economic, environmental, and social objectives conflict. (Goessel 2025, pp. 66–73 and Fig. 2.6.1)

Attributes — MOO problem formulation.

Element Description
Decision variables (x) the parameters being optimised (e.g. renovation strategy, technology choice)
Objective functions (f₁, f₂, …, fₙ) quantities to minimise / maximise (e.g. CGD, embodied carbon, SET-DH)
Constraints feasibility limits (e.g. heritage rules, technical compatibility)
Pareto-dominant solution x₁ dominates x₂ if all f(x₁) ≤ f(x₂) and at least one strict inequality
Pareto front set of all non-dominated solutions in objective space
Decision-aid step choosing one preferred solution from the Pareto front (multi-criteria decision-making)

(Goessel 2025, pp. 66–67)

Notes — solution methods. - Exact methods (linear programming for linear MOO, exhaustive enumeration for small finite cases) — Goessel uses exact enumeration on ~10,000 renovation strategies. - Genetic / evolutionary algorithms (NSGA-II, NSGA-III, MOEA/D) — population-based search; the standard for >100,000 candidate solutions. - Scalarisation — convert multiple objectives to single via weighted sum or epsilon-constraint; gives one solution per weight choice. - Interactive — engage decision-maker to refine preferences progressively.

(Goessel 2025, pp. 68–69, citing Deb 2002 NSGA-II)

Related terms. Pareto dominance / Pareto front; NSGA (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm); building renovation (umbrella); Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); multi-criteria decision-making; K-Means clustering.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: MOO definition, problem formulation, solution-method taxonomy (translated from French).

Mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP)
