Definition. An optimisation framework in which the objective function and/or constraints contain non-linear terms and a subset of decision variables is restricted to integer values. The principal mathematical tool used in hydrogen pipeline network design where (i) topology decisions (which arcs exist) are binary, (ii) discrete commercial pipe diameters are integer, and (iii) gas-flow physics (pressure drop ∝ flow²) are non-linear. Distinguished from MILP (mixed-integer linear programming) — used for problems where the non-linear flow physics is approximated by linear constraints. (Hammond et al. 2025, abstract and Section 1; André et al. 2013, p. 240)

Notes — applications. - Brimberg et al. — Tabu search + Variable Neighborhood Search for South Gabon offshore oil collection (formulated as mixed-integer program). - Middleton & Bielicki SimCSS — MILP for CCUS pipeline networks (linear objective, omits non-linear flow-diameter relations). - Johnson & Ogden HyPAT — MILP for hydrogen pipeline optimisation in GAMS, same simplification. - André et al. ECOTRANSHY — joint topology + diameter sizing in a single non-linear model with local search. - Hammond et al. StObGA — graph-based Steiner tree with Obstacles Genetic Algorithm; native MINLP-equivalent pipe routing.

(André et al. 2013, p. 240; Hammond et al. 2025, Section 1)

Related terms. Hydrogen pipeline network design; Steiner tree (with obstacles); Tabu search; Genetic algorithm; energy system models (100% RE analyses).

Source history. - André et al. 2013 — added 2026-05-08: definition, distinction from MILP, French hydrogen-pipeline application. - Hammond et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: applications inventory, StObGA approach.

Methyl methacrylate (MMA) and PMMA

Aliases. MMA; methyl 2-methyl-2-propenoate; PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate); acrylic; Plexiglas; Lucite; Perspex.

Definition. Methyl methacrylate (CH₂=C(CH₃)-COOCH₃) is a vinyl monomer produced industrially by three competing routes: (i) acetone-cyanohydrin (ACH) — the historical Mitsubishi-Lucite route; (ii) C4-isobutylene-based oxidation (Asahi, Mitsubishi Alpha process); and (iii) methacrolein → methyl methacrylate (Lucite Alpha-2). PMMA is its free-radically polymerised polymer — a transparent, glassy, scratch-resistant amorphous thermoplastic used in optical and lighting applications. (Speight 2019, Chapters 7.3, 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global MMA production ~5 Mt/yr
Global PMMA production ~3 Mt/yr
MMA largest end-use — PMMA ~75%
MMA — coatings, surface adhesives, ink resins ~20%
MMA — copolymers (in PVC modifiers, ABS modifiers) ~5%
PMMA — transparent sheet (Plexiglas, Perspex, Lucite) ~40%
PMMA — automotive lighting (rear lamp lenses) ~25%
PMMA — display screens, optical fibres ~15%
PMMA — paint, dental ~20%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3)

Notes — properties. PMMA Tg ~105 °C, refractive index 1.49, transmits 92% of visible light (better than glass), tensile strength 70 MPa. PMMA is brittle vs PC but more scratch-resistant; PMMA-PC blends combine the advantages of both. PMMA is amorphous (no crystalline phase), so it is fully transparent. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Related terms. Acetone; isobutylene; propylene; engineering plastics (umbrella); free-radical polymerisation; plastic processing (umbrella); cumene process (Hock process — phenol + acetone); high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: MMA production routes, PMMA properties, end-use shares.

Methanol-to-Olefins (MTO)

Definition. A catalytic conversion process that produces light olefins (predominantly ethylene C₂H₄ and propylene C₃H₆) from methanol via dimethyl ether intermediate (CH₃OH → CH₃OCH₃ → C₂H₄, C₃H₆). MTO is the central enabling technology for producing plastics from non-petroleum carbon sources — biomass-derived methanol, e-methanol from CO₂ + H₂, or coal-derived methanol — and is therefore a cornerstone of bio-based plastics and Power-to-Plastic pathways. (Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 30–31)

Attributes.

Parameter Value
Operating temperature 300–500 °C
TRL 6–7 (commercial deployment in China; lab-to-pilot in EU)
Methanol from coal MTO already commercial in China
Methanol from biomass gasification demonstrated (Enerkem Canada: 38 ML/y MeOH from 100 kt waste)
Methanol from CO₂ + green H₂ demonstrated in Iceland (~5 ML/y from power-plant CO₂)

(Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 24–25, 30–31)

Notes. MTO is energy-intensive, partly due to the upstream methanol synthesis (and, in the e-methanol case, the H₂ generation and CO₂ capture). Annual European methanol production is ~1.5 Mt today; if the bio-based and Power-to-Plastic plastic routes scale, demand could reach ~2.2 Mt by 2050. MTO complements the Fischer-Tropsch route within Power-to-X portfolios. (Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 30–31; Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 16)

Related terms. Methanol synthesis; Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process; Power-to-Plastic; e-fuels; chemical recycling; steam cracking; olefins.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — listed in Pending 2026-05-07. - Grimaud and Girard 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, operating window, deployment status; promoted from Pending (translated from French).

Methanol-to-aromatics (MTA)

Aliases. MTA; methanol-to-BTX; methanol-aromatisation.

Definition. A catalytic conversion process that produces aromatic hydrocarbons — predominantly the BTX cluster (benzene, toluene, xylenes) — from methanol over a modified zeolite catalyst (typically Zn- or Ga-modified ZSM-5, or HZSM-5 with hierarchical mesoporosity). MTA is one of three on-purpose methanol-conversion routes (alongside MTO for olefins and MTP for propylene) and provides a non-naphtha, non-reformer aromatic-supply pathway that integrates with the C1 chemistry architecture. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Attributes — Zhang 2024 catalyst benchmarks.

Catalyst Conversion Aromatics selectivity
Zn-ZrO₂/ZSM-5 20% 80%
Zn-CrOx/ZSM-5 16% 73.9%
Ga-ZSM-5 moderate 50–60%

(Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Notes — operating window. MTA typically operates at 350–500 °C and atmospheric to mildly elevated pressure, with methanol feed (15–60 vol% in inert/H₂). Co-feeding hydrogen helps control coke formation. The reaction proceeds via methanol-to-DME → carbon-pool aromatic-cycle/olefin-cycle competition; aromatic selectivity is enhanced by acid-site moderation and metal modification (Zn, Ga, Mo). (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Notes — significance for defossilisation. As BTX demand grows and naphtha steam cracking is increasingly feedstock-constrained or carbon-constrained, MTA becomes important as a non-naphtha aromatic source. Combined with biomethanol (lignocellulose gasification), e-methanol (CO₂ + green H₂) or coal-methanol (with CCS), MTA enables defossilised BTX. As of writing, MTA is at industrial-scale demonstration in China but not yet widely commercialised. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Related terms. Methanol synthesis (electrofuels and biofuels); Methanol-to-Olefins (MTO); BTX aromatics; high-value chemicals (HVCs); Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process; C1 chemistry; synergistic catalysis (OXZEO); near-zero emissions materials.

Source history. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, catalyst benchmarks, role in defossilising BTX.

Methanol-to-Propylene (MTP)

Aliases. MTP; Lurgi MTP; Air Liquide MTP; methanol-to-propylene process.

Definition. A catalytic conversion process that produces propylene as the primary product (rather than as an MTO co-product) from methanol over a modified zeolite catalyst (typically Zn- or P-modified ZSM-5) operated at lower temperature than MTO and tuned for high propylene selectivity. The reaction proceeds via methanol-to-DME → carbon-pool olefin chemistry on the zeolite, with downstream cracking of higher olefins back to propylene to maximise the propylene yield. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Attributes — Lurgi MTP commercial benchmarks.

Indicator Value
Reactor temperature 460–490 °C
Reactor pressure 1.3–1.8 bar
Catalyst modified ZSM-5 (Lurgi MTP catalyst)
Propylene selectivity 65–70 wt% (of total olefins)
Ethylene selectivity 5–10 wt%
C4+ selectivity 20–25 wt% (recycled to MTP for cracking)
Per-pass conversion ~99% (high)
Methanol consumption ~3.0 t / t propylene
First commercial unit Trinidad (~470 kt/yr propylene), since 2008

(Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Notes — vs MTO. MTO targets ethylene + propylene roughly in equal proportions; MTP biases the product slate toward propylene with downstream C4+ recycle. MTP is favoured where the local market specifically needs propylene-enriched output (China shale-gas-deficient context); MTO is favoured where ethylene + propylene co-production fits the polymer market. Both are key non-naphtha sources of olefins under the C1-chemistry umbrella. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Related terms. Methanol (commodity); methanol-to-olefins (MTO); methanol-to-aromatics (MTA); propylene; C1 chemistry; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, Lurgi MTP benchmarks, vs MTO.

Microfibre pollution

Aliases. Synthetic microfibres; clothing-derived microplastics; textile microfibres; laundry-effluent microfibres.

Definition. Tiny fibres (length 100 μm – 5 mm, diameter 10–50 μm) shed from synthetic-textile garments — polyester, polyamide (Nylon), acrylic, polypropylene, elastane — during their life cycle, particularly during washing cycles in domestic and industrial laundry. Released as effluent into wastewater, microfibres pass through wastewater-treatment plants (50–80% removal typical, lower for older plants) and discharge to freshwater rivers and ultimately the marine environment. Microfibres are the single largest source of primary microplastic pollution in the global oceans — ~190,000 t/yr (~35% of total marine microplastic input), exceeding tyre wear, plastic-pellet spillage, and personal-care-product microbeads. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 191, 195–196)

Attributes — emission rate and trajectory.

Indicator Value
Microfibres released per kg garment per wash 1,500–4,500 fibres
Mass-basis emissions per garment-wash 0.1–0.5 g
Total annual marine microfibre input ~190,000 t/yr
Synthetic-textile share of marine primary microplastics ~35%
Wastewater-treatment removal efficiency 50–80% (older plants); >95% (advanced membrane bioreactor)
Top-loading vs front-loading washer fibre release top-loading ~5× more fibres
France microfibre filter mandate 2025 (Loi AGEC) — mandatory filters in new washing machines
EU regulatory framework EU Microplastics Strategy 2023, REACH restrictions

(Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 191, 195–196; OECD 2022; ECHA 2023)

Notes — environmental and human-health impact. Microfibres accumulate in marine sediments, are ingested by zooplankton + filter-feeding bivalves + finfish, and bioaccumulate up the food chain. Human dietary exposure via seafood is documented; airborne exposure from indoor textile dust is also substantial. The persistent organic pollutants (POPs) sorbed onto microfibre surfaces (PCBs, PAHs, pesticides) compound the toxicity concern. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, p. 196)

Notes — mitigation hierarchy. Per EU Microplastics Strategy: 1. Source reduction — substitute synthetic fibres with natural / cellulosic where possible; lyocell (Tencel) closed-loop production. 2. Garment-design intervention — tighter weave, longer-lifetime garments (less wash cycles per garment-life). 3. Washing-machine filters — capture microfibres before discharge to wastewater (mandatory new-machine France 2025). 4. Wastewater treatment upgrade — membrane bioreactors capture >95% but require capital expenditure. 5. Behaviour — wash less frequently, lower temperatures, full loads.

(Niinimäki et al. 2020, p. 196; EU Microplastics Strategy)

Related terms. Microplastics; textile fibres (synthetic and natural); fast fashion; plastic chemicals; polyester (PET); polyamides (Nylon); plastic leakage; mismanaged plastic waste; chemical recycling.

Source history. - Niinimäki et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-08: definition, emission rate, mitigation hierarchy.

Microplastics

Definition. Plastic particles smaller than 5 mm in diameter, originating from primary release (deliberate manufacture, e.g. cosmetic microbeads) or secondary fragmentation of macroplastics. Sources include tyre and brake wear, road markings, textile washing, and progressive UV/mechanical degradation of larger plastic items. (OECD 2022, pp. 21–22, 47, 52)

Attributes — global picture.

Parameter Value
Share of total 2019 plastic leakage 12% (~3 Mt of 22 Mt)
Largest single source tyre wear (and road markings)
OECD share of global microplastic leakage 36%
Detection in human cardiovascular plaque (Naples 2024 study) 150/257 patients positive

(OECD 2022, pp. 21–22, 52; Goel and Tripathi 2024, p. ix)

Notes. Microplastics have been documented in freshwater, terrestrial environments, food and beverages, the air we breathe, and human tissue. Aerial microplastic pollution is highest in highly urbanised areas. The growing exposure prompted the EU REACH restriction on intentionally added microplastics (2023) and is a focus of the global plastic pollution treaty being negotiated under UNEP/INC since 2022. (OECD 2022, pp. 22, 52; Goel and Tripathi 2024, pp. ix–xv)

Related terms. Macroplastics; plastic leakage; mismanaged plastic waste; plastic chemicals.

Source history. - OECD 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, leakage statistics, sources. - Goel and Tripathi 2024 — added 2026-05-08: human-exposure context.

Migration (plastic chemicals)

Definition. The unintended (or intentionally engineered) transfer of chemical substances from a plastic product to a contacting medium — most importantly food, food simulants (FSs), water, saliva, sweat, or air. The migration process consists of four steps: (i) diffusion of compounds through the polymer; (ii) desorption from the polymer surface; (iii) sorption at the plastic–medium interface; (iv) absorption into the contacting medium. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, pp. 187, 190)

Notes — drivers of migration rate. - Higher temperature → faster migration (e.g. retort processing, microwave heating, hot-fill). - Longer contact time → more migration (Fick’s law diffusion). - Higher fat content of food → greater migration of lipophilic plasticizers and slip agents. - Polymer type matters: PA/PE blends, PVC and PS show different migration profiles for the same chemical. - Phthalate plasticizers exhibit some of the highest documented migration rates — up to 350% transfer in PVC gasket-on-olive-oil tests, indicating transfer via the seal as well as the gasket.

(Hahladakis et al. 2018, pp. 187, 190, Table 2)

Related terms. Plasticizers (phthalate esters); antioxidants (plastic additives); chemicals of concern; plastic chemicals; PoTSs (potentially toxic substances).

Source history. - Hahladakis et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, four-step process, rate determinants.

Mismanaged plastic waste

Definition. Plastic waste that is neither recycled, incinerated nor disposed of in a sanitary landfill, but is instead disposed of in uncontrolled dumpsites, openly burned, or littered — and is therefore at high risk of leaking into the environment. Identified by the OECD as the principal source of macroplastic leakage globally. (OECD 2022, pp. 14–15, 21)

Attributes — global plastic waste fates 2019.

Fate Share
Recycled (after recycling losses) 9%
Incinerated 19%
Sanitary landfill ~50%
Mismanaged (dumpsites, open burning, leaked) 22%

(OECD 2022, pp. 14–15)

Notes. Mismanaged-waste leakage has more than doubled in two decades. Closing leakage pathways through sanitary waste-management infrastructure, organised collection and anti-littering policies is identified as the first phase of the OECD’s plastics policy roadmap. Achieving net-zero plastic leakage in low- and middle-income countries is estimated to require ~EUR 25 billion/y in basic waste-management infrastructure investment, of which only ~2% is currently met by official development assistance. (OECD 2022, pp. 21, 26–27)

Related terms. Plastic leakage; macroplastics; microplastics; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR); single-use plastics.

Source history. - OECD 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, fate breakdown, infrastructure-finance gap.

Mismatch energy (VRE storage modelling)

Definition. A normalised time-series describing the imbalance between aggregated renewable generation and electricity load in highly renewable power-system designs. Defined by Heide et al. (2010) as Δ(t) = a·W(t)/⟨W⟩ + b·S(t)/⟨S⟩ − L(t)/⟨L⟩, where W(t), S(t) and L(t) are wind, solar and load time series, ⟨X⟩ denotes average over the modelling period, and a = ⟨W⟩/⟨L⟩, b = ⟨S⟩/⟨L⟩ are the wind and solar coverage shares. For a 100% wind-plus-solar scenario, a + b = 1. (Heide et al. 2010, Section 2 and Eq. 1)

Notes — derived metrics. - Standard deviation σ_Δ — simplest balancing-cost proxy; minimised at a = 0.62 in the Heide 100% wind+solar case. - Required stored energy H_max = max H(t) − min H(t) of the cumulative storage filling H(t) = H(t−1) + η_in·Δ if Δ ≥ 0 else (1/η_out)·Δ — minimised at a = 0.47 (idealised η = 1) or a = 0.57 (using the 90% quantile of stored energy). - Surplus generation factor γ = a + b > 1 to compensate for storage losses; γ ≈ 1.05 (pumped hydro) or γ ≈ 1.28 (hydrogen) at a = b.

(Heide et al. 2010, Section 2 and Figs. 3–4)

Notes. The mismatch energy concept underpins the “seasonal optimal mix” of wind and solar generation in highly renewable Europe — one of the most cited benchmarks in 100% renewable energy systems literature. Switching from monthly to hourly resolution increases storage losses (and thus γ) materially. (Heide et al. 2010, Sections 2–3)

Related terms. Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); seasonal optimal mix; storage efficiency; surplus generation factor; pumped hydro energy storage (PHES); hydrogen storage.

Source history. - Heide et al. 2010 — added 2026-05-08: definition, derived metrics, optimal-mix locations.

Motor fuels (umbrella)

Aliases. Gasoline; petrol; motor spirit; motor gasoline; aviation gasoline; mogas.

Definition. A category of liquid petroleum products with relative density 0.70–0.79 at 60 °F and boiling range 30–220 °C, produced by blending refinery streams (catalytic-reformer reformate, FCC gasoline, hydrocracker naphtha, alkylate, isomerate, butanes, oxygenates) to meet performance specifications for spark-ignition internal combustion engines. Subcategories include automotive gasoline (passenger cars, light commercial vehicles), aviation gasoline (light aircraft; not for turbines), and small-engine fuels (chainsaws, motor mowers, outboard marine). Motor fuel is the largest single end-use of crude oil globally — historically ~50% of refined-product volume. (Addicott 1971, pp. 59–61; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4 fuels chemistry)

Attributes — composition and properties.

Property Value
Relative density (60 °F / 60 °F) 0.70–0.79
Boiling range 30–220 °C
Carbon range C5–C12
Paraffins (n- + iso-) typically 40–60 vol%
Aromatics (BTX) typically 25–45 vol% (legacy >35%; reformulated <35%)
Olefins typically 5–20 vol% (FCC-rich)
Cycloparaffins (naphthenes) typically 5–15 vol%
Sulfur (Tier 3 / Euro 6, post-2017) <10 ppm (vs ~300 ppm legacy)
Lead (banned EU 2000, US 1995) 0 (was 0.6 g/L tetraethyl lead)
RVP (vapour pressure) 7–14 psi (winter higher for cold-start)
Octane (RON, regular) 91–93 (US 87)
Octane (RON, premium) 95–98 (US 91–93)

(Addicott 1971, pp. 60–63 and Tables; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Notes — blending components from the refinery. - Light straight-run gasoline (C5–C6, RON ~65) → isomerised to higher RON. - Heavy straight-run naphtha (RON ~30) → catalytic reforming → reformate (RON ~95). - FCC gasoline (RON 90–95) — major contributor to motor-fuel pool, but high olefin content limits use under reformulated-gasoline rules. - Hydrocracker naphtha (RON ~50–55) → goes to reformer. - Alkylate (RON 92–98) — premium component. - Isomerate (RON ~85–92) — from light-naphtha isomerisation. - Butanes (n-butane, isobutane) — RVP-control component. - Oxygenates (ethanol, MTBE, ETBE) — octane and oxygen-content compliance.

(Addicott 1971, pp. 61–63; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Notes — defossilisation outlook. Bio-ethanol blending (E10 standard in EU; up to E85 / E100 in Brazil) and HVO/HEFA renewable gasoline directly displace fossil motor fuel. Long-term, electrification of light vehicles is projected to drive global motor-fuel demand sharply down, with surviving demand concentrated in legacy markets and aviation gasoline. Refiners increasingly pivot from fuel-oriented to chemicals-oriented configurations (refinery-petrochemical integration). (Cross-ref Refinery-petrochemical integration entry; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024)

Related terms. Petroleum refining (umbrella); naphtha; catalytic reforming; catalytic cracking (FCC); alkylation (refinery); isomerisation (refinery); octane number (RON / MON); knock; high-value chemicals (HVCs); refinery-petrochemical integration.

Source history. - Addicott 1971 — added 2026-05-08: definition, terminology, composition, blending components. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): blending and modern specifications.

Octane number (RON / MON)

Aliases. Octane rating; RON (research octane number); MON (motor octane number); AKI (anti-knock index); PON (pump octane number); octane index.

Definition. A standardised measure of a motor-fuel sample’s resistance to knock (autoignition) under spark-ignition-engine compression, calibrated against reference mixtures of n-heptane (octane = 0) and isooctane / 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (octane = 100). Higher octane = greater knock resistance = supports higher engine compression ratio = higher thermal efficiency. Three measurement standards: RON (Research Octane Number, ASTM D2699, 600 rpm, 52 °C intake) — slow-driving / cruise conditions; MON (Motor Octane Number, ASTM D2700, 900 rpm, 149 °C intake) — high-load / high-speed conditions; AKI = (RON+MON)/2 — the US “pump” rating displayed at filling stations. (Addicott 1971, pp. 64–66; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Attributes — typical octane values.

Component RON MON
n-heptane (reference low) 0 0
isooctane (2,2,4-TMP, reference high) 100 100
n-pentane 62 67
2-methylbutane (isopentane) 92 90
Benzene 102 90
Toluene 121 109
Mixed xylenes ~115 ~108
Ethanol 109 90
MTBE 117 102
Tetraethyl lead (TEL) (banned) additive — raises RON ~3–6 per g/L —
Light straight-run naphtha ~65 ~63
Catalytic reformate (typical) ~95 ~85
FCC gasoline 90–95 78–82
Alkylate 92–98 88–94
HCK naphtha ~50 ~45

(Addicott 1971, p. 64–66 and Table 3; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Notes — refinery octane economics. The “octane gap” between low-octane straight-run streams and the gasoline-pool RON target drives the demand for catalytic reforming, isomerisation, alkylation, and oxygenate blending. Each refinery operates an octane balance: all gasoline-pool components are weighted by their volume share and octane number to ensure final blend ≥ specification. Premium gasoline commands a price premium of ~5–15% over regular due to the higher concentration of high-octane components. (Addicott 1971, pp. 65–66; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Related terms. Motor fuels (umbrella); knock; catalytic reforming; alkylation (refinery); isomerisation (refinery); MTBE; ethanol; aromatic hydrocarbons.

Source history. - Addicott 1971 — added 2026-05-08: definition, RON/MON/AKI distinction, typical values. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): refinery octane balance.

Modulation nucléaire (load-following nuclear)

Aliases. Load-following nuclear; suivi de charge nucléaire; nuclear flexibility; modulating nuclear.

Definition. Operation of a pressurised water reactor at less than full available power, varying its output to follow load and/or to balance variable RES. French nuclear reactors (palier 900 MW, 1300 MW, N4, EPR / EPR2) are designed to modulate over the range ~25–100% of nominal power, with controlled ramp rates (typically up to ~5%/min) and operational constraints linked to xenon transients and fuel-cycle management. Modulation is a key component of French power-system flexibility today and a critical assumption for high-VRE futures. (RTE 2022, Section 7.10.3.2, p. 380, translated from French)

Attributes — RTE 2050 modulation envelope.

Indicator Today (2020) RTE 2050 (M1, M23) RTE 2050 (N1, N2, N03)
Annual nuclear modulation ~50 TWh 200+ TWh in M-scenarios smaller, ~100 TWh
Equivalent hours of CF reduction ~700 h/yr (all units) up to 2,000 h/yr ~1,000 h/yr
Capacity-factor reduction from modulation ~5–8 percentage points up to 15 percentage points ~10 percentage points
Nuclear “modulation” share of total flexibility ~10% ~30% (M-scenarios) ~20% (N-scenarios)
Operating constraint xenon transients, ~20% min stable similar similar

(RTE 2022, Sections 7.10.3.1–7.10.3.2, p. 380, translated)

Notes — drivers of nuclear modulation in 2050. RTE identifies four drivers of nuclear-fleet output reduction: - Service-system reserves — part of nuclear capacity is set aside for FCR/aFRR, immobilising some MW today; by 2050, batteries take over much of this role, freeing nuclear to produce energy. - Fuel-cycle (combustible) management — load-following reduces fuel utilisation efficiency; today’s modulation costs ~700 h/yr of CF reduction. - No-export periods — when interconnection capacity is saturated and domestic demand is low, nuclear must reduce output rather than export. - Curtailment-priority logic — when both RES and nuclear are simultaneously surplus, RTE assumes RES is curtailed first (zero variable cost) and nuclear modulates second; but in M-scenarios with very high RES, nuclear modulation becomes substantial because RES output exceeds export capacity even after RES curtailment. (RTE 2022, Section 7.10.3.2, p. 380)

Notes — economic implication. Modulation is partly free (no marginal cost beyond fuel saving) but reduces capital-cost recovery per MWh produced. RTE’s economic analysis attributes this opportunity cost to the renewable build-out in M-scenarios — i.e. high RES penetration imposes a system cost on nuclear via modulation. Reciprocally, EPR2 build (in N-scenarios) reduces VRE curtailment, reducing the modulation cost of both fleets. (RTE 2022, Sections 7.10.3, 11.6.5)

Related terms. Nuclear power (incl. small modular reactors); Curtailment; Operating reserves; EPR2 programme; RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 scenarios; Capacity factor; Power system flexibility.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, French envelope (~700 h/yr today rising to 2,000 h/yr in M-scenarios), four drivers, economic implication (translated from French).

French residential typologies (Chalandon, maison de bourg)

Aliases. Typologies bâti (FR); building stock typology; archetype housing; case-study housing; representative-building approach.

Definition. A classification framework that groups individual buildings into representative archetypes sharing common characteristics — construction period, structural typology, envelope materials, surface area, heating system — so that renovation and impact studies can be conducted on a manageable number of building types rather than the full ~30-million-dwelling French stock. Two contrasting French residential typologies, both used as case studies in Goessel 2025: - Maison Chalandon (1969–1974) — single-family detached, low-cost mass-produced housing built under French Housing Minister Albin Chalandon’s program; lightweight timber-frame, poor insulation, large window-wall ratio, gas or oil heating typical, ~80–120 m² floor area. Represents the post-war “rapidly-built” housing stock with poor energy performance (Class E–G typical). - Maison de bourg (pre-1915) — heritage-stone single-family house in rural town centres; thick massive stone walls (50+ cm), high thermal mass, traditional construction, often heated by wood stove or oil boiler, ~60–100 m² floor area, often heritage-protected (planning constraints on exterior insulation). (Goessel 2025, pp. 75–80; CSTB typology database)

Attributes — Chalandon vs maison de bourg comparison.

Indicator Chalandon (1969–1974) Maison de bourg (pre-1915)
Construction timber-frame + plasterboard massive stone (calcaire / granite)
Wall thickness 15–30 cm 50–80 cm
Wall U-value (typical) 1.8 W/m²K 1.2 W/m²K
Thermal mass low very high
Heritage protection none often Article L621 / ZPPAUP
ITE compatible yes typically restricted
ITI typical not usual often only option
Window ratio high (~25%) medium (~15%)
Original heating gas / oil boiler wood / oil
Surface area 80–120 m² 60–100 m²
DPE class (unrenovated) E–G E–G

(Goessel 2025, pp. 75–80 and Sections 3.2.1)

Notes — Goessel two-case-study finding. Optimal renovation strategies differ markedly between the two typologies because of structural and heritage constraints: - Chalandon: ITE + heat pump dominate; envelope intervention is the highest-impact lever. - Maison de bourg: ITI + heat pump + passive cooling (the high thermal mass already provides good summer comfort); ITE is regulatorily blocked; deep envelope intervention has limited impact relative to HVAC switching.

This demonstrates that renovation policy cannot be one-size-fits-all — typology-specific guidance is essential for policy effectiveness. (Goessel 2025, pp. 110, 129)

Notes — building-stock archetypes more broadly. TABULA (EU project, 2009–2018) developed standardised residential building archetypes for 20 EU countries. The CSTB / France maintains a national archetype database with ~70 typologies covering single-family + multi-family + non-residential. Goessel uses two of these as case studies; the methodology generalises. (Goessel 2025, pp. 75–80; TABULA / EPISCOPE EU project)

Related terms. Building renovation (umbrella); Building envelope; Interior vs Exterior insulation (ITI / ITE); thermal mass (buildings); DPE (Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique); building energy simulation (BES / SED); RE2020 / RT2012.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: Chalandon + maison de bourg typology definitions, comparison table, optimal-renovation finding, TABULA context (translated from French).

Modern bioenergy

Definition. Bioenergy used in modern energy applications, comprising liquid biofuels (biogasoline, biodiesel, biojet kerosene, other liquid biofuels), biogases (biogas, biomethane) and all solid bioenergy products except the traditional use of biomass. Distinguished from “traditional use of biomass” (basic three-stone fires or low-tier improved cookstoves burning wood, charcoal, agricultural residues or animal dung). (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, pp. 378–379)

Notes. Modern bioenergy is the dominant component of “low-emissions fuels” in IEA scenarios, accounting for ~60% of the projected 2025–2035 growth in low-emissions fuels market value (USD 215 → 390 billion). Biomethane, bioethanol and biodiesel are the most mature segments; biojet kerosene (sustainable aviation fuel, SAF) is projected to require stronger policy support to grow. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 15–16)

Related terms. Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); HEFA pathway; low-emissions hydrogen-based fuels; clean energy technologies; bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS).

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, distinction from traditional biomass, role in low-emissions fuels.

Operating reserves (FCR / aFRR / mFRR / RR)

Aliases. Réserves opérationnelles (FR); ancillary services reserves; balancing reserves.

Definition. Generation, storage or load capacity contracted to be available within specified response times to correct instantaneous deviations between scheduled and actual production/consumption. Reserve products are categorised by activation time: - FCR — Frequency Containment Reserve (réserve primaire) — automatic, fully deployed in 30 s, mutualised across the European synchronous area; sized against the loss of the two largest in-feed units. - aFRR — automatic Frequency Restoration Reserve (réserve secondaire) — automatic, deployed within 30 s–15 min, country-specific. - mFRR — manual Frequency Restoration Reserve (réserve rapide / réserve complémentaire) — manual activation within 15 min. - RR — Replacement Reserve (réserve de remplacement) — for periods up to several hours. (RTE 2022, Sections 7.1.3.1–7.1.3.2, pp. 292–294, translated from French)

Attributes — RTE 2050 reserve volumes (France).

Reserve Today (France) RTE 2050 envelope Driver
FCR (réserve primaire) shared European volume; ~0.5–1 GW France share slight increase but volume-stable Mutualised; sized against loss of 2 largest infeeds (nuclear → offshore wind / interconnections)
aFRR (réserve secondaire) ~0.5–0.8 GW rising with VRE share Forecast errors on wind/solar over min-to-tens-of-min
mFRR + RR (rapid + complementary) a few GW rising substantially Forecast errors over tens of min to hours
Total operational reserves 2050 ~3 GW up to ~9 GW (M0 / M1) RES forecast accuracy
Forecast-quality sensitivity improving forecasts → reduce mFRR+RR RTE prudent assumption: limited improvement —

(RTE 2022, Section 7.1.3.2, Figure 7.4, pp. 293–294)

Notes — FCR technical-spec evolution. With falling system inertia (more inverter-based RES, fewer synchronous machines), frequency excursions become faster for the same imbalance. The volume of FCR remains roughly constant (set by the dimensioning incident — loss of the two largest infeeds), but the technical specification must evolve: faster activation (sub-second response) is required to keep frequency within the same envelope. Modern batteries and modern grid-forming inverters can meet stricter specs; legacy thermal units may not. RTE points to the GB system as a precedent: Britain has already tightened FCR specs because of low inertia. (RTE 2022, Section 7.1.3.1, pp. 292–293)

Notes — aFRR + mFRR + RR scaling with VRE. The volume of aFRR/mFRR/RR scales with forecast uncertainty in real-time RES output. RTE bounds the 2050 reserve need at ~9 GW total under conservative forecast-improvement assumptions. Better short-term wind/PV forecasting, better real-time observability of distributed solar, and incentive design (imbalance settlement) can reduce this need. (RTE 2022, Section 7.1.3.2, p. 294)

Notes — provider mix evolution. Historically, French reserves were primarily provided by nuclear (FCR/aFRR) and hydro reservoir (mFRR). By 2050, RTE projects: batteries dominate FCR and partially aFRR (sub-second response advantage); demand-side flexibility (industrial load-shedding, smart EV charging) dominates mFRR+RR; nuclear retains a residual role mostly in N-scenarios. (RTE 2022, Section 7.4.1, p. 327)

Related terms. Frequency control (power system); Inertia (power system); Rate of Change of Frequency (ROCOF); Battery storage (stationary); Vehicle-to-grid (V2G); Power system flexibility; Modulation nucléaire.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: FCR/aFRR/mFRR/RR taxonomy, France-2050 envelope (~9 GW), spec-evolution under falling inertia, provider-mix evolution (translated from French).

Naphtha

Aliases. Petrochemical naphtha; full-range naphtha; light/heavy naphtha; cracker feed.

Definition. A petroleum-distillate fraction with a boiling range of approximately 30–200 °C (C5–C12 hydrocarbons), comprising a mixture of paraffins, cycloalkanes (naphthenes) and aromatics. Naphtha is recovered from atmospheric crude-oil distillation and from secondary refining processes (hydrocracker, catalytic reformer, FCC, coker). It is the dominant feedstock for the global petrochemical industry: roughly 50% of global ethylene (and an even higher share of co-produced propylene + C4 + BTX) comes from naphtha steam crackers, and naphtha is also reformed to high-octane gasoline. (Speight 2019, Chapters 2.3.2.1 and 6.6.1; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 1)

Attributes — properties and end-uses.

Property Value / range
Boiling range 30–200 °C (light naphtha 30–90 °C; heavy naphtha 90–200 °C)
Carbon range C5–C12
Density ~0.65–0.75 kg/L
LHV ~44 MJ/kg
Global production (2013) ~600 Mt/yr (≈10 EJ/yr energy basis)
Global use as steam-cracker feed ~280 Mt/yr (≈9.2 EJ/yr)
Global use as catalytic-reformer feed ~250 Mt/yr (mostly to gasoline pool)
Steam-cracker ethylene yield (naphtha) ~30% wt
Steam-cracker propylene yield (naphtha) ~15% wt
Steam-cracker C4 olefin yield (naphtha) ~10% wt
Steam-cracker pyrolysis-gasoline (BTX-rich) yield ~20% wt

(Speight 2019, Chapters 2.3, 6.6.1; Levi and Cullen 2018, Table 1 and Fig. 1; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024)

Notes — bionaphtha and recycled naphtha. Bionaphtha (HVO/HEFA-derived light fraction) and naphtha from chemically recycled plastics are emerging drop-in substitutes for fossil naphtha in steam crackers. Zanon-Zotin’s defossilisation scenarios envision bionaphtha steam cracking as one of the principal alternative-feedstock routes to ethylene, alongside bioethanol-dehydration and biomethanol-to-olefins. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 3 and Fig. 3)

Notes — gasoline-naphtha substitutability. Because gasoline and naphtha share a similar C5–C10 carbon range, refiners can re-route hydrocracker / FCC / reformer streams between the two pools as relative demand changes. As gasoline demand falls (transport electrification), this flexibility prolongs the role of fossil oil throughout the 21st century by allowing refineries to shift toward HVC production. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 3)

Related terms. Steam cracking (vapocracking); catalytic reforming; catalytic cracking (FCC); hydrocracking; high-value chemicals (HVCs); BTX aromatics; pyrolysis gasoline (pygas); refinery–petrochemical integration.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, properties, end-uses, cracker yields. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: global mass balance, steam-cracker share. - Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: bionaphtha role, gasoline-naphtha substitutability.

NSGA (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm)

Aliases. NSGA-II; NSGA-III; non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm; multi-objective genetic algorithm.

Definition. A family of evolutionary multi-objective optimisation algorithms developed by Deb et al. (NSGA-II, 2002; NSGA-III, 2014) for solving multi-objective optimisation problems with many objectives and complex constraint structures. NSGA combines non-dominated sorting (ranking solutions into Pareto-front layers) with genetic-algorithm operations (selection, crossover, mutation) to evolve a population of candidate solutions toward the true Pareto front. NSGA-II is the most widely-cited multi-objective optimisation algorithm in the engineering literature; NSGA-III is its extension to many-objective problems (>3 objectives). (Goessel 2025, pp. 14, 68–69, citing Deb 2002 and Deb 2014)

Attributes — NSGA-II core features.

Feature Description
Population size typically 100–500 candidate solutions
Selection binary tournament with crowding-distance ranking
Crossover simulated binary crossover (SBX)
Mutation polynomial mutation
Non-dominated sorting rank into Pareto-front layers F₁, F₂, F₃, …
Crowding distance preserve diversity along Pareto front
Generations 100–1,000 typically (depends on problem complexity)
Convergence test Pareto-front spread + hypervolume indicator
Parallelisable yes — population evaluations independent

(Goessel 2025, pp. 68–69; Deb et al. 2002 NSGA-II paper)

Notes — vs exact methods. NSGA-II/III is a heuristic — it cannot prove optimality but scales to very large search spaces (>10⁶ candidate solutions) where exact enumeration is intractable. Goessel uses exact enumeration (not NSGA) for his ~10,000-strategy renovation search because the search space is small enough; for typical commercial building-design optimisation tools (BEOpt, RENOIR, MOBO) NSGA-II is the standard. (Goessel 2025, p. 14)

Related terms. Multi-objective optimisation (MOO / OMO); Pareto dominance / Pareto front; Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); building renovation (umbrella); genetic algorithm (GA); Mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: NSGA-II definition, core features, vs exact methods (translated from French).

ETP-2026 applies the term to four headline materials: steel from iron ore, aluminium from bauxite, ammonia, and (with cement-kiln CCS) cement. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 378)

Net Zero Energy Building (NZEB) and Passive House (Passivhaus)

Aliases. NZEB (Net Zero Energy Building); nZEB (nearly Zero Energy Building, EU regulatory term); ZEB (Zero Energy Building); Passive House; Passivhaus (German); maison passive (FR); BBC (Bâtiment Basse Consommation, French earlier label).

Definition. Two related but distinct building-performance standards: - NZEB / nZEB — a building that, on an annual balance, produces as much energy as it consumes — typically requiring deep insulation + on-site solar PV + air-source heat pump. The EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) specifies nZEB (nearly-zero) as the standard for new construction since 2021; the 2024 recast tightens this to ZEB (zero-emission) by 2030. France’s RE2020 is consistent with this. - Passive House (Passivhaus) — a more demanding voluntary standard developed by Wolfgang Feist (Darmstadt, 1991) defining specific quantitative thresholds: heating demand ≤15 kWh/m²/yr, primary-energy ≤120 kWh/m²/yr, air-tightness n50 ≤0.6 ach@50Pa, no thermal bridges. Achieved through extreme insulation (300+ mm walls), MVHR with heat recovery, triple glazing, optimised orientation. ~150,000 certified Passivhäuser globally as of 2024. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7; Passivhaus Institut)

Attributes — NZEB / Passive House thresholds.

Indicator nZEB (EU) NZEB (US) Passive House (Passivhaus)
Heating demand <30 kWh/m²/yr net-zero balance ≤15 kWh/m²/yr
Primary energy <80 kWh/m²/yr (varies by climate) net-zero balance ≤120 kWh/m²/yr
Air-tightness (n50) <1.5 ach@50Pa varies ≤0.6 ach@50Pa
MVHR typically required typically required mandatory (≥75% heat recovery)
Triple glazing typical typical required
Thermal bridges minimised minimised eliminated (ψ < 0.01 W/m·K)
On-site renewables part of net-zero balance required not strictly required
Certification body national (CEPHEUS, RE2020) LEED-Zero, NetZero Passivhaus Institut

(Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7; Passivhaus Institut criteria)

Notes — Goessel context. Most of Goessel’s optimal renovation strategies achieve BBC-rénovation level (~80 kWh/m²/yr primary energy) which is roughly equivalent to nZEB-rénovation. Achieving Passivhaus-rénovation level requires substantially more capital + envelope intervention; Goessel’s three-criteria analysis (cost + carbon + summer comfort) shows Passivhaus-rénovation rarely sits on the Pareto front because the embodied-carbon and capital cost grow faster than operational savings at the deep-end of insulation. (Goessel 2025, pp. 110, 129)

Related terms. Building renovation (umbrella); RE2020 / RT2012; EPBD; building envelope; Mechanical ventilation (VMC / MVHR); Glazing technology; thermal bridge; air-tightness.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: NZEB / Passivhaus definitions, threshold table, Goessel-context observation that Passivhaus-rénovation is rarely Pareto-optimal (translated from French).

Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE)

Definition. A normative IEA scenario that maps a global pathway for the energy sector to achieve net-zero CO₂ emissions by 2050, consistent with the long-term goal of limiting the rise in global average temperatures to 1.5 °C (with a 50% probability). In contrast to previous editions, the NZE Scenario used in ETP-2026 is no longer a low-overshoot scenario — it assumes warming exceeds 1.5 °C for several decades before returning below 1.5 °C by 2100. This adjustment reflects persistently high emissions in recent years and the slow deployment of some key technologies. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 378)

Notes. Achieving the NZE pathway requires not only a very rapid transformation of the energy sector but also large-scale deployment of CO₂-removal (CDR) technologies, which remain unproven at large scale. The NZE Scenario sits alongside two exploratory scenarios (CPS and STEPS) in the IEA’s three-scenario framework introduced in ETP-2026 / WEO-2025. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 378; pp. 15–17)

Related terms. Current Policies Scenario (CPS); Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS); carbon dioxide removal (CDR); near-zero emissions materials; low-emissions hydrogen.

Source history. - IEA 2026 (Financing CCUS) — listed in Pending 2026-05-08 (NZE abbreviation). - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: full definition, overshoot revision, role in scenario framework; promoted from Pending.

Nuclear power (incl. small modular reactors)

Definition. Generation of low-emissions electricity (and heat) by controlled fission of heavy nuclei (typically uranium-235 or plutonium-239) in a reactor; the heat is used to raise steam that drives a turbine. ETP-2026 distinguishes large-scale conventional reactors from small modular reactors (SMRs) — designs with electrical output typically below 300 MWe per unit, intended for factory fabrication, modular installation and shorter lead times. Nuclear was the second-largest source of low-emissions electricity after hydropower in 2024, supplying ~9% of global electricity. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 147, 7314–7370)

Rate of Change of Frequency (ROCOF)

Definition. The instantaneous time-derivative of the AC grid frequency (df/dt, in Hz/s), used as a proxy for power-system stress during a contingency event. Higher ROCOF signals lower available system inertia and a faster departure from nominal frequency; ROCOF protection relays trigger generator/load disconnection when the rate exceeds a configured threshold, potentially triggering cascading outages. (Guerra et al. 2022, Section 3.4.3)

Typical 50 Hz ROCOF protection-relay setting 0.1–1.0 Hz/s
Spanish system normal frequency band 49.85–50.15 Hz
Spanish load-shedding threshold 49.5 Hz
Guerra ROCOF sensitivity scan 0.5–3.0 Hz/s

(Guerra et al. 2022, Section 3.4.3, citing ENTSO-E)

Natural climate solutions (NCS)

Definition. A category of carbon-dioxide-removal strategies based on conservation, restoration and improved land management, increasing terrestrial carbon storage or avoiding GHG emissions in forests, wetlands, grasslands and agricultural lands. NCS includes rain-fed afforestation and reforestation, soil carbon sequestration, and related land-use practices. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 8–9)

Notes — coverage in the 100% RE systems database. Despite their importance in climate-mitigation strategies, NCS are very rarely modelled in 100% RE systems analyses — only one study assumed unspecified negative emissions from agriculture, forestry and land-use sectors. Khalili et al. identify this as a major research gap, alongside biochar, enhanced weathering, desalination-based afforestation, and CCUS materials. (Khalili et al. 2026, p. 16)

Related terms. Carbon dioxide removal (CDR); bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS); direct air carbon capture and sequestration (DACCS).

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, coverage in database, research-gap framing.

Net Present Value (NPV)

Aliases. Valor Presente Neto (VPN); Valor Actual Neto (VAN).

Definition. The sum of a project’s expected future cash flows discounted to the present using a chosen discount rate. NPV = Σₜ (CFₜ / (1 + r)ᵗ), where CFₜ is the net cash flow in period t (negative at t=0 for the initial CAPEX) and r is the discount rate (commonly the WACC). A positive NPV indicates that the project creates value at the chosen discount rate; a negative NPV indicates that it destroys value. (Ramírez Del Río 2022, pp. 22–24, citing Damodaran 2012)

Notes. NPV is the canonical project-valuation criterion in corporate finance, complementary to the IRR. NPV maximises absolute value created (and is preferred when comparing mutually exclusive projects), while IRR ranks projects by relative return (and is preferred when comparing projects of different scales). Within an LCOE framework, the LCOE is the unit revenue at which NPV = 0 over the project lifetime. (Ramírez Del Río 2022, pp. 22–24, 25–26)

Related terms. Internal Rate of Return (IRR); Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE); Capital Recovery Factor (CRF); Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC); Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

Source history. - Ramírez Del Río 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, formula, role alongside IRR and LCOE (translated from Spanish).

Non-intentionally added substances (NIAS)

Definition. Plastic chemicals that are unintentionally present in plastic materials and products as impurities, unreacted intermediates, reaction by-products or degradation products, in contrast to intentionally added substances (starting substances, processing aids and additives). Together with intermediates, NIASs constitute one of the four top-level functional classes used in the PlastChem inventory. (Monclús et al. 2025, pp. 349–350, citing Geueke 2018)
