(Monclús et al. 2025, pp. 353–354)

Related terms. Plastic chemicals; plastic additives; chemicals of concern; UVCB substances; PlastChem inventory.

Source history. - Monclús et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-07: definition, share within inventory, simplification context.

Non-energy use of fossil fuels

Aliases. Non-combustion use; feedstock use; chemical-feedstock use; non-energy NEU.

Definition. The fraction of fossil-fuel production that is consumed not for combustion to produce useful energy but rather as feedstocks for chemical, material, or industrial processes (primary chemicals, lubricants, asphalt, solvents, waxes, road bitumen). The carbon in these inputs is largely embedded in long-lived materials (plastics, fertilisers fixed in biomass) or short-lived consumables, making the eventual emissions trajectory dependent on end-of-life management (incineration, landfill, recycling, leakage). (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, pp. 1–2; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1726; IEA-cited in source)

Attributes — global non-energy use breakdown.

Indicator Value
Total global non-energy use (2020s) ~30 EJ/yr (~13% of total fossil-fuel production)
Fraction used as primary-chemicals feedstock ~2/3 (~20 EJ/yr)
Fraction used as lubricants, asphalt, solvents, waxes, etc. ~1/3 (~10 EJ/yr)
Direct CO₂ emissions from chemical sector ~1 GtCO₂/yr
Share of non-energy use in chemical sector total energy ~58% (vs 44% in 1971)
Indicative oil consumed as petrochemical feedstock ~10% of crude oil; 50% as transport fuel; 20% heating; 20% other

(Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 1; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1725; Keim 2010, p. 298)

Notes — climate-policy gap. The 2023 COP28 Global Stocktake calls for “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems” but is silent on non-energy use. Zanon-Zotin et al. argue this is a critical gap: under stringent climate scenarios, the chemical sector’s role as fossil-fuel consumer can become binding on the overall fossil-fuel phase-out, because (i) fossil-fuel processing plants co-produce fuels and feedstocks (naphtha-gasoline substitutability locks in oil refining), (ii) refinery utilisation factors fall when transport fuel demand drops but feedstock demand persists, and (iii) the transition to alternative feedstocks (biomass, CCU, recycling) requires major scale-up of competing carbon resources. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, pp. 1–2)

Notes — defossilisation pathway. Zanon-Zotin’s modelling shows that under restrictive scenarios (limited biomass + limited CCS + no biomaterial carbon storage), oil demand stays high through 2100 (only −22 to −42% reduction vs 2020) primarily because of the chemical sector’s persistent feedstock demand. Conversely, with all alternatives available at scale, the chemical sector can reach −1 GtCO₂/yr (net-negative) by 2050 if biogenic carbon stored in unrecycled bioplastics is counted, and up to 62% of feedstock carbon comes from alternative sources. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, pp. 2–3)

Notes — IEA NEU statistics. IEA energy balances report non-energy use under “industrial non-energy use → of which: chem./petrochem.”, but the line aggregates true feedstock energy with some fuel inputs to chemical-process heat. Levi & Cullen 2018 perform a bottom-up cross-check and find 6% discrepancy at the global aggregate but order-of-magnitude differences for some product categories (coal under-reported, natural gas over-reported). (Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1730 and Table 1)

Related terms. High-value chemicals (HVCs); naphtha; petrochemicals (umbrella); refinery-petrochemical integration; carbon dioxide removal (CDR); plastic chemicals; bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS); near-zero emissions materials; coal gasification (to hydrogen); steam methane reforming (SMR).

Source history. - Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, ~30 EJ/yr scale, climate-policy-gap framing, defossilisation pathway scenarios. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: cross-check vs IEA NEU statistics. - Keim 2010 — added 2026-05-08: 10% of oil for chemical feedstock.

Non-recourse project finance

Definition. A financing structure in which lenders’ claims are limited to the cash flows and assets of a dedicated special purpose vehicle (SPV) created to develop, build and operate a project, without recourse to the project sponsors’ other assets. The SPV “ring-fences” risks within a single project, allowing firms to preserve corporate balance-sheet capacity and distribute financial risk among partners. (IEA 2026, pp. 7, 25, 29)

Attributes — recent CCUS non-recourse landmark deals.

Project Country Year Amount
Net Zero Teesside / Northern Endurance Partnership UK 2024 >USD 10 billion
Trailblazer CO₂ pipeline USA 2024 non-recourse term-loan financing
BECCS Stockholm Sweden 2025 >USD 1 billion
Liverpool Bay CCS UK 2024 mid-sized non-recourse

(IEA 2026, pp. 27, 29, 38)

Notes — context. Over USD 15 billion of commercial debt has been raised across CCUS projects in the past 2 years, predominantly through non-recourse project finance. Transactions typically require large lending syndicates (15–20 commercial banks) — syndication allows lenders to diversify exposure to single projects but limits scale-up. This model demands robust contractual frameworks and predictable revenue streams; in practice it has been mostly viable in jurisdictions with stable revenue support (EU CCfDs, UK regulated asset base, US 45Q tax credits). (IEA 2026, pp. 25, 29, 30)

Related terms. Bankability; final investment decision (FID); special purpose vehicle (SPV); regulated asset base (RAB); carbon contract for difference (CCfD); 45Q tax credit.

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, recent landmark deals, syndication context.

Olefins

Definition. Unsaturated hydrocarbons (ethylene, propylene, etc.) and a key product class of the chemicals sector. Globally produced primarily by steam cracking of naphtha (Europe, Asia) or ethane (North America); also produced from methanol via methanol-to-olefins (MTO). (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 12)

Notes. Decarbonisation pathways include carbon capture on existing crackers, electrification or hydrogen-based heat for cracking, use of bio-naphtha as feedstock, and methanol-to-olefins routes when methanol is itself decarbonised. Petroleum refining additionally produces olefins as part of refining process outputs; refineries account for ~44% of global hydrogen consumption (2023), with 80% of that hydrogen produced on-site, primarily from fossil fuels. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 12)

Notes — natural occurrence in crude oils. Olefins also occur naturally in many crude oils and condensates worldwide, with concentrations 0.3–10 wt% across reservoir ages from pre-Cambrian to Tertiary. Curiale and Frolov identify one primary source (migration with other soluble organics directly from the source rock as olefinic biomarkers) and three secondary sources: (i) migration-contamination by light oils acting as solvents; (ii) “cold” radiolytic dehydrogenation of saturated hydrocarbons (a by-product of decay of uranium, thorium and other reservoir-rock radioactives); and (iii) pyrolysis from igneous-intrusion thermal events. Olefinic biomarkers are useful for oil–oil correlation and reservoir-continuity studies, and radiogenic olefins potentially indicate the time an oil has spent in the trap. (Curiale and Frolov 1998, abstract; pp. 397–398)

Related terms. Carbon capture and storage; steam methane reforming; hydrogen colour taxonomy; steam cracking; methanol-to-olefins (MTO); naphtha cracking.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition, production routes, decarbonisation notes. - Curiale and Frolov 1998 — added 2026-05-08: natural occurrence in crude oils, primary vs secondary origins.

Olefin metathesis (OCT)

Aliases. OCT (olefin conversion technology); olefin metathesis; metathesis; Phillips triolefin process; Lummus OCT.

Definition. A reversible catalytic reaction in which the carbon-carbon double bonds of two olefin molecules are exchanged, redistributing the substituents to form two new olefins. The classic reaction R₁CH=CHR₂ + R₃CH=CHR₄ ⇌ R₁CH=CHR₃ + R₂CH=CHR₄. In refineries and petrochemical complexes, the most economically important application is propylene-from-ethylene-and-2-butene metathesis: 2 C₂H₄ → 1-butene + … (reverse self-metathesis); or CH₂=CH-CH₃ + CH₃-CH=CH-CH₃ ⇌ 2 CH₂=CH-CH₃ (i.e., ethylene + 2-butene → 2 propylene), a major on-purpose propylene route. Catalyst: WO₃/SiO₂ (Lummus OCT) or Re₂O₇/Al₂O₃. Yves Chauvin, Robert Grubbs and Richard Schrock shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the metathesis mechanism and catalyst development. (Speight 2019, Chapters 7.3, 7.4)

Attributes — industrial olefin metathesis.

Variant Reaction Catalyst Use
Phillips triolefin propylene → ethylene + 2-butene (or reverse) WO₃ / SiO₂ propylene production from ethylene + butenes
Lummus OCT ethylene + 2-butene → 2 propylene WO₃ / SiO₂ + MgO propylene from on-purpose route, integrated with naphtha cracker
Self-metathesis (oligomer to α-olefin) various Re₂O₇ / Al₂O₃ or Mo / Al₂O₃ linear α-olefin production
Cross-metathesis RCH=CH₂ + R’CH=CH₂ → RCH=CHR’ + ethylene Grubbs (Ru) homogeneous specialty / fine-chemical

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3)

Notes — propylene supply role. Lummus OCT is now installed at most modern integrated naphtha-cracker complexes (e.g., Saudi Aramco / SABIC, ExxonMobil) to upgrade surplus ethylene + raffinate-2 (mixed butenes) to propylene, balancing the cracker propylene/ethylene ratio with downstream PP demand. Together with PDH and MTP, metathesis is one of the three on-purpose propylene routes that fill the gap left by steam-cracker propylene yields. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727)

Related terms. Propylene; ethylene; propane dehydrogenation (PDH); methanol-to-propylene (MTP); high-value chemicals (HVCs); steam cracking (vapocracking); refinery-petrochemical integration.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, industrial variants, propylene-supply role. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: ~3% of global HVC supply via on-purpose technologies including metathesis.

OSeMOSYS (modelling framework)

Aliases. OSeMOSYS; Open Source Energy Modelling System; GENeSYS-MOD (extension).

Definition. A fully open-source bottom-up Energy System Optimisation Model framework first released in 2011 (Howells et al. 2011) and now maintained by KTH Royal Institute of Technology (Sweden) and a wider community of contributors. OSeMOSYS is the second-most-used ESOM framework globally — Manuel et al. 2025 found it in 13% of pathway studies (14% combined with its derivative GENeSYS-MOD). It is implemented in GLPK / Python / MathProg with LP formulation, perfect foresight, and a deliberately minimalist set of constraints to prioritise transparency and educational accessibility. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8 and Fig. 8a; Howells et al. 2011 cited)

Attributes — OSeMOSYS design features.

Indicator Value
Solver paradigm LP (GLPK or commercial CPLEX/Gurobi)
Programming language Python wrapper (otoole), MathProg, GAMS variants
Foresight perfect foresight (default)
Milestone interpolation none — costs computed only at requested milestones
End-effect mitigation salvage values + discounting
Endogenous learning not standard (extensions exist)
Open-source status fully open (no commercial dependencies in default config)
Cost free
Use cases educational use, low-resource-country studies, UN SDG-7 analysis
Major users KTH, UN-ESCAP, World Bank, African Energy Ministers

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8; Howells et al. 2011)

Notes — significance. OSeMOSYS is the canonical “open” ESOM, deliberately designed with low computational footprint and zero proprietary-software dependencies to make ESOM-based analysis accessible to researchers and ministries in low-resource settings. The Climate Compatible Growth (CCG) programme uses OSeMOSYS for ~30 sub-Saharan African and South Asian country pathways. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); TIMES; MESSAGE; PyPSA; TEMOA; foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); salvage value (modelling); end effects (modelling).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, design features, significance.

Operational carbon (buildings)

Aliases. Operational emissions; in-use emissions; B6+B7 emissions; operational footprint.

Definition. The greenhouse-gas emissions resulting from energy and water use during a building’s operation phase — primarily heating, cooling, ventilation, domestic hot water, lighting, appliances, and equipment plug-loads (B6 module) plus operational water (B7 module under EN 15978). Operational carbon is calculated from annual energy / water consumption multiplied by emission factors of the underlying energy carrier (electricity-grid CO₂ intensity, gas, oil, biomass, district heating). (Goessel 2025, pp. 41–48 and eq. 2.10)

Attributes — operational-carbon factors (France 2025).

Energy carrier Emission factor (kg CO₂eq / kWh final energy)
Electricity (France, 2025 — RTE / SNBC reference) ~0.04 (very low — nuclear-dominant)
Electricity (EU average 2025) ~0.20–0.25
Electricity (coal-heavy regions, India, China) 0.7–1.0
Natural gas ~0.20 (combustion) + ~0.04 (upstream) = ~0.24
Heating oil ~0.32
Biomass / wood <0.05 (with biogenic-carbon credit)
District heating (EU avg) 0.12–0.20 (depends on local mix)
Heat pump (COP 3, French electricity) ~0.013 (~6× lower than gas)

(Goessel 2025, Section 2.5.2 and Annexe A; ADEME 2024 base carbone)

Notes — declining share over time. As electricity grids decarbonise (French SNBC: 0.04 → 0.01 kg CO₂/kWh by 2050) and buildings’ energy efficiency improves, operational carbon falls in absolute terms. Goessel’s prospective LCA captures this: the operational fraction of life-cycle emissions in a renovated French house drops from ~70% (current grid) to ~25% (2050 decarbonised grid), making embodied emissions the new dominant lever. (Goessel 2025, p. 13; Pellan 2024)

Notes — primary vs final vs delivered energy. Operational carbon is calculated from final energy (delivered to the building) using emission factors that include upstream production — so for electricity, the emission factor includes power-plant emissions, transmission losses, and (with prospective scenarios) future grid mix. Primary energy is the related but distinct metric used in energy-efficiency regulations (CEP — Consommation d’Énergie Primaire). (Goessel 2025, pp. 41–48)

Related terms. Embodied carbon (buildings); Life Cycle Assessment (LCA); building renovation (umbrella); EN 15978; heat pump (HP); RE2020; DPE (Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique); abatement cost (greenhouse gas).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, French emission-factor table, declining-share trajectory, primary/final/delivered distinction.

Open cycle gas turbine (OCGT)

Aliases. TAC (FR — Turbine à Combustion); simple-cycle gas turbine; peaker; combustion turbine.

Definition. A simple Brayton-cycle gas turbine driving an electric generator, without a steam-bottoming cycle. Lower capital cost, smaller footprint and faster start-up (~5–15 min cold start) than CCGTs make OCGTs the canonical peaker technology, suitable for very low-capacity-factor operation covering residual-load peaks. Net thermal efficiency on natural gas is ~38–42% (vs ~55–60% for CCGT), and the technology accepts oil distillate as backup fuel. (RTE 2022, Section 4.4, p. 195, translated from French)

Attributes — France-2021 fleet and 2050 projections.

Indicator Value
France OCGT fleet (Sept 2021) ~2 GW total, ~10 sites
Fuel of French OCGT fleet gas or fuel oil
Recent build (2007+) ~2/3 of installed base
OCGT thermal efficiency (NG) ~38–42% (RTE)
OCGT efficiency on H₂ (assumed) ~40%
H₂ OCGT efficiency in P2G2P loop ~40%
Operating hours per year (typical) tens to hundreds of h/year
2050 OCGT capacity factor (RTE) <5% (insurance only)
Cost ratio OCGT vs CCGT (CAPEX) ~1/3 of CCGT per kW
Hydrogen TAC efficiency (P2H2P) ~40% (vs ~60% for H₂-CCGT)

(RTE 2022, Sections 4.4, 7.5.3, Figure 4.27, pp. 195–196, 333)

Notes — peaking role and decarbonised future. OCGTs currently cover the highest-demand hours of the year (very cold winter peak; afternoon summer peaks under air-conditioning load). RTE 2050 envisions OCGTs continuing this role on hydrogen or biomethane fuel, but with capacity factor <5%, used essentially as last-resort capacity. Their lower CAPEX (vs CCGT) makes them economic for very low utilisation; their lower efficiency makes them unattractive for higher utilisation. (RTE 2022, Section 7.5.3, p. 336)

Notes — interaction with RTE flexibility envelope. In the M0/M1 scenarios (100% renewable), OCGTs and CCGTs together can total up to 29 GW of “new decarbonised thermal” by 2050; this falls to 11 GW in N1, 5 GW in N2, and effectively 0 GW in N03 (where existing-nuclear plus new-EPR2 cover residual peaks). The CCGT/OCGT split favours CCGTs for higher-capacity-factor flexibility (~10–15%), OCGTs for the lowest-capacity-factor extreme peaks. (RTE 2022, Section 7.5.3, Figure 7.30 area; scenario flexibility tables)

Related terms. Combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT); Power-to-gas-to-power loop; Capacity adequacy; Peaking plant; Residual load; Modulation nucléaire; RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 scenarios.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: French fleet (~2 GW, ~10 sites), peaking role, ~40% efficiency, role transition to H₂/biomethane in 2050 (translated from French).

Ortho-hydrogen and para-hydrogen

Definition. Two nuclear-spin isomers of molecular hydrogen. At room temperature, normal hydrogen is 75% ortho-hydrogen and 25% para-hydrogen; on cooling to 20 K, ortho-hydrogen content falls towards 0%. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 29)

Notes. During liquefaction, untransformed ortho-hydrogen at low temperature releases the enthalpy of the ortho–para transformation reaction, which can cause additional evaporation of liquid hydrogen and contribute to boil-off losses. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 29)

Related terms. Liquid hydrogen storage; boil-off loss.

Source history. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: spin-isomer definition and liquefaction implication.

Overnight vs transition pathway modelling

Definition. Two complementary energy-system-modelling approaches. Overnight modelling analyses a single target year (e.g. 2040, 2050) under fixed-cost greenfield assumptions, ignoring the legacy capital stock. Transition pathway modelling covers multi-decade trajectories from the present to a target year, typically in 5–10 year time steps, accounting for stranded assets, technology learning curves and capital-replacement schedules. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 9–11)

Attributes — share in the 100% RE systems database.

Approach Share of articles
Overnight greenfield 77%
Transition pathway 23%
First transition-pathway article Weingart 1979

(Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 9, 11)

Notes. The transition modelling pathway is generally more sophisticated — it requires projections about future technologies, energy-consumption trends and policies, and larger amounts of input data. For policy-making, transition models help identify both short- and long-term measures. Overnight modelling demands fewer variables and is simpler to implement, but obscures pathway dynamics and stranded-asset risks. (Khalili et al. 2026, p. 11)

Related terms. Energy system models (100% RE); 100% renewable energy system; nodal resolution; temporal resolution; sector coupling.

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, distribution in database, methodological trade-offs.

Passoire thermique (DPE F+G)

Aliases. Passoire thermique (FR — “thermal sieve”); thermal-sieve dwelling; energy-inefficient housing; Class F+G DPE.

Definition. A French regulatory term (introduced in the Loi Climat et Résilience 2021) for residential dwellings rated F or G on the DPE energy-performance certificate — typically primary-energy consumption >330 kWh/m²/yr or operational CO₂ >70 kg/m²/yr. Passoires thermiques are the worst-performing 17% of the French residential stock (~5.2 million dwellings out of ~30 million total in 2023), concentrated in pre-1948 construction without major renovation. The French government has scheduled their progressive removal from the rental market: G banned from rental from January 2025; F banned from January 2028; E banned from January 2034. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7; Loi Climat & Résilience Aug. 2021)

Attributes — passoire-thermique statistics (France 2023).

Indicator Value
Total residential dwellings ~30 million
Class G (worst) ~1.4 million (~5%)
Class F (worse) ~3.8 million (~13%)
Total Class F+G (“passoires”) ~5.2 million (~17%)
Class F+G in rental sector ~1.6 million
Class F+G in owner-occupied sector ~3.6 million
2025 G-rental ban enforced
2028 F-rental ban scheduled
2034 E-rental ban scheduled
Affected tenant population ~10 million

(Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7; SDES 2024 statistics)

Notes — significance for renovation policy. The passoire-thermique designation is the principal regulatory driver for accelerating French residential renovation through 2034. The progressive rental ban creates urgent renovation demand for landlords; combined with MaPrimeRénov’ subsidies (up to €70,000 for “rénovation d’ampleur” deep renovations) and CEE certificate revenues, it forms the backbone of French building-decarbonisation policy. Goessel’s optimisation methodology is designed precisely for this market — identifying cost-optimal renovation strategies that move passoires through the DPE classes. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7)

Notes — energy-poverty linkage. Many passoire-thermique residents are énergie-précaires (energy-poor) — spending >10% of income on energy bills despite low consumption. The rental ban risks displacing these tenants from their homes; balancing housing affordability with energy decarbonisation is one of the principal political tensions in the French renovation programme. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7)

Related terms. DPE (Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique); building renovation (umbrella); MaPrimeRénov’; CEE (Certificat d’Économie d’Énergie); RE2020 / RT2012; energy poverty (précarité énergétique).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, statistics, rental-ban schedule, energy-poverty linkage (translated from French).

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)

Aliases. “Forever chemicals”.

Definition. A large family of synthetic plastic chemicals containing at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF₃–) or methylene (–CF₂–) group, identified as one of the largest and most persistent groups of plastic chemicals. PFASs are managed as a chemical class under the Stockholm Convention because of their high environmental persistence. (Monclús et al. 2025, p. 353, citing Kwiatkowski et al. 2020; Cousins et al. 2020)

Attributes. PFAS account for 440 of the 16,325 chemicals in the PlastChem inventory and are one of the three largest structural groups of plastic chemicals (alongside alkenes, 802; and silanes/siloxanes/silicones, 443). (Monclús et al. 2025, p. 353)

Notes. Identified as one of 15 priority groups of plastic chemicals of concern (≥40% of group members are chemicals of concern, or strong evidence for the entire group being hazardous). Listed by Monclús et al. as a canonical case where managing the chemical class as a whole — rather than individually — is appropriate, given the common high persistence of every member. (Monclús et al. 2025, p. 353, Fig. 4)

Related terms. Chemicals of concern; plastic chemicals; bisphenol A (BPA); chlorinated paraffins; UVCB substances.

Source history. - Monclús et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-07: definition, group size, priority-group context.

Pay-as-you-throw (PAYT)

Definition. A municipal-waste pricing mechanism in which households pay for waste-disposal services in proportion to the volume or weight of mixed (residual) waste they generate, typically via per-bag charges, weight-based bin charges, or RFID-tagged bins. PAYT creates a strong direct financial incentive for households to sort recyclables and compostables at source — provided a parallel free or low-cost stream is available for those materials. (OECD 2022, pp. 26, 130)

Notes. PAYT is identified as a complementary instrument to deposit-refund schemes within the OECD plastics-policy roadmap. To avoid perverse incentives (e.g. illegal dumping or contamination of free recyclable streams), PAYT must be combined with anti-dumping enforcement and clearly differentiated waste streams. Most successful examples are in Switzerland, Germany, Austria, parts of the United States and a growing number of Northern European municipalities. (OECD 2022, pp. 25–27)

Related terms. Deposit-refund scheme; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR); single-use plastics; mismanaged plastic waste.

Source history. - OECD 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, role in OECD plastics policy roadmap.

Physisorption (hydrogen storage)

Definition. A material-based hydrogen-storage method in which hydrogen molecules adhere to a solid surface via weak van der Waals adsorption forces. Effective hydrogen capacity requires high surface area, low temperatures (below the boiling point of nitrogen, 77 K) and high pressure; the entrapping energy of physisorption is on the order of a few kJ/mol H₂. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, p. 30)

Notes. Promising materials include activated carbon, single- and multi-walled carbon nanotubes, and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), with gravimetric capacities of 5–9 wt% and volumetric capacities of 40–60 g/L under high pressure and 77 K. (AlZohbi et al. 2023, pp. 30–31)

Related terms. Chemisorption; carbon nanotubes; metal-organic frameworks; hydrogen storage.

Source history. - AlZohbi et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, conditions, candidate materials.

Pipeline efficiency (η_pip)

Definition. A correction factor applied to the theoretical isothermal turbulent flow of a compressible fluid through a pipeline to reflect real-world losses (welds, valves, bends). For hydrogen transport, Baufumé et al. retain η_pip = 92%, consistent with the H₂A delivery model. (Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8813, citing the H₂A project [DOE/NREL])

Related terms. Darcy-Weisbach friction factor; compressibility factor.

Source history. - Baufumé et al. 2011 — added 2026-05-07: definition and assumed value for H₂ transport.

Planetary boundaries

Aliases. Planetary boundaries (Rockström); safe operating space; Earth-system thresholds.

Definition. A scientific framework introduced by Rockström et al. 2009 (and updated by Steffen 2015, Persson 2022, Richardson 2023) defining nine global biogeochemical processes that regulate Earth-system stability and that humanity must keep within “safe operating space” thresholds to avoid abrupt and irreversible environmental change at planetary scale. The nine boundaries are: (1) climate change; (2) novel entities (chemical pollution, plastics); (3) stratospheric ozone depletion; (4) atmospheric aerosol loading; (5) ocean acidification; (6) biogeochemical flows (nitrogen + phosphorus); (7) freshwater use; (8) land-system change; (9) biosphere integrity (genetic + functional diversity). (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 607–608; Richardson et al. 2023; Persson et al. 2022)

Attributes — boundary status (Richardson 2023 update).

Boundary Status (2023) Notes
Climate change exceeded (high risk) atmospheric CO₂ ~420 ppm vs 350 ppm boundary
Novel entities (incl. plastics, chemicals) exceeded Persson 2022 — quantification finalised
Land-system change exceeded deforestation + agriculture
Biosphere integrity (genetic) exceeded extinction rates 100–1,000× background
Biogeochemical flows (nitrogen) exceeded excess fertiliser-N runoff
Biogeochemical flows (phosphorus) borderline regional excesses
Freshwater (green water) exceeded (Richardson 2023) new in latest update
Freshwater (blue water) within most river systems
Ocean acidification within (rising fast) pH dropping toward boundary
Stratospheric ozone within (recovering) Montreal Protocol success
Atmospheric aerosols regional only SE Asia exceeds, others within

(Tilsted et al. 2023, p. 608, citing Richardson et al. 2023)

Notes — petrochemical relevance. Tilsted highlights that petrochemicals/plastics drive transgression of several boundaries simultaneously: (i) climate change (4–5% of global GHG); (ii) novel entities (Persson 2022 specifically uses plastics as the central case for crossing the boundary); (iii) ocean acidification (CO₂ from feedstocks); (iv) biosphere integrity (microplastic + chemical exposure). The framework is now central to the “exceedance” framing in environmental policy — production must come within boundaries, not just stop growing. (Tilsted et al. 2023, p. 608; Persson et al. 2022)

Related terms. Petrochemical lock-ins / political economy; plastic chemicals; chemicals of concern; plastic leakage; nitrogen fertilisers (umbrella); microplastics; UN Global Plastics Treaty.

Source history. - Tilsted et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: planetary-boundary definition, boundary-status table, petrochemical relevance.

Plastic additives

Definition. Chemicals intentionally added to plastic materials to provide a desired performance or property. The most prevalent functions, by number of chemicals serving them in the PlastChem inventory, are: colourants (3,674), fillers (1,836), biocides (1,552), plasticisers (883), light stabilisers, antioxidants, flame retardants, antistatic agents, heat stabilisers, lubricants, and odour agents. (Monclús et al. 2025, p. 350 and Fig. 1c)

Notes. Plastic additives are the most diverse top-level functional class, covering 16 major functions and 5,776 chemicals total. At least 4,054 substances have multiple functions at different stages of the plastic life cycle, e.g. bisphenol A which acts as co-monomer, crosslinking agent, intermediate, antioxidant and light stabiliser. Removing chemicals of concern from this class without sacrificing performance is the central challenge of the “simplification of plastics” agenda. (Monclús et al. 2025, pp. 350–351, 353–354)

Related terms. Plastic chemicals; chemicals of concern; non-intentionally added substances (NIAS); bisphenol A (BPA); per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS); essential use concept.

Source history. - Monclús et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-07: definition, function distribution, multi-function note.

Plastic leakage

Definition. The flow of plastic materials from the economic system into the natural environment (rivers, lakes, oceans, soils, atmosphere), in both macro- and microplastic forms. Includes mismanaged solid-waste disposal, littering, and primary microplastic emissions (tyre wear, brake wear, road markings, textile washing). The OECD estimates 22 Mt of plastic materials leaked into the environment in 2019. (OECD 2022, pp. 21–22, 47)

Attributes — accumulation in aquatic environments.

Compartment Stock (cumulative) Annual flux 2019
Rivers 109 Mt accumulated —
Ocean 30 Mt accumulated 6.1 Mt total to rivers, lakes and ocean
Total plastic leakage — 22 Mt

(OECD 2022, pp. 21, 47)

Notes. The build-up of plastics in rivers means leakage into the ocean will continue for decades to come even if mismanaged plastic waste is significantly reduced. As particles fragment progressively into ever-smaller microplastics, cleanup becomes increasingly difficult and costly — strong upstream policy is therefore identified as the dominant cost-effective lever. Achieving “net zero plastic leakage” is the OECD’s headline policy target. (OECD 2022, pp. 21–22, 27)

Related terms. Macroplastics; microplastics; mismanaged plastic waste; single-use plastics; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR); deposit-refund scheme.

Source history. - OECD 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, mass balance, accumulation stocks.

Plastic chemicals

Definition. All chemicals that can be present in plastic materials and products, including the polymer backbone, intentionally added substances (starting substances, processing aids and additives) and non-intentionally added substances (impurities, unreacted intermediates, reaction by-products and degradation products). Whether a chemical has additional uses outside plastics has no bearing on its inclusion. Sorbed contaminants from the environment are excluded. (Monclús et al. 2025, Methods p. 354 and Supplementary Text 1)

Attributes — composition of the PlastChem inventory.

Category Number
Total entries 17,932
Unique chemicals (with valid CAS RN) 16,325
Discrete compounds (organic / inorganic / organometallic) 12,658
UVCBs, mixtures, polymers 3,667
Without CAS RN (excluded from analysis) 1,607

(Monclús et al. 2025, Fig. 1a, p. 350)

Notes. Plastic chemicals can be released throughout the entire plastic life cycle, from feedstock extraction and production to use and waste; specific end-of-life treatments such as uncontrolled landfilling or incineration can further exacerbate chemical releases. Strong epidemiological evidence links certain plastic chemicals to reproductive, neurodevelopmental, immune and metabolic disorders. (Monclús et al. 2025, pp. 349–350)

Notes — global mass balance (Geyer et al. 2017; updated by OECD 2022).

Indicator Value Year
Cumulative virgin plastics ever produced 8,300 Mt (Geyer); 7,800 Mt resins + 1,000 Mt fibres 1950–2015
Cumulative plastic waste ever generated 6,300 Mt 1950–2015
Of which recycled 9% (600 Mt) 1950–2015
Of which incinerated 12% (800 Mt) 1950–2015

(Geyer et al. 2017, pp. 2–3; OECD 2022, pp. 14–15)

Notes — additive composition. On average, nonfiber plastics contain 93% polymer resin and 7% additives by mass; plasticizers, fillers and flame retardants account for ~75% of all additives by mass (Geyer 2017). The seven dominant polymer types together account for 92% of all plastics ever made: PE (36%), PP (21%), PVC (12%), and PET, PUR and PS (<10% each), plus polyester (≈70% of fibre output, mostly PET). (Geyer et al. 2017, pp. 1–2)

PlastChem inventory

Definition. A consolidated open-access global inventory of plastic chemicals, harmonising information from seven prior sources (PlasticMAP, ECHA, LitChemPlast, FCCmigex, Aurisano-Weber-Fantke 2021, CPPdb, FCCdb), containing 16,325 unique plastic chemicals identified by CAS Registry Number. Released as a Zenodo deposit (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.10701706) with all data engineering code on GitHub. (Monclús et al. 2025, Fig. 1a, p. 350; data availability statement p. 355)

Notes. The inventory adds annotations on chemical structure (canonical SMILES, isomeric SMILES, InChI, InChIKey), physicochemical properties (XLogP, monoisotopic mass, molecular weight, topological polar surface area), function, regulatory status (Basel, Stockholm, Minamata Conventions; Montreal Protocol; EU, Japan, Republic of Korea, USA national lists), hazard scoring (P/B/M/T) and use/presence/release evidence. Hazard data come from 15 authoritative regulatory sources, with the latest update August 2023. (Monclús et al. 2025, p. 354 Methods and Supplementary Tables 4–5)

Related terms. Plastic chemicals; plastic additives; non-intentionally added substances (NIAS); chemicals of concern; UVCB substances.

Source history. - Monclús et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-07: definition, source coverage, annotations.

Plasticizers (phthalate esters and other)

Definition. A class of plastic additives — typically of relatively low molecular weight (300–600 g/mol) — that improve the flexibility, durability and stretchability of polymers (especially PVC), reduce shear during processing and improve impact resistance in films. The dominant chemical family is phthalate esters (PAEs), of which DEHP (used in PVC) constitutes about 80% of the plasticizer volume for PVC production. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, pp. 186, 190)

Attributes — common plasticizers by polymer.

Polymer Common plasticizers
PVC DEHP, DiBP, DBP, BBP, DINP, DIDP, DEHA, DEHS
PET DPP, DEHA, DOA, DEP, DBP
PVDC cling-films acetyltributyl citrate (ATBC)
Common adipates DHA, DCHP, HAD, HOA

(Hahladakis et al. 2018, p. 186)

Notes. Plasticizers can migrate from packaging materials into food, becoming indirect food additives. Migration tests typically use food simulants (FSs) at controlled temperature and contact time. Phthalates exhibit some of the highest documented migration rates — Fankhauser-Noti & Grob (cited in Hahladakis) recorded a 350% transfer rate for phthalate plasticizers used in PVC gasket-on-olive-oil tests. Several phthalates (DEHP, DBP, BBP, DiBP, DIDP, DINP) are restricted under EU REACH due to reproductive toxicity. Cooking oil and other fatty foods are the primary migration media; high temperatures and long contact time favour migration. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, pp. 186, 190–191, Table 2)

Related terms. Plastic additives; antioxidants (plastic additives); brominated flame retardants; migration (plastic chemicals); chemicals of concern; PoTSs (potentially toxic substances); plastic chemicals.

Source history. - Hahladakis et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, polymer-specific list, migration behaviour.

Oxidative dehydrogenation (ODH)

Aliases. ODH; oxidative cracking; oxydehydrogenation.

Definition. A catalytic alkane-to-olefin conversion in which a saturated hydrocarbon (ethane, propane, butane, naphtha) is dehydrogenated with an oxidant (O₂ or lattice oxygen of a redox catalyst), producing the corresponding olefin and water rather than olefin and H₂ (as in conventional dehydrogenation): C₂H₆ + ½ O₂ → C₂H₄ + H₂O. The oxidative variant is exothermic (in contrast to endothermic conventional dehydrogenation), shifts the thermodynamic equilibrium decisively toward the olefin, and avoids the coke-formation problem that limits conventional dehydrogenation. ODH is investigated as an alternative to steam cracking (for ethane, naphtha) and to PDH (for propane), with chemical looping ODH (CL-ODH / ROC) emerging as the most promising commercial-scale variant. (Haribal et al. 2018, pp. 714–715, citing oxidative-dehydrogenation literature)

Attributes — typical ODH performance benchmarks.

System Catalyst Conversion Olefin selectivity Comments
Ethane → ethylene (gas-phase O₂) Mo-V-Te-Nb mixed oxide (M1) 60% 80–90% (ethylene) Sabic / Linde / Wacker R&D
Propane → propylene (gas-phase O₂) V-Mg-O / V-K-O 25% 60–70%
Hexane / naphtha (gas-phase O₂) Li/MgO + plasma 28% 60% low T but limited selectivity
Ethane CL-ODH (lattice O₂) Mn-Na₂WO₄ / SiO₂ 60% 80%+ exothermic, no air-separation
Hexane CL-ODH (lattice O₂) Ca-Mn-K mixed oxide 79% 61% Haribal 2018 ROC reference

(Haribal et al. 2018, p. 715, citing Solov’ev, Cavani, Trionfetti et al.)

Notes — significance. ODH addresses two limitations of conventional thermal cracking: (i) endothermicity (cracking requires substantial external heat input and high T), (ii) coke deposition. By making the reaction exothermic and shifting equilibrium toward the olefin, ODH can in principle deliver olefins at lower T and with smaller, simpler reactor design. Chemical looping ODH (CL-ODH / ROC) further eliminates safety hazards from gas-phase O₂/hydrocarbon mixing. (Haribal et al. 2018, pp. 714–715)

Notes — limitations. ODH selectivity is sensitive to catalyst design — over-oxidation of the olefin product to CO/CO₂ (the most common failure mode) destroys both yield and economics. Light olefin yields below 35% have historically limited ODH to laboratory-scale demonstration; CL-ODH and ROC variants are rapidly improving the yields toward commercial relevance. (Haribal et al. 2018, p. 715)

Related terms. Redox oxy-cracking (ROC) / chemical looping cracking; steam cracking (vapocracking); olefins; high-value chemicals (HVCs); propane dehydrogenation (PDH); ethylene; propylene.

Source history. - Haribal et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, performance benchmarks, vs conventional cracking.

Petrochemical lock-ins / political economy

Aliases. Carbon lock-in (petrochemicals); fossil-based growth lock-in; political economy of petrochemicals; petroleum-chemical-plastic nexus.

Definition. A framing introduced by Tilsted et al. 2023 for the technological, institutional, organisational, and behavioural phenomena that collectively hinder transformative change in the petrochemical industry away from fossil feedstocks and excess plastic production. Lock-ins arise from (i) integrated production complexes (fossil extraction → cracking → polymer manufacturing co-located), (ii) consolidated multinational firms spanning fossil + chemical + plastics value chains (Saudi Aramco-Dow Sadara, ExxonMobil, Shell), (iii) historical state subsidisation (post-WWII reconstruction, 1970s nationalisation, ongoing tax breaks), (iv) research and education systems aligned to fossil-petrochemical paradigms, (v) public-finance backing (export credits, infrastructure subsidies). Together these produce a self-reinforcing system that is structurally biased against transitions to alternative feedstocks (biomass, recycled plastics, CO₂-derived). (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 607–610)

Attributes — Tilsted 2023 lock-in taxonomy.

Lock-in dimension Examples
Material / infrastructural integrated cracker-polymer complexes; pipeline networks; petrochemical clusters (Antwerp, Houston, Jubail)
Institutional / regulatory favourable carbon-emission pricing for petrochemicals; non-recognition of plastics under climate frameworks
Organisational consolidated multinationals; long-lived capital assets; fossil-skill pipelines
Knowledge / research fossil-petrochemistry-trained workforces; publication and IP systems aligned to fossil paradigms
Financial public-finance backing of greenfield mega-complexes; sunk-cost defence of stranded assets
Demand-side / cultural low-cost plastic packaging deeply embedded in retail / consumption patterns

(Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 608–610)

Notes — Tilsted 2023 supply-side intervention argument. Tilsted argues that addressing climate-plastic-toxics crises requires supply-side interventions on petrochemical production (caps on virgin-polymer production, fossil-feedstock pricing, removal of subsidies) — not just downstream waste-management and recycling. Without supply-side action, the “treadmill of production” continues: virgin polymer is cheap, recycled polymer is expensive, displacement is incomplete. The UN Global Plastics Treaty negotiations (since 2022) are a key venue for these supply-side debates. (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 607, 612)

Notes — “noxious deindustrialisation” framing. Tilsted cites recent research showing that fenceline communities near petrochemical complexes increasingly face the negative externalities (pollution, health damage) without the positive externalities (jobs, public services) that historically justified the local presence. Combined with stranded-asset risk for petrochemical investors, this creates a political-economy crack that supply-side interventions can leverage. (Tilsted et al. 2023, p. 608)

Related terms. Petrochemicals (umbrella); refinery-petrochemical integration; non-energy use of fossil fuels; plastic chemicals; just transition; Paris Agreement; circular economy; carbon leakage; deep reindustrialisation; UN Global Plastics Treaty.

Source history. - Tilsted et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: lock-in taxonomy, supply-side intervention argument, noxious-deindustrialisation framing. - Bennett 2012 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): historical chemical-industry-fossil-fuel coupling context.

Petrochemicals (umbrella)

Aliases. Petroleum chemicals; primary chemicals; chemical-sector products; chemical industry outputs.

Definition. Chemicals produced from petroleum, natural gas, or coal feedstocks (and increasingly from biomass and recycled materials), forming the molecular building blocks for plastics, synthetic fibres, fertilisers, pharmaceutical precursors, solvents, detergents, paints, adhesives, and many specialty chemicals. The petrochemical sector accounts for ~10% of global crude-oil consumption, ~13% of total fossil-fuel non-energy use, ~7% of global GHG emissions, and is the largest industrial energy consumer (final-energy basis). (Aghdam 2023, pp. 1–2; Keim 2010, p. 298; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1725; Zhang et al. 2024, p. 99)

Attributes — sector framing.

Indicator Value
Share of global oil consumption (feedstock) ~10%
Share of total fossil non-energy use ~13% (≈30 EJ/yr)
Share of global GHG emissions ~7%
Share of CO₂-only emissions ~5.5%
Final energy consumption (2014) ~42.5 EJ (largest industrial sector)
Feedstock-energy share of total energy input ~58% (rising from 44% in 1971)
Direct industrial CO₂ emissions reduction needed (2DS) 30% by 2050 vs 2014, with 2.8× output growth
Building blocks (5 pillars) ethylene, propylene, C4 derivatives, benzene, xylenes
Total chemical-product output ~820 Mt/yr (2013 baseline)
Plastics share of output ~80%
Fibres share ~16%
Synthetic rubber share ~3%

(Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1725; Keim 2010, p. 298; Aghdam 2023, p. 1)

Notes — Keim’s “five pillars”. Keim 2010 frames the petrochemical industry as built on five basic building blocks — ethylene, propylene, C4 derivatives, benzene, and xylenes — from which thousands of intermediates and final products derive. This taxonomy is consistent with Levi & Cullen’s mass-balance categorisation and with Speight’s (2019) handbook organisation. (Keim 2010, p. 298; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1; Speight 2019, Chapters 6–7)

Notes — main product categories. Aghdam groups petrochemicals into four end-use categories: (i) fuels (gasoline, diesel, jet) — the largest tonnage; (ii) plastics and polymers (PE, PP, PVC, PS, PET) — the most visible; (iii) fertilisers and agrichemicals (urea, ammonium nitrate, pesticides); (iv) pharmaceuticals, solvents and specialties (small but high-value). Zhang et al. argue that the relative weight of the material role (categories ii–iv) over the energy role (category i) will rise sharply through 2050 as transport electrifies, leading to a fundamental restructuring of refining. (Aghdam 2023, p. 1; Zhang et al. 2024, pp. 99–100)

Notes — historical evolution. Zhang et al. trace the petrochemical industry’s evolution: distillation (19C kerosene); thermal cracking (1900s, automotive era); catalytic cracking (1940s, gasoline-driven); platinum reforming (1950s, anti-knock); zeolite cracking (1960s); hydrocracking + hydrofining (1980s, environmental); on-purpose technologies (1990s+, MTO/MTP/PDH). The path-dependence on distillation-based unit operations limits the industry’s ability to shift to alternative feedstocks rapidly. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 100)

Related terms. High-value chemicals (HVCs); naphtha; non-energy use of fossil fuels; BTX aromatics; olefins; steam cracking (vapocracking); catalytic cracking (FCC); catalytic reforming; refinery-petrochemical integration; near-zero emissions materials; volatile chemical products (VCPs); plastic chemicals; biorefinery.

Source history. - Keim 2010 — added 2026-05-08: five pillars, 10% of crude oil for chemical feedstock. - Aghdam 2023 — added 2026-05-08: end-use categories framing. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 7% GHG share, 42.5 EJ final-energy consumption, 820 Mt/yr output. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: historical evolution, restructuring outlook.

Petroleum refining (umbrella)

Aliases. Oil refining; refinery process flow; downstream petroleum.

Definition. The industrial conversion of crude oil into a portfolio of saleable products — transport fuels (gasoline, diesel, jet kerosene), heating fuels (heating oil, residual fuel oil), feedstocks for the petrochemical industry (naphtha, ethane, propane, LPG), and specialty products (lubricants, asphalt, waxes, bitumen, petroleum coke). A modern integrated refinery is a sequence of physical-separation units (atmospheric and vacuum distillation), conversion units (FCC, hydrocracking, catalytic reforming, alkylation, isomerisation, coker, visbreaker), and treating units (hydrotreating, sweetening, sulfur recovery), interconnected by streams of intermediate cuts. (Speight 2019, Chapters 1.4 and 4; Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, pp. 1–2)

Attributes — typical product slate from a complex refinery (mass-yield basis).

Crude oil cut Boiling range Yield Typical destination
Refinery gas (C1–C4) <30 °C 1–3% Fuel gas; LPG (propane/butane); ethane to crackers
Light naphtha (C5–C6) 30–90 °C 5–10% Isomerisation → high-octane gasoline blendstock
Heavy naphtha (C7–C10) 90–200 °C 10–20% Catalytic reforming → reformate (BTX, gasoline)
Kerosene / jet (C9–C16) 150–270 °C 10–15% Jet fuel; diesel blendstock
Diesel / gas oil (C12–C20) 200–360 °C 20–30% Diesel; FCC / hydrocracker feed
Vacuum gas oil (C20–C40) 360–540 °C 15–20% FCC feed; hydrocracker feed; lube base oil
Vacuum residue (>C40) >540 °C 10–25% Coker / visbreaker feed; heavy fuel oil; asphalt

(Speight 2019, Chapter 4 and Tables 1.4, 4.1)

Notes — refinery configuration types. Refineries are categorised by complexity: (i) topping refinery — atmospheric distillation only, no conversion; (ii) hydroskimming — adds catalytic reforming and hydrotreating; (iii) cracking refinery — adds FCC and/or hydrocracker for residue conversion; (iv) coking refinery — adds coker for vacuum residue conversion; (v) deep-conversion / integrated — fully integrated with petrochemical units (steam cracker, MTO, PDH). The Nelson Complexity Index (NCI) is the canonical numerical metric, ranging from 1 (topping) to >12 (full deep-conversion + integrated petrochemical). (Speight 2019, Chapter 1.4)

Notes — energy and emissions. A modern complex refinery consumes ~5–10% of crude-oil throughput as process energy (fuel gas + steam + electricity), giving ~150–250 kg CO₂/t crude direct emissions. Hydrogen is a key intermediate (~1–3% of throughput) for hydrotreating, hydrocracking, and lube-oil hydrofinishing; reformer co-produced H₂ + supplementary SMR cover demand. As transport-fuel demand falls (transport electrification), Zanon-Zotin project refinery utilisation falls from ~70% today to 30–50% by 2030 (1.5°C scenarios), with surviving capacity increasingly chemicals-oriented. (Speight 2019, Chapter 1.4; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, pp. 2–3)

Notes — five basic process steps. Speight summarises refining into: (i) separation (atmospheric + vacuum distillation, gas plants), (ii) conversion (cracking, hydrocracking, coking, visbreaking, alkylation, isomerisation, catalytic reforming), (iii) treating (hydrotreating, sweetening, sulfur recovery via Claus), (iv) blending (gasoline/diesel/jet pool blending to spec), (v) auxiliary services (hydrogen, steam, sour water, amine treating, sulfur recovery). The product-quality requirements are set by transport-fuel specifications (octane, cetane, sulphur cap, RVP, distillation envelope, oxygenate content). (Speight 2019, Chapter 4)

Related terms. Atmospheric distillation; vacuum distillation; catalytic cracking (FCC); catalytic reforming; hydrocracking; alkylation (refinery); isomerisation (refinery); delayed coking; visbreaking; hydrotreating (HDS / HDN); naphtha; high-value chemicals (HVCs); refinery-petrochemical integration; petrochemicals (umbrella); steam cracking (vapocracking).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, product slate, Nelson Complexity Index, five-step process, energy and emissions. - Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: utilisation-factor evolution, defossilisation pathway. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): refinery role in chemical-sector mass balance.

Power Purchase Agreement (PPA)

Aliases. PPA; corporate PPA; renewable PPA; physical PPA; financial PPA; virtual PPA; sleeved PPA.

Definition. A long-term contract (typically 10–25 years) in which an electricity buyer agrees to purchase a defined volume of electricity from a specified renewable-energy generator at a pre-agreed price, providing the generator with revenue certainty for project finance and providing the buyer with a hedged renewable-electricity supply. Variants include: (i) physical PPA — buyer takes physical delivery; (ii) financial / virtual PPA — buyer settles the price difference with grid spot prices, no physical delivery; (iii) sleeved PPA — utility intermediates the contract for a fee; (iv) as-produced PPA — buyer takes whatever the generator produces hourly; (v) baseload PPA — generator delivers a flat-shape profile, with grid balancing. (Romero-Piñeiro et al. 2025, pp. 341–342; cross-ref renewable-energy project finance)

Attributes — typical PPA structures.

PPA type Buyer’s commitment Generator’s commitment Use case
As-produced (hourly matching) accept all hourly output at fixed price deliver as generated green-H₂ production (EU REDIII rules from 2030)
Baseload take flat profile deliver flat shape (with battery / firming) industrial process loads needing stable supply
Take-or-pay pay regardless of physical delivery guarantee minimum volume risk-shifting away from buyer
Pay-as-consumed pay only for delivered energy match consumer demand typical commercial buyers
Virtual / financial settle vs spot price settle vs spot price corporate sustainability without grid co-location

(Romero-Piñeiro et al. 2025, p. 342)

Notes — defossilisation linkage. PPAs are the principal financial mechanism enabling corporate procurement of new-build renewable electricity at scale. The European Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) requires that, from 2030, renewable hydrogen must be produced within the same 1-hour period as the renewable-electricity generation — making as-produced hourly-matched PPAs the standard for compliant green-H₂ production. Romero-Piñeiro 2025 use a 40 €/MWh hourly-matched solar PPA with 15% over-sizing as their reference for refinery green-H₂ production. (Romero-Piñeiro et al. 2025, pp. 341–342; EU RED III, cited)

Related terms. Carbon contract for difference (CCfD); regulated asset base (RAB) model; bankability; renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO); low-emissions hydrogen; non-recourse project finance; Variable Renewable Energy (VRE).

Source history. - Romero-Piñeiro et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, PPA structures, RED III hourly-matching requirement, refinery green-H₂ application.

Power-to-X (PtX)

Aliases. Power-to-Gas (PtG); Power-to-Liquid (PtL); Power-to-Methane (PtM); Power-to-Methanol; Power-to-Ammonia; sector coupling pathways.

Definition. A family of technologies that convert (renewable) electricity into chemical energy carriers — gases, liquids or solids — through electrolysis-derived hydrogen and downstream synthesis. The umbrella encompasses PtG (e-hydrogen, e-methane), PtL (e-FTL, e-methanol, e-DME), and product-specific routes (e-ammonia, e-naphtha). PtX is identified as the central enabler of indirect electrification for “hard-to-abate” segments and as a long-duration / inter-annual storage option. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 16, 22)

Notes. Power-to-Gas has the potential to serve as a fuel-storage unit, with both e-hydrogen and e-methane storable across heating, transport and chemical-industry sectors. e-fuels and e-chemicals stand out within sector coupling due to the pivotal role played by e-hydrogen, generated via electrolysis, at the beginning of their conversion chains. The transmission of H₂ and CH₄ via dedicated pipelines is examined in only 5.4% and 3.0% of 100% RE systems articles respectively. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 9, 16, 22)

Related terms. e-fuels; electrofuels; sector coupling; hydrogen storage; hydrogen pipeline.

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: umbrella definition, PtG/PtL/PtM variants, role in sector coupling.

Power system flexibility

Definition. The ability of a power system to balance variable supply and demand across all relevant timescales (sub-second to seasonal) while maintaining frequency, voltage and adequacy constraints. Becomes a binding requirement as the share of variable renewable energy (VRE) rises and as conventional synchronous generation is retired. (Guerra et al. 2022, p. 2; IEA ETP 2026, pp. 145, 153; IEA GER 2026, p. 12)

Attributes — flexibility sources (Guerra et al. 2022).

Source Mechanism
Grid expansion / interconnections spatial smoothing of VRE
Optimal wind/solar ratio seasonal counterbalancing
Curtailment reduce VRE output to match inflexible supply or inertia
Energy storage (battery, PHES, CAES, TES, H₂) shift energy across time
Flexible conventional generation gas, biomass, hydro
Demand response / load shifting move flexible loads to high-VRE periods
Power-to-X (PtG, PtL) absorb surplus and decouple sectors
System diversity / forecast improvement reduce uncertainty

(Guerra et al. 2022, p. 2)

Notes — recent stress events. GER-2026 highlights a Europe-wide stress event in 2025 when poor wind conditions during cold snaps drove up natural gas use in power generation — illustrating the importance of dispatchable capacity and storage as VRE share grows. Drought conditions in Europe and Central/South America also reduced hydropower output, increasing fossil generation. Without these weather effects, global coal demand growth would have been 0.5% rather than 0.4%. (IEA GER 2026, p. 12)

Related terms. Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); curtailment (VRE); inertia (power system); battery storage (stationary); pumped hydro energy storage (PHES); demand response; power-to-X (PtX).

Source history. - Guerra et al. 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, taxonomy of flexibility sources. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: deployment context. - IEA GER 2026 — added 2026-05-08: 2025 stress-event illustrations.

PoTSs (potentially toxic substances)

Definition. A category used in the plastic-chemicals literature to denote any chemical substance present in a plastic product (intentionally added or non-intentionally added) that has the potential to cause harm to human health or the environment if released, even if it has not yet been formally classified as a chemical of concern. Closely related to Monclús et al.’s “chemicals of concern” but used by Hahladakis et al. as a broader operational term covering the full migration-and-release problem space. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, pp. 186–187)

Notes — examples studied for release from plastics. Phthalates, brominated flame retardants (BFRs), bisphenol A (BPA), bisphenol-A diglyceride ether (BADGE), lead/tin/cadmium, formaldehyde and acetaldehyde, 4-nonylphenol, methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), benzene, and various volatile organic compounds. The guideline values for PoTS migration typically do not consider low-dose endocrine-disrupting effects or mixture toxicity. (Hahladakis et al. 2018, p. 187)

Related terms. Chemicals of concern; plastic chemicals; migration (plastic chemicals); plasticizers (phthalate esters); brominated flame retardants; bisphenol A (BPA).

Source history. - Hahladakis et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, scope, example PoTSs.

Power-to-gas-to-power loop (P2G2P)

Aliases. P2H2P (when via H₂); P2CH4P (when via methanation); P2G2P; round-trip H₂/CH₄ storage; long-duration energy storage via gas vector.

Definition. A multi-stage long-duration storage chain in which surplus electricity (typically from VRE oversupply) is converted to a chemical-energy carrier (hydrogen via electrolysis, optionally further methanated to CH₄) for storage; the gas is later reconverted to electricity in a CCGT, OCGT or fuel-cell when the system needs it. The P2G2P loop is one of the few flexibility levers capable of absorbing weeks-to-months mismatches between VRE production and demand. (RTE 2022, Section 7.5.2.3, Figures 7.32–7.33, pp. 333–334, translated from French)

Attributes — RTE 2050 round-trip efficiency by configuration.

Configuration Electrolysis Storage / methanation Power conversion Round-trip efficiency
H₂ + H₂-CCGT ~70% (no methanation) ~60% ~40%
H₂ + H₂-OCGT ~70% (no methanation) ~40% ~28%
H₂ + fuel cell ~70% (no methanation) ~50–55% ~35–40%
CH₄ + biomethane CCGT ~70% ~80% (methanation) ~55–60% ~30%
CH₄ + CH₄ TAC ~70% ~80% (methanation) ~40% ~22%
Best case (H₂-CCGT) 70% — 60% ~42%
Worst case (CH₄ TAC) 70% 80% 40% ~20%

(RTE 2022, Figures 7.32–7.33, p. 333)

Notes — energy losses. RTE quantifies the energy cost of the P2G2P loop: in M-scenarios with strong renewable build-out, conversion losses across the storage chain can reach 20–35 TWh/year (M0: ~35 TWh; M23: ~20 TWh). In N-scenarios with EPR2 displacing some of the storage need, the losses are 3 TWh (N03) to 15 TWh (N1). These are losses the user pays for via the annualised system cost. (RTE 2022, Section 7.10.2, Figure 7.60, p. 378)

Notes — H₂ vs CH₄ trade-off. Methanation adds an extra conversion step (~80% efficient) but yields a fuel that integrates directly with existing gas infrastructure (CH₄ network, storage, end-use). H₂ has higher round-trip efficiency but requires hydrogen-specific (or pipeline-reassigned) network and CCGT/OCGT modifications. RTE flags H₂ as preferred when domestic infrastructure can be built; CH₄ as a fallback when retrofitting existing gas grids is cheaper than building H₂-specific infrastructure. Methanation also requires a CO₂ source (purity > 99% commonly needed), often co-located with biogas digesters. (RTE 2022, Section 7.5.2.3, p. 334)

Notes — long-duration storage role. P2G2P is the only flexibility lever in RTE’s portfolio that can store electricity over weeks-to-months timescales (vs hours for batteries / V2G, days for PHES). Its annual energy throughput in M0 reaches the order of 20–30 TWh into storage and ~10–15 TWh out, vs zero today. The capital cost is dominated by electrolysers and underground gas storage; CCGT/OCGT capital cost is comparatively small. (RTE 2022, Sections 7.5.2.3, 7.10.2, Figures 7.59–7.60)

Related terms. Combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT); Open cycle gas turbine (OCGT); Power-to-X (PtX); Hydrogen Combined Cycle (H₂ CC); Underground hydrogen storage (UHS); Hydrogen pipeline; Battery storage (stationary); Pumped hydro energy storage (PHES); Mismatch energy.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, ~40% (H₂-CCGT) to ~20% (CH₄-TAC) round-trip efficiency, 20–35 TWh/year conversion losses by scenario, role as long-duration storage (translated from French).

Plastic processing (umbrella)

Aliases. Plastics conversion; plastics moulding; plastic forming methods.

Definition. The set of industrial methods that convert thermoplastic resin pellets (or thermoset prepolymers) into finished plastic products with a defined geometry. The dominant plastic processing methods globally, ranked roughly by tonnage processed, are: extrusion (continuous profiles, films, pipes), injection moulding (discrete moulded parts), blow moulding (hollow containers), thermoforming (sheet → shaped product by vacuum), rotomoulding (large hollow tanks), calendering (rigid + flexible sheet/film), and compression / transfer moulding (thermoset parts). (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Attributes — process selection logic.

Process Best for Typical part geometry Tooling cost Production rate
Extrusion constant-section profiles pipes, sheets, films, fibres low continuous (high)
Injection moulding discrete complex parts bumpers, housings, containers high high (10–60 s cycle)
Blow moulding hollow containers bottles, drums, tanks medium high
Thermoforming shallow shapes from sheet trays, packaging, dashboards low medium
Rotomoulding large hollow parts water tanks, kayaks, playground low low
Calendering flat sheet (thick or flexible) flooring, conveyor belts very high high
Compression moulding thermoset parts brake pads, body panels medium low

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Notes — emerging additive manufacturing. 3D printing / additive manufacturing of polymers (FDM, SLA, SLS) is growing rapidly for prototyping and low-volume specialty parts. Tonnage remains tiny vs the seven dominant industrial methods above, but the 3D-printing materials market (FDM filament: PLA, ABS, PETG, PEEK, nylon) intersects with bio-polymers and engineering plastics. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Related terms. Injection moulding; extrusion (plastic processing); blow moulding; thermoforming; rotomoulding; calendering; compounding (plastics); plastic chemicals; petrochemicals (umbrella).

Pareto dominance / Pareto front

Aliases. Pareto front; Pareto-optimal set; non-dominated set; efficient frontier; Pareto-Edgeworth dominance.

Definition. A foundational concept in multi-objective optimisation, named after Vilfredo Pareto (Italian economist, 1848–1923). A solution x₁ dominates solution x₂ if it is at least as good as x₂ on all objectives and strictly better on at least one — i.e. there is no trade-off; x₁ is unconditionally preferred. The set of non-dominated solutions in the search space is the Pareto front — solutions where every objective is at its best given the constraints of the others. The Pareto front is typically a curved or surface-like structure in objective space; choosing one solution from the front requires a separate decision-aid step using preference weights. (Goessel 2025, pp. 66–69)

Attributes — Pareto-front interpretation.

Aspect Description
Geometry typically curved (2D), surface (3D), or higher-dimensional manifold
Number of solutions varies — Goessel finds ~50–200 Pareto-optimal renovation strategies on his front
Trade-offs moving along the front trades one objective for another
Knee point point of “diminishing returns” where modest gains in one objective cost large losses in others
Outliers from front dominated solutions; not Pareto-optimal but may be culturally / heritage-preferred
Convex vs concave front concave fronts may not be reached by weighted-sum scalarisation

(Goessel 2025, pp. 66–69 and Fig. 2.6.1)

Notes — Goessel application. Goessel evaluates ~10,000 renovation strategies for each typology × climate × system configuration, then identifies the Pareto-optimal subset (~50–200 strategies typically) on the (CGD, embodied carbon, SET-DH) 3D Pareto front. The 3D front is then projected to 2D for visualisation, and clustered (K-Means) to identify renovation archetypes — characteristic strategies on the front that share common renovation features. (Goessel 2025, pp. 89–110)

Related terms. Multi-objective optimisation (MOO / OMO); NSGA (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm); K-Means clustering; building renovation (umbrella); multi-criteria decision-making; Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: Pareto-dominance criterion, front geometry, Goessel application (translated from French).

Polybutadiene rubber (BR)

Aliases. BR; cis-1,4-polybutadiene; high-cis BR; trans-PB.

Definition. A synthetic elastomer produced by stereospecific coordination polymerisation of butadiene over a Ziegler-Natta (Ti, Co, Ni) or anionic-living (alkyl-lithium) catalyst, giving high-cis (~98% cis-1,4) microstructure with high elasticity, low heat build-up under cycling, high abrasion resistance, and Tg of −108 °C — the lowest of any commercial elastomer. BR is used predominantly in tyre tread blends (~70%), where it combines with SBR to deliver the rolling-resistance + grip + wear performance triangle. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global BR production ~3 Mt/yr
Stereoregularity (high-cis) ~98% cis-1,4
Tg (cis form) −108 °C
Tg (trans form) −14 °C
End-use — tyre tread + sidewall ~70%
End-use — high-impact polystyrene (HIPS) modifier ~20%
End-use — ABS modifier ~5%
End-use — golf-ball cores, footwear, conveyor belts ~5%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11)

Related terms. Butadiene; styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR); ABS; polystyrene (HIPS); Ziegler-Natta polymerisation; tyre industry; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Polycarbonate (PC)

Aliases. PC; bisphenol-A polycarbonate; Lexan; Makrolon; Calibre.

Definition. An amorphous, transparent, glassy thermoplastic polymer produced by step-growth polymerisation of bisphenol A (BPA) with phosgene (COCl₂) or, in modern green-process plants, with diphenyl carbonate (DPC). The polymer’s signature combination of optical clarity (transmits >90% of visible light), high impact resistance (notched Izod 700–900 J/m, the toughest of common transparent polymers), and high heat resistance (Tg ~145 °C) makes it the dominant material for high-performance optical and impact applications. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production ~5 Mt/yr
Tg 145 °C
Tensile strength 60–70 MPa
Notched Izod impact 700–900 J/m
Synthesis route (legacy) BPA + COCl₂ → PC + 2 HCl (interfacial polycondensation)
Synthesis route (green) BPA + diphenyl carbonate → PC + 2 phenol (melt transesterification)
End-use — optical media (CD, DVD, BluRay) declining (~5% of historical peak)
End-use — automotive (headlamp lenses, glazing) ~25%
End-use — construction glazing (greenhouses, riot shields) ~20%
End-use — electrical / electronics housings ~25%
End-use — water bottles, food packaging (regulated for BPA) declining
End-use — medical devices ~10%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Notes — BPA controversy. BPA leaching from PC into food and water has been a major public-health concern since the early 2000s. EU regulation has banned BPA in baby bottles (2011), thermal-paper receipts (2020), and food-contact packaging (2024); US FDA restrictions are narrower. BPA-free polycarbonate alternatives (Eastman Tritan, copolyester) are commercial and now dominate consumer water-bottle applications. (Cross-ref Bisphenol A entry; Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Related terms. Bisphenol A (BPA); cumene process (Hock process — phenol + acetone); engineering plastics (umbrella); step-growth polymerisation; chemicals of concern; high-value chemicals (HVCs); plastic chemicals.

Polyethylene (HDPE / LDPE / LLDPE)

Aliases. PE; HDPE (high-density); LDPE (low-density); LLDPE (linear low-density); polyethene.

Definition. A family of thermoplastic polymers produced by polymerising ethylene monomer (CH₂=CH₂). The three main commercial grades differ in degree of branching and crystallinity, set by the polymerisation process and catalyst: - LDPE (Low-Density PE): highly branched, amorphous-rich; produced by high-pressure free-radical polymerisation (1,000–3,000 bar, 150–300 °C) — the original 1933 ICI process. - HDPE (High-Density PE): essentially linear (no branching); produced by low-pressure coordination polymerisation (~30 bar, 70–100 °C) over Ziegler-Natta or chromium (Phillips) catalysts. - LLDPE (Linear Low-Density PE): linear with short-chain branches from a comonomer (1-butene, 1-hexene, 1-octene); low-pressure Ziegler-Natta or metallocene catalysts in gas-phase, slurry, or solution reactors. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.1)

Attributes — properties and uses.

Property LDPE HDPE LLDPE
Density (g/cm³) 0.910–0.925 0.941–0.965 0.915–0.935
Crystallinity 40–55% 65–80% 35–55%
Melting point 105–115 °C 125–135 °C 120–130 °C
Tensile strength (MPa) 8–17 22–35 14–25
Process high-P free-radical (autoclave or tubular) Ziegler / Phillips, gas-phase or slurry Ziegler or metallocene, gas-phase or solution
Catalyst radical initiator (peroxide) TiCl₄/MgCl₂ + Et₃Al, or CrO₃/silica TiCl₄ or Cp₂ZrCl₂ metallocene
Largest end-use film for packaging bottles, containers, pipe stretch film, agricultural film

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.1.1–11.3.1.3)

Notes — global production and end-uses. Combined PE production is ~115 Mt/yr globally (HDPE ~50 Mt, LLDPE ~35 Mt, LDPE ~25 Mt), making PE the largest commodity thermoplastic worldwide (~35% of all plastics). Packaging dominates end-use (~65%); pipe and construction (~15%); injection-moulded goods (~15%); other (~5%). Shopping bags, food film, milk jugs, water bottles, drinking straws, cable insulation, geomembranes, gas-distribution pipe, and HDPE-pipe water mains are all PE. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.1; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Notes — recyclability. PE has the highest mechanical-recycling-friendliness of the commodity polymers — chemically inert, no halogens, no nitrogen — but the volume recycled in practice is small (~5–15% globally) due to contamination in mixed-stream MSW and the low cost of virgin PE. Identification: HDPE is resin-code 2; LDPE/LLDPE is resin-code 4. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.1; cross-ref Mechanical recycling)

Related terms. Ethylene; olefins; high-value chemicals (HVCs); Ziegler-Natta polymerisation; metallocene polymerisation; free-radical polymerisation; chromium catalyst; gas-phase polymerisation; slurry polymerisation; solution polymerisation; mechanical recycling; chemical recycling; plastic chemicals.

Polylactic acid (PLA)

Aliases. PLA; polylactide; bio-PLA; Cargill Dow / NatureWorks Ingeo.

Definition. A bio-based, compostable thermoplastic polyester produced by ring-opening polymerisation of lactide (the cyclic dimer of lactic acid) over a stannous-octoate catalyst, or by step-growth polycondensation of lactic acid. Lactic acid is produced industrially by fermentation of sugars (corn dextrose, sugarcane sucrose) by Lactobacillus bacteria. PLA is the most-deployed bio-based plastic globally, with applications in food-service single-use packaging (cups, cutlery), 3D-printing filament (FDM), and biomedical sutures. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section, citing Cargill / NatureWorks)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global PLA production capacity (~2024) ~0.4 Mt/yr (NatureWorks ~150 kt; TotalEnergies-Corbion ~75 kt; others)
Tg 60–65 °C
Tm 150–180 °C (depends on stereochemistry)
Tensile strength 50–70 MPa
Bio-content ~100% (from corn / sugarcane)
Compostability industrially (60 °C / 60% humidity) yes; home-compostable: limited
End-use — biodegradable food-service single-use ~40%
End-use — 3D-printing filament (FDM) ~20%
End-use — biomedical sutures, orthopaedic implants ~5%
End-use — fibre, textile, agricultural film ~35%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Notes — limits. PLA’s Tg of ~60 °C means containers warp in hot beverages or sunlit cars. Mechanical recycling streams confuse PLA with PET (resin code conflict — PLA is sometimes labelled “7”); contamination of PET recyclate by PLA degrades quality. Industrial composting infrastructure is required for compostability — most PLA discarded as MSW does not compost in landfill or marine environments. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Related terms. Modern bioenergy; biorefinery; chemical recycling; compostable plastics; engineering plastics (umbrella); plastic chemicals; lignocellulose; mechanical recycling.

Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA / PHB)

Aliases. PHA; polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB); polyhydroxyvalerate (PHV); P3HB; Mirel; Nodax.

Definition. A family of biopolyesters synthesised intracellularly by certain bacteria (e.g., Cupriavidus necator, Bacillus megaterium) from sugar or vegetable-oil substrates as carbon-and-energy storage granules — analogous to fat in animals. The polymer is harvested by cell lysis and solvent extraction. PHB (3-hydroxybutyrate homopolymer) is the most studied, but commercial materials are typically copolymers (PHBV, PHBHHx) blended for processability. PHA is fully bio-based and biodegradable in soil, freshwater and marine environments — a key advantage over PLA. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section, citing PHA literature; Keim 2010, p. 301)

Indicator Value

Bio-content ~100% (from glucose, fatty acids)
Biodegradability yes — soil, freshwater, marine (the only commodity bioplastic with marine biodegradation)
Tg (PHB homopolymer) 5 °C
Tm (PHB) 175 °C
Tensile strength (PHBV typical) 25–40 MPa

End-use — agricultural mulch film ~15%
End-use — biomedical scaffolds ~10%
End-use — coated paperboard, fibre ~25%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section; Keim 2010, p. 301)

Notes — vs PLA. PHA’s marine-biodegradability is a unique selling point vs PLA (which only composts in industrial conditions). Both face cost barriers vs commodity plastics. PHA scale-up is limited by fermentation productivity and downstream-extraction efficiency. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Polypropylene (PP)

Aliases. PP; isotactic polypropylene (i-PP); homopolymer / copolymer / impact-PP.

Definition. A linear, semi-crystalline thermoplastic polymer of propylene (CH₃-CH=CH₂), produced by stereospecific coordination polymerisation over Ziegler-Natta (TiCl₄/MgCl₂ + Et₃Al with electron-donor) or metallocene catalysts. The dominant commercial form is isotactic PP (all methyl groups on the same side of the chain), which crystallises efficiently and gives the strongest mechanical properties. Atactic PP (random methyl placement) is amorphous and used as a sealant adhesive. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.2)

Attributes — properties and uses.

Property Isotactic PP
Density 0.90–0.91 g/cm³
Crystallinity 60–70%
Melting point 160–175 °C
Glass transition (Tg) −20 to 0 °C
Tensile strength 30–40 MPa
Production process gas-phase (Spheripol, Unipol-PP) or slurry (Mitsui CX-process)
Catalyst 5th-gen Ziegler-Natta with phthalate or diether donor; metallocene
Global production ~80 Mt/yr
Largest end-use rigid packaging (~30%); fibres (~20%); injection-moulded goods (~25%); film (~15%); other (~10%)

Notes — copolymers. PP homopolymer is rigid but brittle at low temperature. Random copolymer PP (1–7% ethylene) lowers crystallinity and improves transparency / impact. Heterophasic / block copolymer PP (in-reactor blend with ethylene-propylene rubber) gives “impact PP” with high low-temperature toughness for automotive and crate applications. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.2)

Notes — applications. PP is the second-largest commodity thermoplastic. Major end-uses: yogurt cups, microwave containers, bottle caps, rigid packaging; carpet fibres, nonwoven fabric (face-mask spunbond layer); automotive bumpers and dashboards; banknotes (Australia); injection-moulded crates and pallets. Resin-code 5. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.6.5)

Polyvinyl chloride (PVC)

Aliases. PVC; vinyl; chloroethene polymer.

Definition. A thermoplastic polymer of vinyl chloride monomer (VCM, CH₂=CHCl) produced predominantly by suspension or emulsion free-radical polymerisation. PVC contains ~57 wt% chlorine, making it intrinsically flame-retardant but generating HCl on incineration. The polymer is amorphous-to-slightly-crystalline; commercial products are formulated with plasticisers (PVC-P, “flexible PVC”) for soft uses or used unplasticised (PVC-U, “rigid PVC”) for pipes and window frames. PVC is the third-largest commodity thermoplastic globally. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.3)

Density 1.38–1.45 g/cm³ 1.20–1.35 g/cm³

Tensile strength 50–80 MPa 10–25 MPa

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.3)

Notes — chlorine balance and end-of-life. PVC’s chlorine content originates in the chlor-alkali process (electrolysis of NaCl brine → Cl₂ + NaOH + H₂); ~30% of global Cl₂ production goes to PVC manufacture. End-of-life PVC: incineration generates HCl (acid gas, neutralised by lime); landfill disposal is dominant; mechanical recycling is hampered by additive content (especially phthalate plasticisers) and chlorine-induced equipment corrosion. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.3; cross-ref Plasticizers entry)
