Polyetheretherketone (PEEK)

Aliases. PEEK; polyaryletherketone (PAEK); Victrex PEEK; Vestakeep.

Definition. A semi-crystalline aromatic-ether-ketone thermoplastic polymer with the highest commercial-engineering-plastic combination of mechanical strength (tensile 100 MPa), heat resistance (Tg 143 °C, Tm 343 °C, continuous-use 250 °C), chemical resistance (insoluble in nearly all common solvents below 250 °C), and radiation resistance. PEEK is produced by step-growth polycondensation of 4,4′-difluorobenzophenone with hydroquinone (or the disodium salt). Originally developed by ICI in 1978 and commercialised by Victrex. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET)

Aliases. PET; PETE; polyester (when in fibre form); BoPET (biaxially-oriented).

Definition. A semi-crystalline thermoplastic polyester produced by step-growth (condensation) polymerisation of terephthalic acid (TPA / PTA) and ethylene glycol (MEG), with water as the condensation by-product: n HOOC-C₆H₄-COOH + n HOCH₂-CH₂OH → [-OC-C₆H₄-CO-O-CH₂-CH₂-O-]ₙ + (2n−1) H₂O. Direct esterification (TPA route, dominant) or transesterification (DMT route, older) produces a low-MW prepolymer, which is then melt-polycondensed to bottle-grade or fibre-grade PET. Solid-state polymerisation (SSP) further increases molecular weight for bottle resin. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.6 and 11.6.1)

PET is the most-recycled commodity polymer (~25–60% recovered in deposit-refund-scheme regions), thanks to high-volume bottle separation, simple mono-material design, and a mature recycling supply chain (rPET). PET-bottle-to-bottle closed-loop recycling is now commercial; rPET fibres dominate sustainable-fashion claims. Resin-code 1. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.6.1; cross-ref Deposit-refund scheme entry)

Notes — bio-PET and chemical recycling. PartialBio-PET (30% bio-MEG + fossil-TPA; Coca-Cola PlantBottle) is commercial; fully bio-PET requires bio-PX → bio-TPA, pre-commercial. Chemical recycling via glycolysis (PET + MEG → BHET → re-polymerise) and methanolysis (Eastman, Loop Industries) are scaling — turning post-consumer PET back into virgin-quality monomers. Polyoxymethylene (POM / polyacetal)

Aliases. POM; polyacetal; polyformaldehyde; Delrin; Hostaform; Celcon; engineering acetal.

Definition. A highly crystalline aliphatic polyether engineering thermoplastic produced by anionic polymerisation of formaldehyde monomer (homopolymer Delrin, DuPont) or by cationic polymerisation of trioxane (the cyclic trimer of formaldehyde) with a small amount of comonomer (typically ethylene oxide; copolymer Hostaform / Celcon). Distinguished by very high tensile strength (65 MPa), low coefficient of friction (self-lubricating), excellent dimensional stability, and high fatigue resistance — ideal for precision moving parts. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.10)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production ~1 Mt/yr
Tg −60 °C
Tm 175 °C
Tensile strength 65 MPa
Crystallinity 70–80%
Friction coefficient 0.10–0.15 (self-lubricating)
End-use — gears, bearings, cams (mechanical) ~40%
End-use — automotive (fasteners, fuel-system parts, aerosol containers) ~25%
End-use — appliances (door handles, dishwasher impellers) ~15%
End-use — plumbing fittings ~15%
End-use — medical, electronics ~5%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.10)

Related terms. Formaldehyde; engineering plastics (umbrella); free-radical polymerisation (cationic variant); plastic processing (umbrella); high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Polyphenylene oxide (PPO / PPE)

Aliases. PPO; PPE (poly(phenylene ether)); 2,6-dimethyl polyphenylene oxide; modified PPO (mPPO); Noryl.

Definition. A high-Tg amorphous engineering thermoplastic produced by oxidative coupling of 2,6-dimethylphenol with O₂ at the para-position over a cuprous-chloride (CuCl) / pyridine catalyst. The pure polymer (Tg 205 °C) has high heat-distortion temperature, low moisture absorption, and excellent electrical insulation — but high melt viscosity and poor solvent resistance limit its standalone applicability. Commercial materials are Noryl — blends of PPO with polystyrene, which retain PPO’s heat resistance while gaining PS’s processability. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.9)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production (incl. blends) ~0.5 Mt/yr
Synthesis 2,6-dimethylphenol + O₂ → PPO (oxidative coupling, CuCl + pyridine)
Tg (pure PPO) 205 °C
Tg (PPO/PS = Noryl, depending on blend) 100–180 °C
End-use — electrical/electronic housings ~40%
End-use — automotive interior ~20%
End-use — medical-device housings ~15%
End-use — water-distribution components, pump housings ~10%
End-use — appliance components (microwave, dishwasher) ~15%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.9)

Related terms. Engineering plastics (umbrella); polystyrene (PS / HIPS / EPS); phenol; high-value chemicals (HVCs); plastic processing (umbrella).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, oxidative-coupling synthesis, Noryl blend, end-uses.

Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)

Aliases. PTFE; Teflon; ETFE / FEP / PFA (related fluoropolymers).

Definition. A highly crystalline fluoropolymer produced by free-radical (or persulfate-initiated) emulsion or suspension polymerisation of tetrafluoroethylene (CF₂=CF₂). The repeating −CF₂−CF₂− unit gives PTFE the lowest known coefficient of friction of any solid material (0.05–0.10), excellent thermal stability (continuous-use 260 °C), exceptional chemical inertness (resists virtually all acids, bases, solvents below 250 °C), low dielectric constant, non-stick surface, and full UV/weather resistance. Discovered accidentally by Roy Plunkett at DuPont in 1938. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production (incl. fluoropolymer family) ~0.2 Mt/yr
Tm 327 °C (no Tg; semi-crystalline at all use temperatures)
Continuous-use temperature 260 °C
Tensile strength 25 MPa (relatively low)
Friction coefficient 0.05–0.10
End-use — non-stick cookware coating ~25%
End-use — chemical / petrochemical seals, gaskets, pipe linings ~25%
End-use — electrical insulation (cable, capacitors) ~20%
End-use — semiconductor processing (etch tanks) ~15%
End-use — Gore-Tex / breathable membranes (expanded PTFE) ~5%
End-use — medical (sutures, vascular grafts) ~5%
End-use — bearings, lubrication additives ~5%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Notes — PFAS controversy. Tetrafluoroethylene polymerisation has historically used perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) as an emulsifier; PFOA is a Group 2B IARC carcinogen and persistent organic pollutant. PFOA was phased out under the EPA Stewardship Program (2015), and modern fluoropolymers use shorter-chain alternatives or fluorine-free emulsifiers. PTFE itself is inert and not classified as PFAS hazard, but the wider fluoropolymer family — including the side-chain-fluorinated polymers (textile DWR coatings) — is the principal regulatory concern under PFAS rules. (cross-ref Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS); Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Related terms. Engineering plastics (umbrella); per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS); free-radical polymerisation; high-value chemicals (HVCs); chemicals of concern.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, properties, applications, PFOA-emulsifier history.

Polystyrene (PS / HIPS / EPS)

Aliases. PS; GP-PS (general-purpose); HIPS (high-impact); EPS (expanded); XPS (extruded).

Definition. A thermoplastic polymer of styrene (C₆H₅-CH=CH₂) produced by free-radical chain polymerisation (bulk, suspension, or solution), giving an amorphous, glassy, transparent polymer with characteristic brittleness at room temperature. Modifications: HIPS is a graft copolymer with polybutadiene (~5–10% rubber), giving impact resistance at the cost of transparency. EPS is a foamed PS made by polymerising styrene in the presence of a hydrocarbon blowing agent (pentane), giving low-density rigid foam used as insulation and packaging. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.4)

Attributes — properties and uses.

Variant Density Tensile strength Use
GP-PS 1.04 g/cm³ 35–55 MPa CD/DVD cases, disposable cutlery, plastic models
HIPS 1.04 g/cm³ 25–35 MPa (with toughness) refrigerator liners, TV housings, food containers
EPS 0.015–0.05 g/cm³ low insulation board, packaging foam, cups
XPS 0.025–0.05 g/cm³ low building insulation
Tg (all PS variants) ~100 °C — —
Global PS production ~25 Mt/yr — resin-code 6

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.4)

Notes — environmental and recycling. PS is among the least-recycled commodity polymers — many municipal collection systems exclude it, and EPS foam contamination by food residues + low bulk density (high transport cost per kg) hurt economics. Resin-code 6 PS is widely banned in single-use food-service applications by various US states / EU member states. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.4)

Related terms. Styrene; ethylbenzene; benzene; ethylene; ABS; SBR (styrene-butadiene rubber); free-radical polymerisation; suspension polymerisation; plastic chemicals; single-use plastics.

Polyamides (Nylon)

Aliases. PA; nylon; Nylon 6; Nylon 6,6; PA6; PA66; PA12; aramid.

Definition. A family of thermoplastic engineering polymers containing the amide (-CO-NH-) functional group in the polymer backbone, produced by step-growth (condensation) polymerisation. The two largest commercial polyamides are Nylon 6,6 (from hexamethylenediamine HMDA + adipic acid) and Nylon 6 (from ε-caprolactam ring-opening polymerisation). Polyamides are characterised by high mechanical strength, high melting points (220–265 °C), good chemical resistance, and excellent fibre-forming properties. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.5 and 11.6.2)

Attributes — main commercial polyamides.

Variant Monomer(s) Tm (°C) Use
Nylon 6,6 HMDA + adipic acid 265 Carpet fibre, automotive, electrical
Nylon 6 ε-caprolactam 220 Tyre cord, fibres, packaging film
Nylon 6,12 HMDA + dodecanedioic acid 220 Tubes, monofilaments
Nylon 11 11-aminoundecanoic acid 198 Cable insulation; Rilsan brand
Nylon 12 laurolactam (12-aminododecanoic acid) 178 Flexible tubing, sports equipment
Aramid (Kevlar / Twaron) aromatic diamine + aromatic diacid chloride decomposes >450 High-strength fibre, ballistic protection
Global PA production ~9 Mt/yr (2/3 Nylon 6, 1/3 Nylon 6,6) — —

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.5)

Notes — feedstock chains. Nylon 6,6’s adipic acid is produced by oxidising cyclohexane (from benzene hydrogenation) → KA-oil → adipic acid; HMDA is produced by hydrogenating adiponitrile (from butadiene + HCN, Invista process). Nylon 6’s caprolactam is produced from cyclohexanone oxime via Beckmann rearrangement. Both chains generate substantial nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions in adipic-acid production — a major industrial GHG source until catalytic abatement (>95% reduction) was deployed in the 2000s. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.5; cross-ref process emissions)

Notes — engineering plastics and high-performance fibres. Beyond commodity Nylon 6 / 6,6, the polyamide family includes high-performance aramid fibres (Kevlar, Twaron) used in body armour, aerospace composites, and ballistic protection — strength >3 GPa per mono-fibre. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.6.2.1–11.6.2.6)

Related terms. Step-growth polymerisation; benzene; butadiene; ammonia; cyclohexane; engineering plastics; high-value chemicals (HVCs); plastic chemicals.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: Nylon 6 / 6,6 / 6,12 / 11 / 12 family, feedstock chains, aramid.

Polyethylene furanoate (PEF)

Aliases. PEF; bio-PET-substitute; furanic polyester; PET alternative.

Definition. A 100% bio-based aromatic polyester produced by step-growth polymerisation of 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) with ethylene glycol. FDCA is produced from 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (5-HMF), which is derived from sugar (fructose, glucose) by acid-catalysed dehydration. PEF has higher gas-barrier performance than PET (~2× better for O₂; ~6–10× better for CO₂), comparable mechanical strength and Tg (88 vs 75 °C for PET), and full bio-content. PEF is positioned as a bottle-resin substitute for PET, especially for carbonated beverages where CO₂ retention is critical. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section, citing Avantium/YXY; Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 3)

Attributes — properties and uses.

Property PEF vs PET
Bio-content 100% (PEF) vs 30% (Bio-PET PlantBottle) vs 0% (fossil PET)
Tg 88 °C (PEF) vs 75 °C (PET)
O₂ barrier improvement 2× better (PEF)
CO₂ barrier improvement 6–10× better (PEF)
H₂O barrier improvement 2–3× better (PEF)
Tm 215 °C (vs 250–265 °C for PET)
Global production capacity (~2024) <50 kt/yr (Avantium Delfzijl plant under construction)
Compostability no (PEF is a stable polyester, like PET)
Mechanical recyclability yes (compatible with PET-recycle stream concerns under study)

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Notes — significance. PEF is the only fully bio-based aromatic polyester at commercial scale. Avantium (Netherlands, with Carlsberg, Coca-Cola HBC, Danone partners) is building the first commercial-scale FDCA / PEF plant in Delfzijl. Successful scaling could displace a meaningful fraction of the PET-bottle market with bio-PEF over the next decade. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 3)

Related terms. PET (polyethylene terephthalate); ethylene glycol (EO/MEG); biorefinery; lignocellulose; modern bioenergy; chemical recycling; near-zero emissions materials; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Polyurethane (PU / PUR)

Aliases. PU; PUR; polyurethane foam; rigid PU; flexible PU.

Definition. A thermoset polymer family produced by step-growth polyaddition of a polyol (HO-R-OH or polyether/polyester polyol) with a polyisocyanate (commonly toluene diisocyanate TDI, or methylenediphenyl diisocyanate MDI). Reaction of the isocyanate group (-N=C=O) with the hydroxyl group (-OH) forms the urethane linkage (-NH-CO-O-). PU products span a wide range of rigid and flexible foams, elastomers, coatings, adhesives, and sealants — making PU one of the most versatile polymer families. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.5.1)

Attributes — categories and uses.

Variant Density Use
Flexible foam 20–80 kg/m³ mattresses, upholstery, automotive seats, foam padding
Rigid foam 30–100 kg/m³ building insulation (refrigerators, walls, roofing)
Elastomers (TPU) 1.1–1.3 g/cm³ shoe soles, automotive parts, cable jacketing
Coatings & varnishes — wood finishes, automotive coatings, marine paints
Adhesives & sealants — construction, footwear, automotive
Global PU production ~25 Mt/yr —
Largest end-use flexible foam (~30%) + rigid foam (~30%) — combined two-thirds is foams

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.5.1)

Notes — toluene diisocyanate (TDI) vs MDI. TDI dominates flexible-foam applications; MDI dominates rigid-foam applications. Both isocyanates are reactive lung sensitisers, with strict workplace exposure limits. The polyol component is either polyether (from EO/PO + initiator, used for flexible foam) or polyester (from glycol + dicarboxylic acid, used for elastomers and rigid foam). (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.5.1)

Notes — defossilisation and bio-PU. Bio-polyols from castor oil, soybean oil, recycled PET, or plant sugars are commercially available (Cargill, Covestro, BASF) and substitute up to 30% of the polyol in commercial formulations. Fully bio-PU (bio-polyol + bio-isocyanate) is pre-commercial; CO₂-based polyols (Covestro cardyon, polyol with up to 20% incorporated CO₂) are commercial. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.5.1)

Related terms. Step-growth polymerisation; toluene diisocyanate (TDI); MDI; ethylene oxide / propylene oxide; thermoset; insulation; high-value chemicals (HVCs); plastic chemicals.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, foam/elastomer/coating variants, TDI vs MDI, bio-PU.

Power-to-Plastic

Aliases. Power-to-Polymer; CCU-to-plastic.

Definition. A pathway that produces plastic monomers from atmospheric or captured CO₂ enriched with electrolytic hydrogen, via methanol synthesis (CO₂ + 3 H₂ → CH₃OH + H₂O) followed by Methanol-to-Olefins (MTO) — yielding ethylene and propylene as plastic feedstocks. The all-electric, carbon-capture-based plastic-production route within the broader Power-to-X family, complementary to direct e-fuel pathways. (Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 30–31)

Notes — example deployments. - Iceland: 5 ML/y e-methanol production from power-plant CO₂ (commercial, TRL 7). - China: MTO already used at commercial scale (mostly with coal-derived methanol). - Germany / EU: pilot-scale demonstrations under the broader Power-to-Liquid family.

Notes — energy and material implications. Producing 15 Mt/y of plastic (≈25% of current EU production) via Power-to-Plastic would require ~516 TWh/y of renewable electricity (≈20% of EU 2030 renewable electricity production), 56 Mt of CO₂ feedstock, and 7.5 Mt of H₂ (vs the EU 2030 target of 10 Mt H₂). The emerging direct-DME and oxidative coupling of methane (OCM) variants are at lab scale and unlikely to reach commercial deployment before 2050. (Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 30–32, Fig. 30)

Related terms. Methanol synthesis; Methanol-to-Olefins (MTO); e-fuels; Power-to-X (PtX); direct air capture (DAC); carbon capture and storage (CCS).

Source history. - Grimaud and Girard 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, deployment status, energy/material requirements (translated from French).

Porous rock hydrogen storage

Definition. Storage of hydrogen in porous rock formations overlain by an impermeable caprock (typically mudstone or evaporite), creating subsurface conditions suited to trap and contain gas alongside the formation brine. The two principal sub-types are saline aquifers and depleted gas fields. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 79)

Extended definition. Porous-rock formations have been proven to securely contain gases over millennia and are considered candidates for inter-seasonal, TWh-scale hydrogen storage. Important experience comes from town-gas storage in saline aquifers (1950s–1970s) in France (Beynes), the Czech Republic (Lobodice) and Germany (Engelborstel, Bad Lauchstaedt). During decades of commercial operation no containment failures have been reported, though some changes in stored-gas composition occurred from bio- and geochemical reactions. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 79, citing Buzek et al. 1994; Kruck and Crotogino 2013; Panfilov 2016)

Attributes. Storage power and discharge time.

Storage type Storage power Discharge duration
Porous rocks (depleted gas fields and deep saline aquifers) ~100 MW – 10 GW week to season

(Miocic et al. 2023, Fig. 2, p. 75)

Notes. Cyclic injection and withdrawal of hydrogen alters pressure and temperature around the well and within the reservoir, changing the stress equilibrium. Geomechanical failure modes include induced caprock/overburden failure, fault reactivation, and well-sealing failure. Risks specific to porous-media storage include load-bearing dissolution–precipitation reactions, swelling/drying of clays, hydrogen–brine wettability change, and gravity overriding and viscous fingering due to low H₂ density and viscosity. Capillary entry pressure of cap and fault rocks must remain above storage pressure to preserve integrity. (Miocic et al. 2023, pp. 79–81, citing Heinemann et al. 2021a, 2021b; Pijnenburg et al. 2019; Peng et al. 2020; Wentinck and Busch 2017; Vavra et al. 1992; Miocic et al. 2019; Paterson 1983; Feldmann et al. 2016)

Related terms. Saline aquifer; depleted gas field; caprock; cushion gas; salt cavern; storage complex.

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, attributes, and risk profile.

Post-combustion capture

Definition. A CCS variant in which CO₂ is removed from the flue gas of a combustion plant after combustion. In Natural Gas Combined Cycle plants, CO₂ is chemically absorbed by a monoethanolamine solution; in steam methane reforming plants, the CO₂ is chemically absorbed after the shift reaction by a methyl diethanolamine solution. (Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8810)

Related terms. Carbon capture and storage; pre-combustion capture; oxyfuel; Natural Gas Combined Cycle; steam methane reforming.

Source history. - Baufumé et al. 2011 — added 2026-05-07: definition and chemistry.

Pre-calcination

Definition. The cement-production stage between preheating (200–750 °C) and the rotary kiln, conducted at 750–1000 °C, in which limestone is partially decarbonated. Pre-calcination and the rotary kiln are the two most energy-intensive and highest-emission stages of clinker production. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 9)

Related terms. Clinker; rotary kiln; process emissions.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition and energy-intensity role.

Pre-combustion capture

Definition. A CCS variant in which CO₂ is removed from a hydrogen-rich syngas stream before combustion. In an Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle, the gasifier produces syngas that undergoes a shift reaction; CO₂ is then absorbed by a commercial physical solvent (Rectisol, Selexol). (Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8810)

Related terms. Carbon capture and storage; post-combustion capture; oxyfuel; Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle; coal gasification.

Source history. - Baufumé et al. 2011 — added 2026-05-07: definition and chemistry.

Primary steel and secondary steel

Definition. - Primary steel. Steel produced from iron ore via reduction (BF-BOF route, DRI-EAF, etc.) — accounts for 76% of global production. - Secondary steel. Steel produced by recycling scrap metal in electric arc furnaces — accounts for 24% of global production. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Notes. Decarbonising secondary steel reduces to decarbonising the electricity that powers EAFs. Primary steel decarbonisation requires changes to the iron-reduction step (e.g. methane, hydrogen, or direct electrolysis). Increasing the share of secondary steel in production is itself a major decarbonisation lever. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 8)

Related terms. BF-BOF route; DRI-EAF pathway; direct reduction; electric arc furnace; hydrogen direct reduction.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definitions and emissions implications.

Process emissions

Definition. CO₂ emissions originating from chemical reactions in industrial process streams (e.g. limestone calcination in cement, soda-ash and limestone heating in glass), as distinct from emissions from fuel combustion. In Europe, process emissions per unit of output have remained largely stable across sectors over the last decade. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, pp. 4, 9, 11)

Notes — sectoral magnitudes (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, pp. 9, 11). - Cement: process emissions from limestone decomposition represent ~⅔ of cement’s direct emissions. - Glass: process emissions account for 13–43% of total emissions, depending on recycling rate and glass type. - Ceramics: process-related emissions account for ~16% of total ceramics emissions; fuel combustion accounts for ~78%.

Related terms. Clinker; pre-calcination; rotary kiln; cullet; carbon capture and storage; Hall-Héroult electrolysis process.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition and sectoral magnitudes.

RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 scenarios (M0 / M1 / M23 / N1 / N2 / N03)

Definition. A set of six contrasted long-run electricity-mix scenarios for France to 2050–2060, published by Réseau de Transport d’Électricité (RTE) in February 2022 after a two-year public consultation. The six headline scenarios articulate around two scenario families based on whether new nuclear reactors are commissioned (“M” = no new nuclear; “N” = new EPR2 build-out), each subdivided by the speed and form of renewable deployment. All six are paired with a reference electricity-demand trajectory (~645 TWh ± 100 TWh in 2050) and three demand variants: reference, sufficiency (sobriété) and deep reindustrialisation. (RTE 2022, Sections 5.2 and 3.1, translated from French)

(RTE 2022, Section 5.2 figures and infographics; M23 specific renewables values not extracted but noted as “high renewable” with concentration in large parks.)

Notes — distinguishing logic. - M0 — exit from existing nuclear by 2050; ~10 → 200+ GW solar PV, ~75 GW onshore wind, ~62 GW offshore wind. Most ambitious renewable build-out and flexibility envelope; conditioned on rapid scale-up of decarbonised thermal. - M1 — diffuse renewable rollout (small/large rooftop PV, citizen / local-actor projects), nuclear exit smoothed to 2060 (excluding Flamanville EPR), 16 GW remaining. - M23 — renewable rollout via large parks to capture scale economies; 100% renewable by 2060. - N1 — programme of 8 new EPR2 by 2050 (~1 pair every 5 years from 2035 commissioning) plus M23-like renewable build; 26% nuclear / 74% renewable in 2050. - N2 — accelerated EPR2 programme beyond first six pairs; 36% nuclear / 64% renewable in 2050. - N03 — all four levers maximised (existing-fleet life extension, beyond-60-year extensions, max EPR2 rate, SMRs); ~50 GW nuclear by 2050 (~50% generation share). Industrial-constraint-driven, not political-choice-driven.

(RTE 2022, Sections 5.2.1–5.2.2)

Notes — three demand variants. All six mix scenarios are run on three demand trajectories: reference (645 TWh ± 100 TWh in 2050, driven by sectoral electrification), sufficiency (sobriété; ~−40 TWh vs reference) and deep reindustrialisation (+~50 TWh vs reference). Sufficiency reduces flexibility-capacity needs by ~20%; deep reindustrialisation requires more renewable build-out and additional thermal capacity. (RTE 2022, Sections 3.4–3.5, 7.11–7.12)

Related terms. Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); Power system flexibility; Sufficiency (sobriété); Deep reindustrialisation; Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE); Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC); EPR2 programme; nuclear power (incl. small modular reactors).

Propane dehydrogenation (PDH)

Aliases. PDH; on-purpose propylene; UOP Oleflex; Lummus Catofin; Lummus CB&I PDH.

Definition. A catalytic on-purpose propylene production process in which propane is dehydrogenated to propylene + hydrogen (CH₃-CH₂-CH₃ → CH₂=CH-CH₃ + H₂) over a Pt-Sn (UOP Oleflex) or Cr₂O₃ (Lummus Catofin) catalyst at 540–680 °C and sub-atmospheric to moderate pressure. PDH is one of three on-purpose propylene routes (alongside MTP and metathesis) that have grown rapidly since 2010, fed by abundant low-cost shale-gas-derived propane. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3 olefin chemistry; Zhang et al. 2024, p. 109)

Attributes — commercial PDH technologies.

Technology Catalyst Temperature Cycle Conversion Selectivity
UOP Oleflex Pt-Sn / Al₂O₃ 600–680 °C continuous moving-bed (CCR) 35–45% 88–92%
Lummus Catofin Cr₂O₃ / Al₂O₃ 540–620 °C cyclic fixed-bed 50–55% 86–90%
STAR (Krupp Uhde) Pt-Sn / ZnAl₂O₄ 580 °C continuous tubular 30–40% ~93%
FBD (Snamprogetti / Yarsintez) Cr₂O₃ ~590 °C fluidised ~40% ~90%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3)

Attributes — global PDH deployment.

Indicator Value
Global PDH capacity (~2024) >15 Mt/yr propylene
China PDH capacity share >70% (largest deployment region)
First commercial unit Saudi Arabia (Petro-Rabigh, 2010s)
Hydrogen co-product ~3 wt% of feed; valuable refinery H₂ supply
Energy intensity ~10 GJ / t propylene (endothermic, requires furnace heat)
Coke deposition (Catofin cyclic) requires regeneration every ~10–30 min

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3; Zhang et al. 2024)

Notes — significance. PDH is now a major non-cracker propylene source, accounting for ~15–20% of global propylene by tonnage as of 2024 (rising). Its growth is enabled by the low cost of shale-gas-derived propane in the US Gulf Coast and the Middle East. The endothermic dehydrogenation requires substantial process heat — defossilising PDH means electrifying the furnace duty (electric heaters at >600 °C are technically demanding) or replacing fossil-fuel furnaces with green-H₂ combustion. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.3)

Related terms. Propylene; propane; methanol-to-propylene (MTP); olefin metathesis (OCT); high-value chemicals (HVCs); steam cracking (vapocracking); catalytic cracking (FCC); on-purpose technologies; refinery-petrochemical integration.
