PyPSA (modelling framework)

Aliases. PyPSA; Python for Power System Analysis; PyPSA-Eur; PyPSA-Earth.

Definition. A fully open-source bottom-up Energy System Optimisation Model framework developed at TU Berlin and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), first released in 2018 (Brown et al. 2018) and now maintained by a wider research community. PyPSA is implemented in Python (using pyomo / linopy) with linear programming and is distinguished by its sector-coupled modelling capability, very high temporal resolution (hourly across full year is standard), and open data availability via the PyPSA-Eur (Europe) and PyPSA-Earth (global) reference datasets. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8; Brown et al. 2018, Zeyen et al. 2023 cited)

Attributes — PyPSA design features.

Indicator Value
Solver paradigm LP (default); MILP (with extensions)
Programming language Python (open-source)
Foresight perfect (default); myopic / limited via extensions
Temporal resolution hourly across full year (8760 h) standard
Spatial resolution very high (Europe: 100s of nodes; world: 1000s)
Sector coupling electricity + heat + transport + hydrogen + e-fuels integrated
End-effect mitigation annuity factors
Open-source status fully open (Apache 2.0 licence)
Open data PyPSA-Eur and PyPSA-Earth provide fully open, reproducible datasets
Major users TU Berlin / KIT / Aarhus / TU Delft / Frankfurt Inst. Adv. Studies

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8; Brown et al. 2018, Zeyen et al. 2023)

Notes — significance. PyPSA is the most rapidly-growing ESOM framework, distinguished by its hourly temporal resolution (much finer than the typical-day 8–48 timeslices of TIMES / OSeMOSYS) and full transparency / reproducibility (open code + open data). It is increasingly the framework of choice for academic 100% RE / sector-coupled studies in Europe. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); TIMES; OSeMOSYS; MESSAGE; TEMOA; sector coupling; annuity factor (modelling); foresight (perfect / limited / myopic).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, design features, significance, open-data orientation.

PMV / PPD (Fanger thermal-comfort model)

Aliases. Predicted Mean Vote (PMV); Predicted Percentage of Dissatisfied (PPD); Fanger model; ISO 7730 model.

Definition. A pair of related thermal-comfort indices proposed by P.O. Fanger (1970) and standardised in ISO 7730 (and ASHRAE 55, alongside SET). The PMV predicts the mean thermal sensation vote of a large group of occupants on a 7-point scale: −3 (cold), −2 (cool), −1 (slightly cool), 0 (neutral), +1 (slightly warm), +2 (warm), +3 (hot). The PPD translates the PMV into the percentage of occupants likely to be dissatisfied with the thermal environment: PPD ≈ 100 − 95·exp(−0.03353·PMV⁴ − 0.2179·PMV²). The PMV/PPD model takes six inputs: air temperature, mean radiant temperature, relative humidity, air velocity, occupant clothing insulation (clo), occupant metabolic rate (met). (Goessel 2025, pp. 27–31, citing ISO 7730 and Fanger 1970)

Attributes — PMV / PPD relationship.

PMV Thermal sensation PPD (%)
0 neutral 5% (minimum dissatisfied)
±0.5 slightly cool / warm 10%
±1.0 cool / warm 26%
±1.5 (intermediate) 50%
±2.0 cold / hot 76%
±3.0 very cold / very hot 100%
ASHRAE 55 acceptable comfort zone −0.5 ≤ PMV ≤ +0.5 PPD < 10%

(Goessel 2025, p. 27 and Fig. 2.4; ISO 7730)

Notes — limitations. PMV/PPD is built on steady-state heat-balance physiology and assumes a static occupant in a moderate thermal environment (PMV between −2 and +2). At thermal extremes or with rapidly-varying conditions, the model loses validity; adaptive thermal comfort (de Dear-Brager) is preferred for naturally-ventilated buildings, and SET is preferred for heat-stress conditions. PMV also underestimates female thermal discomfort (originally calibrated on male office workers). (Goessel 2025, pp. 27–28; Vellei 2017 cited)

Notes — usage in building design. PMV/PPD remains the dominant thermal-comfort metric in EU building-services design (ISO 7730 categories I/II/III for HVAC system sizing). Most commercial dynamic-thermal-simulation software (EnergyPlus, IDA-ICE, COMETh) computes PMV/PPD at hourly time-step output. Its limitation in extreme-heat scenarios is the principal motivation for Goessel’s switch to SET-DH for renovation-impact assessment. (Goessel 2025, p. 27)

Related terms. Standard Effective Temperature (SET); Thermal comfort (umbrella); adaptive thermal comfort; ISO 7730; ASHRAE 55; building renovation (umbrella); building energy simulation (BES / SED).

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: PMV/PPD definition, sensation scale, ISO 7730 limits, vs SET adaptation.

Pumped hydro energy storage (PHES)

Definition. A bulk electricity-storage technology in which surplus electricity (e.g. from wind or solar) is used to pump water from a lower reservoir (sea, river, artificial pool) to a higher reservoir; during periods of high demand, the stored water is released back through a turbine to generate electricity. PHES is one of the most traditional and mature storage solutions and offers reliable peak-demand balancing. (Khalili et al. 2026, p. 7)

Notes — coverage and outlook. PHES is the third most common storage technology in the 100% RE systems database, present in 29.8% of articles (after batteries 60.2% and e-hydrogen 45.5%). Khalili et al. argue that PHES could be an overlooked option because its potential has not been fully incorporated in 100% RE systems analyses, despite its maturity, low operating cost and relatively low environmental footprint. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 16)

Related terms. Compressed air energy storage (CAES); thermal energy storage (TES); battery; vehicle-to-grid (V2G); hydrogen storage.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — listed in Pending 2026-05-07 (PHS abbreviation). - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, share in 100% RE database, “overlooked option” framing; promoted from Pending.

Pyrolysis gasoline (pygas)

Aliases. Pygas; pyrolysis naphtha; py-gas; raw pygas.

Definition. A liquid co-product of naphtha (and heavier-feed) steam cracking, comprising C5–C10 hydrocarbons rich in aromatics (BTX) and olefins/diolefins. After hydrotreatment to saturate diolefins (first-stage HDS) and to remove sulfur (second-stage), pygas is fractionated to recover BTX aromatics and a remaining gasoline-blending stock. Pygas is the dominant non-reformer source of aromatic hydrocarbons globally. (Speight 2019, Chapters 6.5–6.6; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Attributes — typical composition and yield.

Property Value
Yield from naphtha steam cracker 18–22 wt% of feed
Aromatic content (raw) 50–70%
Diolefin content (raw) 15–25% (requires hydrogenation)
Sulfur content 100–500 ppm
Octane (RON) ~95 (after hydrogenation)
Principal aromatic recovery benzene, toluene, mixed xylenes
Global pygas production ~80–100 Mt/yr
Global pygas-derived BTX ~50–60 Mt/yr

(Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Notes — extraction and reformer-pygas balance. Liquid-liquid extraction (sulfolane process) or extractive distillation recovers BTX from hydrotreated pygas. Globally, ~57% of BTX comes from pygas (heavy-feed crackers) and ~40% from catalytic reformers; on-purpose MTA contributes ~3%. Light-feed (ethane) crackers produce essentially no pygas. (Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727)

Related terms. Steam cracking (vapocracking); BTX aromatics; naphtha; catalytic reforming; hydrocracking; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, composition, hydrotreatment chain. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: pygas vs reformer share of global BTX.

p-Xylene and Terephthalic acid (TPA / PTA)

Aliases. p-Xylene (PX); para-xylene; terephthalic acid (TPA); purified terephthalic acid (PTA); dimethyl terephthalate (DMT).

Definition. p-Xylene (C₈H₁₀) is one of three xylene isomers (ortho-, meta-, para-) recovered from catalytic-reformer reformate or steam-cracker pyrolysis gasoline by selective crystallisation (sub-zero) or sorption (UOP Parex / Mobil MX-Sorbex). Terephthalic acid (HOOC-C₆H₄-COOH, TPA) is produced by the catalytic liquid-phase oxidation of p-xylene with air over a Co/Mn/Br catalyst (Amoco/MC process) at 175–230 °C and 15–30 bar in acetic acid solvent, then purified by hydrogenation (PTA). TPA + ethylene glycol → polyethylene terephthalate (PET). (Speight 2019, Chapter 8.2; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global p-xylene production ~50 Mt/yr
Global TPA production ~80 Mt/yr (TPA includes PTA)
p-xylene from reformate ~70%
p-xylene from pygas ~15%
p-xylene from toluene disproportionation (TDP) ~10%
p-xylene from m-/o-xylene isomerisation ~5%
Selectivity for PX in mixed-xylene ~24% (equilibrium); pushed to >99% by adsorption
TPA / PTA end-use ~70% PET fibre (polyester clothing); ~25% PET bottle resin; ~5% other

(Speight 2019, Chapter 8.2; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Notes — bio-PET routes. Bio-PET combines bio-ethylene-glycol (from sugar fermentation) with conventional fossil-TPA (Coca-Cola PlantBottle: 30% bio-content). Fully bio-PET requires bio-PX from bio-isobutanol or bio-furanics — pre-commercial. Polyethylene furanoate (PEF) is a fully bio-based PET-substitute polymer with similar mechanical properties (Avantium); pre-commercial. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 3)

Related terms. BTX aromatics; xylene; benzene; toluene; PET (polyethylene terephthalate); ethylene oxide / ethylene glycol (EO / MEG); catalytic reforming; pyrolysis gasoline (pygas).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, p-xylene recovery routes, TPA Amoco/MC oxidation chemistry. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: ~50 Mt/yr p-xylene, ~80 Mt/yr TPA, end-use breakdown.

Pathways (vs scenarios)

Aliases. Energy-system pathway; transition pathway; mitigation pathway; capacity-expansion trajectory; multi-stage scenario.

Definition. A pathway is a trajectory describing the year-by-year (or decade-by-decade) evolution of an energy / climate / techno-economic system over a multi-decadal horizon — typically 2020 → 2050 or 2020 → 2100 — including the sequence of investment decisions, retirements, and operational shifts. The term is often used interchangeably with scenario, but Manuel et al. 2025 distinguish: a scenario may describe only the end-state of the system (e.g., 100% renewables in 2050) without specifying the route; a pathway explicitly traces the multi-period evolution. Pathways can be qualitative (narrative-driven) or quantitative (model-driven, typically by ESOM or IAM). (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 1–2; cross-ref Energy System Optimisation Model entry)

Attributes — pathway taxonomy.

Type Description Example
Normative pathway reverse-engineered from a desired end-state “1.5 °C by 2100” pathways
Exploratory pathway forward simulation of plausible developments IEA WEO STEPS / CPS
Backcasting start from end-state, identify required steps NetZero scenario design
Forecasting start from current state, project trends business-as-usual analyses
Snapshot scenario describes only end-state, no trajectory not a pathway under Manuel definition

(Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 1–2 and Fig. 2)

Notes — pathway vs scenario in IPCC context. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) uses the SSP×RCP framework (Shared Socioeconomic Pathway × Representative Concentration Pathway): SSPs describe the socio-economic narrative, RCPs describe the radiative-forcing trajectory. Each SSP×RCP combination, when run through an IAM, generates a specific pathway. The IEA’s World Energy Outlook and Energy Technology Perspectives publish three reference pathways annually: STEPS (Stated Policies), APS (Announced Pledges), NZE (Net Zero by 2050). (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 1)

Notes — quality criteria. Manuel et al. 2025 emphasise that high-quality pathway studies should disclose: (i) the foresight regime used (perfect / limited / myopic); (ii) the decision horizon and any horizon extension beyond the target year; (iii) the milestone-interpolation method; (iv) the discount rate and whether salvage values / annuity factors are used; (v) the use (or absence) of endogenous learning and early retirement; (vi) the temporal and spatial resolution. Currently, only a minority of published pathway studies disclose all of these. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 8–11)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); Integrated Assessment Model (IAM); foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); end effects (modelling); investment milestones; Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE); Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS); Current Policies Scenario (CPS); RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 scenarios.

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, pathway taxonomy, vs scenario distinction, quality criteria.

Pyrolysis (PL)

Definition. A thermochemical process that converts dry biomass into bio-oil, gases and biochar in the absence of oxygen. Fast pyrolysis operates at relatively high temperatures (450–550 °C; 723–823 K) and ambient pressure with short gas-phase residence times (<2 s); biomass feedstock must be finely ground (<5 mm) and dried to <10% moisture content. Slower-temperature pyrolysis instead favours biochar. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 9)

Notes. Pyrolysis is the upstream step of the HDCJ-PL aviation biofuel pathway. Pyrolysis bio-oil has higher acidity, weaker thermal stability and higher oxygen content than HTL bio-oil and so requires more extensive upgrading (catalytic cracking, steam reforming, hydrotreating) before fractionation into naphtha, kerosene and diesel. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 9)

Related terms. Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL); HDCJ pathway; integrated hydropyrolysis and hydroconversion (IH2); methane pyrolysis.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, fast-pyrolysis operating conditions, comparison with HTL.

ReFuelEU Aviation

Definition. A proposed EU Regulation (released July 2021 as part of the Fit for 55 package) intended to boost the supply and demand for sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) at EU airports through a binding obligation on fuel suppliers and obligations on EU airports to provide hydrogen-refuelling and electric-recharging infrastructure. ReFuelEU defines SAF as RED-compliant biofuels (advanced biofuels listed in RED II Annex IX Parts A and B) plus electrofuels (synthetic fuels). (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 25, 26)

Attributes — minimum SAF share required at EU airports (proposal version).

Year Minimum SAF share Of which electrofuels (e-fuels)
2023 2 vol% —
2030 (intermediate) 0.7 vol% of overall SAF
2050 63 vol% (Parliament endorsement: 85 vol%) 28 vol% of overall SAF

(Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 26)

Notes. Until 2035, fuel suppliers may meet the SAF target via a SAF certificate trading mechanism. To mitigate “tankering” (the use, prior to entering the EU, of more fuel than required for the flight in order to reduce SAF consumption and save on fuel costs), ReFuelEU proposes that airlines tank at least the whole required amount for their subsequent flight. A Sustainable Aviation Fund has been proposed to support cleaner aviation deployment. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 26)

Related terms. Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); CORSIA; renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO); EU Renewable Energy Directive.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, mandated minimum SAF shares, anti-tankering provision.

Renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO)

Definition. A sub-category of renewable fuels introduced in the European Commission’s July 2021 amendment to the EU Renewable Energy Directive II (RED II), encompassing electrofuels, renewable hydrogen and renewable electricity. The amendment proposes a minimum share of 2.6% RFNBO in the overall transport sector by 2030, alongside the existing minimum-share requirement for advanced biofuels. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 25)

Related terms. Electrofuels; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); ReFuelEU Aviation; EU Renewable Energy Directive.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition and 2.6% target.

Regulated asset base (RAB) model

Definition. A revenue-support framework in which a private operator builds and operates a piece of long-lived infrastructure (here, CO₂ transport-and-storage networks) in exchange for a regulated tariff structured to recover capital and operating costs plus a reasonable rate of return on the regulated asset base. The tariff is set transparently and emitters that use the infrastructure must pay it, providing the operator with revenue certainty and the user with predictable access charges. (IEA 2026, pp. 26, 43, 47)

Notes — UK Track-1 application. The United Kingdom is applying the RAB approach to develop regional CO₂ transport-and-storage networks. Government commitments include a mix of direct capital expenditures and funds to support long-term CCfD-style contracts, regulated transport-and-storage tariffs, and risk guarantees, totalling ~USD 28 billion across the first two CCUS hubs. RAB is identified as a key innovation that translates risk-allocation frameworks into bankable infrastructure financing structures. (IEA 2026, pp. 26, 28, 43, 47)

Related terms. Carbon contract for difference (CCfD); take-or-pay/store-or-pay contract; cross-chain risk; bankability; non-recourse project finance; hub and cluster model.

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition and UK Track-1 application.

Residual load (consommation résiduelle)

Aliases. Consommation résiduelle (FR); residual demand; net load; net demand.

Definition. Total electricity demand at a given instant minus the simultaneous output of “fatal” non-dispatchable production — primarily wind, solar PV, run-of-river hydro and other must-take RES. Residual load is the demand that dispatchable sources (nuclear, thermal, hydro reservoir, storage discharge, imports) must cover at each instant. As VRE penetration rises, residual load decouples from total load — peak residual load shifts in time and can become the binding sizing constraint of the dispatchable fleet. (RTE 2022, Section 3.8.5, p. 143, translated from French)

Attributes — RTE 2050 residual-load metrics (France).

Indicator Today (2020) 2050 (RTE scenarios)
Total demand peak (1-in-10 year cold) ~95 GW up to ~120 GW (and beyond in some hours)
Probability of demand >100 GW 0.02% (rare) ~2.4% of hours
Residual peak load (1-in-10 year) ~85 GW 82–88 GW (across scenarios)
Daily VRE-driven residual swings small large; can drive residual to <0 (export/curtailment)
Demand-flex contribution to residual peak ~3 GW today 16–18 GW by 2050

(RTE 2022, Sections 3.8.5–3.8.6, Figures 3.43–3.45, pp. 143–144)

Notes — sizing implication. Historically, system capacity adequacy was sized against the one-in-ten-year total-load peak; with high VRE the relevant indicator becomes the residual peak. RTE notes a paradox: total demand can reach extreme highs (e.g. 120 GW with widespread heat-pump uptake) while residual demand stays modest (82–88 GW) because solar and wind cover much of the non-peak. The sizing constraint thus shifts from raw demand to residual demand, with significant implications for the size of the thermal / nuclear / storage fleet. (RTE 2022, Section 3.8.5, Figure 3.45, p. 144)

Notes — sub-zero residual load. During strong-wind / strong-PV days, residual load can be negative (i.e. fatal production exceeds demand), forcing exports, storage charging, electrolysis dispatch or curtailment. RTE Figure 3.44 shows residual load reaching near-zero or negative values during 100+ GW total-demand peaks, depending on simultaneous wind/PV. These events are the principal driver of curtailment and of seasonal/long-duration storage need. (RTE 2022, Section 3.8.5, Figure 3.44)

Related terms. Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); Curtailment; Power system flexibility; Capacity adequacy; Mismatch energy; Combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT); Open cycle gas turbine (OCGT); RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 scenarios.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, French 2050 metrics, sizing implication, sub-zero residual load (translated from French).

Redox oxy-cracking (ROC) / chemical looping cracking

Aliases. ROC; chemical looping oxidative cracking; CL-ODH; oxygen-carrier-mediated cracking.

Definition. A two-step intensified process for naphtha or ethane cracking that replaces the conventional fired-furnace + steam-dilution scheme with a chemical-looping arrangement. In step 1 (the reducer / cracker), naphtha is cracked at ~775 °C in contact with a circulating mixed-oxide redox catalyst (e.g., alkali-doped CaO–Mn₃O₄), which selectively combusts the H₂ produced by cracking using its own lattice oxygen and supplies the endothermic cracking heat from its sensible heat. In step 2 (the regenerator), the reduced oxide is re-oxidised in air at ~935 °C, releasing heat and being recharged with O₂. The two reactor sections are connected by a circulating-solid loop. ROC eliminates the parasitic steam dilution, the need for an air-separation unit, and the safety hazards of mixed-O₂/hydrocarbon operation. (Haribal et al. 2018, pp. 714–717)

Attributes — Haribal 2018 ROC vs conventional steam-cracking reference case.

Indicator Steam cracking ROC
Reactor type fired furnace + steam dilution reducer-regenerator with circulating Mn-oxide
Cracking T 750–900 °C (radiant zone up to 1100 °C) 775 °C (reducer)
Steam dilution 0.5 kg steam / kg feed none
Energy intensity 20–40 GJ/t ethylene (32.5 GJ/t reference) 67% lower in upstream section
Ethylene yield (kg / kg naphtha) reference +28% (incl. propylene)
Compression work reference −25%
Total energy + CO₂ savings vs SC reference −52%
Direct CO₂ emissions 1.8–2.0 kg CO₂ / kg ethylene substantially reduced (need for amine CO₂ capture)
Redox catalyst n/a Ca-Mn-K mixed oxide; Mn₃O₄ ↔︎ MnO redox couple
Safety flammable mixtures avoided by design gas-phase O₂ absent in cracker
TRL 9 (commercial) 4–5 (lab-to-pilot)

(Haribal et al. 2018, pp. 715–719 and Tables 2, 5)

Notes — chemical looping fundamentals. ROC is a member of the broader chemical looping family — chemical looping combustion (CLC), chemical looping oxidative dehydrogenation (CL-ODH), chemical looping reforming (CLR) — all of which use a circulating metal-oxide oxygen carrier instead of direct gas-phase O₂ contact. The benefits are (i) intrinsic CO₂ separation (CO₂ leaves the reducer pure, ready for capture), (ii) no NOₓ formation in the cracker (no air contact), (iii) no air-separation unit, (iv) tighter T control via solids circulation. The same redox-catalyst design principles inform CL-ODH for ethane, with ~60% C₂–C₄ olefin selectivity at 30% conversion in the lab. (Haribal et al. 2018, pp. 714–715, citing Neal et al. 2014, 2017)

Notes — defossilisation linkage. ROC is one of the candidate routes for reducing the embodied CO₂ footprint of cracker-derived olefins (~2 kg CO₂ / kg ethylene) without requiring full electrification of the cracker furnace. Combined with green-H₂ (or biomethane) for any residual furnace duty, ROC could halve the cracker-CO₂ footprint at modest CAPEX premium. Pilot demonstration is the next milestone. (Haribal et al. 2018, pp. 720–721)

Related terms. Steam cracking (vapocracking); olefins; high-value chemicals (HVCs); naphtha; oxidative dehydrogenation (ODH); methanol-to-olefins (MTO); refinery-petrochemical integration; ethylene; chemical looping (umbrella concept).

Source history. - Haribal et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, two-step process flow, 52% energy / CO₂ reduction, ASPEN process simulation results.

RE2020 / RT2012 (French building regulations)

Aliases. RE2020 (Réglementation Environnementale 2020); RT2012 (Réglementation Thermique 2012); RT (Réglementation Thermique, generic); BBC label.

Definition. Successive French building thermal/environmental regulations setting mandatory energy and (since RE2020) carbon performance standards for new buildings: - RT2012 (2012, mandatory from 2013) — set primary-energy consumption limits (Cep_max ~50 kWh/m²/yr modulated by climate zone) and required envelope-quality performance. Inspired by the BBC (“Bâtiment Basse Consommation”) label. - RE2020 (2020, mandatory from 2022 for residential) — supersedes RT2012; adds embodied-carbon limits (life-cycle GWP100 of construction materials), summer-comfort indicator (DH degré-heure thresholds), and a tighter primary-energy limit. RE2020 is the world’s first national building regulation to formally cap embodied carbon. (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7, 75–88; French Code de la Construction)

Attributes — RE2020 and RT2012 performance thresholds.

Indicator RT2012 RE2020 (residential)
Bbio_max (heating + cooling demand, points) ~60 (modulated) varies by climate zone
Cep_max (primary energy, kWh/m²/yr) ~50 (modulated) ~80 (with bonus for biomass)
Ic_construction (embodied GWP, kg CO₂eq/m²) not regulated <640 (2022) → <415 (2031, post-2024 trajectory)
Ic_énergie (operational GWP, kg CO₂eq/m²/yr) not regulated varies
DH (summer overheating, K·h above 26 °C) not regulated <350 (typical) — exceeding triggers “passoire de chaleur” warning

(Goessel 2025, pp. 80–86; CCH RE2020 specifications)

Notes — climate-zone modulation. Both RT2012 and RE2020 modulate their thresholds by climate zone (H1a, H1b, H1c, H2a, H2b, H2c, H2d, H3) — H1a is coldest (Strasbourg, Lille), H3 is warmest (Mediterranean coast). Goessel’s two case studies use H1a (Vélizy, near Paris — cold winter) and H3 (Nîmes — Mediterranean) to span this spectrum. (Goessel 2025, pp. 80–82, Fig. 3.3)

Notes — for renovation. RE2020 governs new buildings; existing-building renovations are governed by the separate RT existant rules + the DPE / Loi Climat & Résilience prohibition on Class F/G rentals. Renovations exceeding €500 / m² (“rénovation lourde”) trigger element-by-element thermal-performance requirements (e.g., insulation thickness minimum, glazing U-value minimum). Goessel’s renovation case studies aim broadly at the BBC-rénovation level (~80 kWh/m²/yr primary energy). (Goessel 2025, pp. 1–7; Code de la Construction)

Related terms. DPE (Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique); building renovation (umbrella); building envelope; embodied carbon (buildings); operational carbon (buildings); Standard Effective Temperature (SET); INIES / FDES / PEP.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: RE2020 / RT2012 definitions, performance thresholds, climate-zone modulation, renovation context (translated from French).

Reverse water gas shift reaction (rWGS)

Definition. The reverse of the conventional water gas shift reaction: CO₂ + H₂ ↔︎ CO + H₂O. Used in electrofuel production pathways to convert hydrogen and captured CO₂ into syngas. It can be catalysed (typically copper-based catalysts) at 300–800 °C (573–1073 K), or driven jointly with water thermal splitting in a high-temperature solid-oxide co-electrolyser. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 11–12)

Notes. For an FT-electrofuel route producing 1 mole of C₁₂H₂₆, 12 moles of CO₂ are first reacted with 12 moles of H₂ via rWGS, and the resulting CO is then reacted with another 25 moles of H₂ in the FT reactor — yielding ~169 Mt H₂ required to satisfy the projected 2045 aviation demand of 16.73 EJ. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 28)

Related terms. Co-electrolysis; solid oxide electrolysis (SOE); Fischer–Tropsch (FT) process; methanol synthesis; electrofuels.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, operating window, FT-electrofuel stoichiometry.

Reid Vapour Pressure (RVP)

Aliases. RVP; Reid vapour pressure; ASTM D323; volatility metric.

Definition. A standardised measure of the volatility of motor gasoline and other volatile petroleum products, defined as the absolute vapour pressure exerted by the sample at 37.8 °C (100 °F) in a sealed bomb apparatus — measured in psi or kPa. RVP is the principal regulatory metric controlling gasoline evaporative emissions (which contribute to ozone formation), and it determines the seasonal “winter grade” vs “summer grade” formulation in temperate countries: high-RVP winter gasoline (~14 psi / ~95 kPa) for cold-start performance; low-RVP summer gasoline (~7–9 psi / ~50–60 kPa) for evaporative-emissions control. (Addicott 1971; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Attributes — typical RVP regulatory limits.

Region / Season RVP limit
US summer (high-ozone areas) 7.0 psi (48 kPa)
US summer (low-ozone areas) 9.0 psi (62 kPa)
US winter 13–15 psi (90–103 kPa)
EU summer (Class A) 60 kPa max
EU winter (Class A1) 90 kPa max
Brazilian gasoline up to 62 kPa
Aviation gasoline (tighter) 38–49 kPa

(Addicott 1971, p. 65; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Notes — refinery butane balance. RVP is dominantly controlled by the light-end content of gasoline (n-butane, isobutane, isopentane). Refiners adjust RVP by varying butane addition: more butane in winter (raises RVP, improves cold-start), less in summer (reduces evaporative emissions). The ~1 psi of RVP-control flexibility at the gasoline-pool level is one of the principal levers in seasonal-blending operations. (Addicott 1971, p. 65)

Notes — ethanol blending. Ethanol-blended gasoline (E10) has higher RVP than the same gasoline without ethanol despite ethanol’s lower individual RVP — because the ethanol-gasoline binary forms an azeotrope. This “RVP boost” of ~1 psi is regulated under the US RFG (reformulated gasoline) rules. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Related terms. Motor fuels (umbrella); Octane number (RON / MON); knock; ethanol; secondary organic aerosol (SOA); volatile chemical products (VCPs); naphtha.

Source history. - Addicott 1971 — added 2026-05-08: definition, ASTM D323 measurement, seasonal-grading. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): regulatory limits, ethanol-blending RVP boost.

Refinery-petrochemical integration

Aliases. Crude-oil-to-chemicals (COTC); integrated refinery-petchem; chemicals-oriented refinery.

Definition. A refinery configuration in which the product slate is shifted away from transport fuels (gasoline, diesel, jet) and toward petrochemical building blocks (HVCs: ethylene, propylene, BTX) by re-routing intermediate streams (FCC C3, reformer aromatics, naphtha) and by adding petrochemical-oriented unit operations (steam cracker, propane dehydrogenation, methanol-to-X). Integration ranges from “fuel-oriented with chemical co-products” (the historical norm, ~5–20% chemical share) to “chemicals-oriented” (>30% chemical share, the emerging design for new greenfield plants in China and the Middle East). (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, p. 2; Speight 2019, Chapter 6; Zhang et al. 2024, Section 4)

Attributes — Zanon 2024 modelling outputs.

Indicator Value
Today’s refinery utilisation factor ~70%
2030 utilisation factor (1.5C scenario) 30–50%
2050 utilisation factor (1.5C scenario) recovers to ~50–60%
Refining capacity 2010 ~191 EJ/yr (oil input)
Refining capacity 2050 (1.5C) 103 EJ/yr
Refining capacity 2050 (all-restrictions scenario) 132 EJ/yr
Refining capacity 2070 44–77 EJ/yr
Refinery-sourced chemicals reduction by 2050 −49 to −77%
Petrochemical integration of surviving refineries 2050 up to +15% vs current

(Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, pp. 2–3)

Notes — 21st-century driver. Zanon-Zotin’s principal finding: as transport-fuel demand falls (electrification of mobility), refineries do not simply close; they reshape toward higher chemicals integration. The “last greenfield fuel-oriented refineries” are those currently under construction; new builds are chemicals-led. This dynamic prolongs fossil-oil use through 2100 (oil declines only −22 to −42% by 2100 in 1.5C scenarios) because chemicals demand is harder to substitute than fuel demand. (Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024, pp. 2–3)

Notes — chemicals-oriented greenfield examples. Chinese chemicals-oriented megaprojects (Yantai, Zhoushan, Hengli) achieve 35–45% chemicals output share. Middle-East projects (Saudi Aramco/SABIC Yanbu, Reliance Jamnagar) similarly target high integration. ExxonMobil’s Singapore “crude-oil direct cracking” pilot (Zhang 2024) takes integration to its logical extreme: skipping conventional refining and feeding crude directly into a steam cracker, with light-fraction yield of 76% to chemicals at 40–50% chemicals output. (Zhang et al. 2024, pp. 105–106)

Related terms. Catalytic cracking (FCC); catalytic reforming; hydrocracking; naphtha; high-value chemicals (HVCs); non-energy use of fossil fuels; petrochemicals (umbrella); steam cracking (vapocracking); crude-oil direct cracking (COTC).

Source history. - Zanon-Zotin et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, capacity-and-utilisation modelling output, prolonged-oil-use mechanism. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: ExxonMobil COTC pilot, Chinese megaproject integration levels. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): historical refinery-petchem integration framing.

Reynolds number (Re)

Definition. A dimensionless parameter classifying gas-pipeline flow as laminar (Re < 2,000), transitioning (2,000 < Re < 4,000) or turbulent (Re > 4,000). Defined as Re = V_avg · D · ρ_avg / µ, where V_avg is average gas velocity (m/s), D is internal pipe diameter (m), ρ_avg average gas density (kg/m³), and µ gas viscosity (kg/m·s). (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 12–13)

Notes. In practice, most gas pipelines (including hydrogen) operate at flow rates that produce high Reynolds numbers (well above 4,000), placing them firmly in the turbulent flow regime. For Khan et al.’s 1,500 km, 36-inch H₂ transmission pipeline case study, Re ≈ 1.65 × 10⁷. Within this regime the Darcy friction factor is computed from the Colebrook-White equation (which must be solved iteratively). (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 13, 22)

Related terms. General flow equation; Darcy-Weisbach friction factor; Colebrook-White law; erosional velocity; hydrogen pipeline.

Source history. - Khan et al. 2021 — added 2026-05-08: definition, regimes, hydrogen-pipeline values.

Recycling (materials and critical minerals, umbrella)

Definition. The umbrella process of recovering materials from end-of-life products and waste streams for reuse as secondary feedstock, distinct from primary production from virgin ore or fossil resources. ETP-2026 distinguishes recycling of bulk materials (steel, aluminium, paper, copper) from recycling of critical minerals (lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare earth elements) extracted from end-of-life batteries, electronics and clean-energy-technology components. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 143, 6432–6440, 7185–7220)

Attributes — current recycling rates by material.

Material / category Recycling rate Year
Steel, aluminium, copper (bulk) 40–80% globally 2024
Aluminium and paper stable / modest gains 2024
Lithium (from batteries) ~20% (up from 4% in 2015) 2024
Battery minerals (overall) well below bulk-material rates 2024
Recycled lithium/nickel projected share of demand only ~5% by 2035 2035
WEEE collection: Europe / North America 40–50% 2024
WEEE collection: Japan / Korea ~30% 2024
WEEE collection: Asia / Latin America <5% 2024
WEEE collection: Africa ~1% (no improvement since 2010) 2024

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 7185–7220, 6432–6440)

Notes — strategic levers. Improved recycling processes for lithium and nickel could reduce global demand for these minerals by ~25% by 2025; recycled cobalt could offset ~40% of demand. The pace of recycling growth depends on how quickly materials reach end-of-life. Innovation and shifting technology choices (e.g. uptake of LFP batteries, which contain no cobalt and less nickel than NMC/NCA) can also limit recycling potential for specific minerals. ETP-2026 highlights tolling models, traceability, certification and harmonised waste regulations as priority policy actions. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 6432–6440, 7220–7235)

Related terms. Mechanical recycling; chemical recycling; solvolysis; secondary plastics market; critical materials; battery storage (stationary); plastic chemicals.

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: umbrella definition for materials recycling, regional WEEE rates, battery-mineral outlook.

Oil supply shock (demand-side response)

Definition. A sudden, large reduction in global crude-oil supply or refined-product flows that drives prices upward and threatens energy affordability for households and businesses. The principal IEA framework distinguishes (i) supply-side responses (emergency stock releases by IEA member countries — collective releases coordinated by the IEA Governing Board) and (ii) demand-side responses (10 IEA-recommended levers across road transport, aviation, cooking and industry). (IEA Sheltering From Oil Shocks 2026, pp. 3–4)

Attributes — IEA’s 10 recommended demand-side options.

Lever Potential national savings Individual driver savings
Three additional remote workdays/week 2–6% of car oil use ~20%
Lower highway speed limits by ≥10 km/h 1–6% of car oil use 5–10%
Encourage public transport / cycling / walking 1–3% of car oil use —
Alternate-day private-car access 1–5% of car oil use —
Increase car sharing + eco-driving 5–8% of car oil use —
Eco-driving for commercial vehicles + load optimisation 3–5% of road-freight oil use —
Divert LPG from transport preserves LPG for cooking —
Avoid air travel where alternatives exist (≈40% business flight cut) 7–15% of jet-kerosene demand —
Switch from LPG to electric / modern cooking mitigates cooking-fuel shortages —
Industrial-fuel switching where possible mitigates LPG/diesel shortages —

(IEA Sheltering From Oil Shocks 2026, pp. 3–4)

Notes — context. The 2026 report was published in response to the largest supply disruption in global oil-market history caused by the near-halt of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz (~20% of global oil consumption). On 11 March, IEA member countries released 400 million barrels of emergency reserves — the largest stock release in IEA history — alongside the demand-side options above. The Strait-of-Hormuz disruption highlighted the maritime-chokepoint vulnerability also discussed in ETP-2026. (IEA Sheltering From Oil Shocks 2026, pp. 3–4; IEA ETP 2026, p. 378)

Related terms. Maritime chokepoint; total cost of ownership (TCO); battery electric vehicle (BEV); electric cars; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF); modern bioenergy.

Source history. - IEA Sheltering From Oil Shocks 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, 10 demand-side levers, supply-shock context.

Rotomoulding (rotational moulding)

Aliases. Rotational moulding; rotational casting; rotomoulding.

Definition. A plastics processing method in which finely-ground polymer powder (typically LLDPE) is loaded into a heated mould that rotates biaxially (around two perpendicular axes) inside an oven at 250–350 °C. The polymer melts and coats the inside of the mould uniformly under gravity; the mould then cools while still rotating and the part is demoulded. Rotomoulding produces large, hollow, seamless, stress-free parts at low tooling cost — economic for low-volume, large-volume-per-part applications. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Attributes — typical applications.

Indicator Value
Typical polymer LLDPE (>80%), HDPE, PP, PVC plastisol
Output range 1 L (small bottles) to >50,000 L (water tanks, road tankers)
Wall thickness 1.5–10 mm
Cycle time 10–60 min (slow!)
Tooling cost low ($5,000–$50,000) — economic for batch sizes 100–10,000
End-use — water tanks (rural, on-site) ~40%
End-use — kayaks, canoes, surfboards ~10%
End-use — playground equipment ~10%
End-use — road tankers, agricultural sprayers ~15%
End-use — automotive (fuel tanks, instrument panels — niche) ~10%
End-use — toys, leisure (LEGO base plates etc.) ~15%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Related terms. Polyethylene (HDPE / LDPE / LLDPE); blow moulding; injection moulding; plastic processing (umbrella).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, biaxial rotation, large-part applications.

Rotary kiln

Definition. A high-temperature (1200–1450 °C) rotating cylindrical furnace used in cement production for heating preheated and pre-calcined raw materials to produce clinker. (Raillard-Cazanove 2024, p. 9)

Related terms. Clinker; pre-calcination; process emissions.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition and operating temperature.

Saline aquifer

Definition. A porous rock formation saturated with saline formation brine and overlain by an impermeable caprock; one of two principal candidate formation types for porous-rock hydrogen storage (the other being depleted gas fields). (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 79)

Notes. Saline aquifers represent largely unexplored capacity for large-scale seasonal H₂ storage; in the absence of pre-existing infrastructure or production history, they require additional pre-operational characterisation relative to depleted gas fields. Recent assessment indicates that only one offshore depleted gas field on the UK continental shelf has sufficient static capacity to meet UK domestic heating demand, motivating attention to alternative low-carbon options including saline aquifer storage. (Miocic et al. 2023, pp. 81–82, citing Heinemann et al. 2021a; Mouli-Castillo et al. 2021; Scafidi et al. 2021)

Related terms. Porous rock hydrogen storage; depleted gas field; caprock; cushion gas; town gas.

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition and capacity context.

Salvage value (modelling)

Aliases. Residual value; SV; horizon-end credit; SVᵢ,ₘ,ᵣ.

Definition. A correction term in finite-horizon energy-system optimisation models that subtracts the expected residual benefit of investments still operating beyond the model horizon, so that technologies with long lifetimes are not unfairly disadvantaged relative to short-lifetime technologies. The salvage value typically represents the discounted value of the future benefits not captured within the foresight horizon, calculated from the remaining lifetime, the technology’s annuity, and the discount rate. Frameworks using salvage values include TIMES (Loulou et al. 2016) and OSeMOSYS (Howells et al. 2011). (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 4 and eqs. 5–6)

Attributes — typical salvage-value formulation (Howells et al. 2011 / OSeMOSYS-style).

Term Definition
If m + Lifeᵢ − 1 ≤ mₘₐₓ SV = 0 (full lifetime within horizon)
Else SVᵢ,ₘ,ᵣ = ICᵢ,ₘ × ncᵢ,ₘ,ᵣ × [1 − ((1+d)^(mₘₐₓ−m+1) − 1) / ((1+d)^Lifeᵢ − 1)]
ICᵢ,ₘ overnight installation cost of technology i installed in milestone m
ncᵢ,ₘ,ᵣ newly-installed capacity of technology i in milestone m, region r
d discount rate
Lifeᵢ technical lifetime of technology i
mₘₐₓ last milestone year in horizon

(Manuel et al. 2025, eqs. 5–6, citing Howells et al. 2011)

Notes — limits. Salvage values reduce but do not eliminate end-effect distortions; modellers must still extend the horizon beyond the target year to obtain reliable mid-horizon results. Salvage values implicitly assume future system conditions resemble present ones, which can be violated under steep technology cost-decline curves. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 4–5)

Related terms. End effects and decision horizon (modelling); annuity factor (modelling); Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); discount rate; investment milestones.

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, formulation, frameworks using, limits.

Annuity factor (modelling)

Aliases. AFᵢ; capital-recovery factor (modelling-context); annuitised investment cost; payment-stream method.

Definition. A correction-method in energy-system optimisation models that subdivides total CAPEX into annuitised yearly payments over the technology’s lifetime, weighted by a technology-specific WACC, so that only the within-horizon payments are charged to the model. This avoids the truncation distortion of charging full CAPEX while crediting only within-horizon OPEX. Used by frameworks including TEMOA (Hunter et al. 2013) and PyPSA (Zeyen et al. 2023). (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 4 and eqs. 7–9)

Attributes — typical annuity-factor formulation (Hunter et al. 2013 / TEMOA-style).

Term Definition
AFᵢ = WACCᵢ / (1 − (1+WACCᵢ)^(−LifeEoHᵢ,ₘ)) annuity factor for technology i in milestone m
LifeEoHᵢ,ₘ = min(Lifeᵢ, mₘₐₓ−m+1) within-horizon remaining lifetime
CAPEXₘᴬᶠ = Σᵢ,ᵣ (AFᵢ × ICᵢ,ₘ,ᵣ × ncᵢ,ₘ,ᵣ) annuitised CAPEX charged in milestone m
WACCᵢ technology-specific weighted-average cost of capital

(Manuel et al. 2025, eqs. 7–9, citing Hunter et al. 2013)

Notes — vs salvage value. Annuity factors and salvage values are mathematically equivalent for technologies whose lifetime ends within the horizon; they differ in how they handle technologies still operating at horizon end. Annuity factors charge only the within-horizon payments (no future credit); salvage values charge full CAPEX with a future credit. Both methods leave residual end-effect distortions (Krishnan & McCalley 2017). (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 4)

Related terms. Salvage value (modelling); end effects and decision horizon (modelling); Capital Recovery Factor (CRF); Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC); Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, formulation, frameworks using.

Salt cavern

Definition. Cavity solution-mined within suitable, halite-dominated salt formations using fresh water to dissolve the salt rock. The surrounding salt provides low permeability, high sealing capability, inert chemical behaviour with respect to hydrogen, and favourable mechanical properties that allow repeated withdrawal and extraction cycles, enabling secure storage of fluids over long periods of time. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 77, citing Li et al. 2019; Urai et al. 2019; Evans et al. 2021; Lux 2009)

Attributes. Storage power and discharge duration.

Property Value
Storage power ~10 MW – 1 GW
Discharge duration day to month

(Miocic et al. 2023, Fig. 2, p. 75)

Notes — operational H₂ sites. Practical experience in pure-hydrogen salt-cavern storage is limited to four operational projects providing hydrogen for the chemical industry: Teesside (UK; bedded salt; 95% H₂; mean depth 350 m; in operation since 1972) and Clemens, Moss Bluff and Spindletop (USA; domal salt; 95% H₂; mean depths 1000–1340 m; from 1983, 2007 and 2017). Kiel (Germany) stored town gas (62% H₂) in a salt cavern in the 1960s–1970s. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 77 and Table 3, p. 78, citing Crotogino 2016; Panfilov 2016)

Notes — integrity and design. Internal cavern pressure must remain below the dilatancy boundary to preserve integrity. Cavern geometry — slim shafts with large depth-to-radius ratios and capsule (ovoidal) shapes — is preferred to reduce roof-collapse risk; with increasing burial depth, pressure differentials and storage capacity rise. Salt’s near-isotropic stress state, ductility and viscoplastic creep allow it to heal induced cracks, but non-halite interbeds can compromise permeability and alter steady-state creep, creating strain partitioning. (Miocic et al. 2023, pp. 79–80, citing Urai et al. 2019; Tarkowski 2019; Taheri et al. 2020; Hunsche and Hampel 1999; Khaledi et al. 2016; InSPEE 2016)

Notes — cycling. Salt caverns are likely to experience faster cycling rates than porous stores. The integrity and stability of a cavern is related to geomechanical and geological factors of the salt and the cavern shape, as well as the pressure of the stored gas. Thermal and geomechanical stresses may also affect the wellbore/cement/salt-formation interface, since creep deformation or interbed slip could lead to casing collapse or loss of well sealing. (Miocic et al. 2023, pp. 79–80, citing Ozarslan 2012; Ramesh Kumar et al. 2021; Spiers et al. 1990; Asgari et al. 2020; Leister et al. 2018)

Related terms. Caprock; dilatancy boundary; cushion gas; cyclic loading; town gas; bedded salt; domal salt.

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, operational sites, integrity/design and cycling notes.

Slow Strain Rate Test (SSRT)

Definition. A tensile-strength test performed at a controlled, gradual deformation rate, recognised for closely simulating the actual stress conditions encountered by materials in service applications. Used to assess hydrogen embrittlement (HE) susceptibility. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 376)

Notes. SSRT and Conventional Strain Rate Test (CSRT) have produced nearly identical results when evaluating localised conditions such as local stress and local hydrogen distribution at the fracture initiation point. (Ghadiani et al. 2024, p. 376)

Related terms. Hydrogen embrittlement; hydrogen charging; fatigue crack growth rate test; Conventional Strain Rate Test.

Source history. - Ghadiani et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-07: definition and comparison with CSRT.

Sector coupling

Definition. The integration and interaction of multiple energy sectors (power, heat, transport, industry, desalination, CDR) through electrification and the use of common energy carriers and infrastructure. Direct sector coupling occurs through electrification of end-use (BEVs, heat pumps); indirect sector coupling occurs through power-to-X (PtX) products such as e-hydrogen, e-methane and e-methanol used as feedstocks or fuels in non-power sectors. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 3, 22)

Notes. Sector coupling provides opportunities to harness synergies across energy sectors: BEVs link transport to power via grid charging and V2G; heat pumps link the heat sector to power; PtX links power to chemicals/fuels. e-hydrogen sits at the start of nearly all PtX conversion chains. Out of the 1,067 articles in the 100% RE systems database, only 30% conduct a full energy-system analysis covering all of power, heat and transport — Khalili et al. identify expanded multi-sector coverage as a key research gap. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 3, 22, 24)

Related terms. Power-to-X (PtX); e-fuels; battery electric vehicle (BEV); heat pump (HP); 100% renewable energy system; energy system models.

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, direct vs indirect coupling, research-gap framing.

Secondary plastics market

Definition. The market for plastic resins produced from recycled end-of-life plastic items, as opposed to “primary” (virgin) plastics produced from fossil-feedstock cracking. Secondary plastics are mainly considered substitutes for primary plastics rather than a valuable resource in their own right, making the market small and vulnerable to primary-price fluctuations. (OECD 2022, pp. 23–24, 84)

Attributes — global secondary plastics production.

Year Production Share of total feedstock
2000 6.8 Mt ~3%
2019 29.1 Mt ~6%
Cumulative growth (2000–2019) >4× —

(OECD 2022, p. 23)

Notes — push and pull policies. Several countries have strengthened secondary-plastics markets through a combined “push” of supply (Extended Producer Responsibility schemes) and “pull” of demand (recycled-content targets, public-procurement requirements). The recent decoupling of European primary- and secondary-PET prices (mainly food-grade rPET) is the first clear signal that the policy combination is working. China’s 2017 “National Sword” import ban on plastic waste, and subsequent amendments to the Basel Convention and OECD Decision on Transboundary Movements of Waste, have on-shored recycling capacity in advanced economies. (OECD 2022, pp. 23–24)

Related terms. Mechanical recycling; chemical recycling; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR); deposit-refund scheme; pay-as-you-throw (PAYT); plastic chemicals.

Source history. - OECD 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, deployment, push-pull policy framework.

Solar PV

Aliases. Solar photovoltaics; PV.

Definition. A power-generation technology that converts solar irradiation directly into electricity using semiconductor cells (predominantly crystalline silicon today, with growing market shares for heterojunction technology, HJT, and Tunnel Oxide Passivated Contact, TOPCon). One of the IEA’s six “clean energy technologies” and the dominant variable renewable energy (VRE) source by capacity. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 144–145, Glossary p. 374; Khalili et al. 2026, p. 6)

Single-use plastics

Definition. Plastic items designed and intended to be used once, for a short duration, and then discarded — including bags, beverage bottles, food packaging, cutlery, straws, cups and personal protective equipment (PPE). A leading source of macroplastic litter and a primary target of plastics-policy bans, taxes and design restrictions. (OECD 2022, pp. 18, 21–26)

Attributes.

Stat Value
Countries with single-use plastic bans/taxes (2022) >120
Plastic items in circulation with <1-year use phase >40% globally
“Word of the year” (Collins Dictionary) “single-use” (2018)

(OECD 2022, pp. 18, 25; Grimaud and Girard 2024, p. 13)

Notes. Single-use plastics are the principal driver of the rapid growth of plastic waste; their abundance and visibility make them an effective policy entry point but most existing bans target small-volume items (bags, straws) rather than larger packaging streams. Avoidance of single-use plastics is identified by the OECD and Grimaud as the most effective lever for upstream demand reduction, alongside re-use, refill systems and product-design improvements. (OECD 2022, pp. 25–27; Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 13–15)

Related terms. Plastic leakage; mismanaged plastic waste; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR); deposit-refund scheme; macroplastics.
