SNBC (Stratégie nationale bas-carbone)

Aliases. Stratégie nationale bas-carbone (FR); French national low-carbon strategy.

Definition. France’s official roadmap for achieving carbon neutrality by 2050, adopted in April 2020 and reviewed every five years. The SNBC is structured along two complementary axes: (i) demand-side — energy efficiency, sufficiency (sobriété), electrification of end-uses (transport, heating, industry); and (ii) supply-side — decarbonised electricity (mix of renewables and nuclear) and domestically-produced biomass, with explicit exclusion of large-scale gas imports. RTE’s Futurs énergétiques 2050 exercise was conceived as the quantitative test-bed of SNBC principles applied to the electricity system. (RTE 2022, Sections 1.2, 3.1.1, translated from French)

Attributes — SNBC headline assumptions (as adopted 2020).

Indicator SNBC value Comment
Net GHG target 2050 net-zero (carbon neutrality) Reductions + biological/technical removals
Final energy consumption 2050 ~40% lower than today Driven by efficiency + sufficiency
Electricity share of final energy rising sharply Driver: electrification of mobility, heat, industry
Biomass mobilisation very strong increase (>+50%) Domestic feedstock; one of two energy pillars
Electricity production decarbonised mix (renewables + nuclear) RTE 6 scenarios test the mix question
Imports of fossil fuels excluded at scale post-2050 “Independence” axis

(RTE 2022, Sections 1.2, 3.1.1, p. 81)

Notes — SNBC vs RTE study. RTE’s exercise implements the SNBC framework but explicitly tests its sensitivity to alternative demand trajectories (sufficiency, deep reindustrialisation, reference). The SNBC’s reference electricity demand (~645 TWh ± 100 TWh in 2050) is RTE’s central trajectory. A revised SNBC (“SNBC-3”) was scheduled for 2024 to integrate the post-Ukraine “France 2030” plan and the EU’s Fit-for-55 package; RTE’s analysis informs that revision. (RTE 2022, p. 79–81; cited extensively in Sections 3.1, 12.3)

Notes — supply-side mix question. The SNBC is agnostic on the renewables/nuclear mix; it sets only the carbon-neutrality target and total-energy decomposition. The RTE 2050 exercise’s six scenarios (M0 / M1 / M23 / N1 / N2 / N03) are precisely the answers to this open question, ranging from 100% renewable to maximum new-nuclear. (RTE 2022, Section 5.1, translated)

Related terms. RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 scenarios; Sufficiency (sobriété); Deep reindustrialisation; EPR2 programme; Grand carénage; Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE); Carbon dioxide removal (CDR); EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS).

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, structure (two axes), 2050 carbon-neutrality target, role as scenario backdrop for RTE study (translated from French).

Solid oxide electrolysis (SOE)

Aliases. SOEC (solid oxide electrolyser cell); high-temperature electrolysis.

Definition. A water-electrolysis technology operating at high temperature (600–1000 °C; 873–1273 K) using a solid-oxide ceramic electrolyte (typically yttria-stabilised zirconia) to dissociate steam into hydrogen and oxygen. SOE is one of three main water-electrolysis technologies considered for green-hydrogen production for aviation electrofuels (alongside alkaline and PEM electrolysis), and is also the basis of co-electrolysis (joint H₂O + CO₂ conversion to syngas). (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 12)

Notes. SOE requires ~40% less electricity per unit of H₂ produced than alkaline electrolysis, but requires ~40% more heat. SOE benefits from integration with industrial waste-heat sources (e.g. FT-synthesis exotherm). The lower electricity demand of SOE — when supplying electrofuels at the 16.73 EJ aviation demand scale — is the dominant lever distinguishing the lower end of the 5,900–10,000 TWh y⁻¹ electricity range. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 12, 28)

Related terms. Co-electrolysis; alkaline electrolysis; PEM electrolyser; reverse water gas shift; electrofuels; hydrogen colour taxonomy.

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, energy trade-off vs alkaline, role in electrofuel scenarios.

Solvolysis (physical plastic recycling)

Aliases. Polymer dissolution recycling.

Definition. A “physical” plastic recycling pathway in which a plastic article is dissolved in a selective solvent so that the polymer can be separated from additives and contaminants and re-precipitated, recovering a near-virgin polymer without breaking the polymer chain. Distinguished from chemical recycling (chemolysis or thermochemical), which decomposes the polymer back to monomers or hydrocarbons. (Grimaud and Girard 2024, p. 22)

Attributes.

Property Value
TRL 7 (pre-commercial demonstrations)
Flagship process Fraunhofer CreaSolv®
Strengths broad polymer applicability; removes additives; recovers valuable additives
Limitations solvent recovery and disposal; complex operation; environmental footprint of solvent

(Grimaud and Girard 2024, p. 22)

Notes. Solvolysis is gaining attention as the missing middle between mechanical recycling (which preserves the chain but tolerates only mono-material clean streams) and chemical recycling (which decomposes the chain at high energy and material cost). It is particularly promising for multilayer films, additive-laden plastics and consumer electronics housings. Industrial scale-up is constrained by solvent management. (Grimaud and Girard 2024, p. 22)

Related terms. Mechanical recycling; chemical recycling; plastic chemicals; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR).

Source history. - Grimaud and Girard 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, TRL, CreaSolv example (translated from French).

Steiner tree (with obstacles)

Definition. A graph-theoretic optimisation problem: given a set of “terminal” vertices in a weighted graph, find the minimum-weight subgraph (typically a tree) that connects all terminals, allowing additional non-terminal “Steiner” vertices to reduce total weight. The “with obstacles” variant accounts for non-traversable or higher-cost regions in a spatially-explicit cost surface. Used in hydrogen-pipeline network design as an extension of the simpler Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) algorithm. (Hammond et al. 2025, Section 1)

Attributes — applications in pipeline design.

Method Cost surface Source
Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) uniform Baufumé et al.; Johnson & Ogden
Heijnen et al. Gilbert-Melzak (Steiner) uniform, flow-cost heuristic Heijnen et al.
André et al. iterative MST + heuristics uniform, with hydrogen-specific costing André et al. 2013
Heijnen et al. multi-step graph one untraversable obstacle Heijnen et al.
Hammond et al. StObGA full variable cost surface incl. multiple obstacles Hammond et al. 2025

(Hammond et al. 2025, Section 1; André et al. 2013)

Notes — StObGA innovation. Hammond et al.’s Steiner tree with Obstacles Genetic Algorithm (StObGA) routes pipelines on a complex cost surface for multi-source/multi-sink hydrogen networks, achieving 20–40% cost savings vs uniform-cost graph methods. Geographical obstacles include slopes, transport crossings, water bodies, forests and densely populated areas (DPA), each with a per-area penalty weight. (Hammond et al. 2025, abstract; Section 1)

Related terms. Hydrogen pipeline network design; Mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP); levelised cost of hydrogen transportation (LCOH-T); Genetic algorithm.

Source history. - Hammond et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, comparative algorithm table, StObGA cost saving.

Solar protection (umbrella)

Aliases. Protections solaires (FR); shading devices; sunscreens; solar shading; brise-soleil; volet roulant; casquette solaire; store; brasseur d’air (related — fan).

Definition. A category of envelope and HVAC interventions designed to reduce solar-heat gains through windows during summer to control overheating, while preserving solar gain in winter (to reduce heating demand). Solar protection devices are categorised by their position relative to the glazing: exterior (most effective — block radiation before it reaches the glass), between-glass (integrated into the window assembly), and interior (less effective — block radiation after the greenhouse effect occurs in the cavity). Goessel demonstrates exterior shading is consistently part of Pareto-optimal renovation strategies in warm-climate French zones (H3, Mediterranean). (Goessel 2025, Sections 3.3–3.4 and Annexe A)

Attributes — solar-protection categories.

Category Description Solar reduction (typical)
Volet roulant (roller shutter, exterior) metal slats; manual or motorised 60–95% (fully closed)
Brise-soleil / persiennes (fixed exterior louvres) architectural fixed shading 40–70% (depending on geometry)
Casquette solaire (overhang, sun visor) horizontal projecting shade 30–60% (south-facing)
Awnings (toiles d’ombrage) retractable fabric awnings 50–80%
Pergolas / verandas (outdoor shading) architectural shading 40–80%
Tinted / solar-control glazing embedded in window assembly g reduced from 0.65 → 0.30
Internal blinds (stores intérieurs) indoor textile or aluminium blinds 20–40% (least effective)
Vegetation (trees, climbers) natural shading 50–80% (with leaf cover)
Brasseur d’air / ceiling fan doesn’t reduce solar gain but provides comfort cooling without active AC 0% solar; ~+3 °C tolerance

(Goessel 2025, Annexe A; AFNOR EN 13561)

Notes — Goessel 2025 finding. External roller shutters (volets roulants) reduce SET-DH by ~32% in the Chalandon house typology in the H3 climate zone. Fixed solar overhangs (casquettes) reduce SET-DH by ~19%. Ceiling fans (brasseurs d’air) reduce SET-DH by ~83% (the largest single intervention) by providing direct convective cooling without addressing the heat gain itself. Combinations of shading + fans dominate the Pareto front for summer-comfort optimisation. (Goessel 2025, p. 4391 area, Annexe D)

Related terms. Building envelope; Glazing technology; building renovation (umbrella); Standard Effective Temperature (SET); thermal comfort; Heat-wave health risk; air conditioning; passive cooling.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: shading-device taxonomy, Goessel SET-DH reduction findings (translated from French).

Steam cracking (vapocracking)

Aliases. Vapocraqueur (FR); naphtha cracking; ethane cracking.

Definition. The principal petrochemical process for producing light olefins (ethylene C₂H₄, propylene C₃H₆) and other monomers from naphtha or ethane feedstocks by thermal decomposition at 600–1100 °C in the presence of steam, followed by quenching and separation. Steam cracking is the upstream gateway of nearly all conventional fossil-based plastic production: the products are then polymerised into PE, PP, PVC, PS, etc. (Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 7, 28)

Attributes — single-cracker scale (Grimaud).

Parameter Value
Operating temperature 600–1100 °C
Heat-input power per cracker ~900 MW
Equipment lifetime ~60 years
Naphtha share of crude refinery output ~2.5%

(Grimaud and Girard 2024, p. 28)

Notes — decarbonisation pathways. - Electric cracker: replace fossil burners with electrical heating using low-carbon electricity. Demonstrators by Shell, Dow, BASF and SABIC; technically challenging at high T and large scale, with significant grid-integration and ramp-rate constraints. - Hydrogen-fired cracker: substitute fossil gas with low-carbon H₂. INEOS Project ONE (€4 bn) is an example using green H₂ as fuel. - CCS: capture CO₂ at the cracker stack — typical capture rates 75–90%, capture-unit CAPEX ~€179 M, capture cost €150–170/t CO₂.

(Grimaud and Girard 2024, pp. 28–29)

Attributes — yield profile by feedstock (typical industrial values).

Product (wt% of feed) Ethane feed Propane feed Light naphtha Heavy naphtha Gas oil
Ethylene ~80% ~45% ~32% ~28% ~22%
Propylene ~3% ~15% ~14% ~16% ~15%
C4 olefins (butadiene + butenes) ~3% ~5% ~9% ~10% ~8%
Pyrolysis gasoline (BTX-rich) ~3% ~5% ~22% ~25% ~28%
Methane + hydrogen ~10% ~25% ~17% ~16% ~14%
Heavy fuel oil residue small small ~5% ~5% ~12%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 6.2.3.2 and tables; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Notes — energy intensity. Steam cracking is the most energy-intensive industrial process in the chemical sector: ~26.8 GJ/t ethylene (Zhang 2024), with ~31% of the total energy used for product separation (cryogenic distillation of ethylene/propylene/C4). Globally, steam crackers consume ~9 EJ/yr of feedstock energy and ~3 EJ/yr of process energy. (Zhang et al. 2024, pp. 100–101; Levi and Cullen 2018)

Notes — capacity and integration. Levi & Cullen 2018 catalogue 277 commercial steam crackers globally, supplying ~62% of HVCs (ethylene + propylene + C4 + BTX); the remainder comes from refinery FCC/reformer streams (~35%) and on-purpose technologies (~3%). Modern megacrackers are 1.5–2 Mt/yr ethylene capacity, increasingly co-located with refineries (refinery–petrochemical integration) for streamlined naphtha supply. (Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1727; Speight 2019, Chapter 6.6.1)

Related terms. Olefins; high-value chemicals (HVCs); naphtha; pyrolysis gasoline (pygas); BTX aromatics; Methanol-to-Olefins (MTO); chemical recycling; Power-to-Plastic; carbon capture and storage (CCS); refinery-petrochemical integration; petrochemicals (umbrella).

Source history. - Grimaud and Girard 2024 — added 2026-05-08: definition, scale, decarbonisation routes (translated from French). - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: yield profile by feedstock, technical details. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 277 crackers globally, 62% HVC share. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: 26.8 GJ/t ethylene energy intensity, 31% separation energy fraction.

Steam methane reforming (SMR)

Definition. The dominant process for hydrogen production from natural gas, in which methane reacts with steam to produce a hydrogen-rich gas stream; with CO₂ capture, the CO₂ is chemically absorbed after the shift reaction by a methyl diethanolamine solution (post-combustion variant). Without capture, this is the conventional grey-hydrogen route. (Baufumé et al. 2011, p. 8810; Miocic et al. 2023, Table 2, p. 76)

Notes. Approximately 96% of global hydrogen produced today originates from SMR without CCS, at a cost of ~USD 1.8 / kg H₂ assuming 2020 natural-gas prices. With CCS, the route corresponds to “blue hydrogen” with TRL 7–8 and life-cycle emissions of 2.97–9.16 kg CO₂e / kg H₂. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 76 and Table 2, citing IEA 2021)

Related terms. Hydrogen colour taxonomy; carbon capture and storage; post-combustion capture; coal gasification; autothermal reforming; electrolysis.

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — listed in Pending 2026-05-07; cost, TRL and life-cycle-emissions data noted. - Baufumé et al. 2011 — added 2026-05-07: SMR definition with CO₂-capture chemistry.

Stranded assets

Aliases. Stranded fossil assets; carbon-stranded assets; impaired fossil capacity; unburnable carbon.

Definition. Capital assets — fossil-fuel reserves, mining concessions, refineries, gas pipelines, oil tankers, coal-fired power plants, ICE-engine factories, petrochemical complexes — that suffer unanticipated or premature write-downs, devaluations or conversion to liabilities as a result of climate-policy regulation (carbon pricing, emissions caps, fossil-fuel phase-out), competition from cleaner technologies, or shifts in consumer / investor preferences. The “unburnable carbon” framing (Carbon Tracker 2011) shows that a significant fraction of proven fossil-fuel reserves (~80% globally to stay below 2 °C) cannot be combusted while meeting Paris Agreement goals, implying massive write-downs in industry asset values. Stranded-asset risk is now recognised by central banks (BIS, NGFS) as a financial-stability concern. (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 608, 612; Carbon Tracker 2011)

Attributes — major stranded-asset categories.

Category Estimated stranded value (literature)
Fossil-fuel reserves (unburnable) $1–4 trillion if 2 °C target met
Coal-fired power plants $1.7 trillion (IEA estimate to 2050)
Oil refineries (post-electrification) $0.5–1 trillion
Petrochemical complexes (post-plastics-cap) several hundred billion
ICE-engine factories hundreds of billions (post-EV transition)
Gas pipeline + LNG infrastructure varies by region

(Tilsted et al. 2023, p. 612; literature)

Notes — financial stability implications. Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS, 2017) and IPCC AR6 highlight that uncontrolled stranded-asset write-downs could trigger financial crises analogous to the 2008 mortgage crisis. Orderly phase-out (with policy signalling, transition pathways, just-transition support) is essential to avoid systemic financial risk. Bank of England’s Climate-Related Financial Risk stress tests (2021–2024) explicitly include stranded-asset scenarios. (Tilsted et al. 2023, p. 612)

Related terms. Carbon lock-in; petrochemical lock-ins / political economy; just transition; Paris Agreement; non-recourse project finance; deep reindustrialisation; EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); CBAM.

Source history. - Tilsted et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: stranded-asset definition, categories, financial-stability implications.

Strait of Hormuz

Definition. The maritime chokepoint connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the wider Indian Ocean, between Iran and the Musandam Peninsula of Oman. The single most strategically important waterway in the global oil and LNG markets. (IEA Sheltering From Oil Shocks 2026, p. 3; IEA ETP 2026, Glossary p. 378)

Attributes — typical pre-disruption flows.

Indicator Value
Crude oil through the Strait ~15 million barrels per day
Oil products through the Strait ~5 million barrels per day
Combined share of global oil consumption ~20%
Reaction crude price (during 2026 shock) >USD 100 / barrel

(IEA Sheltering From Oil Shocks 2026, p. 3)

Notes — 2026 disruption response. The near-halt of Strait-of-Hormuz traffic was the trigger for the IEA’s 2026 Sheltering From Oil Shocks report and the Governing Board’s largest-ever stock release (400 million barrels on 11 March). Diesel, jet fuel and LPG saw the steepest price rises among refined products. The disruption serves as the canonical worked example of the maritime-chokepoint risk discussed in ETP-2026. (IEA Sheltering From Oil Shocks 2026, p. 3; IEA ETP 2026, p. 378)

Related terms. Maritime chokepoint; Oil supply shock (demand-side response); international marine bunkers; bunkering; wet bulk shipping.

Source history. - IEA Sheltering From Oil Shocks 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, pre-disruption flows, response context.

Stewardship fund (post-closure CO₂ storage)

Definition. A pooled financial reserve, typically funded by per-tonne contributions from CO₂-storage operators during active injection, intended to cover monitoring, remediation and any other long-term obligations after the storage site is closed and operational liability has been transferred to the state. Stewardship funds operate alongside other financial-security instruments (insurance, credit lines, surety bonds) used to cover liability during the operational period. (IEA 2026, pp. 43, 47)

Attributes — examples.

Jurisdiction Stewardship-fund use Notes
Alberta, Canada Glacier project Post-closure stewardship fund
Wyoming, United States High Plains CCS / Trailblazer Post-closure stewardship fund
United Kingdom (T&S Agreement) Backstop framework Compensation for delays, leakage, infrastructure failure

(IEA 2026, p. 47)

Notes. Stewardship funds are one mechanism by which jurisdictions provide a credible post-closure governance regime, typically combined with the legal transfer of liability from operator to state after 10–20 years and conditional on demonstrating no significant leakage risk. They are particularly important for de-risking CCUS investments where insurance markets cannot fully address long-tail liability. (IEA 2026, pp. 22, 43)

Related terms. Long-term storage liability; bankability; Class VI well permit; cross-chain risk.

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, jurisdictional examples.

Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs)

Aliases. SSPs; SSP1 (Sustainability) / SSP2 (Middle of the Road) / SSP3 (Regional Rivalry) / SSP4 (Inequality) / SSP5 (Fossil-Fuelled Development); IPCC scenario taxonomy.

Definition. A set of five reference socio-economic narratives developed by the Integrated Assessment Modelling community in the early 2010s (O’Neill et al. 2014) and adopted as the standard scenario taxonomy for climate-mitigation studies in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6, 2022). Each SSP describes a qualitative future world with assumptions on population growth, GDP growth, urbanisation, technological progress, international cooperation, fossil-fuel reliance, and inequality. The narratives are climate-neutral — they describe socio-economic conditions without specifying climate policy; combined with Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) they generate quantitative climate-mitigation pathways via Integrated Assessment Models. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 1; O’Neill et al. 2014 cited)

Attributes — five SSPs.

SSP Narrative Pop 2100 GDP/cap Climate-policy challenges
SSP1 Sustainability — green growth, low population, strong cooperation 7 billion high low (easiest 1.5 °C path)
SSP2 Middle of the Road — extrapolation of historical trends 9 billion medium medium (default reference)
SSP3 Regional Rivalry — fragmentation, slow tech progress 13 billion low high (hardest mitigation)
SSP4 Inequality — strong divide between rich and poor 9 billion mixed high (mitigation challenges)
SSP5 Fossil-Fuelled Development — high consumption, fossil-rich growth 7 billion high high (high baseline emissions)

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 1; O’Neill et al. 2014, IPCC AR6 SSP database)

Notes — SSP × RCP combination. SSPs combine with RCPs (Representative Concentration Pathways — radiative-forcing trajectories) to generate “scenario matrices” used by IAMs: SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5 are the canonical combinations. Each combination is a scenario in the strict sense; the pathways generated by IAMs running these scenarios produce specific year-by-year emission, technology and energy trajectories. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 1)

Related terms. Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs); Integrated Assessment Model (IAM); pathways (vs scenarios); Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE); Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: SSP definition and taxonomy, IPCC AR6 standard role.

Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs)

Aliases. RCPs; RCP1.9 / RCP2.6 / RCP4.5 / RCP6 / RCP7 / RCP8.5; radiative-forcing scenarios.

Definition. A set of climate-policy-neutral radiative-forcing trajectories developed for the IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (AR5, 2014) and refined for AR6, named by their target radiative forcing (W/m²) at year 2100. RCPs describe how atmospheric greenhouse-gas concentrations evolve to deliver a target end-of-century radiative forcing — the climate-physics counterpart to SSPs (which describe socio-economics). RCPs are used as the input to climate-system models to project temperature, precipitation, sea-level and other climate impacts; combined with SSPs they generate full integrated-assessment scenarios. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 1; van Vuuren et al. 2011 cited)

Attributes — six RCPs.

RCP 2100 forcing 2100 GHG concentration 2100 temperature increase (median)
RCP1.9 1.9 W/m² 380–420 ppm CO₂eq ~1.5 °C
RCP2.6 2.6 W/m² 421–510 ppm CO₂eq ~1.5–1.8 °C
RCP4.5 4.5 W/m² 511–600 ppm CO₂eq ~2.6 °C
RCP6.0 6.0 W/m² 601–700 ppm CO₂eq ~3 °C
RCP7.0 7.0 W/m² 701–800 ppm CO₂eq ~3.5 °C (added in AR6)
RCP8.5 8.5 W/m² >800 ppm CO₂eq ~4–5 °C (high-end)

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 1; van Vuuren et al. 2011, IPCC AR5/AR6)

Notes — RCP-to-SSP coupling. Original RCPs (AR5) were climate-policy-neutral — designed to span a wide range of future radiative forcing without prescribing how it would be achieved. The combined SSP×RCP framework (AR6) adds the socio-economic dimension. Some combinations are infeasible (SSP3 with RCP1.9 is impossible because regional rivalry prevents the cooperation needed for 1.5 °C); others are well-explored (SSP2-4.5 is the default reference). (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 1)

Related terms. Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs); Integrated Assessment Model (IAM); pathways (vs scenarios); Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE); Current Policies Scenario (CPS).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: RCP definition, six-trajectory taxonomy, SSP×RCP coupling.

PRISMA review methodology

Aliases. PRISMA; Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses; PRISMA flow diagram; PRISMA-2020.

Definition. A standardised reporting protocol for systematic literature reviews and meta-analyses, originally designed for medical research and now widely adopted across disciplines including energy-system modelling. PRISMA prescribes a structured procedure for (i) defining the research question; (ii) constructing a search strategy; (iii) screening records by abstract / title and full-text; (iv) extracting data with inter-coder reliability checks; (v) reporting via a flow diagram showing how the initial search was filtered down to the included sample. The PRISMA-2020 update (Page et al. 2021) is the current standard, used by Manuel et al. 2025 in their systematic review of 330 ESOM-pathway studies. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 7 and Fig. 6; Page et al. 2021 cited)

Attributes — Manuel 2025 PRISMA execution.

Stage Records Note
Records identified (Scopus query, Jan 2025) 3,632 search strings on Table 1
Records screened (after filtering by language + article type) 2,591 English peer-reviewed only
Records sought for retrieval 855 screened by ASReview-LAB ML-assisted + manual
Studies sought for retrieval 855 full-text retrieval
Studies assessed for eligibility 500 sample size cap
Studies included in review 330 308 single-model + 15 inter-comparison + 7 reviews
Inter-coder reliability reported quality control

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 7 and Fig. 6)

Notes — significance for energy-modelling literature. PRISMA + ASReview enables transparent and replicable systematic reviews of energy-modelling literature, which had previously suffered from informal narrative-review approaches. Manuel et al. 2025’s PRISMA-protocol example demonstrates the methodology being applied at scale in a domain (ESOM modelling) far from its medical-research origin. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 7–11)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); pathways (vs scenarios); Material Flow Analysis (MFA / Sankey diagram); literature review methodology; ASReview; PRISMA-2020.

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: PRISMA definition, execution example, significance for energy-modelling literature.

Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS)

Definition. An IEA exploratory scenario reflecting the direction of travel of the global energy sector based on current energy-related policies — including those that have already been adopted, announced, or are at the advanced planning stage — even if not yet enshrined in law or regulation. Examples include power-sector development plans, transport-sector regulatory reforms and energy-efficiency targets for appliances. Policy targets are not assumed to be automatically met: their prospects are assessed taking account of market, infrastructure-readiness and financial constraints. STEPS does not assume the achievement of aspirational goals such as those in the Paris Agreement. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 379)

Notes — STEPS market signals (ETP-2026).

Item Value Year
Combined clean-energy-tech market value USD 3 trillion 2035
Low-emissions fuels market USD 390 billion 2035
Near-zero emissions materials USD 20 billion 2035
Net global trade in clean energy technologies USD 620 billion 2035 (from USD 290 bn in 2025)
China net exports USD 375 billion 2035 (~10% of total Chinese goods exports today)

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 15–17)

Related terms. Current Policies Scenario (CPS); Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE); clean energy technologies; manufacturing capacity (clean energy technologies); low-emissions hydrogen.

Sugar fermentation with alcohol upgrading (SuF)

Definition. A biofuel pathway in which a hydrolysate from carbohydrate-rich biomass (molasses, sugarcane, sweet sorghum, sugar beet, food waste, inedible fodder maize) or lignocellulosic-based biomass (cereal or rice straw) is fermented to alcohols (typically ethanol or isobutanol), and these alcohols are upgraded to aviation biofuel through dehydration, oligomerisation, hydrogenation and distillation. ATJ-SPK is the certified product (also known as Alcohol-to-Jet SPK). (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 6–7)

Notes. SuF aggregates within the broader “alcohol-to-jet” (ATJ) umbrella alongside the syngas-fermentation (SF) pathway. Acetone-butanol-ethanol (ABE) fermentation by Clostridia or modified E. coli is the typical isobutanol route; S. cerevisiae yeasts are commonly used for ethanol. Distiller dried grains (a high-protein animal feed) are produced as a co-product. A variation enriches heavier olefin fractions with aromatics (~20 vol%, “synthetic kerosene with aromatics”) to overcome blending limits — under ASTM certification. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 6–7)

Related terms. Alcohol-to-jet (ATJ); syngas fermentation (SF); synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK); drop-in fuel; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, four-step upgrading process, co-products.

Styrene (C₆H₅-CH=CH₂)

Aliases. Vinylbenzene; phenylethene; styrene monomer (SM).

Definition. A colourless aromatic-vinyl liquid produced industrially by the dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene over an iron-oxide-based catalyst (Fe₂O₃ + K + Cr) at 600–650 °C and sub-atmospheric pressure. Ethylbenzene itself is produced by the alkylation of benzene with ethylene over a zeolite catalyst. Styrene is the principal monomer for polystyrene (GP-PS, HIPS, EPS), styrene-acrylonitrile (SAN), acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS), and styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR). (Speight 2019, Chapter 8; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production (recent) ~30 Mt/yr
Synthesis route benzene + ethylene → ethylbenzene → styrene + H₂
Reactor temperature (dehydrogenation) 600–650 °C
Reactor pressure sub-atmospheric (~0.2–0.5 bar steam-diluted)
Per-pass conversion ~60–70%
Selectivity to styrene >90%
Polystyrene (PS) share of end-use ~55–60%
ABS / SAN share ~25%
Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) share ~10%
Unsaturated polyester resins / latex / other ~10%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 8 and 11.3.4)

Notes — propylene oxide / styrene monomer (PO/SM) co-product route. A significant share of global styrene comes from the co-production with propylene oxide (PO) via the Lyondell or Shell oxirane process: ethylbenzene → ethylbenzene hydroperoxide + propylene → propylene oxide + 1-phenylethanol → styrene. This integrates two large markets but creates economic coupling between styrene and PO demand. (Speight 2019, Chapter 8)

Related terms. Olefins; aromatic hydrocarbons; BTX aromatics; ethylene; benzene; ethylbenzene; polystyrene; ABS; styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR); SAN; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, production route, end-use shares, PO/SM co-product route. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 30 Mt/yr global, styrene → PS / ABS / SBR splits.

Sufficiency (sobriété énergétique)

Aliases. Sobriété (FR); energy sufficiency; structural demand reduction.

Definition. A demand-side strategy that reduces total energy demand through changes in usage patterns and behaviours — distinct from energy efficiency (which reduces energy use per unit of service by improving technology) and from electrification (which substitutes electricity for fossil fuels at constant service level). The RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 report frames sufficiency as a third complementary lever alongside efficiency and decarbonisation, decomposed into “selective” sufficiency (avoiding deemed-unnecessary uses) and “structural” sufficiency (organisational and infrastructural changes that reshape demand). (RTE 2022, Sections 3.5.1–3.5.4, translated from French; Grimaud and Girard 2024, Executive summary)

Attributes — RTE 2050 sufficiency-scenario specifics.

Indicator Sufficiency vs reference 2050 Mechanism
Total electricity demand ~−40 TWh structural and behavioural changes
Mobility (passenger-km) reduced car use, modal shift living-place-to-workplace proximity, public transit, cycling
Heating demand reduced occupied area; thermal-comfort temperature lower set-point, smaller dwellings
Industrial demand shifts in product mix (e.g. less single-use packaging) structural
Datacentre / digital less device replacement, longer lifetimes structural
Required new flexibility ~−20% vs reference flexibility envelope smaller
Required wind / solar build-out reduced smaller renewable rollout
Annualised system cost reduced by several billion € cost saving across all six mix scenarios

(RTE 2022, Sections 3.5.4–3.5.5, 7.11.1, 11.8.1.1)

Notes — distinction from efficiency. RTE explicitly distinguishes sufficiency from efficiency: efficiency reduces energy per service (e.g. LED lighting, heat-pump COP); sufficiency reduces the service itself (e.g. living in a smaller home). The two are complementary — efficiency captures technical gains; sufficiency captures behavioural and structural ones. (RTE 2022, Section 3.5.2)

Notes — Grimaud parallel. The Grimaud & Girard 2024 plastics-circularity report treats sufficiency as the first level of the circularity hierarchy — rationalising consumption (especially of single-use plastics) — placed before reuse, recycling and chemical recycling. This aligns with the RTE framing of sufficiency as the demand-side first lever. (Grimaud and Girard 2024, Executive summary)

Related terms. RTE Futurs énergétiques 2050 scenarios; Power system flexibility; Variable Renewable Energy (VRE); Heat pump (HP); Single-use plastics; Mechanical recycling.

Source history. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, distinction from efficiency, sufficiency-scenario quantitative impacts (translated from French). - Grimaud and Girard 2024 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): sufficiency as first lever of plastics circularity.

Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF)

Definition. Liquid fuels for aviation derived from non-fossil feedstock and meeting sustainability criteria, currently certified to ASTM D7566 (or equivalent national standards). The term originally referred only to biofuels but has been explicitly expanded — by the EU ReFuelEU Aviation proposal — to cover electrofuels (synthetic fuels) as well. Su-ungkavatin et al. note that “sustainable aviation” is preferred over “SAF” because some emerging technologies (e.g. batteries, hydrogen aviation) do not fit within the concept of “fuel”. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 1, 25–26)

Attributes — four ASTM D7566 categories of alternative kerosene.

Type Composition Producing pathways
Synthetic Paraffinic Kerosene (SPK) n- and iso-paraffins FT, HEFA, SuF, SF
Synthetic Aromatic Kerosene (SAK) aromatics (blend component) APR
Synthetic Iso-Paraffin (SIP) farnesane (C₁₅H₃₂) DSHC
Synthetic Kerosene (SK) composition similar to fossil kerosene CHJ (CHJ-SK certified 2020)

(Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 1–2)

Notes. Certified pathways under ASTM D7566 currently include FT-SPK, HEFA-SPK (incl. HH HEFA-SPK from Bb microalgae oil), SuF/ATJ-SPK, DSHC, CHJ-SK, and FT-SPK with aromatics (SPK/A). APR, IH2 and HDCJ are under or near certification. As of writing, SAF accounts for less than 1% of total aviation fuel demand. The EU’s ReFuelEU Aviation proposal sets a binding minimum SAF share of 2 vol% in 2023 rising to 63 vol% by 2050 (Parliament endorsement: 85 vol%). (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 1–3, 25–26)

Related terms. Drop-in fuel; electrofuels; HEFA pathway; Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process; alcohol-to-jet (ATJ); CHJ; DSHC; APR; ReFuelEU Aviation; CORSIA; renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO).

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — listed in Pending 2026-05-07. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, four ASTM categories, certified pathways, EU regulatory share targets; promoted from Pending.

Sulfur compounds in crude oil

Aliases. Crude-oil sulfur species; mercaptans; sulfides; disulfides; thiophenes; benzothiophenes; dibenzothiophenes (DBTs).

Definition. Sulfur is naturally present in all crude oils at concentrations of 0.1–3 wt% (sweet crudes <0.5 wt%; sour crudes >0.5 wt%, often >2 wt% in heavy sour crudes like Maya, Arabian Heavy). The volatile species (H₂S, light mercaptans) are removed at the wellhead during oil-and-gas processing; the refinery faces a wide range of bound sulfur compounds distributed across distillation cuts. The four principal classes — mercaptans (R-S-H), sulfides (R-S-R’), disulfides (R-S-S-R’), and thiophenes (heterocyclic 5-ring with S) — each have distinct hydrodesulfurization (HDS) reactivity and removal-difficulty. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, p. 5)

Attributes — sulfur-compound classes by HDS difficulty.

Class Structure Distillation cut HDS difficulty
Hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) gaseous gases (removed at wellhead) trivial
Mercaptans R-S-H naphtha, jet, diesel easy (mild HDS)
Sulfides R-S-R’ naphtha, jet, diesel easy (mild HDS)
Disulfides R-S-S-R’ jet, diesel moderate
Thiophenes five-ring + S naphtha, kerosene moderate
Benzothiophenes (BTs) benzene + thiophene fused diesel, gas oil hard (deep HDS)
Dibenzothiophenes (DBTs) two benzene + thiophene fused diesel, gas oil hard
4,6-dimethyl-DBTs (sterically hindered) DBT with methyl groups diesel very hard (controlling factor for ULSD)

(H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, p. 5; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Notes — distribution across distillation cuts. Sulfur compounds concentrate in heavier cuts: naphtha typically 100–500 ppm S; diesel 0.1–1 wt%; vacuum gas oil 1–3 wt%; vacuum residue 3–6 wt%. Sour crudes therefore put more burden on heavy-end conversion processes (FCC, hydrocracker, coker) than on naphtha hydrotreating. This is one driver of the price spread between sweet and sour crudes. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, p. 5)

Related terms. Hydrodesulfurization (HDS); Hydrotreating (HDS / HDN / HDM); Claus process (sulfur recovery); ULSD (ultra-low-sulfur diesel); sweet vs sour crude; petroleum refining (umbrella); naphtha; diesel fuel.

Source history. - H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017 — added 2026-05-08: four-class taxonomy, HDS-difficulty hierarchy, distribution across distillation cuts. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): refinery context.

Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄)

Aliases. H₂SO₄; oil of vitriol; battery acid (in dilute form); contact-process sulfuric acid.

Definition. A strong inorganic mineral acid (H₂SO₄), the largest-volume industrial chemical produced globally (~250 Mt/yr) and the cornerstone of phosphate-fertiliser manufacture, sulfate-pulp processing, alkylation acid catalysis, ore leaching, lead-acid batteries, and many specialty-chemical reactions. Sulfuric acid production is so ubiquitous that its annual production volume is conventionally used as an indicator of national industrial activity. Industrial production proceeds through the contact process: (i) S + O₂ → SO₂ (sulfur combustion or smelter off-gas capture); (ii) SO₂ + ½ O₂ → SO₃ over V₂O₅ catalyst at 400–600 °C; (iii) SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 6–7; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production ~250 Mt/yr
Largest end-use — phosphate fertiliser (DAP, MAP, SSP, TSP) ~60–65%
Caprolactam / Nylon 6 (Beckmann rearrangement) ~5%
Alkylation (refinery) ~1% (small volume)
Hydrofluoric acid + other inorganic chemistry ~5%
Ore leaching (Cu, U, Ni) ~5–10%
Lead-acid batteries ~3%
Other (TiO₂, dyes, detergents, water treatment) ~10–15%
Sulfur-source split ~75% from refinery + NG sulfur recovery (Claus); ~10% from smelter off-gas; ~15% from voluntary mining (Frasch process, declining)
Primary global producers China, US, Morocco, Russia, India

(H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, p. 6; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Notes — phosphate fertiliser linkage. Sulfuric acid is the dominant reagent for converting phosphate rock (Ca₅(PO₄)₃F) into wet-process phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄), the precursor to DAP / MAP / TSP fertilisers. ~60% of global H₂SO₄ goes through this route. The downstream gypsum (CaSO₄ · 2H₂O) co-product is largely landfilled (phosphogypsum). Together with the Claus process (sulfur recovery) and refinery hydrotreating (HDS), sulfuric acid is at the centre of the global sulfur cycle in industry. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, p. 6)

Notes — sulfur-mining displacement. US sulfur production was historically dominated by Frasch-process mining of underground deposits along the Gulf of Mexico (Louisiana, Texas), commercialised in the early 1900s. By 2000, recovered sulfur from petroleum + natural-gas processing had completely displaced Frasch mining — making the modern sulfuric-acid industry effectively a by-product industry of fossil-fuel processing. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 6–7)

Related terms. Claus process (sulfur recovery); hydrotreating (HDS / HDN / HDM); sulfur dioxide (SO₂); phosphate fertiliser; sweet vs sour crude; alkylation (refinery); chemicals of concern.

Source history. - H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017 — added 2026-05-08: definition, contact process, phosphate-fertiliser linkage, Frasch-displacement. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): industrial chemistry context.

Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) air pollution

Aliases. SO₂; sulphur dioxide emissions; acid rain precursor; PM2.5 precursor.

Definition. A toxic gas (SO₂) released to the atmosphere by combustion of sulfur-containing fuels (coal, fuel oil, untreated diesel, residual fuel) and by metallurgical smelting of sulfide ores. Atmospheric SO₂ (i) directly damages the human respiratory system — particularly children, the elderly, and asthma sufferers; (ii) oxidises in the atmosphere to sulfate (SO₄²⁻) aerosol, a primary component of fine particulate matter (PM2.5); (iii) reacts with atmospheric water to form sulfuric acid, the principal driver of acid rain (ecological damage to forests, soils, freshwater fish populations, building stone). SO₂ is regulated globally as a criteria air pollutant. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 1–2)

Attributes — US emissions trajectory and inventory.

Indicator Value
Total US SO₂ emissions (2013) ~5.17 Mt/yr
Power-plant (coal) share dominant single source (>40%)
Mobile sources (gasoline + diesel) share <2% (after 2017 Tier 3 / ULSD rules)
Refinery share ~5–10%
Smelter (non-ferrous metals) share ~10%
Pre-Clean-Air-Act US emissions (1970) ~30 Mt/yr (peak)
Reduction in mobile-source SO₂ via ULSD (2006+) >99.5%
Health-effect threshold (WHO 24-h average) 20 μg/m³

(H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 1–6; EPA NEI database)

Notes — hydrogen-enabled SO₂ reduction. The Praxair / Linde white paper computes that US refineries consume ~1.33 billion scf/day (~3 Mt/yr) of hydrogen specifically for desulfurisation (HDS) of liquid fuels, equivalent to avoiding ~21.9 Mt SO₂/yr. The downstream EPA Tier-3 rule (gasoline sulfur <10 ppm, effective 2017) and the global ULSD diesel rules have effectively eliminated mobile-source SO₂ as a significant emissions category. Industrial SO₂ regulation focuses on power-plant flue-gas desulfurisation (FGD scrubbers) and sour-gas processing. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 4–6)

Notes — IMO 2020 marine fuel rule. The International Maritime Organization’s “IMO 2020” rule capped marine bunker fuel sulfur at 0.5 wt% (down from 3.5 wt%) globally as of January 2020, with 0.1 wt% in Emission Control Areas. The rule reshaped global refining: heavy fuel oil (HFO, traditionally 2–3 wt% S) demand collapsed, and complex refineries with hydrocrackers + cokers absorbed the displaced low-value residue into transport-fuel pools. The rule eliminated several Mt/yr of marine SO₂ emissions, particularly in coastal cities. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017 — referenced; IEA 2020 Outlook on IMO impact)

Related terms. Hydrotreating (HDS / HDN / HDM); Claus process (sulfur recovery); sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄); motor fuels (umbrella); chemicals of concern; sweet vs sour crude; secondary organic aerosol (SOA); volatile chemical products (VCPs).

Source history. - H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017 — added 2026-05-08: definition, US emissions inventory, hydrogen-enabled SO₂ reduction, ULSD impact.

Synergistic catalysis (OXZEO)

Aliases. Bifunctional catalyst; oxide-zeolite (OXZEO) catalyst; tandem catalysis; relay catalysis.

Definition. A catalyst design strategy in which two distinct catalytic functions — typically a metal-oxide for CO/CO₂ activation and a zeolite for selective C–C coupling/cracking — are physically combined (or layered) so that the products of the first reaction become the substrates of the second within a confined micro-environment. In the OXZEO architecture, syngas (CO + H₂) is converted on the oxide to reactive intermediates (methanol, dimethyl ether, ketones) which are immediately funnelled into zeolite pores where they couple to light olefins, propylene or aromatics with selectivities that exceed the Anderson-Schulz-Flory (ASF) ceiling of conventional Fischer-Tropsch synthesis. (Zhang et al. 2024, pp. 109–110, citing Bao group and others)

Attributes — Zhang 2024 OXZEO performance benchmarks.

Reaction Catalyst CO conversion Target product selectivity
Syngas → light olefins Zn-CrOx/MOR high C2=–C4= ~73% (vs ASF cap 58%)
Syngas → light olefins ZnAl₂O₄/MOR high ethylene 65%
Syngas → light olefins Ge-AlPO-18/oxide optimised yield 48%
Syngas → aromatics Zn-ZrO₂/ZSM-5 20% aromatics 80%
Syngas → aromatics Zn-CrOx/ZSM-5 16% aromatics 73.9%
Syngas → light olefins (high single-pass) acid-density tuned 85% light olefins >80%

(Zhang et al. 2024, p. 110, citing experimental references)

Notes — mechanism. OXZEO breaks the canonical FT mechanism into two distinct steps: (i) on the oxide, CO is hydrogenated to a CHₓO intermediate (methanol, ketene, dimethyl ether); (ii) on the zeolite, the intermediate is selectively converted to the target product (light olefin via MTO-like chemistry; aromatic via MTA-like chemistry). The oxide’s role is to avoid CH₄ formation; the zeolite’s role is to select the target carbon-number range via shape-selectivity. The two catalysts must be chosen and physically arranged so that intermediates transfer efficiently without back-reaction. (Zhang et al. 2024, pp. 109–110)

Notes — significance for net-zero chemicals. Synergistic catalysis is the key technological enabler of Zhang’s “simplified petrochemical industry” vision: by escaping ASF’s selectivity ceiling, FT-like syngas chemistry can deliver target HVCs at high purity, dramatically reducing downstream separation energy and CO₂ emissions. Combined with green-H₂ + electrocatalytic CO₂-to-CO, OXZEO becomes the centerpiece of the C1-chemistry future. (Zhang et al. 2024, p. 110)

Related terms. Anderson-Schulz-Flory (ASF) distribution; Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process; Methanol-to-Olefins (MTO); methanol-to-aromatics (MTA); C1 chemistry; high-value chemicals (HVCs); zeolite catalyst.

Source history. - Zhang et al. 2024 — added 2026-05-08: OXZEO mechanism, performance benchmarks, role in defossilising HVCs.

Standard Effective Temperature (SET)

Aliases. SET; SET* (asterisk variant); Gagge SET; effective temperature.

Definition. A thermal-comfort index proposed by A.P. Gagge (1971) that equates a real environment (with given air temperature, mean radiant temperature, humidity, air velocity, occupant clothing and metabolic rate) to a standardised reference environment (50% relative humidity, 0.1 m/s air velocity, mean radiant temperature equal to air temperature, sedentary metabolic rate, light clothing). The SET value is the temperature in this reference environment that would produce the same physiological response (skin temperature + skin wetness) as the real environment. SET is more comprehensive than simple operative temperature because it integrates thermo-physiological response (sweating, vasoconstriction/dilation) — making it suitable for assessing thermal stress in hot or cold extremes. (Goessel 2025, pp. 27–31, citing ASHRAE 55 and Gagge 1971)

Attributes — SET-based thermal-sensation classes (ASHRAE 55).

SET range Sensation class Description
<17 °C very cold discomfort cold
17–22 °C cold mild cold discomfort
22–25 °C slightly cold acceptable cool
25–30 °C thermal-neutral / comfortable comfort zone
30–34 °C slightly warm mild warm discomfort
34–37 °C warm discomfort warm
37–41 °C hot thermal stress
>41 °C very hot severe heat stress, health risk

(Goessel 2025, p. 30 and Fig. 2.5, ASHRAE 55-2020)

Notes — SET-Degree-Hours (SET-DH) as renovation indicator. Goessel uses SET-Degree-Hours above 25 °C (DH = Σ over hours when SET > 25 °C of (SET − 25)) as the third optimisation indicator (alongside CGD and embodied carbon) — capturing the cumulative summer thermal discomfort experienced by occupants over a year. SET-DH is a continuous metric (vs binary “comfort/discomfort” thresholds) and integrates exposure intensity × duration. A value above ~5,000 K·h indicates severe summer-discomfort building — typical of poorly-insulated French residential without air-conditioning. (Goessel 2025, pp. 31, 89, Annexe D)

Notes — vs PMV/PPD models. SET is one of three principal thermal-comfort approaches alongside PMV/PPD (Predicted Mean Vote / Percentage Dissatisfied) and adaptive-comfort models. PMV/PPD requires more inputs (clothing, metabolic, air-velocity assumptions) and is less suited to extreme-heat scenarios because the underlying Fanger model breaks down beyond moderate ranges. SET retains physiological validity in heat-wave conditions where PMV cannot be reliably extrapolated. (Goessel 2025, pp. 27–31, citing Katić 2016 review)

Related terms. Thermal comfort (umbrella); PMV / PPD (Fanger model); adaptive thermal comfort; degree-hours; building renovation (umbrella); heat wave (climate); ASHRAE 55.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: SET definition, classes, SET-DH renovation indicator, vs PMV/PPD comparison (translated from French).

Synthetic rubbers (SBR / BR / NBR / EPDM / IIR / CR)

Aliases. Synthetic elastomers; synthetic rubber; SR; commodity-rubber family.

Definition. A family of elastomeric polymers produced from olefin and diolefin monomers (predominantly butadiene, styrene, isoprene, isobutylene, and chloroprene) by emulsion / solution / coordination polymerisation. After polymerisation, the rubber is vulcanised (cross-linked with sulfur or peroxides) to convert the linear polymer into the elastic, springy three-dimensional network that gives rubber its characteristic recovery from large deformations. Synthetic rubbers complement natural rubber (NR, from Hevea brasiliensis latex) — together accounting for ~30 Mt/yr global production, with synthetic ~60% and natural ~40%. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11)

Attributes — major synthetic-rubber types.

Type Monomers Production Tg Key applications
SBR (styrene-butadiene rubber) styrene + butadiene ~5 Mt/yr −55 °C (cold-emulsion E-SBR) tyre tread (>70%), shoe soles, conveyor belts
BR (polybutadiene) butadiene ~3 Mt/yr −108 °C (high-cis) tyre tread + sidewall (~70%), HIPS modifier
NBR (nitrile-butadiene rubber) acrylonitrile + butadiene ~0.5 Mt/yr −20 to −50 °C (depending on AN content) oil-resistant gaskets, fuel hoses, gloves (medical, lab)
EPDM (ethylene-propylene-diene) ethylene + propylene + ENB diene ~1 Mt/yr −55 °C weather-resistant roofing, automotive seals, garden hose
IIR / butyl (isobutylene-isoprene rubber) isobutylene + small amount of isoprene ~0.4 Mt/yr −68 °C inner tubes, tyre inner liners (very low gas permeability)
CR / Neoprene (chloroprene rubber) chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene) ~0.3 Mt/yr −40 °C flame-resistant + oil-resistant — wetsuits, gaskets
HNBR (hydrogenated NBR) NBR + H₂ small −30 °C oilfield seals, automotive timing belts
FKM (fluoroelastomer / Viton) vinylidene fluoride + HFP small −20 °C very high-T chemical-resistant seals

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11)

Notes — tyre industry coupling. The tyre industry consumes ~70% of all rubber globally — natural + synthetic combined, ~21 Mt/yr. SBR + BR dominate tread compounds; butyl rubber dominates inner liners; halobutyl variants resist O₂ permeation in tubeless tyres. The tyre industry’s olefin-monomer demand (butadiene + styrene + isoprene) ranks alongside plastics as a major HVC consumer. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11; cross-ref Butadiene entry)

Notes — vulcanisation. Charles Goodyear’s 1839 discovery of sulfur vulcanisation transformed natural rubber from a sticky, temperature-sensitive material into a useful elastomer; the same chemistry applies to most synthetic rubbers. Modern vulcanisation uses sulfur + accelerators (thiazoles, thiurams) at 130–180 °C, or peroxide-curing for sulfur-sensitive applications. Cross-link density determines the modulus and recovery characteristics. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.11)

Related terms. Butadiene; styrene; acrylonitrile; isoprene; isobutylene; chloroprene; polybutadiene rubber (BR); high-value chemicals (HVCs); olefins; emulsion polymerisation; tyre industry; natural rubber.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: synthetic-rubber family taxonomy, monomer chains, end-use shares, vulcanisation chemistry.

Syngas fermentation (SF)

Definition. A biofuel pathway in which lignocellulosic biomass is first gasified to syngas (mostly H₂, CO; with CO₂, CH₄, N₂ and impurities), the cleaned syngas is fermented by acetogenic bacteria (e.g. Clostridium ljungdahlii, Clostridium autoethanogenum) to ethanol, and the ethanol is then upgraded to aviation biofuel via the alcohol-to-jet (ATJ) route to ATJ-SPK. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 7–8)

Notes. SF is an alternative to chemical (Fischer–Tropsch) gas-to-liquid conversion of biomass-derived syngas, allowing operation at lower temperature and tolerating greater syngas-composition variability. LanzaTech has demonstrated SF at commercial scale, including conversion of CO-rich industrial waste gases (e.g. from steel mills) into ethanol and 2,3-BDO co-product. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 7–8, 14)

Related terms. Alcohol-to-jet (ATJ); sugar fermentation with alcohol upgrading (SuF); Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process; sustainable aviation fuels (SAF).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, biomass-to-syngas-to-ethanol-to-ATJ chain.

TEMOA (modelling framework)

Aliases. TEMOA; Tools for Energy Model Optimisation and Analysis.

Definition. A bottom-up Energy System Optimisation Model framework developed by NC State University in the US, first released in 2013 (Hunter et al. 2013) as a fully open-source pyomo-based ESOM with deliberate emphasis on uncertainty-handling and multi-stage stochastic programming. TEMOA is implemented in Python (pyomo) with LP / MILP / stochastic-LP formulation, perfect foresight, and annuity-factor end-effect mitigation. Manuel et al. 2025 found TEMOA in 3% of single-model pathway studies. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8; Hunter et al. 2013 cited)

Attributes — TEMOA design features.

Indicator Value
Solver paradigm LP / MILP / stochastic-LP (pyomo)
Programming language Python (fully open)
Foresight perfect or stochastic (Monte Carlo + scenario tree)
Milestone interpolation constant interpolation between milestones
End-effect mitigation annuity factors
Stochastic programming yes — distinctive feature (multi-stage uncertainty)
Open-source status fully open (custom licence)
Major users NC State, US national-laboratory research, US grid-planning analyses

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8; Hunter et al. 2013)

Notes — uncertainty focus. TEMOA’s distinctive feature is its support for stochastic optimisation — solving the model over a tree of future-state scenarios with assigned probabilities, delivering a “robust” investment plan that performs reasonably across all scenarios rather than optimising for a single deterministic future. This is particularly relevant under deep climate-policy uncertainty. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); TIMES; OSeMOSYS; MESSAGE; PyPSA; annuity factor (modelling); foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); stochastic optimisation.

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, design features, stochastic-optimisation focus.

Technology Warming Potential (TWP)

Aliases. TWP; time-resolved warming impact; dynamic GWP; technology-specific climate forcing.

Definition. A time-dependent climate metric, distinct from the static GWP100 used in standard LCA, that quantifies the cumulative radiative forcing of a technology’s emissions over a specified time horizon — taking into account the differing atmospheric lifetimes of the gases involved (CO₂ ~ centuries; CH₄ ~12 yr; N₂O ~120 yr). TWP is particularly important for analysing technologies where short-lived but powerful greenhouse gases (especially methane CH₄, with GWP100 ~30 but GWP20 ~85) play a major role — e.g., natural gas systems, blue ammonia, biogas, livestock, landfills. (Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 8–10, citing Edwards-Trancik 2014, Tanaka 2019)

Attributes — TWP vs static-GWP framework.

Aspect Static GWP100 TWP (time-dependent)
Time horizon 100 yr (default IPCC) user-selectable (10, 20, 50, 100 yr)
Methane weighting ~30 (GWP100) 85 (GWP20) → 30 (GWP100) → 7 (GWP500)
N₂O weighting ~273 (GWP100) similar magnitude
CO₂ weighting 1 (reference) 1 (reference)
Use case retrospective inventory prospective technology-comparison
Captures methane near-term impact poorly well
LCA standardisation yes emerging

(Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 8–10)

Notes — Mayer 2023 application to blue ammonia. Mayer et al. apply TWP to compare blue and green ammonia and find that methane upstream leakage (3% in some natural-gas value chains) substantially worsens blue ammonia’s climate performance in short time horizons — TWP10 of blue NH₃ exceeds brown NH₃ if methane leakage is high. In long time horizons (TWP100+), blue NH₃ outperforms brown. Green ammonia is consistently better across all time horizons, but its electricity intensity makes its TWP sensitive to grid-decarbonisation trajectory. (Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 8–10 and Fig. 5)

Notes — significance for climate-policy debate. TWP is increasingly relevant because climate-policy actually faces near-term stabilisation targets (2030 emissions peak, 2050 net-zero) — making short-time-horizon impacts disproportionately important. A technology with low GWP100 but high GWP20 (typical of biogas or blue NH₃ with leakage) may be inappropriate for 2030 climate goals even if it’s fine for 2100 goals. (Mayer et al. 2023, p. 8)

Related terms. Global Warming Potential (GWP); Pouvoir de Réchauffement Global (PRG); Life Cycle Assessment (LCA); methane leakage; Blue ammonia and green ammonia; natural gas; biogas; methane.

Source history. - Mayer et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: TWP definition, vs static GWP, ammonia-LCA application, climate-policy significance.

Take-or-pay / store-or-pay contract

Definition. A long-term commercial contract in which the off-taker (typically an emitter using a CO₂ transport-and-storage service, or a buyer in an LNG/pipeline analogue) commits to pay for a contracted volume even if it does not actually take the service — providing the infrastructure operator with revenue certainty against under-utilisation risk. Variants include “store-or-pay” (storage-specific), “ship-or-pay” (transport-specific), and minimum volume commitments (MVCs). (IEA 2026, pp. 22, 42, 44)

Notes — recent CCUS applications. Take-or-pay and minimum-volume-commitment contracts were critical to reducing volumetric risks at recent FIDs, including the Tallgrass Energy Trailblazer CO₂ pipeline (United States) and the expansion phase of Northern Lights (Norway). LNG and pipeline developments in oil and gas have long relied on take-or-pay contracts to underpin revenues for capital-intensive midstream assets — providing a template for adapting these instruments to CCUS, although CO₂ disposal carries long-term liability rather than intrinsic market value, requiring some adjustments to credit profiling. (IEA 2026, pp. 44–45)

Related terms. Cross-chain risk; bankability; minimum volume commitment; regulated asset base (RAB); hub and cluster model.

Source history. - IEA 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, CCUS applications, oil and gas analogues.

Technological innovation system (TIS)

Definition. A systemic framework for assessing innovation around a specific technology, in which the diffusion and adoption of technologies is conceptualised as a set of “functions” (related sets of activities) contributing to the path-dependent evolution of the system. Used by Kushnir et al. to evaluate the conditions for hydrogen direct reduction (H-DR) adoption in the Swedish steel industry. (Kushnir et al. 2020, pp. 2–3, citing Bergek et al. 2008, 2015; Hekkert et al. 2007, 2011)

Notes — analytical steps. The five-step process used in this analysis is: (1) define the technology and system boundaries; (2) identify components (actors, artefacts, institutions) and stage of development; (3) evaluate functions based on evidence from indicators; (4) identify blocking and inducement mechanisms; (5) discuss potential policy mechanisms to address barriers. (Kushnir et al. 2020, p. 2)

Related terms. TIS functions; HYBRIT.

Source history. - Kushnir et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-07: framework definition and analytical-steps note.

TIS functions

Definition. The set of system-level functions used in TIS analysis to characterise innovation-system performance. (Kushnir et al. 2020, p. 2 and Table 1, p. 3, adapted from Bergek et al. 2008)

Attributes — function and indicator types (Kushnir et al. 2020, Table 1).

Function Indicator types
Knowledge development patent and paper analysis (citations, volume, trajectories); R&D project size and orientation; learning curves
Influence on direction of search visions, expectations, beliefs; actor perceptions; regulations and policy; demand articulation; technical bottlenecks; crises in current business
Legitimation level of legitimacy; alignment between TIS, current legislation, and value base; influence on demand, legislation, firm behaviour
Resource mobilisation changing volume of capital (incl. seed/venture); changing human resources; changes in complementary assets
Entrepreneurial experimentation number of new entrants (incl. diversifying established firms); number of application types; breadth of technologies and complementary technologies
Developing external economies emergence of pooled labour markets; emergence of specialised intermediate goods/service providers; information flows and knowledge spill-overs
Market formation customer groups, application types, sales, etc.

Related terms. Technological innovation system.

Source history. - Kushnir et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-07: full functional list and indicator types.

Thermal bridge (pont thermique)

Aliases. Pont thermique (FR); thermal bridge; cold bridge; structural thermal bridge.

Definition. A localised path through the building envelope where heat flows preferentially because the local thermal resistance is lower than that of the surrounding envelope — typically at junctions (intermediate floor / external wall, partition wall / external wall, balcony / floor slab, window-frame to wall jamb, corners). Thermal bridges (i) increase heat-loss coefficient (additive to the U-value loss), (ii) lower interior surface temperature locally, creating condensation risk and mould growth, and (iii) reduce thermal comfort near affected surfaces. Quantified by the linear heat-transfer coefficient ψ (W/m·K) for line bridges (junctions) and point heat-transfer coefficient χ (W/K) for point bridges (anchors, fasteners). (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35; AFNOR EN ISO 14683)

Attributes — typical thermal-bridge ψ values.

Junction ψ (W/m·K) — uncorrected ψ — well-designed
Intermediate floor / external wall (legacy ITI) 0.6–1.0 0.10–0.15
Intermediate floor / external wall (ITE) 0.05–0.10 <0.05
Partition wall / external wall 0.2–0.4 0.05
Balcony / floor slab (cantilevered) 0.6–0.9 0.10–0.15 (with structural break)
Window-frame to wall jamb 0.05–0.15 0.02–0.05
Foundation / external wall 0.5–0.8 0.10–0.20

(Goessel 2025; AFNOR EN ISO 14683)

Notes — significance for renovation. Thermal bridges typically account for 15–30% of total envelope heat loss in unrenovated French residential. Interior insulation (ITI) does NOT correct most thermal bridges (the wall is insulated but the floor slabs aren’t), giving a partial improvement. Exterior insulation (ITE) wraps the entire envelope and dramatically reduces thermal bridging — one of its main advantages over ITI in terms of total heat-loss reduction. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35, 89–110; ITI vs ITE entry)

Related terms. Building envelope; Interior vs Exterior insulation (ITI / ITE); building renovation (umbrella); RE2020 / RT2012; building energy simulation (BES / SED); thermal bridge ψ.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, typical ψ values, ITI-vs-ITE thermal-bridge consequence.

Thermal mass / thermal inertia (buildings)

Aliases. Inertie thermique (FR); thermal mass; building thermal capacitance; effective heat-storage capacity.

Definition. The thermal-energy storage capacity of a building’s structural mass — concrete floors, brick walls, stone walls, masonry partitions — that absorbs heat during warm periods and releases it during cool periods, dampening interior temperature fluctuations. Quantified by effective thermal capacitance (J/K per m² floor) or thermal inertia (mass × specific-heat × thickness, kJ/m²K). High thermal mass is desirable for passive summer cooling (slow heating during the day, releasing heat at night) and for winter solar gain capture; low thermal mass causes rapid temperature swings and dependence on active heating/cooling. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35; AFNOR EN ISO 13786)

Attributes — typical building thermal-mass classifications.

Class Effective heat capacity (kJ/m²K) Examples
Very low <50 timber-frame, lightweight panels
Low 50–110 metal-frame + plasterboard, with no exposed mass
Medium 110–200 concrete slab, exposed brick (one face)
High 200–300 exposed concrete + brick (multiple faces)
Very high >300 massive stone walls (pre-1948 maison de bourg, châteaux)

(Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35; AFNOR EN ISO 13786)

Notes — Goessel typology relevance. Goessel’s pre-1915 maison de bourg typology has very high thermal mass (massive stone walls 50+ cm thick), making it inherently more resistant to summer overheating than the Chalandon (1969–1974) lightweight timber-frame typology. This explains part of the difference in renovation strategies: Chalandon needs active cooling and fans; maison de bourg can rely more on passive cooling + night ventilation. (Goessel 2025, pp. 75–80; Annexe A)

Notes — interaction with insulation. Interior insulation (ITI) thermally decouples the indoor space from the structural mass, reducing the effective thermal mass available for passive cooling. Exterior insulation (ITE) preserves the mass, keeping the benefit. This is one of several reasons why ITE is preferred for building physics, especially in warm climates. (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35)

Related terms. Building envelope; Interior vs Exterior insulation (ITI / ITE); building renovation (umbrella); Standard Effective Temperature (SET); passive cooling; Heat-wave health risk; building thermal mass.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: thermal-mass classification, Goessel typology relevance, ITI vs ITE interaction (translated from French).

Thermal energy storage (TES)

Definition. A storage technology that retains thermal energy by heating or cooling a storage medium (water, molten salt, rock, phase-change material) for later use in heating, cooling or power generation. The most widely deployed configuration is tank TES, often coupled with traditional heat-generation technologies for short-term variations in demand or, in some cases, for seasonal storage. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 16)

Notes — coverage in the 100% RE systems database. TES is the fourth most common storage option in 100% RE systems analyses, present in 19.4% of the 1,067 reviewed articles (after batteries 60.2%, e-hydrogen 45.5%, PHES 29.8%). It is particularly relevant where district heating with heat pumps or combined heat and power is the dominant heat-supply technology. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 16)

Related terms. Heat pump (HP); district heating (DH); concentrated solar power (CSP); pumped hydro energy storage (PHES); compressed air energy storage (CAES).

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, share in 100% RE database.

Techno-Economic Assessment (TEA)

Aliases. TEA; techno-economic analysis; techno-economic evaluation; LCOA / LCOH / LCOE evaluation; project-level financial-engineering analysis.

Definition. A structured methodology — closely related to but distinct from Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) — that quantifies the technical performance and economic viability of an industrial process, technology, or system, integrating capital and operational costs with technical-yield and energy-balance data. TEA outputs typically include: (i) the Levelised Cost of the product (LCOH for hydrogen, LCOA for ammonia, LCOE for electricity, LCOP for production, LCOH₂T for hydrogen transport); (ii) Net Present Value (NPV) over project lifetime; (iii) Internal Rate of Return (IRR); (iv) sensitivity to key parameters (CAPEX, OPEX, feedstock prices, lifetime, discount rate). TEA is often combined with LCA (together: “techno-economic-environmental analysis”) to evaluate decarbonisation technologies on both economic and environmental criteria. (Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 3–6; Khan et al. 2021; Romero-Piñeiro et al. 2025)

Attributes — TEA workflow.

Step Description
1. Define system boundary input + output flows, sub-process scope
2. Quantify mass + energy balances yield, energy intensity, water consumption
3. Estimate CAPEX scaling laws, vendor quotes, factor-based estimation
4. Estimate OPEX feedstock, energy, labour, maintenance, waste-disposal
5. Compute discounted-cash-flow NPV at chosen discount rate over project life
6. Compute Levelised Cost dominant output: LCOA / LCOH / LCOE / etc.
7. Sensitivity analysis one-at-a-time + Monte-Carlo on key parameters
8. Compare alternatives base case vs decarbonised options

(Mayer et al. 2023, pp. 3–6)

Notes — TEA outputs for ammonia (Mayer 2023).

Configuration LCOA (€/t NH₃) Carbon intensity (kg CO₂eq/kg NH₃)
Brown ammonia (SMR-based) 200–400 1.6–2.5
Brown ammonia (coal-based) 250–500 4.0–5.0
Blue ammonia (SMR + CCS) 350–600 0.5–0.8 (no CH₄ leak); 1.8 (3% leak)
Green ammonia (PV + PEM) 600–1,200 0.05–0.4
Green ammonia (wind + alkaline) 600–1,000 0.04–0.2

(Mayer et al. 2023, Table 3)

Notes — combination with LCA. Modern TEA is increasingly coupled with LCA in integrated assessment — Romero-Piñeiro 2025 (refinery green-H₂), Mayer 2023 (blue/green ammonia), Goessel 2025 (building renovation). The combination identifies sweet-spot technologies that are both economically feasible and environmentally preferred, vs. those competitive on only one dimension. (Mayer et al. 2023; Romero-Piñeiro et al. 2025; Goessel 2025)

Related terms. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA); Life Cycle Costing (LCC); Levelised Cost of Energy (LCOE); Levelised cost of hydrogen (LCOH); Net Present Value (NPV); Internal Rate of Return (IRR); Total Capital Investment (TCI); Total Cost of Ownership (TCO); blue and green ammonia.

Source history. - Mayer et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: TEA workflow, ammonia-LCOA outputs, integration with LCA. - Khan et al. 2021 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): hydrogen-pipeline TEA precedent. - Romero-Piñeiro et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): refinery green-H₂ TEA + LCA.

Total Capital Investment (TCI)

Aliases. Total Installed Cost (TIC) + Indirect Costs.

Definition. The total capital expenditure required to bring a project from concept to operational readiness, comprising the Total Installed Cost (TIC) of equipment and labour plus the indirect costs of design, engineering, permitting, contingency and site preparation. In the HDSAM hydrogen-pipeline cost framework, indirect costs typically equal 40% of TIC. (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 17–18)

Attributes — TCI components in HDSAM-style hydrogen pipelines.

Component Share of TIC
Site preparation 5%
Engineering and design 10%
Project contingency 10%
Permitting 3%
(Other indirect, summing to 40%) balance

(Khan et al. 2021, p. 18)

Notes. TCI is annualised via the Capital Recovery Factor (CRF) when computing the Levelized Cost of Hydrogen (LCOH). For Khan et al.’s 1,500 km, 36-inch H₂ pipeline case study, the inlet compressor TCI = 192 M C$ and the enroute compressor stations TCI = 275 M C$ (2019 C$). (Khan et al. 2021, pp. 26, 28)

Related terms. Capital Recovery Factor (CRF); Levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH); hydrogen pipeline; total installed cost (TIC).

Source history. - Khan et al. 2021 — added 2026-05-08: definition, indirect-cost composition, TCI usage.

Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)

Definition. The total costs associated with acquiring, operating and maintaining an asset over its full lifecycle, including purchase price, fuel/energy costs, maintenance and operating costs, insurance and end-of-life disposal/decommissioning. Distinguished from upfront cost (sticker price) by accounting for time-discounted cash flows over the asset’s useful life. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 379)

Notes — example: electric vs internal-combustion cars. - In China in 2024, two-thirds of electric cars sold were priced upfront lower than their ICE counterparts (vs. half in 2021); EVs already match or undercut ICEs on TCO across most market segments. - In Germany, the average upfront price premium for small battery electric cars was just over 40% above equivalent small ICE models in 2024 — but TCO favours BEV when fuel and maintenance are included. - ETP-2026 uses TCO as the comparative metric for cars, heat pumps and clean-energy-technology end-uses where lifetime costs differ markedly from purchase cost.

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 5910–5950)

Related terms. Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE); Levelised Cost of Production (LCOP); Net Present Value (NPV); battery electric vehicle (BEV); fuel cell electric vehicle (FCEV); heat pump (HP).

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, EV-vs-ICE TCO context.

Thermoforming (plastic processing)

Aliases. Vacuum forming; pressure forming; sheet thermoforming; cup forming.

Definition. A plastics processing method in which a thermoplastic sheet (typically pre-extruded HIPS, PP, PVC, PET, ABS, or APET) is heated to its softening temperature and then pulled or pressed against a mould surface — usually by vacuum (vacuum forming) or by combined vacuum + air pressure (pressure forming) — where it cools and retains the shape. Thermoforming produces shallow-draw, large-area shapes at relatively low tooling cost, and is the dominant production method for disposable cups, food packaging trays, blister packs, and large parts like dashboards and refrigerator liners. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Attributes — typical applications.

Indicator Value
Common polymers HIPS, PP, PET (APET), PVC, ABS, HDPE
Sheet thickness range 0.05–6 mm
Mould draft angle 5–10° (deeper than injection moulds)
Tooling cost low–medium (much cheaper than injection-mould tooling)
Cycle time 5–30 s (small parts in continuous “form-fill-seal” lines)
End-use — disposable cups, food trays ~30% (industrial scale, continuous)
End-use — blister packaging (pharma, electronics) ~20%
End-use — refrigerator liners, automotive interior ~25%
End-use — bath tubs, swimming-pool shells ~10%
End-use — agricultural pots, signs ~15%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.4 plastic forming methods)

Related terms. Injection moulding; extrusion (plastic processing); blow moulding; rotomoulding; calendering; polypropylene (PP); polystyrene (PS / HIPS / EPS); plastic processing (umbrella).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, applications, vacuum vs pressure forming.

Tetraethyl lead (TEL)

Aliases. TEL; (C₂H₅)₄Pb; tetraethyllead; lead anti-knock additive; Ethyl Corporation TEL.

Definition. An organolead compound (Pb(C₂H₅)₄, a colourless liquid with a sweet smell) added to gasoline at 0.6–0.8 g Pb/L since 1923 (US) as the dominant anti-knock additive — raising the effective octane number (RON) of low-octane refinery streams by 3–6 points per gram of lead, allowing higher-compression engines without engine knock. Phased out globally over the 1970s–2010s due to severe public-health and environmental harms: lead is a potent neurotoxin, especially harmful to children’s cognitive development; combustion converts TEL to atmospheric lead aerosol that settled on soils, water and food, causing population-wide blood-lead elevation. The TEL phase-out is one of the largest single global public-health successes of 20th-century environmental regulation. (Addicott 1971, p. 65; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4 historical context)

Attributes — TEL deployment and phase-out timeline.

Period Status
1923 (US) TEL commercialised by GM / Standard Oil / DuPont (Ethyl Corp)
1973 (US) EPA begins phasing out leaded gasoline due to catalytic-converter incompatibility (lead poisons the converter)
1995 (US) Leaded gasoline banned for on-road use
2000 (EU) Leaded gasoline banned EU-wide
2011 (Algeria) last European-region country eliminates leaded gasoline
2021 (Algeria) leaded petrol globally eliminated for road vehicles (UNEP confirmation)
Aviation low-lead “100LL” avgas remains in use for piston-engine aircraft
Replacement high-octane refinery streams (alkylate, reformate); oxygenates (MTBE, ethanol)

(Addicott 1971; Speight 2019; UNEP 2021)

Notes — public-health benefit. US population-average blood-lead levels fell from ~16 μg/dL (1976) to <1 μg/dL (2016) — a >90% reduction — driven primarily by TEL phase-out. Global IQ gains from lead phase-out are estimated in the literature at ~1–7 IQ points per child, potentially generating trillions of USD in cumulative economic benefit. The TEL phase-out is also one of the few major air-quality regulations driven primarily by neurodevelopmental concerns rather than respiratory or cancer endpoints. (EPA, UNEP, public-health literature)

Related terms. Octane number (RON / MON); knock; motor fuels (umbrella); aviation gasoline; MTBE; ethanol; chemicals of concern; alkylation (refinery).

Source history. - Addicott 1971 — added 2026-05-08: TEL function, anti-knock dosage, refinery context. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): phase-out timeline, public-health rationale.

Toluene diisocyanate (TDI) and Methylenediphenyl diisocyanate (MDI)

Aliases. TDI; MDI; diisocyanates; pMDI (polymeric MDI); 4,4′-MDI; 2,4-TDI / 2,6-TDI.

Definition. Two industrial diisocyanates that anchor the polyurethane (PU) supply chain. TDI (typically 80:20 mixture of 2,4- and 2,6-toluene diisocyanate isomers) is produced by phosgenation of toluenediamine (TDA), itself from toluene + nitric acid → dinitrotoluene → hydrogenation. MDI is produced by phosgenation of methylenedianiline (MDA), itself from aniline + formaldehyde condensation. TDI is preferred for flexible-foam applications; MDI is preferred for rigid-foam, elastomer, and coating applications.
