Both are powerful respiratory sensitisers and require strict workplace exposure controls. (Speight 2019, Chapters 8, 11.5.1)

Attributes — production and end-uses.

Indicator TDI MDI
Global production ~3 Mt/yr ~10 Mt/yr (incl. polymeric MDI)
Synthesis route toluene + 2 HNO₃ → DNT + 4H → TDA + 2 COCl₂ → TDI aniline + HCHO → MDA + 2 COCl₂ → MDI
Boiling point 251 °C 196 °C (4,4′-MDI)
Largest end-use — flexible PU foam ~70% (TDI dominates) ~10%
Largest end-use — rigid PU foam (insulation) ~10% ~50%
Largest end-use — elastomers, coatings, sealants ~15% ~25%
Largest end-use — adhesives ~5% ~15%
Health classification respiratory sensitiser, skin sensitiser same

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.5.1)

Notes — hydrogen demand. TDA + MDA production from dinitrotoluene + dinitrobenzene requires substantial hydrogen for reduction (hydrogenation). Together with hydrocracker and hydrotreater H₂ demand, isocyanate manufacturing is one of the largest industrial-H₂ consumers — making H₂ supply (and its decarbonisation via electrolysis) directly relevant to PU supply chains. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.5.1)

Related terms. Polyurethane (PU / PUR); benzene; toluene; aniline; formaldehyde; phosgene; chlor-alkali process; hydrogen; high-value chemicals (HVCs); plastic chemicals; chemicals of concern.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, TDA/MDA → diisocyanate routes, end-use shares, hydrogen demand.

Time-series aggregation (modelling)

Aliases. Typical-day clustering; representative-day method; time-slice aggregation; k-medoids clustering; chronological-extreme-period method.

Definition. A computational technique used in Energy System Optimisation Models (ESOMs) to reduce the temporal resolution of input time series (electricity demand, wind/solar capacity factors) from full hourly resolution (8,760 h/year) to a smaller set of representative timeslices, typical days, or representative weeks — typically 4 to 200 representative periods per year. The aggregated input dramatically reduces computational complexity (especially for multi-decade pathways) at the cost of accuracy in capturing extreme weather events and renewable variability. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 5–6; Pfenninger 2017, Kotzur et al. 2018 cited)

Attributes — common time-series aggregation methods.

Method Description Trade-off
Time-slice aggregation (TIMES) divide year into ~12 seasons × 4 day-types × 4 day-segments = 192 slices loses chronology; preserves seasonality
Typical-day clustering (k-medoids) cluster days into K representative days, weight by frequency best for medium resolution (8–48 typical days)
Typical-week clustering similar but at week level preserves weekly chronology
Hierarchical clustering nested aggregation flexibility
Chronological extreme-period method preserve worst-case days as additional clusters captures extreme events crucial for adequacy
Full hourly (PyPSA-Eur default) no aggregation high accuracy, high computational cost

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 6; Pfenninger 2017)

Notes — distortion. Coarse time-series aggregation (<8 typical days) systematically distorts model outputs against renewables (which need hourly variability captured) and toward dispatchable thermal generation. Pfenninger 2017 demonstrates >10% LCOE distortion at typical-day counts below 8. Modern best practice uses >100 typical periods per year for high-renewable systems. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 6; Pfenninger 2017)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); spatial aggregation (modelling); investment milestones (modelling); pathways (vs scenarios); Variable Renewable Energy (VRE).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, methods, distortion implications.

Spatial aggregation (modelling)

Aliases. Spatial resolution; nodal aggregation; transmission-network aggregation; regional aggregation; cluster-and-network reduction.

Definition. A complementary technique to time-series aggregation that reduces the spatial resolution of an Energy System Optimisation Model — collapsing the full transmission network and detailed sub-regional supply/demand into a smaller number of nodes and links — to make the model computationally tractable. Methods range from single-region national aggregation (most ESOM studies) to high-resolution multi-node power-flow representation (PyPSA-Eur with several hundred nodes) to full-detailed unit-commitment models. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 6; Frysztacki et al. 2023, Siala & Mahfouz 2019 cited)

Attributes — spatial-aggregation levels.

Level Resolution Use case
Single region 1 node national-aggregate models
Multi-region (continental) 5–30 nodes EU-wide / global IAM aggregation
State-level / utility-level 30–200 nodes US ReEDS, Ofgem analyses
Sub-regional / TSO-zone 100–1000 nodes PyPSA-Eur 256 nodes typical
Full bus-bar 10,000+ nodes unit-commitment / detailed grid studies

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 6)

Notes — Frysztacki distortion finding. Frysztacki et al. 2023 show that aggregating a 256-node power-flow PyPSA-Eur model to 37 nodes overestimates wind capacity by 28% and underestimates costs by 15%. Higher spatial resolution always reduces distortion in renewable-siting and transmission-investment studies; the modeller’s challenge is to find the resolution that captures system constraints without making the model intractable. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 6; Frysztacki et al. 2023)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); time-series aggregation (modelling); transmission network; pathways (vs scenarios); PyPSA framework.

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, levels, Frysztacki distortion finding.

Interior vs Exterior insulation (ITI / ITE)

Aliases. ITI (Isolation Thermique par l’Intérieur — French); ITE (Isolation Thermique par l’Extérieur — French); internal wall insulation (IWI); external wall insulation (EWI / ETICS — exterior thermal insulation composite system).

Definition. Two principal approaches for adding thermal insulation to an existing exterior wall: - ITI — insulation panels attached to the interior face of the wall, then covered with plasterboard. Less expensive, can be done room-by-room without scaffolding, doesn’t change the building’s exterior appearance — important for heritage / Article 4 / co-ownership constraints. Drawbacks: reduces interior floor area; creates thermal bridges at intermediate floors and partition walls; more risk of interstitial condensation; loses building’s thermal mass benefit. - ITE — insulation system attached to the exterior face of the wall, then rendered or clad. More expensive, requires scaffolding, changes the exterior appearance (challenge for heritage). Advantages: no loss of interior space; eliminates thermal bridges; preserves building’s thermal mass; better building envelope performance; eligible for additional renovation subsidies in France (MaPrimeRénov’). (Goessel 2025, pp. 32–35, 89–92)

Attributes — typical performance and cost (French context).

Indicator ITI ITE
Typical U-value achievable 0.30 W/m²K 0.20 W/m²K (better — no thermal bridges)
Insulation thickness needed 100–140 mm 120–160 mm
Cost (typical 2024) ~80–130 €/m² ~150–250 €/m²
Loss of interior surface ~5–10% 0%
Heritage / planning constraint none typically strict in protected zones (e.g. pre-1948 stone buildings)
Embodied-carbon (insulation) ~20–60 kg CO₂eq/m² ~30–80 kg CO₂eq/m²
Thermal-bridge correction partial (corner, junction) excellent
Implementation disruption high (occupant displacement) low (occupant remains)

(Goessel 2025, Annexe A and Sections 3.3.2)

Notes — Goessel optimisation finding. ITE consistently appears more frequently in Pareto-optimal renovation strategies than ITI (Goessel Sections 3.3, 3.4 results) when planning constraints allow it. ITE’s advantage is most pronounced in the Chalandon (1969–1974) typology where the building is already a poor performer; ITI is preferred for the heritage-constrained pre-1915 maison-de-bourg typology where ITE is regulatorily blocked. (Goessel 2025, pp. 100–110, 123–130)

Related terms. Building envelope; building renovation (umbrella); heat pump (HP); RE2020 / RT2012; DPE (Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique); embodied carbon (buildings); thermal bridge.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: ITI vs ITE definition, performance/cost table, optimisation finding (translated from French).

Investment milestones (modelling)

Aliases. Milestone years; decision years; investment periods; planning periods.

Definition. Discrete time steps within an Energy System Optimisation Model’s investment horizon at which the model makes capacity-investment decisions — distinguishing investment-decision points from the operational sub-time-steps that occur between them. The number of milestones (|M|) and their spacing determine both the resolution of the investment trajectory and the model’s computational tractability. Inter-milestone interpolation methods (no interpolation, constant, linear) determine how investment costs and capacity utilisation are accounted for in years between milestones. (Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 5–7 and Fig. 5)

Attributes — typical milestone configurations.

Configuration Example Used in
1-year milestones every year (most precise) UK National Grid Future Energy Scenarios
5-year milestones 2025, 2030, 2035, …, 2050 most ESOM literature; TIMES default
10-year milestones 2025, 2035, 2045, 2050 computationally cheap, low resolution
Variable spacing 5-year early; 10-year late captures near-term policy detail
Custom (year-by-year early, decade later) 2025, 2026, …, 2030, 2040, 2050 hybrid

(Manuel et al. 2025, pp. 5–6 and Fig. 5)

Notes — inter-milestone distortions. Models with sparse milestones can introduce inter-milestone effects — the misalignment between milestone length (MLₘ) and remaining lifetime of an asset (LifeRemᵢ,ₘ) can artificially extend an asset’s effective lifetime within the model. TEMOA and MESSAGE scale down distorted capacity by remaining-lifetime / milestone-length ratio to mitigate; TIMES has more elaborate corrections; OSeMOSYS leaves the distortion uncorrected. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 6 and eqs. 10–12)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); time-series aggregation (modelling); spatial aggregation (modelling); end effects (modelling); foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); inter-milestone effects.

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, configurations, inter-milestone-distortion mechanism.

Knowledge-stock effects (modelling)

Aliases. Knowledge stock; experience accumulation; tacit-knowledge effects; technology familiarity.

Definition. A constraint mechanism in Energy System Optimisation Models in which the rate at which a country / region can deploy a given technology is endogenously linked to the past deployment of that technology in that location — capturing the real-world phenomenon that local industrial capacity, workforce expertise, regulatory familiarity, and supply-chain maturity all accumulate with deployment. Without it, ESOMs may schedule unrealistically rapid deployment of a previously-absent technology. Knowledge-stock effects are a subset of deployment-growth constraints used to mitigate opportunistic investment behaviour. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 7; Mannhardt et al. 2024 cited)

Attributes — typical formulations.

Aspect Description
Stock variable accumulated knowledge K(t) decays slowly absent deployment
Growth limit new deployment in milestone m ≤ f(K(t), market size)
Decay rate typical 5–10% per year (loss of expertise without active deployment)
Cross-region transfer partial — international expertise spillovers
Origin Mannhardt et al. 2024 implementation in IAM context

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 7; Mannhardt et al. 2024)

Notes — significance. Knowledge-stock effects are one of the principal mechanisms used to anchor ESOM pathways in real-world deployment dynamics, preventing the unrealistic “everything-deployed-at-once” outcomes that perfect-foresight ESOMs sometimes produce. They are gaining popularity in post-2020 modelling but remain inconsistently applied. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 7)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); endogenous learning (modelling); endogenous early retirement; deployment-growth constraints; opportunistic investment behaviour; foresight (perfect / limited / myopic).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, formulation, significance.

Opportunistic investment behaviour (modelling)

Aliases. Investment delay pathology; cost-decline-waiting; learning-curve gaming; perfect-foresight artefact.

Definition. A pathological behaviour exhibited by Energy System Optimisation Models with perfect foresight and endogenous (or assumed-exogenous) cost-decline curves: the model delays deployment of a learning-prone technology until later milestones to take advantage of the future cost reductions, missing the very deployment that drives those cost reductions in reality. This produces unrealistic pathways where decarbonisation appears to wait for technological maturity rather than driving it. Identified by Manuel et al. 2025 as a fundamental challenge in long-term ESOM design. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 7; Heuberger et al. 2017 cited)

Attributes — manifestation and mitigation.

Aspect Description
Manifestation model defers solar PV / battery / electrolyser deployment to last decade
Underlying cause perfect foresight + exogenous cost decline; or endogenous learning under the same
Mitigation 1 deployment-growth constraints (cap on annual additions)
Mitigation 2 knowledge-stock effects (deployment unlocks faster future deployment)
Mitigation 3 endogenous learning + deployment-growth caps combined
Mitigation 4 switch to limited / myopic foresight

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 7)

Notes — significance. Opportunistic-investment behaviour is the modelling-pathology counterpart to the policy-debate question of whether front-loaded decarbonisation (deploy now to drive learning) or back-loaded (wait for cheaper technology) is preferable. Heuberger et al. 2017 showed it can shift carbon-budget pathways by 10–20%. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 7)

Related terms. Endogenous learning (modelling); knowledge-stock effects; foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); pathways (vs scenarios); Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); investment milestones.

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, manifestation, mitigation strategies.

Linear / mixed-integer / non-linear programming (LP / MILP / NLP)

Aliases. LP; MILP; NLP; mathematical-programming formulations; convex / non-convex optimisation.

Definition. Three broad classes of mathematical-optimisation problems differing in (i) whether decision variables are continuous-only (LP), continuous + integer (MILP), or general non-linear (NLP), and (ii) whether the objective and constraint functions are linear or non-linear: - LP (Linear Programming) — both objective and constraints linear, all variables continuous; solvable in polynomial time by simplex / interior-point methods. - MILP (Mixed-Integer Linear Programming) — adds integer variables (often binary 0/1, e.g. for unit-commitment, technology-selection); NP-hard but tractable for moderately-sized problems via branch-and-bound + cutting planes. - NLP (Non-Linear Programming) — non-linear objective or constraints; convex NLP solvable; non-convex NLP can have multiple local optima.

In Manuel et al. 2025’s review of ESOMs, LP dominates (67% of studies), MILP is the second-most-used (16%), and non-linear approaches are rare (~3%). (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8 and Fig. 8b)

Attributes — formulation choice trade-offs.

Formulation Strengths Limitations
LP fast, polynomial-time, large-scale tractable can’t represent unit-commitment, integer technology choices
MILP represents binary choices (on/off, build/no-build), unit commitment NP-hard, computational cost rises sharply
NLP (convex) smooth non-linearities (e.g. quadratic costs) requires convexity for global optimum
NLP (non-convex) full reality (efficiency curves, gas-flow Weymouth) local optima; unreliable solutions

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8)

Notes — typical ESOM choice. LP is the workhorse for capacity-expansion ESOMs (TIMES, OSeMOSYS, PyPSA, MESSAGE-default). MILP is added when unit-commitment matters (PyPSA with extensions, PLEXOS). Non-linear formulations are rare because they sacrifice tractability for marginal accuracy gain in long-term planning. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); TIMES; OSeMOSYS; PyPSA; TEMOA; MESSAGE; mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: LP/MILP/NLP definitions, ESOM share, formulation trade-offs.

Tier 3 / Euro 6 fuel standards

Aliases. EPA Tier 3; Euro 6 (vehicle); EN 228 (gasoline); EN 590 (diesel); ULSD + ULSG; reformulated gasoline (RFG).

Definition. Modern motor-fuel-quality regulations issued by the US EPA (Tier 3, 2017) and the EU (Euro 6 vehicle standard + EN 228 / EN 590 fuel standards) that set strict limits on sulfur content (≤10 ppm), aromatic content, benzene content, RVP, oxygenate content, and other parameters in motor gasoline and diesel sold for on-road use. The standards are co-designed with vehicle emission-control system requirements (catalytic converters, particulate filters, selective catalytic reduction) which are poisoned or impaired by sulfur and other contaminants in fuel. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, p. 6; Addicott 1971; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Attributes — key limits.

Parameter EPA Tier 3 (US, 2017+) Euro 6 / EN 228 (EU)
Gasoline sulfur ≤10 ppm ≤10 ppm
Diesel sulfur ≤15 ppm Tier 2; <10 ppm planned ≤10 ppm
Gasoline benzene ≤0.62 vol% ≤1.0 vol%
Gasoline aromatics ≤22 vol% ≤35 vol%
Gasoline olefins ≤8 vol% ≤18 vol%
Gasoline oxygenate up to 10 vol% ethanol (E10) up to 10 vol% ethanol
RVP (summer high-ozone) 7.0 psi 60 kPa Class A
Diesel cetane ≥40 ASTM D975 #2 ≥51 EN 590

(H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, p. 6; EPA Tier 3 final rule; EU Directive 2009/30/EC)

Notes — global cascade. US Tier 3 + Euro 6 + Japan / S Korea J-OBDII / Bharat Stage VI together cover ~80% of global on-road vehicles. Lower-income markets (sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Latin America) historically retained higher-S fuel, but UNEP-led campaigns since 2010 have driven progressive sulfur-reduction commitments. China’s National VI standard (2020) mirrors Euro 6. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, p. 6; UNEP Africa Cleaner Fuels)

Related terms. Motor fuels (umbrella); diesel fuel; ULSD; sulfur dioxide (SO₂) air pollution; hydrotreating (HDS); octane number; Reid Vapour Pressure; tetraethyl lead (TEL); ethanol.

Source history. - H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017 — added 2026-05-08: Tier 3 specifications, regulatory cascade. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): EU EN 228 / EN 590 limits.

Top-18 chemicals (Levi & Cullen / IEA framing)

Aliases. Top-18; chemical-sector dominant chemicals; HVC + ammonia + methanol + others.

Definition. A pragmatic framing of the global chemical sector around the 18 largest-tonnage chemicals that, together, account for 63% of process energy consumption and 75% of GHG emissions in the chemical sector. Used by the IEA in Energy Technology Perspectives and by Levi & Cullen 2018 as the canonical scope for sector-wide decarbonisation analysis. The 18 chemicals (volumes in Mt/yr, ~2013 baseline): (Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1726; IEA 2017 Energy Technology Perspectives, cited)

Attributes — the 18 chemicals.

Chemical Volume Use
Ammonia ~170 Mt/yr fertilisers, urea, nitric acid
Methanol ~110 Mt/yr formaldehyde, MTBE, MTO/MTP, fuels
Ethylene ~150 Mt/yr polyethylene, EO/MEG, EDC/VCM, ethylbenzene/styrene
Propylene ~110 Mt/yr polypropylene, propylene oxide, acrylonitrile, cumene
Butadiene ~12 Mt/yr SBR, BR, ABS, HMDA
Benzene ~46 Mt/yr styrene, cumene, cyclohexane, nitrobenzene → MDI
Toluene ~21 Mt/yr TDI, solvent, → benzene + xylene (TDP)
p-Xylene ~50 Mt/yr terephthalic acid → PET
o-Xylene ~5 Mt/yr phthalic anhydride
Mixed xylenes balance solvent, isomerise to PX
Ethylene oxide / glycol (MEG) ~30 Mt/yr each PET, polyols, antifreeze
Vinyl chloride monomer (VCM) ~50 Mt/yr PVC
Styrene ~30 Mt/yr polystyrene, ABS, SBR
Acrylonitrile ~6 Mt/yr ABS, acrylic fibre, NBR
Carbon black ~14 Mt/yr tyres, pigments
Urea ~190 Mt/yr (fertiliser) fertiliser, melamine
Nitric acid ~78 Mt/yr ammonium nitrate fertiliser, adipic acid, TDI/MDI precursor
Sulfuric acid ~250 Mt/yr phosphate fertiliser, alkylation acid, lead-acid battery

(Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1726, Fig. 1; cross-ref individual entries)

Notes — significance for decarbonisation. The Top-18 framing makes chemical-sector mitigation tractable: efforts targeting these 18 chemicals capture the bulk of the abatement potential. Levi & Cullen show that ~10 first-tier intermediate transformations (ammonia → urea, ethylene → polyethylene, etc.) dominate chemical-feedstock consumption; fertilisers + thermoplastics together account for >60% of chemical-product output. Defossilising these flows requires alternative carbon sources (biomass, CO₂, recycled feedstock) plus electrified process heat plus green H₂. (Levi and Cullen 2018, p. 1731)

Related terms. Petrochemicals (umbrella); high-value chemicals (HVCs); Material Flow Analysis (MFA / Sankey diagram); ammonia; methanol; ethylene; propylene; benzene; non-energy use of fossil fuels; near-zero emissions materials.

Source history. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 18-chemical taxonomy, 63%/75% energy-and-emission share, abatement-prioritisation logic.

Typical Meteorological Year (TMY)

Aliases. TMY (Typical Meteorological Year); année-type (FR); IWEC (International Weather for Energy Calculations — close variant); reference weather year.

Definition. A synthetic 8,760-hour climate file (one full year, hour-by-hour) constructed from 20–30 years of historical meteorological observations to be statistically representative of the long-term climate at a given location. The TMY is the standard input format for building-energy-simulation software (EnergyPlus EPW format, COMETh, IDA-ICE) and avoids the need to simulate the building over many years to capture average behaviour. Constructed by selecting, for each calendar month, the most representative historical month from the multi-decadal observation record (typically using the Finkelstein-Schafer statistics on temperature, humidity, radiation, wind). (Goessel 2025, pp. 60–61, citing AFNOR EN ISO 15927-4)

Attributes — TMY construction.

Step Description
1. Source data 20–30 yr hourly meteorological observations
2. Calendar-month statistics for each year × month, compute monthly distributions of T, RH, GHI, wind
3. Finkelstein-Schafer score rank each historical month by closeness to long-term distribution
4. Smooth concatenation join 12 selected months with smooth transitions to avoid discontinuities
5. Output format EPW (EnergyPlus Weather), TM2, TMY3, IWEC
Variables included T_air, RH, T_dew, T_global, T_diffuse, T_normal, wind_speed, wind_direction, P, cloud, precip

(Goessel 2025, p. 61; AFNOR EN ISO 15927-4)

Notes — prospective TMY (Goessel). Goessel constructs prospective TMY climate files representing the period 2020–2058 (the renovated-building lifetime), built from EURO-CORDEX 11 RCP8.5 projections after CDF-t bias correction. This delivers a single 8,760-hour climate file that captures the average mid-21st-century French climate, suitable as a single-pass BES input. Without prospective TMY, BES must be run for many individual climate years — computationally prohibitive for 1000s of renovation strategies in optimisation. (Goessel 2025, p. 61 and Sections 2.5.1)

Related terms. EURO-CORDEX; Bias correction (climate); building energy simulation (BES / SED); RE2020 / RT2012; building renovation (umbrella); Cooling and Heating degree days (CDD / HDD); Climate risk in power-system planning.

Source history. - Goessel 2025 — added 2026-05-08: TMY definition, construction steps, prospective-TMY innovation (translated from French).

TIMES (modelling framework)

Aliases. TIMES; The Integrated MARKAL-EFOM System; ETSAP-TIAM (global TIMES); MARKAL (legacy predecessor).

Definition. A bottom-up, multi-period, technology-rich Energy System Optimisation Model framework developed and maintained by the IEA’s Energy Technology Systems Analysis Programme (ETSAP). TIMES is the most-used ESOM framework globally — Manuel et al. 2025 found it in 28% of pathway studies (34% combined with its predecessor MARKAL). The framework is implemented in GAMS, supports linear programming (LP) with mixed-integer extensions, perfect or limited foresight, and includes salvage values and discounting end-effect mitigation. National variants (UK-TIMES, US TIMES, ETSAP-TIAM) and regional variants (TIMES-Europe) are widely used in government energy-policy analysis. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8 and Fig. 8a; Loulou et al. 2016 cited)

Attributes — TIMES design features.

Indicator Value
Solver paradigm LP / MILP (GAMS)
Foresight perfect (default); limited (rolling-horizon) supported
Milestone interpolation linear interpolation between investment milestones (sophisticated)
End-effect mitigation salvage values + discounting
Endogenous learning optional
Endogenous early retirement optional
Spatial resolution flexible (single-region to multi-region)
Temporal resolution typical-day clustering (4–48 timeslices/year typical)
Major users IEA, EU Commission JRC, UK BEIS, US EPA, Mexico SENER, India NITI Aayog
Open-source status partially open (model code; commercial GAMS solver required)

(Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8; Loulou et al. 2016 documentation)

Notes — significance. TIMES is the inheritor of MARKAL (Brookhaven National Laboratory, 1970s) and EFOM (European Commission, 1980s). The IEA-ETSAP programme maintains TIMES as a community-supported framework with periodic updates. TIMES outputs underpin many national long-term decarbonisation studies and feed into IEA Energy Technology Perspectives and government roadmaps. (Manuel et al. 2025, p. 8)

Related terms. Energy System Optimisation Model (ESOM); OSeMOSYS; MESSAGE; PyPSA; TEMOA; Integrated Assessment Model (IAM); foresight (perfect / limited / myopic); end effects (modelling); salvage value (modelling); endogenous learning (modelling).

Source history. - Manuel et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-08: definition, share of literature, design features, significance.

Textile fibres (synthetic and natural)

Aliases. Fibres textiles (FR); synthetic fibres; natural fibres; cellulosic fibres; polyamide / nylon textile; cotton; viscose / lyocell; polyester (textile); acrylic.

Definition. A taxonomy of yarns and fabrics used in clothing and home-textile manufacture, comprising: - Synthetic fibres — polyester (PET-textile, ~52% of global production), polyamide (Nylon 6 / 6,6), acrylic (PAN), polypropylene, elastane (Lycra). All petrochemical-derived (mainly from naphtha steam cracker). - Natural fibres — cellulosic — cotton (~25% of global production), flax/linen, hemp. - Natural fibres — protein — wool, silk, cashmere (small share, high value). - Cellulose-derived synthetic — viscose, modal, lyocell (Tencel), cupro — produced from wood pulp via chemical regeneration. - Recycled — rPET (from PET bottles), mechanical-recycled cotton, Renewcell circulose. Small but growing share (~2% in 2018, target ~30% by 2030 in EU). (Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 189–192; Speight 2019)

Attributes — global textile-fibre production (2018, ~110 Mt/yr).

Fibre Share (%) Global tonnage (2018) Source
Polyester (PET-textile) 52% ~57 Mt naphtha steam cracking → PTA + MEG → PET
Cotton 25% ~26 Mt natural cellulose (water-intensive)
Polyamide (Nylon 6 / 6,6) 5% ~5.5 Mt benzene → cyclohexane → caprolactam / adipic acid + HMDA
Cellulosics (viscose, lyocell) 6% ~6.6 Mt wood-pulp regeneration
Wool, silk, others 4% ~4.4 Mt animal-derived
Polypropylene textile 3% ~3.3 Mt propylene polymer
Acrylic (PAN) 2% ~2.2 Mt acrylonitrile polymer
Recycled (rPET, etc.) <2% <2 Mt growing rapidly
Other (elastane, polyimide, aramid) <1% small specialty

(Niinimäki et al. 2020, p. 191 and Fig. 1)

Notes — synthetic-fibre microplastic pollution. Polyester, polyamide, acrylic and polypropylene fabrics shed microfibres during washing — typically 1,500–4,500 fibres per kg garment per wash cycle. Globally these sum to ~190,000 t/yr of primary marine microplastic pollution (~35% of total marine microplastic input) — the single largest source. Microfibre filters in washing machines (mandatory France 2025) and front-loading vs top-loading machine choice substantially affect emissions. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 191, 195)

Notes — water-and-chemical footprint by fibre type. Cotton has the highest water footprint (~10,000 L/kg garment), followed by viscose. Polyester has the lowest water footprint but highest carbon footprint (5–10 kg CO₂eq/kg garment). Lyocell (Tencel) is the lowest-impact cellulosic fibre — closed-loop solvent recycling makes it ~50–80% less impactful than viscose. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 191–193)

Related terms. Fast fashion; polyester (PET); polyamides (Nylon); polypropylene (PP); microplastics; mechanical recycling; chemical recycling; petrochemicals (umbrella); steam cracking (vapocracking); Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR); circular economy.

Source history. - Niinimäki et al. 2020 — added 2026-05-08: textile-fibre taxonomy, global production share, microfibre pollution, water-and-chemical-footprint comparison. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): polymer-chemistry origins of synthetic fibres.

Town gas

Definition. A gaseous mixture produced from coal gasification, in which oxygen and steam oxidise coal to yield approximately 50–60% hydrogen plus c. 30% CH₄ and c. 20% CO₂ and CO. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 79)

Notes. Town gas with ~50–60% H₂ was stored commercially in saline aquifers in France (Beynes), the Czech Republic (Lobodice) and Germany (Engelborstel, Bad Lauchstaedt) from the 1950s through the 1970s; some changes in composition during storage are attributed to bio- and geochemical reactions. A separate cavern at Kiel, Germany stored town gas with 62% hydrogen in the 1960s–1970s. (Miocic et al. 2023, p. 79 and Table 3, p. 78, citing Buzek et al. 1994; Kruck and Crotogino 2013; Panfilov 2016)

Related terms. Hydrogen; salt cavern; porous rock hydrogen storage; saline aquifer.

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: composition and historical-storage notes.

Turboelectric propulsion

Definition. An electric-powertrain configuration for aviation in which a (hydrogen) gas turbine drives a generator, which in turn powers electric motors connected to the propulsors (turbofan, turboprop or turboshaft). No batteries are used (HE = 0). In the full turboelectric configuration HP = 1; in the partial turboelectric configuration the gas turbine partially diverts mechanical power to the generator/electric-motor circuit while the rest is delivered directly to the propulsor (HE = 0; 0 < HP < 1). (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, p. 24)

Notes — example projects. NASA’s STARC-ABL (Single-aisle Turboelectric AiRCraft with an Aft Boundary-Layer propulsor) demonstrated 12% fuel-burn reduction versus a conventional baseline. The Wright ECO-150R (≤150 seats, ~3,000 km range) demonstrated ~44% fuel-burn reduction. NASA’s N3-X turboelectric blended-wing-body design demonstrated ~63% energy and 90% NOₓ reductions versus conventional configurations and is proposed as the next-generation architecture to meet environmental targets. Turboelectric propulsion can use hydrocarbon-based fuels (biofuels, electrofuels) or H₂ instead of fossil kerosene. (Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023, pp. 24, 31)

Related terms. Hybrid electric propulsion; fuel cell (aviation); hydrogen aviation; blended wing body (BWB); lithium-ion battery (aviation).

Source history. - Su-ungkavatin et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: definition, full vs partial variants, NASA project benchmarks.

Urea (CO(NH₂)₂)

Aliases. Carbamide; urea fertiliser; urea (industrial); CH₄N₂O.

Definition. A solid organic compound (CO(NH₂)₂, white crystalline solid) and the largest-volume single nitrogen fertiliser globally — accounting for ~50% of all synthetic-N applied to crops worldwide. Industrial urea is produced by reacting anhydrous ammonia with carbon dioxide at 150–200 °C and 100–250 bar via two reversible reactions: (1) NH₃ + CO₂ → ammonium carbamate (NH₂COONH₄); (2) ammonium carbamate ↔︎ urea + H₂O. Urea is preferred over direct ammonia application because of its high N content (46% by weight), solid form (easier transport, storage, application), and reduced volatility / ammonia-loss compared to ammonium-based fertilisers. (Mingolla & Rosa 2025, p. 3 and Fig. 1; Royal Society 2020)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global urea production ~190 Mt/yr (largest single nitrogen-fertiliser product)
N content (mass basis) 46%
End-use — agricultural fertiliser ~80% (~150 Mt/yr)
End-use — non-agricultural ~20% (~40 Mt/yr) — urea-formaldehyde resins, urea-AdBlue, animal-feed supplement, melamine, plywood adhesives
Synthesis temperature 150–200 °C
Synthesis pressure 100–250 bar
Per-pass conversion 50–80% (with recycle to total ~99%)
Energy intensity ~7 GJ / t urea (above and beyond the ammonia input)
CO₂ feedstock requirement ~0.74 t CO₂ / t urea

(Mingolla & Rosa 2025; Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5)

Notes — CO₂-utilisation balance. Each tonne of urea produced consumes ~0.74 t of CO₂ as feedstock — making urea synthesis one of the largest commercial CO₂-utilisation streams globally (~140 Mt CO₂/yr captured into urea production). However, the CO₂ is released back to the atmosphere when urea is field-applied and hydrolyses (urea + H₂O → 2 NH₃ + CO₂). The net carbon balance of urea is therefore neutral on the CO₂-cycle but the nitrogen end-use creates substantial N₂O emissions (the dominant fertiliser GHG impact). (Mingolla & Rosa 2025; cross-ref nitrogen-fertilisers entry)

Notes — AdBlue / DEF. A 32.5% urea aqueous solution (AdBlue / DEF — Diesel Exhaust Fluid) is injected into diesel engine exhaust after catalytic converter (SCR — Selective Catalytic Reduction) to reduce NOₓ emissions to N₂. Mandatory in modern diesel passenger cars and trucks (Euro 6 / 6d). Global AdBlue production ~30 Mt/yr. (Speight 2019, Chapter 6.5)

Related terms. Ammonia (as hydrogen carrier); Nitrogen fertilisers (umbrella); Haber-Bosch process; carbon capture and utilisation (CCU); formaldehyde; urea-formaldehyde resin; nitrous oxide (N₂O).

Source history. - Mingolla & Rosa 2025 — added 2026-05-08: urea definition, statistics, agricultural and non-agricultural end-uses. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): industrial-process specifics + AdBlue.

UN Global Plastics Treaty (INC)

Aliases. Global Plastics Treaty; INC (Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee on Plastic Pollution); UN Plastics Treaty; UNEP Plastics Treaty.

Definition. A multi-stage UN-led international treaty negotiation, formally launched in March 2022 (UNEP Resolution 5/14), aiming to develop a legally-binding global agreement to end plastic pollution across the full plastics life cycle — including upstream production, downstream waste-management, and chemical hazards. Five INC sessions took place between 2022 and 2025 (Punta del Este, Paris, Nairobi, Ottawa, Busan), with the treaty text expected to be finalised in subsequent rounds. The treaty is the first major UN environmental agreement specifically targeting an industrial product category (rather than emissions, biodiversity, or waste-management generic frameworks) and represents a key venue for upstream (production-side) interventions on petrochemical lock-in. (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 607, 612–613; UNEP Resolution 5/14)

Attributes — INC negotiating-session timeline.

Session Date Location Outcome
INC-1 November 2022 Punta del Este, Uruguay scope agreed, framing for negotiations
INC-2 June 2023 Paris, France options paper, “high-ambition coalition” emerges
INC-3 November 2023 Nairobi, Kenya draft “zero” treaty text
INC-4 April 2024 Ottawa, Canada continued draft refinement
INC-5 November–December 2024 Busan, South Korea major sticking points (production caps, chemicals, finance)
INC-5.2 August 2025 Geneva continuation; treaty text not finalised
Future sessions 2025+ TBD depends on diplomatic progress

(UNEP INC documentation)

Notes — Tilsted 2023 framing. Tilsted argues the INC must include upstream production-side interventions (caps on virgin-polymer production, fossil-feedstock pricing, removal of subsidies) — not just downstream waste-management. The “high-ambition coalition” (~70 countries, Norway-Rwanda-led) supports this; the “petrochemical alliance” (Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iran, India, China) opposes production caps. Treaty effectiveness will depend on how this fault line is resolved. (Tilsted et al. 2023, pp. 612–613)

Notes — comparison with other UN treaties. The Global Plastics Treaty mirrors structurally the Paris Agreement (climate), Convention on Biological Diversity (biodiversity), and Stockholm Convention (POPs). Key innovations include: (i) full-life-cycle scope (production → use → waste); (ii) financial mechanism for technology transfer; (iii) reporting + verification; (iv) potential trade restrictions for non-compliant parties. (Tilsted et al. 2023, p. 612)

Related terms. Petrochemical lock-ins / political economy; planetary boundaries; plastic leakage; mismanaged plastic waste; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR); single-use plastics; Plastic chemicals; non-energy use of fossil fuels; just transition.

Source history. - Tilsted et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-08: INC negotiating timeline, supply-side argument, UN-treaty comparison.

Underground hydrogen storage (UHS)

Aliases. Subsurface hydrogen storage.

Definition. Large-scale storage of hydrogen gas in subsurface geological formations, expected to play a key role in the energy transition and in near-future renewable energy systems by providing inter-seasonal, TWh-scale balancing capacity. Candidate geological options include salt caverns, saline aquifers, depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs, engineered rock caverns and abandoned mine shafts. (Miocic et al. 2023, abstract and p. 73)

Extended definition. Surface-based hydrogen storage facilities (pipelines, surface tanks for gas or liquid hydrogen, liquid organic hydrogen carriers, ammonia/methanol carriers) have limited discharge capacity (MW h, hours–days), whereas subsurface storage in salt caverns and porous media has the potential to supply energy on a much larger scale (GW h/TW h; weeks–seasons). (Miocic et al. 2023, pp. 73–74, citing Mouli-Castillo et al. 2021; Yin and Ju 2020; Abdin et al. 2021)

Notes — operational risks. The cyclical nature of UHS operations causes pressure and stress changes in the reservoir that can affect the integrity of the well, the reservoir, the caprock and the entire subsurface storage complex. To minimise geomechanical leakage risks, optimisation of storage operation is crucial; understanding the pressure and stress history of the storage site, optimising well locations, and identifying the reservoir-specific cushion-gas-to-working-gas ratio are highlighted as priorities. (Miocic et al. 2023, abstract; pp. 79–81)

Related terms. Salt cavern; saline aquifer; depleted gas field; engineered rock cavern; abandoned mine shaft; caprock; cushion gas; storage complex; cyclic loading.

Source history. - Miocic et al. 2023 — added 2026-05-07: umbrella definition, scale comparison, and operational-risk note.

ULSD (ultra-low-sulfur diesel)

Aliases. ULSD; ultra-low-sulfur-diesel; near-zero-sulfur diesel; <10 ppm S diesel.

Definition. Diesel fuel with sulfur content limited to ≤15 ppm (US Tier 2 / EPA 2007) or ≤10 ppm (US Tier 3 / EU EN 590 since 2009 / EU Stage III/IV). The ULSD specification was driven by two motives: (i) protect modern diesel-particulate-filter (DPF) and selective-catalytic-reduction (SCR) emission-control systems, which are poisoned by sulfur; (ii) reduce direct SO₂ and sulfate-PM2.5 emissions from diesel exhaust. Achieving ULSD requires deep hydrotreating of diesel-pool blendstocks, with hydrogen consumption ~70 scf H₂/barrel/% S removed (~0.5 wt% H₂ at typical feed sulfur). (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 3–6; Speight 2019, Chapter 4.4)

Attributes — ULSD regulatory limits and impact.

Indicator Value
US legacy (pre-2006) on-road diesel 500 ppm S
US Tier 2 (2006–2017) 15 ppm S
US Tier 3 (2017+) 10 ppm S (gasoline) — same hydrotreating logic
EU EN 590 (since 2009) 10 ppm S
Marine — ECA (Emission Control Area) 0.1 wt% S
Marine — global (IMO 2020) 0.5 wt% S
H₂ demand for ULSD (US) ~1.33 billion scf/day refinery total
SO₂ avoided (US, vs pre-ULSD) ~21.9 Mt SO₂/yr
Black-carbon co-benefit DPF enabled by ULSD reduces PM2.5 by >90%

(H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 4–6; EPA Tier 3 standards)

Notes — significance. ULSD is a textbook case of a systemic regulation that cascades through several technical layers: low-S diesel enables aftertreatment which enables low-NOₓ engines which enables urban-air-quality compliance. The sulfur-removal step in refining requires substantial hydrogen, providing ~20% of the rationale for refinery hydrotreating capacity globally. Replacing the SMR-based H₂ supply with green H₂ would therefore directly decarbonise the diesel-quality value chain. (H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017, pp. 5–6)

Related terms. Diesel fuel (umbrella); hydrotreating (HDS / HDN / HDM); hydrodesulfurization (HDS); sulfuric acid; sulfur dioxide (SO₂) air pollution; Tier 3 fuel standards; petroleum refining (umbrella); steam methane reforming (SMR).

Source history. - H2-for-sulfur-removal 2017 — added 2026-05-08: definition, regulatory levels, hydrogen-demand impact, SO₂ avoidance. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08 (cross-ref): refinery context.

UVCB substances

Definition. Substances of Unknown or Variable composition, Complex reaction products, or Biological materials — a class of plastic chemicals with ambiguous chemical compositions that cannot be assessed with confidence. The PlastChem inventory contains 3,667 such substances (≈23% of unique entries), encompassing UVCBs, mixtures and polymers; defined chemical structures and properties for these are lacking in the public domain. For around 1,500 of them the available structural information refers only to a minor part of the compounds they contain. (Monclús et al. 2025, pp. 350, 355, citing Lai et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2021)

Notes. Despite this ambiguity, regulatory information supports the identification of 619 UVCBs/mixtures/polymers as chemicals of concern. The fact that more than 10% of polymers are hazardous challenges the long-standing view that polymers do not pose serious hazards owing to their high molecular weight. Improving structural identifiers and developing automated cheminformatics tools for grouping UVCBs is identified as a priority for the next phase of the chemicals-in-plastics agenda. (Monclús et al. 2025, pp. 351, 354–355)

Related terms. Plastic chemicals; PlastChem inventory; chemicals of concern; per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

Source history. - Monclús et al. 2025 — added 2026-05-07: definition, share of inventory, polymer-hazard implications.

Utilisation rate (manufacturing capacity)

Definition. The proportion of the maximum nominal capacity of a manufacturing facility (or other production asset) which is used on average over a set period of time — most commonly a calendar year. ETP-2026 uses utilisation rate as a key parameter for projecting investment requirements, levelised cost of production (LCOP), and surplus-capacity dynamics in clean-energy-technology supply chains. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 379)

Notes. ETP-2026 assumes a default maximum practical utilisation rate of 85% for manufacturing facilities. The recent decline in global manufacturing investment (USD 220 bn in 2023 → ~USD 200 bn in 2024 → continued gentle decline in 2025) is largely explained by a surplus of installed capacity relative to current demand for solar PV and batteries — i.e. existing facilities are operating at sub-target utilisation rates, dampening greenfield investment. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 17–19, 379)

Related terms. Manufacturing capacity (clean energy technologies); Levelised Cost of Production (LCOP); investment overnight; clean energy technologies.

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, default 85%, recent demand-vs-capacity context.

Value added (industrial)

Definition. A national-accounts and industrial-economics measure that reflects the value generated by producing goods and services. Calculated as the value of output minus the value of intermediate consumption (raw materials, components, services purchased from other firms). Used in ETP-2026 to characterise how each step of a clean-energy-technology supply chain contributes to GDP and to compare cross-country industrial competitiveness. (IEA ETP 2026, Glossary, p. 379)

Related terms. Manufacturing capacity (clean energy technologies); Levelised Cost of Production (LCOP); local content requirements (LCRs); revealed comparative advantage (RCA).

Source history. - IEA ETP 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, supply-chain-economics role.

Vacuum distillation (refinery)

Aliases. Vacuum distillation unit (VDU); vacuum pipe still; vacuum tower.

Definition. A refinery distillation step performed at sub-atmospheric pressure (typically 25–80 mmHg, ~30–100 mbar) on the atmospheric residue from the CDU. Vacuum operation lowers the effective boiling points of heavy hydrocarbons, allowing fractionation of vacuum gas oil (VGO) and lubricating-oil cuts without exceeding ~400 °C feed-coil temperature, beyond which thermal cracking would degrade product quality and form coke. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.2)

Attributes — typical operating envelope.

Indicator Value
Feed atmospheric residue (boiling point >360 °C)
Column top pressure 25–80 mmHg (vacuum)
Feed coil outlet temperature 380–420 °C (limit to avoid cracking)
Number of side-stream cuts 3–5 (light/medium/heavy VGO + lube cuts + slop wax)
Vacuum residue yield 20–50% of VDU feed
VGO yield 30–60% of VDU feed
Vacuum source 3–5 stage steam ejectors or liquid-ring pumps

(Speight 2019, Chapter 4.2)

Notes — downstream destinations. VGO is the primary feed to FCC and hydrocracker units; vacuum residue is fed to coker (delayed or fluid coker), visbreaker, or used as heavy fuel oil / asphalt blend. Lubricating-oil VDUs include narrower cuts (light/medium/heavy neutral, brightstock) which then go to solvent extraction or hydroprocessing for lube basestock manufacture. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.2)

Related terms. Atmospheric distillation; petroleum refining (umbrella); catalytic cracking (FCC); hydrocracking; delayed coking; visbreaking.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, conditions, downstream destinations.

Vehicle-to-grid (V2G)

Definition. A bidirectional charging architecture in which a battery electric vehicle (BEV) sends electricity from its battery back to the grid during peak demand or grid stress, allowing the BEV fleet to act as distributed grid-connected storage. V2G is one of the seven major storage options examined in 100% RE systems analyses. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 16)

Notes. V2G emerged as a recognised grid-connected storage technology in 2009, likely due to the resolution of previous limitations in power-sector studies (the integration of BEVs and the transport sector is essential for this storage option). V2G appears in 11.6% of the 1,067 100% RE systems articles. It is identified as a very valuable flexibility complement to smart charging. (Khalili et al. 2026, pp. 7, 16)

Related terms. Battery electric vehicle (BEV); sector coupling; pumped hydro energy storage (PHES); thermal energy storage (TES); compressed air energy storage (CAES).

Source history. - Khalili et al. 2026 — added 2026-05-08: definition, history, share in 100% RE database.

Volatile chemical products (VCPs)

Aliases. VCPs; volatile organic products; consumer-product VOC sources.

Definition. A category of chemical-end-use products — including pesticides, paints and coatings, printing inks, adhesives, household and industrial cleaning agents, and personal-care products — that contain volatile organic compound (VOC) solvents. VCPs release VOCs to the atmosphere during application, drying, or normal use and have emerged in industrialised cities as the largest petrochemical source of urban anthropogenic VOC emissions, exceeding the contribution of mobile-source (vehicle exhaust + evaporative) emissions. (McDonald et al. 2018, pp. 760–761)

Attributes — VCP vs mobile-source VOC emissions (US, ~2012).

Source VOC emissions (Tg/yr) Notes
All VCPs (US) 7.6 ± 1.5 ~2× mobile sources
All mobile sources 3.5 ± 1.1 tailpipe + evaporative + upstream
Coatings, inks, adhesives 4.4 ± 1.2 Largest VCP sub-category
Cleaning products 0.66 ± 0.38
Personal care (within other) smaller absolute, large per-capita
Pesticides 1.1 ± 0.7
Gasoline exhaust 1.7 ± 0.8
Diesel exhaust 0.33 ± 0.12
Gasoline (evaporative) 1.5 ± 0.8

(McDonald et al. 2018, p. 761 and Fig. 1)

Notes — mechanism shift. Decades of US/EU controls on tailpipe VOC emissions (catalytic converters, evaporative emission controls) have driven on-road VOC contributions sharply down — gasoline-exhaust mixing ratios in Los Angeles fell markedly from 1990–2010 — while VCP-derived markers (e.g., acetone) rose. McDonald shows that VOC emission factors per unit product use of VCPs are 1–2 orders of magnitude higher than from gasoline combustion (because most fuel-VOCs are oxidised to CO₂ in the engine + catalyst, whereas most VCP-VOCs evaporate intact). (McDonald et al. 2018, pp. 761–763 and Fig. 2)

Notes — secondary organic aerosol and ozone implications. VCP emissions contribute to (i) tropospheric ozone formation via NOₓ-VOC photochemistry, and (ii) secondary organic aerosol (SOA), a major component of urban PM2.5. McDonald argues human exposure to fossil-derived carbonaceous aerosols is transitioning away from transportation-related sources toward VCPs. US regulation has historically focused on ozone and air toxics; many SOA-relevant chemicals are exempt from current VCP rules. (McDonald et al. 2018, p. 760)

Notes — significance for petrochemical sector. McDonald’s mass balance places VCPs squarely in the chemical sector’s air-quality footprint: while crude-oil and natural-gas extraction, refineries and chemical-manufacturing plants account for some upstream VOC emissions (4.8 ± 1.4 Tg/yr in the US), the largest downstream atmospheric impact comes from how solvent-containing chemical products are used. This complements Levi & Cullen’s mass-balance perspective on chemical production with an end-use-emissions perspective. (McDonald et al. 2018, p. 761; Levi and Cullen 2018)

Related terms. Plastic chemicals; Chemicals of concern; PoTSs (potentially toxic substances); migration (plastic chemicals); petrochemicals (umbrella); non-energy use of fossil fuels; per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS); secondary organic aerosol (SOA).

Source history. - McDonald et al. 2018 — added 2026-05-08: definition, US mass balance (7.6 Tg VCP vs 3.5 Tg mobile), emission-factor differential, ozone/SOA implications.

Vinyl chloride monomer (VCM)

Aliases. Chloroethene; chloroethylene; VCM.

Definition. A colourless gas (CH₂=CHCl) produced from ethylene via a two-step “balanced” process: (1) direct chlorination of ethylene with Cl₂ over FeCl₃ catalyst → ethylene dichloride (EDC, 1,2-dichloroethane); (2) thermal cracking of EDC at 480–530 °C → VCM + HCl. The HCl is recycled to oxychlorination of ethylene with O₂ (CuCl₂/Al₂O₃ catalyst) → additional EDC, closing the chlorine balance. VCM is the precursor to polyvinyl chloride (PVC), the third-largest commodity thermoplastic. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2 and 11.3.3; Levi and Cullen 2018, Fig. 1)

Attributes — production and uses.

Indicator Value
Global production ~50 Mt/yr
Boiling point −13 °C
Process balanced chlorination + oxychlorination
Direct chlorination temperature 90–130 °C
EDC cracking temperature 480–530 °C
Per-pass EDC conversion 50–60%
VCM selectivity >99% from EDC cracking
End-use ~99% to PVC; ~1% to other (chlorinated solvents)
EDC (intermediate) global production ~70 Mt/yr

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2)

Notes — environmental and health concerns. VCM is a Group 1 IARC carcinogen (causes liver angiosarcoma); modern plants operate at ppb-level worker exposure with closed-loop sampling. PVC’s chlorine content (~57%) means VCM-derived plastics generate HCl on incineration, complicating end-of-life management. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2)

Related terms. Ethylene; ethylene dichloride (EDC); polyvinyl chloride (PVC); chlor-alkali process; high-value chemicals (HVCs); plastic chemicals; chemicals of concern.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, balanced-process chemistry, PVC linkage. - Levi and Cullen 2018 — added 2026-05-08: 50 Mt/yr global production.

Variable Renewable Energy (VRE)

Definition. Renewable electricity sources whose output is determined by ambient resource availability (wind speed, solar irradiation) rather than by operator dispatch — primarily wind power and solar photovoltaics (PV). VRE generation is non-dispatchable, location-specific, intermittent, and subject to forecast uncertainty, raising the system-flexibility and -stability requirements of the host power system. (Guerra et al. 2022, p. 1 and Section 1; Heide et al. 2010; Khalili et al. 2026)

Attributes — Guerra Spanish-system thresholds and limits.

Indicator Value
2030 ST scenario VRE share (power generation) 33%
2040 ST scenario VRE share 35%
Resulting CO₂ emissions intensity (2030 / 2040) 157 / 159 kg CO₂/MWh
Required threshold to meet Paris targets (above which new tech required) ~39% VRE
Required emissions intensity for new tech ≤ ~113 kg CO₂/MWh
Required inertia constant ≥ 5 s
Maximum LCOE for new tech ~€134/MWh

(Guerra et al. 2022, abstract and Table 4)

Notes — seasonal optimal mix (Heide et al. 2010). For a 100% wind-plus-solar Europe, the seasonal optimal mix is ~55% wind / 45% solar, derived from the minimum required stored energy. Wind generation is much stronger in winter, while solar dominates summer; combining the two in the ~60/40 to 55/45 ratio counterbalances seasonal load. For sub-100% renewable shares the optimal wind fraction increases. Storage-loss assumptions affect required surplus generation factor γ = a + b: γ ≈ 1.05 (pumped hydro) and ≈ 1.28 (hydrogen storage) when a = b. The seasonal optimal mix location is robust to storage efficiency. (Heide et al. 2010, abstract and Sections 2–3)

Notes — flexibility sources. Sources of flexibility for VRE integration include grid expansion, optimal wind-solar ratios, curtailment, energy storage, flexible conventional generation, demand response, Power-to-X, system diversity, forecast improvement and institutional changes. (Guerra et al. 2022, p. 2)

Related terms. Solar PV; wind power; curtailment (VRE); inertia (power system); Rate of Change of Frequency (ROCOF); flexibility (power system); battery storage (stationary); pumped hydro energy storage (PHES); seasonal optimal mix.

Source history. - Guerra et al. 2022 — added 2026-05-08: definition, Spanish thresholds, flexibility sources. - Heide et al. 2010 — added 2026-05-08: seasonal optimal mix in 100% wind+solar Europe, surplus generation factors.

Wobbe index (W_s)

Definition. A measure of the interchangeability of fuel gases as inputs to a given burner without re-tuning, defined as W_s = HHV / √d, where HHV is the higher heating value (MJ/Nm³) and d is the relative density compared to air. Two gases with the same Wobbe index will deliver the same heat input through a fixed orifice at fixed pressure, regardless of their composition. The Wobbe index is the principal regulatory indicator for safely substituting one gas for another in a distribution grid. (Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007, p. 1383 and Section 4)

Attributes — typical Wobbe-index ranges.

Gas family HHV (MJ/Nm³) Wobbe index range (MJ/Nm³)
Lean NG (L-gas, e.g. Slochteren) ~37.7 41–47
Rich NG (H-gas) ~40+ 48–58
Hydrogen (100%) 13 ~48
Flexible burners (France, Belgium) — 41–58 (full range)

(Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007, p. 1383, Fig. 3)

Notes — H₂-into-NG limits set by Wobbe. When mixing H₂ into NG and using lean-NG burners, up to 98 vol% H₂ stays within 41–47 MJ/Nm³. For rich-NG burners, only ~45 vol% H₂ can be added before the mixture’s Wobbe falls below 48 MJ/Nm³. Adding H₂ raises burner flame speed (flashback risk), so end-use applications, sealings and flame-detection systems may need adjustment regardless of the Wobbe band. (Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007, Section 4)

Related terms. Hydrogen-natural gas blending; higher heating value (HHV); lower heating value (LHV); hydrogen pipeline; linepack.

Source history. - Haeseldonckx and D’haeseleer 2007 — added 2026-05-08: definition, Wobbe-index ranges, blending implications.

Wacker process (acetaldehyde from ethylene)

Aliases. Wacker oxidation; Wacker-Hoechst process; ethylene oxidation to acetaldehyde.

Definition. A homogeneous-catalysis industrial process in which ethylene is oxidised by oxygen over a soluble palladium-chloride / copper-chloride redox-coupled catalyst in aqueous solution to produce acetaldehyde: C₂H₄ + ½ O₂ → CH₃CHO. The process operates at 90–120 °C and 3–10 bar with a single-step (Wacker-Hoechst, ethylene + O₂ + catalyst together) or two-step (Wacker, separate ethylene oxidation and catalyst regeneration) variant. Although acetaldehyde demand has fallen as VAM production has shifted to ethylene-acetic-acid routes, the Wacker mechanism remains a milestone in homogeneous-catalysis education and is the basis for many modern Pd-catalysed C–H activation reactions. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2)

Attributes — process and current status.

Indicator Value
Catalyst PdCl₂ / CuCl₂ in aqueous HCl
Temperature / pressure 90–120 °C / 3–10 bar
Per-pass conversion 35–45%
Selectivity >94%
Global acetaldehyde production ~1 Mt/yr (declining)
Current Wacker-process share <10% (most replaced by ethanol-dehydrogenation or biomass-fermentation routes)
Historical 1960s–1980s peak ~5 Mt/yr
Key Wacker chemistry Pd(II) + alkene → Pd(0) + carbonyl; Pd(0) + Cu(II) + O₂ → Pd(II) + Cu(I); Cu(I) + ½O₂ → Cu(II)

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2)

Notes — historical significance. The Wacker process was a landmark in industrial homogeneous catalysis when commercialised by Wacker-Chemie (1959) — demonstrating that aqueous Pd-Cl₂ chemistry could replace the prior ethanol-dehydrogenation route for acetaldehyde. Modern direct routes from ethanol or biomass have largely displaced it, but the Wacker mechanism remains foundational for understanding Pd-catalysed olefin activation. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2)

Related terms. Ethylene; acetaldehyde; vinyl acetate (VAM); homogeneous catalysis; palladium catalysis; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, mechanism, current status, historical significance.

Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)

Definition. The blended cost of a firm’s (or project’s) financing, weighted by the market-value share of equity and debt in the capital structure. Formally: WACC = (E/(E+D)) · K_e + (D/(E+D)) · K_d · (1 − t), where E and D are the market values of equity and debt, K_e is the cost of equity (commonly estimated by CAPM as K_e = R_f + β · (R_m − R_f) + R_p), K_d is the cost of debt, and t is the tax rate. WACC is the canonical discount rate for project NPV/IRR analysis and a primary determinant of LCOE and LCOH. (Ramírez Del Río 2022, pp. 22–24, citing Damodaran 2012; Khan et al. 2021, p. 20)

Notes. Khan et al.’s hydrogen-pipeline case study uses 8% WACC, while Ramírez Del Río’s PV-vs-hydroelectric Colombia analysis runs sensitivity analyses across a representative WACC range. The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) is the standard method for estimating the cost of equity, parameterised by the risk-free rate, market premium, sector beta and country risk premium. WACC sensitivity dominates the present-value calculus of capital-intensive infrastructure (CCUS hubs, offshore wind, hydrogen pipelines). (Ramírez Del Río 2022, pp. 23–24, 55–69; Khan et al. 2021, p. 20)

Cross-source comparison — WACC reference values.

Source Reference value Range / by technology Comment
RTE 2022 (Futurs énergétiques 2050) 4% (uniform across technologies) 1–7% sensitivity Reference for full-system 2050 economic comparison
IEA WEO 2021 differentiated by technology nuclear ~7–8%; renewables 2.5–4% (with support) / 6.5–9.5% (no support) Splits market vs regulated regimes
ADEME 2018 differentiated by technology nuclear ~7.5%; PV ~5.25%; wind onshore ~5%; offshore ~7.5% French national agency
Polzin et al. 2021 differentiated by technology renewables 3.4–6.3% by country European cross-country study
Nuclear Energy Agency 2020 uniform 7% typical for socio-economic studies Cited in RTE Figure 11.3
Shirizadeh et al. 2020 uniform 3% sensitivity to technology cost uncertainty Academic French 100% RE study
Khan et al. 2021 8% hydrogen-pipeline case study Canadian project economics
Ramírez Del Río 2022 sensitivity range typically 6–14% in Latin American context CAPM-derived

(Compiled from RTE 2022, Section 11.2.2, Figures 11.2–11.3, pp. 540–541; Khan et al. 2021, p. 20; Ramírez Del Río 2022, pp. 22–24, 55–69)

Notes — RTE rationale for uniform 4%. RTE adopts a uniform 4% across all technologies to (i) preserve scenario comparability, (ii) reflect socio-economic discounting rather than market-driven private discounting, (iii) avoid implicit penalisation of capital-intensive technologies (nuclear) when public-support mechanisms are available. RTE explicitly notes that differentiating WACC by technology would simply re-encode the support-policy difference and that uniform WACC isolates the technology-cost question. Sensitivity analyses on WACC dominate scenario rankings: at WACC = 7% (high-private-financing case), nuclear-heavy scenarios become more expensive than renewable-heavy scenarios; at WACC = 1–4% (close to public-finance cost), nuclear-heavy scenarios are cheapest. (RTE 2022, Section 11.2.2, pp. 540–541; Sections 11.6.5.6, 11.6.5.7)

Related terms. Capital Recovery Factor (CRF); Net Present Value (NPV); Internal Rate of Return (IRR); Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE); Levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH); Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM); Annualised electricity system cost (RTE 2050); EPR2 programme.

Source history. - Raillard-Cazanove 2024 — listed in Pending 2026-05-07. - Khan et al. 2021 — added 2026-05-08: usage in hydrogen-pipeline case study (8%). - Ramírez Del Río 2022 — added 2026-05-08: full formula, CAPM derivation, sensitivity analysis (translated from Spanish); promoted from Pending. - RTE 2022 — added 2026-05-08: uniform 4% reference, 1–7% sensitivity range, cross-source comparison table with IEA WEO 2021, ADEME 2018, NEA 2020, Polzin 2021, Shirizadeh 2020 (translated from French).

Vinyl acetate (VAM) and PVAc / PVOH

Aliases. VAM (vinyl acetate monomer); PVAc (polyvinyl acetate); PVOH (polyvinyl alcohol); EVA (ethylene-vinyl acetate copolymer).

Definition. Vinyl acetate (CH₂=CH-O-COCH₃) is produced industrially by the gas-phase reaction of ethylene with acetic acid and oxygen over a Pd / Au / KOAc on silica catalyst at 150–180 °C and 5–10 bar (BP / Celanese process; replaced the older liquid-phase Wacker variant). VAM is the principal monomer for polyvinyl acetate (PVAc) — used in white wood-glue and paint emulsions — and for EVA (ethylene-vinyl acetate copolymer, used in shoe soles, hot-melt adhesives, photovoltaic backsheets). PVAc can be hydrolysed (with NaOH/methanol) to polyvinyl alcohol (PVOH), the only major water-soluble commercial polymer, used in paper sizing, textile sizing, packaging films, and biomedical hydrogels. (Speight 2019, Chapters 7.2, 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Indicator Value
Global VAM production ~7 Mt/yr
End-use VAM — PVAc emulsions (white glue, paint) ~30%
End-use VAM — EVA copolymer ~20%
End-use VAM — PVOH ~25%
End-use VAM — solvent-based / specialty polymers ~25%
Catalyst Pd / Au / K-acetate on silica
Conversion (per pass) 8–10% (with recycle)
Selectivity >92%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2)

Notes — solar-PV connection. EVA is the standard polymer encapsulant in crystalline-silicon PV modules — laminated between the glass front-sheet and the cell array. Global EVA demand is increasingly driven by solar-PV deployment (~5 g EVA / W_p installed); a 1 GW solar-PV manufacturing plant requires ~5,000 t of EVA-encapsulant feedstock annually. (Speight 2019, Chapter 7.2)

Viscose / Lyocell / Modal (cellulosic synthetic fibres)

Aliases. Viscose; rayon; modal; lyocell; Tencel (Lenzing brand); cupro; man-made cellulosic fibres (MMCF).

Definition. A family of textile fibres produced from natural cellulose (wood pulp from beech, eucalyptus, pine, bamboo) that has been chemically dissolved and re-spun into synthetic filaments — bridging the gap between natural (cotton) and synthetic (polyester) fibres. The principal commercial variants: - Viscose / rayon — oldest commercial process (1910s); cellulose dissolved with carbon disulfide (CS₂) + sodium hydroxide (xanthate) and re-spun. Major emissions/waste issues — CS₂ is highly toxic. - Modal — improved viscose with stronger wet-strength; same chemistry, refined process. - Lyocell (Tencel) — modern closed-loop process developed by Courtaulds (1980s) and Lenzing AG (commercialised 1990s) using N-methylmorpholine N-oxide (NMMO) solvent that is recovered >99.5% — eliminating the toxicity and waste issues of viscose. - Cupro (Bemberg) — cellulose dissolved with copper-ammonia complex; minor but premium. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, pp. 191, 196; Lenzing AG; Clark 2022)

Attributes — global cellulosic-fibre production.

Viscose ~5–6 Mt/yr CS₂ + sulphur emissions; legacy issue apparel, lining, filling
Modal ~0.4 Mt/yr improved viscose luxury underwear, bedding
Lyocell (Tencel) ~0.5 Mt/yr closed-loop, ~80% lower than viscose premium apparel, denim alternatives
Cupro ~0.05 Mt/yr small-scale luxury linings
Total cellulosics ~6.5 Mt/yr (~6% of textile fibres) varies sharply varies

(Niinimäki et al. 2020, p. 191 and Fig. 1; Clark 2022)

Notes — wood-pulp sustainability concerns. Cellulosic-fibre production requires ~1.5 t wood pulp per tonne fibre. Supply chains have historically been linked to ancient and endangered forests (Canopy NGO investigation): Indonesia, Brazil rainforest. FSC-certified and PEFC-certified sustainable wood pulp is now mandatory for major lyocell brands; Renewcell (Sweden) demonstrates recycled-cotton-to-lyocell loops as a wood-free alternative. (Niinimäki et al. 2020, p. 196; Clark 2022)

Notes — comparison to cotton. Lyocell has ~50% lower water footprint than cotton, no pesticide use (wood-grown), and full biodegradability — making it the most-preferred textile fibre for sustainability-conscious brands (Patagonia, Eileen Fisher, Stella McCartney). Cost premium ~30–80% vs cotton; market-share growth driven by sustainability commitments and mandatory EU EPR for textiles (2025). (Niinimäki et al. 2020, p. 196)

Related terms. Textile fibres (synthetic and natural); cotton; fast fashion (and slow fashion); microfibre pollution; circular fashion; mechanical recycling; chemical recycling; FSC certification.

Visbreaking (refinery)

Aliases. Viscosity-breaking; thermal cracking (mild); resid visbreaker.

Definition. A mild thermal-cracking refinery process in which atmospheric or vacuum residue is heated to 440–490 °C at moderate pressure (~20 bar) for short residence time (1–3 minutes) to crack heavy molecules just enough to lower viscosity and pour point — without producing solid coke. The cracked product is fractionated into a small amount of refinery gas + naphtha + gas oil + a fluid residue suitable for use as low-viscosity fuel oil. Visbreaking is much milder than delayed coking, with the trade-off of less complete residue conversion. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Attributes — typical operating envelope.

Indicator Value
Furnace outlet temperature 440–490 °C
Residence time 1–3 min (coil) or 5–30 min (soaker drum)
Pressure ~20 bar (coil) or 5–15 bar (soaker)
Conversion (to lighter products) 5–15 wt%
Visbreaker naphtha yield 2–5 wt%
Visbreaker gas oil yield 5–15 wt%
Visbreaker residue yield 80–90 wt%
Coke formation minimal (residue stays liquid)

(Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Notes — vs coker. Visbreaking targets fuel-oil-blend-stock viscosity reduction and modest distillate yield; delayed coking targets full conversion of residue to lighter distillates plus solid petcoke. Visbreaking dominates European refineries (where heavy fuel oil markets persist and petcoke markets are small); coking dominates US Gulf Coast and Asia (high coke demand, low residual fuel oil demand). (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Notes — soaker vs coil variants. Coil visbreakers crack purely in the heater coil (short residence time, higher temperature). Soaker visbreakers add a downstream soaking drum to extend residence time at lower temperature, reducing fuel consumption per barrel of conversion. (Speight 2019, Chapter 4.3)

Related terms. Delayed coking; vacuum distillation; petroleum refining (umbrella); thermal cracking; hydrocracking.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, conditions, vs delayed coking, soaker vs coil variants.

Wind power

Definition. A power-generation technology that converts the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity using turbines mounted on land (onshore wind) or fixed-bottom or floating platforms at sea (offshore wind). One of the IEA’s six “clean energy technologies” and a complementary variable renewable energy source to solar PV. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 144–145, Glossary p. 374; Khalili et al. 2026, p. 6)

Attributes — capacity, costs and outlook (ETP-2026).

Projected onshore wind cost decline to 2035 ~−10% 2024–2035
Onshore wind cost trajectory by region falling in China; stagnant elsewhere; widening price gap 2015–2025
Share of global electricity capacity additions in 2024 (with solar) ~80% 2024
2024 wind installation growth slightly above 2023 (record year) 2024
Installed wind capacity doubles by 2035 in CPS and STEPS — 2025–2035
NZE 2035 capacity multiplier ~4× 2025–2035
Average wind curtailment in China <5% in 2024 (down from >15% peak in 2016) 2016–2024

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 144–145, 5925–5926, 7905–7910, 10173–10220)

Notes — onshore vs offshore. Onshore wind operates as a relatively mature segment with two-sided contracts for difference, improved auction design, and increasing focus on permitting and grid access. Offshore wind remains at the scaling-and-technological-maturation stage, with port and vessel infrastructure (wind turbine installation vessels, WTIVs) identified as a key bottleneck globally outside China. Component costs include turbines, towers and blades; ~75% of the China-vs-elsewhere manufacturing cost gap on blades stems from labour. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 1745, 12414–12734)

Notes — value-adjusted economics. New solar PV and onshore/offshore wind have similar or lower average LCOEs than new coal, gas and nuclear in major STEPS markets. Even when accounting for dispatchability, the Value-Adjusted Levelised Cost of Electricity (VALCOE) of a solar or wind plant operating at a 95% capacity factor could be comparable to dispatchable sources in major markets in 2035. (IEA ETP 2026, p. 5926, citing IEA 2025g)
