Ziegler-Natta polymerisation

Aliases. ZN polymerisation; coordination polymerisation; insertion polymerisation; stereospecific catalysis.

Definition. A coordination-insertion polymerisation in which an α-olefin monomer (typically ethylene or propylene) inserts into a metal-carbon bond of a transition-metal catalyst (Ti or V on a MgCl₂ support, activated by an alkylaluminium co-catalyst) to grow a linear polymer chain. The reaction proceeds at low pressure (~5–35 bar) and moderate temperature (50–110 °C), and is stereospecific: the catalyst surface controls the orientation in which each monomer adds, producing isotactic polypropylene (iPP), syndiotactic, or atactic polymer depending on catalyst design. Discovered independently by Karl Ziegler (1953, ethylene polymerisation at low pressure) and Giulio Natta (1954, isotactic polypropylene), Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1963. (Speight 2019, Chapters 11.3.1.2, 11.3.2)

Attributes — generations of ZN catalysts.

Generation Catalyst Activity (kg PP / g cat) Stereoregularity
1st (1954) TiCl₃ + Et₃Al, no support low (~1) low (~85% isotactic)
2nd (1970) TiCl₃-AA modified moderate (~5) moderate
3rd (1980) TiCl₄/MgCl₂ + benzoate donor + Et₃Al high (~30) high (>92%)
4th (1990) TiCl₄/MgCl₂ + phthalate donor + alkylsilane external donor very high (~80) very high (>97%)
5th (2000s) TiCl₄/MgCl₂ + diether donor >50 >98%
6th / metallocene (1990s+) Cp₂ZrCl₂ + MAO co-catalyst >100 >99%

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.2)

Notes — catalyst function. The MgCl₂ support provides high surface area and cocrystallises with TiCl₄ to expose stereoselective active sites. The alkylaluminium (Et₃Al, TEA) co-catalyst alkylates the Ti centre and scavenges impurities. Internal/external Lewis-base donors (phthalates, succinates, diethers, alkoxysilanes) tune stereoselectivity. Modern catalysts give “particle-form” polymerisation: the catalyst particle replicates into the polymer particle, which exits the reactor as a free-flowing powder. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.2)

Notes — significance. Ziegler-Natta polymerisation underpins HDPE, LLDPE, isotactic polypropylene, EPDM rubber, and many specialty polyolefins — together >150 Mt/yr of polymer. It enabled the polypropylene industry (which has no equivalent free-radical-polymerisable form) and the linear polyethylene industry (LDPE was historically the only PE before ZN). (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.1)

Related terms. Metallocene polymerisation; free-radical polymerisation; polyethylene (HDPE / LLDPE); polypropylene (PP); tacticity; gas-phase polymerisation; slurry polymerisation; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, catalyst generations, mechanism, significance.

Metallocene polymerisation

Aliases. Single-site polymerisation; constrained-geometry catalysts (CGC); MAO-activated polymerisation; post-metallocene catalysis.

Definition. A coordination polymerisation analogous to Ziegler-Natta but using a single-site organometallic complex — typically a group-4 transition metal (Zr, Ti, Hf) sandwiched between two cyclopentadienyl (Cp) ligands or related η⁵-bonded aromatic ligands — activated by methylaluminoxane (MAO) or boron-based co-catalyst. Metallocene catalysts deliver narrower molecular-weight distribution (MWD ~2 vs ZN ~4–8), more uniform comonomer incorporation, and superior stereo- and regio-control than classical Ziegler-Natta. They underpin specialty polyethylene grades (e.g., Exxon Exact, Dow Engage / Affinity), syndiotactic polystyrene (Idemitsu), and metallocene-PP grades. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.1)

Attributes — catalyst design and outputs.

Element Description
Active metal Zr (most common), Ti, Hf
Ligand framework bis-Cp, bridged ansa-metallocene, half-sandwich constrained-geometry, post-metallocene (FI, phenoxy-imine)
Co-catalyst MAO (methylaluminoxane) at high Al/Zr ratio; or borate (B(C₆F₅)₃) at near-stoichiometric ratio
Activity 10–50 t polymer / g Zr / h
Molecular-weight distribution (PDI) 2.0–2.5 (vs 4–8 for ZN)
Comonomer incorporation uniform across chains
Stereoselectivity chiral catalysts give isotactic; achiral give atactic; some give syndiotactic
Polymerisation processes used gas-phase, solution, slurry

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.1)

Notes — significance for polyolefin variety. Metallocenes enable polymers with precisely controlled architectures unattainable with Ziegler-Natta — e.g., octene-LLDPE plastomer (Dow Affinity), syndiotactic PP, syndiotactic polystyrene, and cyclic-olefin copolymers (COC, used in optical applications). Metallocene-PE grades have high-clarity packaging applications (food films, medical pouches) and metallocene-PP gives high-strength fibres. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.1)

Related terms. Ziegler-Natta polymerisation; polyethylene (LLDPE); polypropylene (PP); syndiotactic polystyrene; cyclic-olefin copolymer; tacticity; high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, single-site mechanism, narrow MWD, polymer variety.

Free-radical polymerisation

Aliases. Radical chain polymerisation; addition polymerisation (radical); FRP.

Definition. A chain-growth polymerisation mechanism in which a free-radical initiator (typically a peroxide or azo compound, generated thermally, photochemically, or redox-driven) adds to a vinyl monomer to form an active radical chain end. The chain propagates by sequential addition of monomers to the radical end and terminates by combination or disproportionation of two radical chains (or chain transfer to solvent / monomer / chain transfer agent). Free-radical polymerisation is the dominant route for LDPE (high-pressure), polystyrene, polyvinyl chloride (PVC), polyacrylonitrile, and most acrylic and methacrylic polymers. (Speight 2019, Chapters 11.3.1.1, 11.3.4)

Attributes — kinetics and process variants.

Step Description
Initiation I₂ → 2 I•; I• + M → I-M•
Propagation I-Mₙ• + M → I-Mₙ₊₁• (rate constant kp ~10²–10⁴ L/mol·s)
Termination combination (kt-c) or disproportionation (kt-d)
Chain transfer to solvent, monomer, polymer, transfer agent
Average MW Mₙ ∝ kp/√(kd·kt)
MWD (PDI) 1.5–4.0 (broader than ZN due to statistical termination)

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Notes — process variants. FRP is implemented in four reactor configurations: bulk (no solvent, e.g., PMMA cast sheet, PS), solution (in inert solvent, easy heat removal), suspension (monomer droplets in water with stabiliser, e.g., PVC suspension grade — most common globally), emulsion (monomer micelles + surfactant + water-soluble initiator, e.g., PVC paste-grade, latex, SBR rubber). Each variant balances heat removal, MW control, particle morphology, and downstream processing. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.3)

Notes — controlled radical polymerisation. Modern controlled / living radical polymerisation methods (ATRP, RAFT, NMP) introduced in the 1990s narrow the MWD to <1.5 and allow block-copolymer architectures previously possible only with anionic / cationic / metallocene methods. These remain mostly specialty / academic; commodity polymers still use uncontrolled FRP. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Related terms. Ziegler-Natta polymerisation; metallocene polymerisation; step-growth polymerisation; polyethylene (LDPE); polystyrene (PS); polyvinyl chloride (PVC); suspension polymerisation; emulsion polymerisation.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, kinetic steps, process variants, commodity polymers.

Step-growth (condensation) polymerisation

Aliases. Step polymerisation; condensation polymerisation; polycondensation; polyaddition (when no by-product).

Definition. A polymerisation mechanism in which the polymer chain grows by step-wise reaction between functional groups on monomers or oligomers — e.g., -COOH + HO- → -COO- + H₂O (esterification), or -COOH + H₂N- → -CONH- + H₂O (amidation). Each reaction step is independent: dimers, trimers, tetramers, oligomers, and finally polymer chains form sequentially. High molecular weight is reached only at very high conversion (>99% per the Carothers equation, DP = 1/(1-p)). The dominant route for polyesters (PET), polyamides (Nylon 6,6), polycarbonates, polyurethanes, phenolic and urea-formaldehyde resins. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section, Chapter 11.5.1)

Attributes — step-growth vs chain-growth comparison.

Property Step-growth Chain-growth (e.g., FRP, ZN)
Monomer types bifunctional (or trifunctional) mono-vinyl
MW evolution gradually with conversion rapidly, then plateau
High-MW reached at ≥99% conversion even at low conversion
By-product often (H₂O, MeOH) typically none
Equilibrium-driven yes (in many cases) no
Control mechanism drive equilibrium (vacuum, solvent, T) initiator/catalyst
Examples PET, Nylon 6,6, PU, polycarbonate, phenolic PE, PP, PS, PVC

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Notes — process implementation. Step-growth often requires melt polycondensation under vacuum or with sweep gas to remove the small-molecule by-product and drive equilibrium toward higher conversion. PET production combines low-temperature esterification with high-temperature melt polycondensation (~280 °C, vacuum) and optional solid-state polymerisation (~210 °C, vacuum) to reach bottle-grade MW. Nylon 6,6 uses melt polycondensation of the salt (HMDA · adipate) at 270 °C. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.6)

Related terms. Free-radical polymerisation; Ziegler-Natta polymerisation; metallocene polymerisation; PET (polyethylene terephthalate); polyamides (Nylon); polyurethane (PU); high-value chemicals (HVCs).

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, vs chain-growth comparison, melt polycondensation, examples.

Polymerisation reactor types

Aliases. Bulk; solution; suspension; emulsion; gas-phase; slurry; loop; melt-polycondensation reactors.

Definition. The five-to-six canonical industrial reactor configurations for polymer manufacture, distinguished by the medium in which polymerisation occurs (monomer alone, solvent, water suspension, water emulsion, gas, or condensed slurry). Reactor choice determines heat-removal capacity, MW control, particle morphology, downstream processing requirements, and capital cost. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Attributes — reactor types compared.

Reactor Medium Heat removal Polymer form Examples
Bulk (mass) monomer + initiator poor (very viscous melt) block / sheet / casting PMMA cast sheet; some PS
Solution monomer in inert solvent good (low-viscosity) dissolved → precipitated or dried metallocene-LLDPE; some EPDM
Suspension monomer droplets in water + stabiliser excellent (water heat capacity) beads / pearls (50–500 μm) PVC suspension grade; expandable PS (EPS)
Emulsion monomer in micelles + surfactant + water-soluble initiator excellent latex (50–500 nm particles) PVC paste-grade; SBR rubber; ABS
Gas-phase fluidised bed gaseous monomer + supported solid catalyst good (gas circulation + cooling) free-flowing solid powder HDPE (Unipol); PP (Spheripol gas-phase)
Slurry monomer in light hydrocarbon diluent good polymer slurry HDPE (Phillips loop); some Spheripol PP
Loop slurry propylene as both monomer and diluent (supercritical) excellent concentrated slurry Spheripol PP first stage
Melt polycondensation molten polymer / oligomer poor viscous melt PET, Nylon 6,6
Solid-state polymerisation (SSP) solid pellets at T<Tm by gas sweep solid pellets with raised MW PET bottle-grade; Nylon 6,6 high-MW

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section, with Chapter 11.3.3 for PVC)

Notes — economics and trade-offs. Suspension polymerisation is the workhorse for PVC because the water medium provides excellent heat removal for the highly exothermic VCM polymerisation. Emulsion polymerisation gives small (<500 nm) particles directly suitable for paint, adhesive, or paste applications. Gas-phase polymerisation has dominated new HDPE and PP capacity since the 1980s due to its low capital cost and absence of solvent recovery. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3 polymer chemistry section)

Related terms. Free-radical polymerisation; Ziegler-Natta polymerisation; metallocene polymerisation; step-growth polymerisation; polyethylene; polypropylene; polyvinyl chloride; PET.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: five reactor types, heat-removal trade-offs, example polymers.

Tacticity (polymer stereoregularity)

Aliases. Stereoregularity; isotactic / syndiotactic / atactic; isotacticity index (II).

Definition. The relative spatial arrangement of substituent groups (e.g., methyl in polypropylene, chlorine in PVC, phenyl in polystyrene) along a polymer backbone. Isotactic polymers have all substituents on the same side of the backbone (highly crystalline, strong, dense); syndiotactic polymers have alternating side placement (also crystalline, slightly different properties); atactic polymers have random placement (amorphous, soft, weak). Tacticity is set by the polymerisation catalyst — Ziegler-Natta and metallocene catalysts can produce highly stereoregular chains, while free-radical polymerisation produces atactic chains (or near-random for non-stereosensitive monomers). (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.2)

Attributes — polymer property dependence on tacticity.

Polymer Atactic Isotactic Syndiotactic
Polypropylene amorphous, soft, sticky (sealant adhesive) semi-crystalline (60–70%), Tm 165 °C, strong semi-crystalline, Tm 130–140 °C, transparent
Polystyrene atactic = standard PS, amorphous, brittle, transparent (Tg 100 °C) isotactic = no commercial use syndiotactic-PS (Idemitsu Xarec, Tm 270 °C, semi-crystalline, engineering plastic)
PVC almost-atactic dominant (slightly syndiotactic-rich at low T) not commercial not commercial
1-Butene polymer atactic = sticky i-PB Tm 125 °C —

(Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.2)

Notes — isotacticity index. Commercial isotactic polypropylene has isotacticity index ~95–99% (the rest being syndiotactic / atactic defects). Higher II → higher crystallinity, melting point, modulus, but also higher brittleness; lower II → improved transparency and toughness. Modern 4th–5th-generation Ziegler-Natta catalysts deliver II >97% in commodity-grade i-PP. (Speight 2019, Chapter 11.3.2)

Related terms. Ziegler-Natta polymerisation; metallocene polymerisation; free-radical polymerisation; polypropylene; polystyrene; polymer crystallinity.

Source history. - Speight 2019 — added 2026-05-08: definition, isotactic/syndiotactic/atactic distinction, polymer property dependence.

Zero-emission trucks

Aliases. ZE trucks; battery electric trucks (BETs); fuel cell electric trucks (FCETs).

Definition. Heavy-duty (gross vehicle weight >15 t) and medium-duty (3.5–15 t) trucks powered by zero-emission propulsion: battery electric (BEV) or fuel cell electric (FCEV). The principal decarbonisation pathway for road freight, complementing electric cars. (IEA ETP 2026, pp. 127, 6674–6710)

(IEA ETP 2026, pp. 127, 6674–6710, 4435)

Notes — TCO parity. In China, a relatively wide gap between diesel and electricity prices (per unit of energy), combined with the higher energy efficiency of electric powertrains, means battery-electric trucks already offer lower TCO than diesel for some applications. TCO parity is expected in more regions later this decade. Hydrogen refuelling for trucks remains under-built — most existing H₂ stations were designed for cars and may not be suitable for FCETs due to insufficient dispensing pressure or physical constraints. Changelog

  • 2026-05-08 — Sources processed (round 13): Niinimäki et al. 2020 (fast fashion); Tilsted et al. 2023 (petrochemical political economy); Bennett 2012 (climate-change implications for petrochemicals); Clark 2022 (circular fashion + green chemistry); Mingolla & Rosa 2025 (low-carbon ammonia for agriculture); Royal Society 2020 (ammonia zero-carbon fertiliser/fuel briefing); Mayer et al. 2023 (blue + green ammonia LCA); EVOLEN 2023 (e-fuels Note de synthèse, FR). New entries added (12): Fashion / textile (3): Fast fashion (and slow fashion — Niinimäki 92 Mt waste/yr + 79 trillion L water/yr + 35% marine microfibre share); Textile fibres (synthetic + natural — polyester 52% + cotton 25% global production); Microfibre pollution (~190 kt/yr marine + France 2025 mandatory filter). Petrochemical political economy (2): Petrochemical lock-ins / political economy (Tilsted 6-dimension lock-in taxonomy); Just transition (Tilsted petrochemical-extension argument). Ammonia (3): Blue ammonia and green ammonia (production routes, Mingolla land/water trade-off, Mayer methane-leakage warning); Nitrogen fertilisers (umbrella — Mingolla 107 Mt N/yr, 1.8 bn people supply-vulnerable); Urea (CO(NH₂)₂, ~190 Mt/yr largest single N-fertiliser). E-fuels (2): E-fuels — molecule-by-molecule (e-methane / e-methanol / e-kerosene / e-ammonia / e-diesel from EVOLEN); Methanation (Sabatier reaction — catalytic + biological routes). Climate methodology (1): Technology Warming Potential (TWP — Mayer dynamic-GWP framework with methane-leakage relevance). Bibliography updated: added 9 new sources (Bennett 2012, Clark 2022, EVOLEN 2023, Mayer 2023, Mingolla & Rosa 2025, Niinimäki 2020, Royal Society 2020, Tilsted 2023). Translation note: French content from EVOLEN 2023 systematically translated. Round 13 deliberately extends the dictionary into adjacent decarbonisation domains (fast fashion, ammonia + agriculture food security, political-economy framings) showing the dictionary’s utility beyond strict energy-systems-modelling.
  • 2026-05-08 — Round 12b: deeper building-renovation pass on user request. Added 17 more building-specific entries to give the renovation/HVAC/policy layer the depth equivalent to other domain coverage in the dictionary: HVAC sub-systems (5): Coefficient of Performance (COP / SCOP — typical values by HP type, temperature sensitivity); Mechanical ventilation (VMC / MVHR — single-flux/double-flux/hygro variants); Domestic Hot Water (DHW / ECS — production technologies including CET); HVAC umbrella (taxonomy); Condensing gas boiler (95–110% η, declining role under EPBD). Building physics (4): Thermal bridge (pont thermique with ψ values); Air-tightness (n50/Q4 with French stock benchmarks); Glazing technology (double/triple/low-E + frame conduction); Thermal mass / inertia (5-class taxonomy with Goessel typology relevance). Heating technologies (1): Biomass heating (wood pellet boiler, log boiler, stove with emissions concerns). RE2020 indicators (1): Bbio / Cep / DH / Ic_construction (full RE2020 indicator hierarchy). Comfort (2): Adaptive thermal comfort (de Dear-Brager model); Solar protection (umbrella with shading-device taxonomy and Goessel SET-DH reductions). Policy / regulation (3): Passoire thermique (DPE F+G with rental-ban schedule); MaPrimeRénov’ / CEE / Eco-PTZ (French subsidies bundle); EPBD (EU Directive 2024/1275 + Renovation Wave). Energy poverty (1): Energy poverty (précarité énergétique with split-incentive problem). Standards (1): NZEB and Passive House (Passivhaus thresholds, Goessel observation that Passivhaus-rénovation rarely Pareto-optimal). Typologies (1): French residential typologies (Chalandon vs maison de bourg comparison + TABULA context). With 24 entries from round 12 + 17 from round 12b, building science now has 41 dedicated entries plus updates to several existing entries (heat pump, etc.). Bibliography unchanged at 38 sources.
  • 2026-05-08 — Source processed (round 12): Goessel 2025 (PhD thesis on residential-building renovation methodology). A different field — building science, life cycle assessment, thermal comfort, and climate-prospective methodology applied to French residential renovation. Added 21 entries to extend the dictionary into this adjacent domain: Renovation & buildings (5): Building renovation (umbrella with renovation-category taxonomy + Goessel optimisation findings); Building envelope (with French U-value table + ITI-vs-ITE optimisation finding); Interior vs Exterior insulation (ITI / ITE — French context, performance/cost table); Building energy simulation (BES / SED — COMETh 5RC model); DPE (Diagnostic de Performance Énergétique — French A–G class with rental-ban schedule). Life cycle methodology (5): Life Cycle Assessment (LCA — ISO 14040/14044, EN 15978 building-LCA structure, prospective LCA); Life Cycle Costing (LCC — ISO 15686-5 with CGD French variant); Embodied carbon (buildings — life-cycle module split + intensity table); Operational carbon (buildings — French emission factors + declining-share trajectory); Functional Unit (FU — definition + sector examples); INIES / FDES / PEP (French environmental databases — quality hierarchy + international counterparts). Thermal comfort (3): Standard Effective Temperature (SET — Gagge model with ASHRAE 55 sensation classes); PMV / PPD (Fanger model — ISO 7730); Heat-wave health risk (vague de chaleur — French canicule definition + 2003/2022 mortality + adaptation policy). Climate prospective (5): EURO-CORDEX (regional climate ensemble — 0.11° resolution, uncertainty decomposition); General Circulation Model (GCM) and Regional Climate Model (RCM); Bias correction (climate downscaling); Typical Meteorological Year (TMY — construction + prospective-TMY innovation). Multi-objective optimisation (4): Multi-objective optimisation (MOO / OMO — formulation); Pareto dominance / Pareto front (geometry + Goessel application); NSGA (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm — NSGA-II/III); K-Means clustering (renovation archetype identification). Policy / regulation (2): RE2020 / RT2012 (French building regulations — performance thresholds + climate-zone modulation); Carbon payback time (TRC — typical periods + vs investment payback). Bibliography updated: added Goessel 2025 (one new source). Pending list: removed all of the above. Translation note: French content systematically translated into English with French aliases preserved (e.g. ACV → LCA, vague de chaleur, sobriété, ITE / ITI). The extension into building science demonstrates the dictionary’s utility beyond the energy-systems-modelling core into adjacent decarbonisation-relevant domains.

  • 2026-05-08 — Round-8 follow-up (round 9): closing-gap entries on user request. Added 35 entries to close the remaining gaps in the petrochemicals → plastics-industry chain. Tier-1 monomers and on-purpose routes: Acetic acid (~17 Mt/yr, Cativa/Monsanto); Acrylonitrile (~6 Mt/yr, SOHIO ammoxidation); Adipic acid + HMDA + caprolactam (Nylon-feedstock chain, with N₂O emissions framing); Cumene process (Hock — phenol + acetone, ~12 Mt phenol + 7 Mt acetone /yr, BPA coupling); Cyclohexane (~6 Mt/yr, benzene hydrogenation, Nylon gateway); Formaldehyde (~30 Mt/yr, silver / Formox processes, IARC Group 1); Methyl methacrylate (MMA, ~5 Mt/yr) + PMMA (~3 Mt/yr); Methanol-to-Propylene (MTP, Lurgi); Olefin metathesis (Phillips triolefin, Lummus OCT, Nobel 2005); Propane dehydrogenation (PDH, Oleflex / Catofin / STAR / FBD, >15 Mt/yr global); Hydroformylation / oxo synthesis (~12 Mt/yr aldehydes/alcohols, plasticiser-precursor link); Wacker process (acetaldehyde from ethylene, declining); Vinyl acetate (VAM, ~7 Mt/yr) + PVAc/PVOH/EVA (solar-PV encapsulant linkage); Toluene diisocyanate (TDI) + MDI (PU precursors, ~13 Mt/yr combined). Plastics processing methods: Plastic processing (umbrella, 7 dominant methods); Injection moulding (10–60 s cycles, 500–2,000 bar); Extrusion (continuous profiles, blown-film, twin-screw); Blow moulding (EBM/IBM/ISBM); Thermoforming (vacuum/pressure forming); Rotomoulding (large hollow parts); Calendering (PVC sheet/film); Compounding (additive categories with typical loadings, master-batch concept). Bio-polymers: Polylactic acid (PLA, ~0.4 Mt/yr, lactic-acid fermentation, NatureWorks); Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA/PHB, ~50 kt/yr, marine-biodegradable); Polyethylene furanoate (PEF, FDCA + EG, Avantium scale-up). Engineering plastics: Engineering plastics (umbrella with taxonomy table); Polycarbonate (PC, ~5 Mt/yr, BPA + phosgene → PC, BPA controversy); Polyetheretherketone (PEEK, ~10 kt/yr, aerospace + medical); Polyoxymethylene (POM/polyacetal, ~1 Mt/yr, gears + bearings); Polyphenylene oxide (PPO/PPE, Noryl blend); Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE/Teflon, ~0.2 Mt/yr, PFOA emulsifier history).
